question: A 16-year-old girl with the given physical findings develops mitral regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse. Eye examination reveals bilateral dislocation of the lens. This condition most commonly results from an inherited defect in which of the following proteins?

explanationHtml:
The mode of inheritance of Ehler–Danlos syndrome (EDS) encompasses two Mendelian patterns, namely:

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Autosomal recessive

The biosynthesis of collagen can be disturbed by genetic errors that may affect any one of the numerous structural collagen genes or enzymes necessary for posttranscriptional modifications of collagen. Such molecular heterogeneity results in the expression of EDS as a clinically variable disorder, with varied patterns of inheritance.
question:
Which of the following mode of inheritances is seen in Ehler–Danlos syndrome?

  1. Autosomal dominant
  2. Autosomal recessive
  3. Mitochondrial
  4. X-linked dominant
  5. Genomic imprinting

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of the kyphoscoliotic form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS). This was previously known as Type VI EDS.

The kyphoscoliotic form of EDS is caused by the deficient activity of the enzyme procollagen-lysine, 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1 (PLOD1, or lysyl hydroxylase 1).

It is a generalized connective tissue disorder characterized by:

  • Friable hyperextensible skin
  • Thin scars
  • Easy bruising
  • Generalized joint laxity
  • Severe muscular hypotonia at birth
  • Progressive scoliosis may be present at birth or may develop within the first year of life

X-ray Findings:
The left panel shows a marked scoliosis — a lateral curvature of the spine.
The right panel shows kyphosis — an exaggerated forward curvature of the thoracic spine.
Together, this demonstrates kyphoscoliosis.
question: A 20-year-old woman presents with back pain and weakness. On examination, she is found to have lax skin. X-ray findings are shown below. Lab reports show a deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Classic Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) type involves type V collagen (defects in genes COL5A1 and COL5A2).

Types I and II of EDS are termed as classic forms. Type I is severe, while type II is milder.

It has an autosomal-dominant type of inheritance. Clinically, this type is characterized by skin and joint hypermobility, atrophic scars, and easy bruising.
question: What type of collagen is involved in the classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

correctAnswer: C. Spinal muscular atrophy - Autosomal dominant
explanationHtml:
Spinal muscular atrophy has an autosomal recessive inheritance, not an autosomal dominant.

It is most commonly caused by mutations in the SMN1 gene. Both parents must be carriers for a child to be affected.
question: Which of the following pair is incorrectly matched?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Wolman disease. It is due to a deficiency of the lysosomal acid lipase enzyme. It is an autosomal recessive disease.

It leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides. It presents in the first few weeks of life with:

  • Failure to thrive
  • Vomiting
  • Abdominal distention
  • Steatorrhea
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Extensive bilateral calcifications of the adrenal glands

It is effectively treated with help of enzyme replacement therapy using sebelipase alfa.
question: A 1-month-old infant diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bilateral adrenal calcification was noted radiologically. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hurler disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis caused by a deficiency in α-L-iduronidase, which leads to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), not sphingolipids

Sphingolipidoses are a group of lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of sphingolipids. It includes:

  • Niemann–Pick disease
  • Fabry disease
  • Krabbe disease
  • Gaucher disease
  • Tay–Sachs disease
  • Metachromatic leukodystrophy
question: Which of these is not a form of sphingolipidoses?

explanationHtml:
Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.

It is an autosomal recessive disorder that results from a lack of the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase and accumulation of glucocerebroside in mononuclear phagocytic cells.
question: What is the most common lysosomal storage disorder?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and hexosaminidase α-subunit deficiency are seen in Tay–Sachs disease(the most common form of GM2 gangliosidosis).

Sphingolipidoses with their deficient enzymes:

  1. GM1 Gangliosidoses - GM1 Ganglioside β-galactosidase deficiency
    • Type 1- infantile, generalized
    • Type 2- juvenile
  2. GM2 Gangliosidosis:
    • Tay–Sachs disease - Hexosaminidase α-subunit
    • Sandhoff disease - Hexosaminidase β-subunit
    • GM2 Gangliosidosis variant AB - Ganglioside activator protein

Note: GM2 ganglioside accumulation primarily affects neurons, especially in the central nervous system, the autonomic nervous system, and the retina, although it may also accumulate in other tissues, such as the heart, liver, and spleen.
question: An 8-month-old child presents with mental retardation, blindness, and muscle weakness. On evaluation, deficiency of hexosaminidase α-subunit is found. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Whorled configurations within mitochondria are seen
explanationHtml:
In Tay–Sachs disease, an electron microscope shows whorled configurations within lysosomes composed of onion-skin layers of membranes.

Infants with Tay–Sachs disease appear normal at birth, but symptoms begin around 6 months. Neuronal involvement in the CNS, ANS, and retina dominates the clinical picture. Progressive motor and mental decline starts with incoordination and lethargy, followed by flaccidity, blindness, and dementia. Within 1–2 years, the child becomes vegetative, with death by age 2–3.

Tay–Sachs disease involves GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons of the CNS, autonomic nervous system, and retina. This causes retinal ganglion cell swelling, leading to a pale retina with a contrasting cherry-red macula, where the normal choroidal color is accentuated. This cherry-red spot is characteristic of Tay–Sachs and other neuronal storage disorders.

Histologic examination shows neurons ballooned with cytoplasmic vacuoles, each representing a markedly distended lysosome filled with gangliosides. These lipid accumulations stain positive with Oil Red O and Sudan Black B

The image given below shows a cherry-red spot on the retina:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Affected infants are normal at birth
Neurons in the CNS, ANS, and retina are affected
Accumulations stain positive for oil red O and Sudan black B
Whorled configurations within mitochondria are seen

question: Which of the following statements is false about Tay–Sachs Disease?

explanationHtml:
Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive condition caused by the deficiency of arylsulfatase A.

This enzyme deficiency leads to the accumulation of cerebroside sulfate (sulfatides), which causes white matter injury, demyelination, and gliosis.

In affected tissues, macrophages with vacuolated cytoplasm are scattered throughout the white matter. These macrophages contain metachromatic material, which can be detected in the urine and peripheral nerves using toluidine blue staining.
question: Patients with metachromatic leukodystrophy will have which of the following enzyme deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Krabbe disease is due to the deficiency of galactosylceramidase.

Symptoms typically begin between 3 and 6 months of age and are dominated by motor signs such as stiffness and weakness. Most affected infants do not survive beyond 2 years.

Pathologically, the brain shows loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes, with similar demyelination affecting the peripheral nerves. A hallmark of Krabbe disease is the presence of globoid cells—engorged macrophages that accumulate in the brain parenchyma and around blood vessels, which are characteristic and diagnostic of the disease.
question: Which of the following enzyme is deficient in patients with Krabbe disease?

explanationHtml:
Ceramide trihexoside (also known as globotriaosylceramide) is accumulated in Fabry disease.

The enzyme defect seen in this disease is α-galactosidase A.

Clinical features:

  • Painful acroparaesthesia
  • Hypohidrosis
  • Abdominal cramping
  • Diarrhea
  • Small petechiae around the umbilicus
  • Lenticular opacities
  • Corneal dystrophy
question: Patients with which of the following diseases will have ceramide trihexoside accumulation?

correctAnswer: A. Inherited deficiency of aryl sulfatase is present
explanationHtml:
Niemann–Pick disease types A and B are two related disorders that are characterized by lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase.

The disease is typically inherited as an autosomal recessive condition on chromosome 11.

Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive neurologic involvement, marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin, progressive wasting, and early death within the first 3 years of life.

Type B disease patients have organomegaly, but generally no central nervous system involvement. They usually survive into adulthood.

options.text: Inherited deficiency of aryl sulfatase is present

question: Which of the following statements is false about Niemann–Pick disease?

explanationHtml:
The electron microscopy image shows zebra bodies—lamellated, myelin-like structures within lysosomes, as indicated by the yellow arrows. These represent accumulated lipid material and are suggestive of Niemann–Pick disease, particularly types A and B, where sphingomyelin accumulates due to sphingomyelinase deficiency.

Similar zebra bodies may also be seen in other lysosomal storage disorders, such as the mucopolysaccharidoses.
question: Given below is an electron microscopy picture of lysosomes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. It is a glycogen storage disorder
explanationHtml:
Inclusion-cell (I-cell) disease, also referred to as mucolipidosis II, is a part of the lysosomal storage disease family.

It is characterized by the deficiency of phosphorylating enzymes essential for the formation of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker.

Acid hydrolases lacking the recognition marker cannot be targeted to the lysosomes. Instead, they are secreted extracellularly, leading to the accumulation of undigested substrates inside lysosomes (the “inclusion bodies” seen in cells)

It is characterized by:

  • Coarse facial features
  • Gingival hyperplasia
  • Clouded corneas
  • Restricted joint movements
  • Claw hand deformities
  • Kyphoscoliosis
  • High plasma levels of lysosomal enzymes

[[figure-1]]

options.text: It is characterised by defective phosphorylating enzymes
It is a glycogen storage disorder
It is associated with gingival hyperplasia
High levels of hydrolytic enzymes in plasma are seen

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding I-cell disease?

correctAnswer: D. Hunter syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant disease
explanationHtml:
All the mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited as autosomal recessive traits except Hunter syndrome. It is inherited as an X-linked recessive disease.

The mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs) are a group of closely related syndromes that result from genetically determined deficiencies of enzymes involved in the degradation of mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans).

Mucopolysaccharides are abundant in the ground substance of connective tissues. In the absence of enzymes involved in their degradation, they accumulate within lysosomes in various tissues and organs of the body. Two among these are:

  • Hurler syndrome - deficiency of α-L-iduronidase
  • Hunter syndrome - deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase

options.text: Hunter syndrome is due to a deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase
Hurler syndrome is due to a deficiency of α-L-iduronidase
They are inherited as autosomal recessive traits, except Hunter syndrome
Hunter syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant disease

question: Which of the following is false about mucopolysaccharidosis?

explanationHtml:
Glycogen storage disorder type II, also known as Pompe disease, is the only glycogen storage disease characterized by a defect in lysosomal metabolism.

It is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder. It is caused by the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome due to a deficiency of the lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme.
question: Which glycogen storage disorder is a lysosomal storage disease?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and bone marrow aspiration images, showing necrotic bone with a lack of osteocytes in the lacunae (Image A) and Gaucher cells (Image B), are suggestive of Gaucher's disease. This condition has a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.

Gaucher cells are plump macrophages that characteristically have a crumpled tissue paper appearance (Image B) of the cytoplasm. It is due to the accumulation of glucocerebrosides.

They can be seen in Virchow–Robin spaces (perivascular fluid-filled cavities that surround perforating arteries and veins in the brain parenchyma) in patients with cerebral involvement.
question: A 4-year-old boy presented with severe pain in his left leg which worsened over the last few months. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly and developmental delays were noticed. Labs revealed the following findings on light and oil immersion respectively of the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is deficient in this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Type 1 has no detectable enzyme activity
explanationHtml:
In type 1, enzyme activity is reduced but detectable- there is some residual activity of the deficient enzyme (glucocerebrosidase).

Gaucher disease has two types:

Type 1: Chronic non-neuropathic form

Type 2: Acute neuronopathic form

The central nervous system is involved

 Has no predilection for Jews

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Gaucher’s disease?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Gierke disease. It is due to the deficiency of the glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme.

The condition usually manifests as:

  • Failure to thrive
  • Stunted growth
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Renomegaly

Hypoglycemia is due to the failure of glucose mobilization, which often leads to convulsions. Lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia result from deranged glucose metabolism. Many patients also develop gout, skin xanthomas, and bleeding tendency (due to platelet dysfunction).

With treatment, most patients survive and develop late complications (e.g., hepatic adenomas).
question: A 1-year-old child presents with growth retardation and abdominal distension. On examination, the child has characteristic doll-like facies with thin extremities. Blood investigations reveal hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia. USG abdomen shows hepatomegaly and renomegaly. What deficiency causes the given clinical condition?

explanationHtml:
McArdle’s syndrome is caused due to the deficiency of muscle phosphorylase.

In the skeletal muscles, as opposed to the liver, glycogen is used predominantly as a source of energy during physical activity. If enzymes that hydrolyze glucose are deficient, there will be an accumulation of glycogen in the muscles. This will cause muscle weakness due to impaired energy production.

Enzyme deficiencies leading to muscle glycogen storage include:

  • McArdle disease/type V glycogenosis - deficiency of muscle phosphorylase
  • Type VII glycogen storage disease - deficiency of muscle phosphofructokinase

Typically, individuals with myopathic forms present with muscle cramps after exercise. This is because lactate levels in the blood fail to rise after exercise due to a block in glycolysis.
question: Which enzyme is deficient in McArdle’s syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Standard karyotyping refers to an arrangement of chromosomes from a cell that is undergoing mitosis at metaphase.

At other mitotic stages, the chromosomes are not sufficiently condensed or are too dispersed to allow for the counting and comparison of pairs under the microscope. In a metaphase spread, the individual chromosomes take the form of two chromatids connected to the centromere.

A variety of staining methods are available to identify the individual chromosomes on the basis of a distinctive and reliable pattern of alternating light and dark bands. The most common method used involves a Giemsa stain and is hence called G-banding. Standard G-banding can detect approximately 400 to 800 bands per haploid set.

The image below shows G-banding (karyogram of human male using Giemsa staining):

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Chromosomal Disorders And Other Genetic Disorders
question: At what stage of mitosis is standard karyotyping performed?

explanationHtml:
The short arm of a chromosome (marked as 1) is designated p (for petite), and the long arm (marked as 2) is referred to as q (the next alphabet).

[[figure-1]]

In a banded karyotype, each arm of the chromosome is divided into two or more regions bordered by prominent bands. The regions are numbered (e.g., 1, 2, 3) from the centromere outward. Each region is further subdivided into bands and sub-bands, and these are ordered numerically as well.

[[figure-2]]
lessonTitle: Chromosomal Disorders And Other Genetic Disorders
question: In cytogenetic terminology, how are the following marked structures designated?

explanationHtml:
A ring chromosome is an aberrant chromosome whose broken ends fuse together to form a ring.

Ring chromosomes behave abnormally in meiosis or mitosis and usually result in serious consequences. In rare cases, the telomeres at the ends of a chromosome fuse without any loss of genetic material, which results in a normal phenotype. A ring chromosome is denoted by the symbol r in human genetics.

[[figure-1]]

The following image shows a representative karyotype from a well-differentiated transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. The chromosome indicated by 'r' represents a ring chromosome. Also evident are monosomy 9, 18, and X and trisomy 7.

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option A: In a translocation, a segment of one chromosome is transferred to another.

Option C: Inversion refers to a rearrangement that involves two breaks within a single chromosome, with reincorporation of the inverted, intervening segment.

Option D: Isochromosome formation results when one arm of a chromosome is lost and the remaining arm is duplicated. It results in a chromosome consisting of two short arms only or of two long arms.
lessonTitle: Chromosomal Disorders And Other Genetic Disorders
question: What aberration occurs when a break occurs at both ends of a chromosome with the fusion of the damaged ends?

explanationHtml:
Inversion involves only a rearrangement of the genetic material. There is no change in the genetic material.

It occurs as a result of two breaks within a single chromosome. The intervening segment between the breaks gets inverted and reincorporated. It is of two types:

  • Paracentric - inversion involving only one arm of the chromosome
  • Pericentric - inversion involving opposite sides of the centromere

Inversions are often fully compatible with normal development.

Note: Transversions are mutations where a purine base pair is replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa.

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following is not associated with the change in genetic material?

correctAnswer: A. Leukemia is the major cause of death in early childhood
explanationHtml:
In Down's syndrome, the major cause of death in infancy and early childhood is cardiac disease, not leukemia.

Down's syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder and is a major cause of mental disability. Maternal age is a strong risk factor. This condition can occur through the following mechanisms:

  • The majority of cases - meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in the ovum
  • Rarely - Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)

The clinical features of Down's syndrome include:

  • Mental retardation
  • Facial dysmorphism - flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures, and epicanthic folds
  • Congenital heart disease - endocardial cushion defects (ASD, VSD, AV valve malformations)
  • Atresia of the esophagus and small bowel
  • Neuropathologic changes characteristic of Alzheimer's disease in patients > 40 years
  • Increased risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7)
  • Predisposition to autoimmune diseases and serious lung infections

[[figure-1]]

  • Short neck
  • Overlapping fingers
  • Congenital heart defects

explanationHtml:
Lyon's hypothesis states the idea of the inactivation of the X chromosome.

It states the following:

  • Only one of the X chromosomes is genetically active
  • The other X undergoes heteropyknosis and is rendered inactive (known as Barr body)
  • Inactivation of either the maternal or paternal X occurs at random among all the cells of the blastocyst on or about day 5.5 of embryonic life
  • Inactivation of the same X chromosome persists in all the cells derived from each precursor cell.

The molecular basis of X inactivation involves the XIST gene.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated.

The clinical features include:

  • Eunuchoid body habitus - elongated body and long legs (increased length between the soles and the pubic bone)
  • Absence of secondary sexual characteristics - lack of body and facial hair, deep voice
  • Small atrophic testes
  • Micropenis
  • Gynecomastia
  • Lower IQ, but no mental retardation

The following hormonal variations are seen in these patients:

  • Elevated FSH
  • Elevated estradiol
  • Low testosterone
  • Insulin resistance - increased incidence of type 2 diabetes

Patients with Klinefelter syndrome are at a higher risk for:

  • Male breast cancer (20x more common than in normal males)
  • Extragonadal germ cell tumors
  • Autoimmune diseases - systemic lupus erythematosus

question: A 25-year-old man was referred for infertility evaluation. On examination, he was tall with a lack of body hair. Gynecomastia and micropenis were also noted. Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype. Which of the following statements is not true about the condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of Turner's syndrome. In this condition, the most common karyotypic abnormality seen is a missing entire X chromosome, seen in more than half the cases.

Less commonly, structural abnormalities of the X chromosome and mosaicism can also occur. The common feature of the structural abnormalities is to produce partial monosomy of the X chromosome.

In order of frequency, the structural abnormalities of the X chromosome include the following:

  • An isochromosome of the long arm, 46,X,i(X)(q10), resulting in the loss of the short arm
  • Deletion of portions of both long and short arms, resulting in the formation of a ring chromosome - 46, X,r(X)
  • Deletion of portions of the short or long arm - 46X,del(Xq) or 46X,del(Xp).

The mosaic patients have a 45,XO cell population along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal cell types.

Few patients with this condition also have Y-chromosome sequences, either as a complete Y chromosome or as fragments of Y chromosomes translocated on other chromosomes. These patients are at a higher risk for the development of a gonadal tumor (gonadoblastoma).

question: A 16-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and short stature. Examination shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and absent secondary sexual characteristics. USG abdomen shows a small uterus and streak ovaries. What is the most common karyotypic abnormality seen in individuals with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Huntington's disease is caused by a CAG (trinucleotide) repeat mutation in the coding region of the gene, not the non-coding region.

Expansion of trinucleotide repeats is an important genetic cause of human disease, particularly neurodegenerative disorders. The causative mutations are associated with the expansion of a stretch of trinucleotides that usually share the nucleotides G and C. In all cases, the DNA is unstable, and an expansion of the repeats above a certain threshold impairs gene function.

Expansions affecting noncoding regions will cause a loss-of-function mutation. They include:

  • Fragile X syndrome
  • Myotonic dystrophy
  • Friedreich ataxia

Expansions affecting coding regions cause a gain-of-function mutation. They include:

  • Spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease)
  • Huntington disease
  • Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (Haw–River syndrome)
  • Spinocerebellar ataxia types 1, 2, 3, 6, 7

explanationHtml:
Macro-orchidism (large testicles) is seen in fragile X syndrome, not micro-orchidism.

Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common). It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation, characterized by multiple tandem repeats of the CGG sequence in the FMR1 gene, which is associated with familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1). It is associated with the phenomenon of anticipation, where the disease phenotype worsens over generations within a family.

The affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

The characteristic phenotypic features include the following:

  • Long face with a large mandible
  • Large everted ears
  • Macro-orchidism
  • Hyperextensible joints
  • High arched palate
  • Mitral valve prolapse

The given image shows a child suffering from fragile X syndrome.

question: All of the following are features of fragile X syndrome except:

explanationHtml:
CGG premutations in the FMR1 gene are characteristic of fragile X ataxia. It is also known as fragile X tremor and fragile X-associated primary ovarian failure.

Normally, the FMR1 gene is methylated and silenced, and the number of CGG repeats remains < 55. However, abnormalities in this gene lead to the accumulation of CGG-containing FMR1 mRNAs, which are toxic to the cell. Depending on the type of mutation, there are 2 distinct syndromes:

  • Fragile X ataxia syndrome (FXTAS): 55-200 repeats (premutation), which causes a gain of function
  • Fragile X syndrome (FXs): 200- 4000 repeats (full mutation) leading to loss of function

More than half of the individuals with FXTAS develop a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome starting in their 6th decade. It is characterized by intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia and may progress to Parkinsonism.

Other options:

Option B: Prader-Willi syndrome is associated with the deletion of paternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the maternal allele.

Option D: Friedreich ataxia is due to GAA repeat sequences in the noncoding regions.

explanationHtml:
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is an example of mitochondrial inheritance. It is inherited along the maternal line, as shown in image 4.

[[figure-1]]

In diseases following the mitochondrial pattern of inheritance, all children of an affected mother and a normal father develop the disease. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother do not inherit the disease. Hence, only the daughters of the affected mother will transmit the disease.

This is because this condition is due to a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria. The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa have very few mitochondria, if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy:

LHON is a neurodegenerative disease that manifests as progressive bilateral loss of central vision. Visual impairment starts between the ages of 15 and 35, leading eventually to blindness. Other features include cardiac conduction defects and minor neurologic manifestations.

correctAnswer: A. It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder
explanationHtml:
Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide repeat disorder.

It is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats (>40). It occurs due to a gain-of-function (expansion) mutation in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p.

The disease shows genetic anticipation and has an early-onset (2-3 decades) if inherited from the father.

Cognitive impairment is an early feature. Pathologically, atrophy of caudate and putamen with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly is seen. Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia and decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea.

Treatment consists of haloperidol and tetrabenazine.

explanationHtml:
Cancer cells are insensitive to growth-inhibitory signals.

All cancer cells are known to show around 8 fundamental physiological changes in the cell, which are considered as the hallmarks of cancer. These changes include the following:

  1. Self-sufficiency in growth signals - once activated, tumors can proliferate without external stimuli
  2. Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals - tumors do not respond to inhibitors of cell growth. This is attributed to the inactivation of the tumor-suppressor genes in cancer cells
  3. Altered cellular metabolism - tumor cells switch to aerobic glycolysis, called the Warburg effect
  4. Evasion of apoptosis
  5. Limitless replicative potential
  6. Sustained angiogenesis
  7. Ability to invade and metastasis
  8. Ability to evade the host immune response
question: Which of the following is not a hallmark of malignancy?

correctAnswer: C. Conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the HMP pathway
explanationHtml:
Increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the glycolytic pathway (not HMP).

Even in the presence of ample oxygen, cancer cells demonstrate a distinctive form of cellular metabolism. This is characterized by high levels of glucose uptake and increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid via the glycolytic pathway. This phenomenon is called the Warburg effect.

Aerobic glycolysis provides rapidly dividing tumor cells with metabolic intermediates that are required for the synthesis of cellular components, whereas mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation does not.

correctAnswer: B. Pleomorphic adenoma is an example
explanationHtml:
Pleomorphic adenoma is an example of a mixed tumor consisting of epithelial and myoepithelial cells with or without stromal components.

Adenomas are benign epithelial tumors. They can arise from:

  • Glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example, follicular adenomas of the thyroid, which arise from the thyroid gland and forms glandular structures
  • Glandular cells but form non-glandular structures - for example, heterogeneous mass of adrenal cortical cells growing as a solid sheet
  • Non-glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example, benign epithelial neoplasm that arises from renal tubular cells growing in the form of numerous tightly clustered small glands

Hemangioblastoma is not a small round blue cell tumor.

Hemangioblastomas are tumors of central nervous system that originate from vascular tissues. They demonstrate the proliferation of capillaries with variable sized, closely packed, and thin walled vessels as seen in the image below.

Small round blue cell tumors consist of small round cells that stain blue on routine H&E staining sections. They include:

  • Neuroblastoma

Other options:

Option D: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells. They contain recognizable mature or immature cells or tissues belonging to more than one germ cell layer, and sometimes all three germ layers.

Option C: Papillomas are benign epithelial neoplasms. They are characterized by microscopically or macroscopically visible finger-like or warty projections from epithelial surfaces.

Loss of polarity is a microscopic finding in malignant neoplasm, like metastatic breast cancer.

question: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer. Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in the microscopic examination of the resected tumor?

explanationHtml:
Once the tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the tumor is said to be invasive.

Progression of cancer occurs in the following stages: dysplasia→carcinoma in situ→invasive carcinoma

In situ carcinoma is when dysplastic changes are marked and involve the full thickness of the epithelium, but the lesion does not penetrate the basement membrane. It is a pre-invasive neoplasm.

The tumor is said to be invasive when the basement membrane is breached by the tumor cells.

explanationHtml:
The first node in a regional lymphatic basin that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor, is the sentinel lymph node, which is is often used to assess the presence or absence of metastatic lesions in the lymph nodes microscopically.

Sentinel node mapping can be done by the injection of radiolabeled tracers or colored dyes. Examination of frozen sections of the sentinel lymph node is often performed during surgery. It can guide the surgeon to the appropriate therapy.

Sentinel node examination has also been used for detecting the spread of:

Hirschsprung's disease is caused by mutations in other genes encoding proteins involved in enteric neurodevelopment. These include:

  • RET ligand glial-derived neurotrophic factor
  • Endothelin
  • Endothelin receptor

Note: Medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasias, types 2A and 2B, are usually due to gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.

question: Which of the following is associated with loss of function mutation in RET proto-oncogene?

explanationHtml:
Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is a membrane-bound receptor tyrosine kinase. When aberrantly expressed, it is associated with neuroblastoma pathogenesis. It serves as a therapeutic target.

Neuroblastoma is one of the most common solid cancers among children.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: Which of the following tumors is associated with a mutation of the ALK receptor?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and fundus examination are suggestive of uveal melanoma which is associated with a point mutation of GNAQ protein or GNA11 genes.

Uveal melanomas (UM) originate from melanocytes in the interior wall of the eye. This includes the iris, ciliary body, and the choroid with marked differences in light exposure (from dark anterior to illuminated posterior).

GNAS mutation causes pituitary adenoma and other endocrine tumors.

The 3 RAS genes in humans (H-RAS, K-RAS, and N-RAS) are the most common oncogenes in human cancer. They code for a family of proteins called GTP-binding (G) proteins, which are involved in transmitting signals within cells (cellular signal transduction). When RAS is 'switched on' by incoming signals, it subsequently switches on other proteins, which ultimately results in cell growth, differentiation, and survival.

Mutations in RAS genes can lead to the production of permanently activated RAS proteins. As a result, this can cause unintended and overactive signaling inside the cell, even in the absence of incoming signals. Because these signals result in cell growth and division, overactive RAS signaling can ultimately lead to cancer.

question: A 60-year-old man presents with a painless loss of vision. Fundus examination reveals the lesion shown in the image. Which of the following GTP-binding proteins show point mutations in this condition?

explanationHtml:
MYC oncogene codes for nuclear regulatory proteins. It is the most commonly involved transcription factor in tumors.

The MYC proto-oncogene MYC activates the expression of many genes that are involved in cell growth. It upregulates the expression of telomerase and reprograms somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells.

question: Which of the following are coded by the MYC genes?

explanationHtml:
Translocation of cyclin D1 is seen in mantle cell lymphoma.

Mantle cell lymphoma is an uncommon lymphoid neoplasm that is characterized by overexpression of cyclin D1. It is a type of non Hodgkins lymphoma that involves (11;14) translocation i.e. between IgH locus on chromosome 14 and the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11.

question: Which of the following is associated with the translocation of cyclin D1?

correctAnswer: A. Familial type is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
explanationHtml:
Retinoblastoma is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

Knudson's hypothesis, also known as the two-hit hypothesis or multiple-hit hypothesis states that cancer is the result of accumulated mutations in a cell's DNA. Two mutations (hits), involving both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q14, are required to produce retinoblastoma.

In familial cases, children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene in the germline (the first hit), and the other copy is normal. Retinoblastoma develops when the normal RB allele is mutated in retinoblasts as a result of a spontaneous somatic mutation (the second hit). Most individuals inheriting a germline defect in one RB allele develop unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma as it is an autosomal dominant disease.

Sporadic cases are comparitively rare. In sporadic cases, both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast (two hits).

The image given below shows the Knudson's two-hit hypothesis:

[[figure-1]]

It involves both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q14
In sporadic cases, both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast
In familial cases, children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene and the other copy is normal

question: Which of the following is false about Knudson's two-hit hypothesis theory on retinoblastoma?

correctAnswer: B. Cell cycle will stop at G1
explanationHtml:
If the retinoblastoma (RB) gene is hypophosphorylated, it is active and the cell cycle will stop at G1.

RB is a cell-cycle regulator because it binds to and inactivates a transcription factor (E2F). This is necessary for the transcription of certain genes necessary for the progression from the G1 to S phase. The phosphorylation of RB results in the release of E2F. This activates gene transcription and cell-cycle progression occurs.

The image given below shows the cell cycle regulation by RB gene:

[[figure-1]]

Cell cycle will stop at G1
There will be no effect on cell cycle as RB gene phosphorylation is not needed
The cell cycle progresses and cell divides

question: If the RB gene is hypophosphorylated, which of the following will happen?

correctAnswer: B. P53 inactivation causes cell cycle arrest at G2-M
explanationHtml:
P53 is the tumor suppressor gene, and activation (not inactivation) causes cell cycle arrest at the G1-S and G2-M phases of the cell cycle.

P53 regulates:

  • Cell cycle progression
  • DNA repair
  • Cellular senescence
  • Apoptosis

It is activated by:

  • Anoxia
  • Inappropriate signaling by mutated oncoproteins
  • DNA damage

It is the most frequently mutated gene in cancers. It upregulates the expression of proteins such as the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, thereby causing cell-cycle arrest at the G1-S. It also transactivates and transrepresses the target gene to induce G2/M arrest. A mutation in the p53 gene causes resistance in tumors to radiation and chemotherapy.

The E6 protein of human papillomavirus (HPV) binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase, thereby helping in the longevity of the cells. E6 from high-risk HPV types has a higher affinity for p53 than E6 from low-risk types.

Note: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder due to a defect in the tumor suppressor gene P53 located on chromosome 17.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity

Cancers demonstrate biallelic loss of function mutations in TP53
p53 can be inactivated by E6 protein of HPV

question: Which of the following statements is false about p53?

explanationHtml:
p63 is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia.

p63 is a member of the p53 gene family (which includes p53, p63, and p73).It plays a crucial role in epithelial development.p53 is ubiquitously expressed, while p63 and p73 show more tissue specificity.

p73 has strong pro-apoptotic effects after DNA damage induced by chemotherapeutic agents.

question: Which of the following is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Cowden syndrome. This condition is caused by to germline loss-of-function mutation in the PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) gene.

PTEN is a membrane-associated phosphatase encoded by a gene on chromosome 10q23 that is mutated.

Cowden syndrome is characterized by skin appendage tumors and an increased incidence of epithelial cancers, particularly of the breast, endometrium, and thyroid.

question: A 22-year-old man was found to have multiple GI polyps. He was operated on for thyroid cancer  2 years back. His family history is significant for breast cancer in his mother and endometrial cancer in his aunt. Germline loss-of-function mutations of which gene is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and MRI findings are suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2). Merlin, a cytoskeletal stability protein ,is mutated in NF-2, sporadic schwannomas, and meningiomas.

Cells lacking Merlin do not establish stable cell-to-cell junctions. They are insensitive to normal growth arrest signals generated by cell-to-cell contact.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: A 24-year-old woman presented with hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI was done and showed the presence of bilateral acoustic schwannomas. Which protein involved in cytoskeletal stability is mutated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Germline loss-of-function mutations of the PTCH1 gene cause Gorlin syndrome.

Gorlin syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. Clinical features include:

  • Multiple basal cell carcinomas
  • Highly characteristic facies - large forehead
  • Bifid or misshapen ribs
  • Vertebral and other skeletal anomalies
  • Pits of the skin of the palms and soles
  • Dysgenesis of the corpus callosum
  • Calcification of the falx cerebri - at an earlier age than is seen in non‐affected individuals
  • Macrocephaly

Note: Acquired biallelic loss-of-function mutations of PTCH1 cause sporadic basal cell carcinomas and medulloblastoma.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: Germline loss-of-function mutation of which gene causes Gorlin syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

Loss-of-function mutations of STK11 cause the Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. The STK11 gene, also known as LKB1, encodes a serine/threonine kinase that is an important regulator of cellular metabolism.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. It is associated with arborizing polyps of the gastrointestinal tract (small intestine > colon > stomach). It increases the risk of multiple epithelial cancers, particularly of colon, breast, lung, pancreas, and thyroid.

question: A 25-year-old man patient presents with anemia and abdominal pain. On examination, he has pigmented macules over the palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Further investigations reveal loss-of-function mutations of the STK11 gene. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast which involves mutated E-cadherin protein. In this condition, the histopathological examination shows infiltrating small monomorphic discohesive tumor cells arranged in an Indian-file or single-file pattern.

The image below shows the single file pattern seen in lobular carcinoma of the breast.

[[figure-1]]

Reduced cell surface expression of E-cadherin is seen in carcinomas of:

  • Breast
  • Esophagus
  • Colon
  • Ovary
  • Prostate

E-cadherin is a cell-surface protein that maintains intercellular adhesiveness. Loss of E-cadherin causes disaggregation of cells, which can then invade locally or metastasize.

Germline loss-of-function mutations of the E-cadherin gene lead to familial gastric carcinoma. Sporadic gastric carcinomas are also associated with the loss of E-cadherin expression.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with complaints of a palpable mass in both breasts. Histopathology examination shows the following finding. Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positivity. Which protein that maintains cell adhesion, and thereby inhibits cell motility, is mutated in this condition?

correctAnswer: B. BRCA1 mutation causes well-differentiated cancer
explanationHtml: BRCA2 (not BRCA 1) mutation causes well-differentiated cancer.

question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the BRCA genes?

correctAnswer: B. Extrinsic apoptotic pathway is more frequently disabled in cancer cells
explanationHtml:
The intrinsic apoptotic pathway is most frequently disabled in cancer cells to evade cell death.

Other options:

Option A: p53 is an important pro-apoptotic protein that induces apoptosis in cells that are unable to repair DNA damage.

Option C: Chemotherapy and radiation therapy kill cancer cells mainly by inducing apoptosis via the intrinsic pathway.

Option D: In greater than 85% of follicular B-cell lymphomas, the anti-apoptotic gene BCL2 is overexpressed due to a (14;18) translocation.

question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding apoptosis?

explanationHtml:
SNAIL and TWIST, which encode transcription factors, promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).

In EMT, carcinoma cells downregulate certain epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and upregulate certain mesenchymal markers (e.g. vimentin and smooth muscle actin). This favors the development of a promigratory phenotype that is essential for metastasis. EMT has been documented mainly in breast carcinoma.

question:
Which of the following genes promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition in epithelial tumors?

  1. MYC
  2. SNAIL
  3. TWIST
  4. BRCA1
  5. RET

explanationHtml:
ABL is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase.

Tyrosine kinases may be receptors and non-receptors.

Nonreceptor tyrosine kinases normally localize to the cytoplasm or the nucleus. These are:

  • ABL - translocation causes CML and point mutation causes ALL
  • JAK mutation - seen in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and myelofibrosis as well as other myeloproliferative disorders

Receptor tyrosine kinases:

  • VEGFR
  • PDGFR
  • EGFR

In chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and some acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the ABL gene is translocated from its normal abode on chromosome 9 to chromosome 22 where it fuses with the BCR gene forming the Philadelphia chromosome. The resultant chimeric gene encodes a constitutively active, oncogenic BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: Which of the following is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase?

explanationHtml:
Enhancer deletion does not convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene.

A proto-oncogene is a normal gene that can become an oncogene due to mutations or increased expression. Oncogenes drive cancer by promoting uncontrolled cell growth.

Mechanisms of activating oncogenes:

Mechanism Activation of oncogenes
Mutation A mutation activates the gene. A classic example is the point mutation of the RAS oncogene.
Promoter insertion Insertion of a viral promoter region near a gene activates it.
Enhancer insertion Insertion of a viral enhancer region near a gene activates it.
Chromosomal translocation One chromosome is split off and joined to another. An example is the Philadelphia chromosome.
Gene amplification Abnormal multiplication of a gene resulting in many copies. This can occur with oncogenes and genes involved in tumor drug resistance.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: The mutations/changes that convert proto-oncogene to oncogene include all except:

explanationHtml:
RAS is an oncogene that undergoes mutation and serves as a tumor antigen.

Tumor cells express antigenic molecules on their surface that elicit an immune response. These are called tumor antigens. Some tumor cells evade the immune response, resulting in the growth of the tumor.

Note: Mutated RAS proteins produce abnormal peptides that can be recognized as tumor-specific antigens by the immune system.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: Mutation in which of the following oncogenes can serve as a tumor antigen?

correctAnswer: A. Inhibition of PD-1 receptor on T-cells
explanationHtml:
Inhibition of PD-1 receptor (programmed death-1 receptor) on T cells causes activation of immunity against the tumor cells, not evasion.

PD-1 receptors present on T cells inhibit T-cell activation. This allows tumors to evade host immunity by upregulating the expression of factors like PD-L1 and PD-L2, which act on PD-1 receptors.

Other options:

Option B: Tumor cells upregulate PD-L1, which binds to PD-1 on T-cells. This inhibits T-cell activity, allowing the tumor to escape immune attack.
Option C: Tumors can produce galectins (like Galectin-1), which induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T-cell activation.
Option D: Tumors can recruit or expand regulatory T-cells (Tregs), which play a critical role in suppressing effector T-cells and other components of the antitumor immune response.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity

options.text: Inhibition of PD-1 receptor on T-cells

question: Which of the following mechanisms does not lead to immune evasion by the tumor cells?

correctAnswer: B. Defective DNA nucleotide excision repair
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is caused by a defect in the DNA nucleotide excision repair pathway, resulting in an inability to repair pyrimidine dimers.

Clinical features of xeroderma pigmentosum:

  • Actinic keratosis
  • Hyperkeratotic lesions
  • Multiple lentigos
  • Xerosis
  • Corneal scarring

The image of a child with xeroderma pigmentosum is given below:

question: An 8-year-old girl is referred with recurrent blistering rashes over the face and upper limbs which worsened following exposure to sunlight. There is a history of similar skin lesions in her family and 2 of her uncles were diagnosed with skin cancers at young ages. Examination reveals the presence of multiple lentigos and xerosis. What is the likely pathological mechanism of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Fanconi syndrome is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism. It is a rare disorder of kidney tubule function.

Diseases with defects in DNA repair by homologous recombination:

  • Bloom syndrome and ataxia–telangiectasia triggered by DNA-damaging agents such as ionizing radiation
  • Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in multiple genes responsible for coding for proteins that participate in DNA repair pathways and are triggered by DNA-crosslinking agents like chemotherapeutic drugs.
  • Familial breast cancer is due to inherited gene defects in BRCA1 and BRCA 2 genes

question: Which of the following disorders is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history and biopsy findings are suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma and the translocation involved is t(8;14).

Burkitt lymphoma, also known as small non-cleaved-cell lymphoma, is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation and deregulation of the c-myc gene on chromosome 8.

The classic t(8;14)(q24;q32) reciprocal translocation results in the transposition of the c-myc proto-oncogene on chromosome 8 with one of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) genes on chromosome 14. This results in activation of the c-myc gene and is considered responsible for tumor proliferation.

[[figure-1]]

question: A 30-year-old patient presents with right iliac fossa pain. Imaging shows the presence of an ileocaecal mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a starry sky pattern. What is the translocation involved in this tumor?

explanationHtml:
MLL2 is an epigenomic regulatory gene that is mutated in most follicular lymphomas. It results in histone methylation.

Epigenetics refers to factors other than the sequence of DNA that regulate gene expression. These factors involved in epigenetics are:

  • Histone modifications
  • DNA methylation
  • Nucleosome positioning/ chromatin remodeling

question: Which epigenomic regulatory gene is mutated in most of the follicular lymphomas?

explanationHtml:
The loss of miR-15 leads to upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2.

miR-15 and miR-16 are tumor-suppressive miRNAs involved in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Onco-miRNAs include:

  • miR200 - promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transitions that promote tumor invasion and metastasis
  • miR155 - involved in human B-cell lymphomas

Note: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that promotes cell survival and is often overexpressed in cancers to help tumor cells avoid programmed cell death.
lessonTitle: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity
question: The loss of which of the following micro RNAs leads to upregulation of BCL-2?

correctAnswer: A. Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers
explanationHtml:
Anti-CTLA-4 antibody - Ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) plays an important inhibitory role in the control of T-cell activation.

Ipilimumab is a fully-humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4).

It has been postulated that anti-CTLA-4 antibodies act by blocking inhibitory signals from effector T-cells, allowing costimulatory signaling and generation of antitumor T-cell responses. In vitro studies also demonstrated that the antitumor activity of CTLA-4 blockade is mediated by Fc gamma receptor-expressing macrophage and hypothesized a possible role of regulatory T-cell depletion in the tumor microenvironment.

Other options:

Option B - Mutation of tumor suppressor genes is associated with increased risk of cancer. Antigen toxicity is when the immune response to an antigen is excessive or misdirected, causing damage to tissues or organs.

Option C - PD1/PDL1 is an immune checkpoint whose activation inhibits T-cell function and helps with immune tolerance. Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction using immune checkpoint inhibitors reactivates T cells and enhances immune responses against tumors.

Option D - CD28 is primarily involved in providing the second signal required for T cell activation. The first signal comes from the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Without CD28-mediated costimulation, T cells that only receive the TCR signal (without the second signal) can become anergic.

question: Identify the correct statement regarding immune surveillance.

Multi-step carcinogenesis is best studied in colon carcinoma.

The molecular model for the evolution of colorectal cancers is described as the Fearon-Vogelstein adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

question: Which of the following tumors is best suited to study the mechanism of multi-step carcinogenesis?

explanationHtml:
Cyclophosphamide is a directly-acting carcinogen that does not require metabolic activation.

Carcinogens can be direct-acting or indirect-acting based on their activation.

Direct-acting carcinogens require no metabolic conversion to become carcinogenic. Most are weak carcinogens, but some are important because they are cancer chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g., alkylating agents). The direct-acting carcinogens include:

  • Alkylating Agents:
    • β-Propiolactone
    • Dimethyl sulfate
    • Diepoxybutane
    • Anticancer drugs (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nitrosoureas, and others)
  • Acylating Agents:
    • 1-Acetyl-imidazole
    • Dimethylcarbamyl chloride

Indirect-acting carcinogens (procarcinogens) are chemicals that require metabolic conversion to become active carcinogens. The carcinogenic product of metabolism is called an ultimate carcinogen. The indirect-acting carcinogens include:

  • Polycyclic and heterocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons:
    • Benz[a]anthracene
    • Benzo[a]pyrene
    • Dibenz[a,h]anthracene
    • 3-Methylcholanthrene
    • 7,12-Dimethylbenz[a]anthracene
  • Aromatic amines, amides, azo dyes:
    • 2-Naphthylamine (β-naphthylamine)
    • Benzidine
    • 2-Acetylaminofluorene
    • Dimethylaminoazobenzene (butter yellow)
  • Natural plant and microbial products:
    • Aflatoxin B1
    • Griseofulvin
    • Cycasin
    • Safrole
    • Betel nuts
    • Others
    • Nitrosamine and amides
    • Vinyl chloride, nickel, chromium
    • Insecticides, fungicides
    • Polychlorinated biphenyls
lessonTitle: Carcinogenesis, Paraneoplastic Syndromes And Tumor Markers
question: Which of the following procarcinogens does not require metabolic activation?

explanationHtml:
Seborrheic keratosis is not associated with exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from sun exposure.

UV rays derived from sun exposure are associated with the increased incidence of:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma
  • Basal cell carcinoma
  • Melanoma of the skin

Actinic keratosis is a precancerous skin condition that can cause squamous cell cancer if untreated.
lessonTitle: Carcinogenesis, Paraneoplastic Syndromes And Tumor Markers
question: A 45-year-old man presents with a hyperpigmented lesion on his face. He is a farmer by occupation and works for long hours with sun exposure. He is at increased risk for all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
UVB (ultraviolet B) causes cutaneous cancers due to the formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA.

When DNA absorbs energy from UVB, there is a covalent crosslinking of pyrimidine bases and a distortion of the DNA helix. This prevents proper pairing of the dimer with bases in the opposite DNA strand.

Normally, these defects are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair pathway. Defects in the nucleotide excision repair pathway result in xeroderma pigmentosum.

UV portion of the solar spectrum is divided into three wavelength ranges:

Spectrum Wavelength
UVA 320-400 nm
UVB 280-320 nm
UVC 200-280 nm

Note: UVC is the most potent mutagen, but it is not considered significant as it is filtered out by the ozone layer.
lessonTitle: Carcinogenesis, Paraneoplastic Syndromes And Tumor Markers
question: Which form of radiation is responsible for cutaneous cancer?

explanationHtml:
Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of myeloid leukemia.

Carcinogenic radiations include:

  • Electromagnetic radiation -
    • X-rays
    • γ rays
  • Particulate radiation -
    • α particles
    • β particles
    • Protons
    • Neutrons

Cancers due to ionizing radiation:

  • Most frequent - myeloid leukemia and thyroid cancer
  • Intermediate frequency - cancers of breast, lungs, and salivary glands
  • Relatively resistant cancers - cancers of skin, bone, and gastrointestinal tract

question: Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of which of the following malignancies?

explanationHtml: Adenocarcinoma of the lung is not associated with microbial etiopathogenesis. It is primarily associated with non-infectious causes like smoking and genetic predispositions.

question: Which of the following tumors is not caused by microbes?

explanationHtml:
Human T-cell leukemia-lymphoma virus (HTLV-1) causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).

HTLV-1 encodes the viral protein Tax, which leads to polyclonal expansion of T cells. It exhibits tropism for CD4+ T cells.

Human infection requires transmission of infected T cells through sexual intercourse, blood products or breast feeding. Leukemia develops only in 3-5% of infected individuals, typically after a long latent period of 40-60 years.

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. This virus is not implicated in follicular lymphoma.

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpesvirus family, has been implicated in:

  • African form of Burkitt lymphoma
  • B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed
  • A subset of Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  • Gastric carcinoma - most common EBV associated malignancy
  • T-cell lymphoma and natural killer (NK) cell lymphoma

question: A 13-year-old child presents to the OPD with fever, pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Peripheral smear showed a predominance of lymphocytes. The heterophile agglutination test is positive. The causative organism of this condition is not implicated in which of the following tumors?

correctAnswer: A. EBV infection always results in Burkitt lymphoma
explanationHtml:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection does not always result in Burkitt lymphoma.

EBV infection is highly prevalent even in areas where Burkitt lymphoma is not found. It commonly causes infectious mononucleosis.

EBV uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach to and infect B cells. EBV genome triggers B-cell signaling pathways inducing B-cell growth and transformation.

The infection of B cells is latent as there is no viral replication and the cells are not killed. However, B cells latently infected with EBV express viral proteins that result in the ability to propagate indefinitely in vitro. In the absence of T-cell immunity, EBV-infected B cells can rapidly grow out as aggressive B-cell tumors.

It uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach and infect B cells
It is implicated in B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed people
It is a potent inducer of B-cell growth and transformation

question: Which of the following statements about Epstein-Barr virus is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) is a gamma-herpesvirus associated with Kaposi sarcoma, multicentric Castleman disease, and primary effusion lymphoma.

They are lymphoproliferative diseases that are most commonly observed in immunocompromised individuals. The viral genome expresses genes responsible for inhibition of apoptosis, cell cycle entry, and angiogenesis.

question: Which of the following pathogens is implicated in the causation of primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and histopathological image showing follicular hyperplasia of lymph nodes are suggestive of Castleman disease.

Castleman disease (angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia) is a lymphoproliferative disorder that can be associated with HHV-8 (multicentric Castleman disease or MCD) or idiopathic (unicentric Castleman disease or UCD)

There are 3 major histological subtypes:

  • Hypervascular (UCD) -
    • Lollipop appearance - atrophic germinal centers with radially penetrating blood vessels
    • Onion skin appearance of the mantle zone around germinal centers
  • Plasma cell subtype (UCD or MCD) - hypertrophic germinal centers, increased vascularity
  • Mixed variant (MCD) - a mix of hypervascular and plasma cell subtype features in the same lymph node

The clinical features include:

  • Multiple enlarged lymph nodes
  • Night sweats
  • Weight loss
  • Weakness and fatigue
  • Hepatosplenomegaly

As this condition is associated with elevated levels of IL-6, the treatment involves IL-6 inhibitors like siltuximab and tocilizumab.

Note: Hodgkin's lymphoma has characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells in the histopathological section of lymph nodes.

Cushing syndrome is the most common endocrinopathy caused by tumors.

Endocrinopathy refers to ectopic hormone production by non-endocrine tumors. Approximately, 50% of the individuals with Cushing syndrome as endocrinopathy have carcinoma of the lung, chiefly the small-cell type.

Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome. Cancer-associated hypercalcemia occurs due to:

Thymomas are unusual neoplasms of thymic epithelial tissue, ranging from small indolent tumors to aggressive thymic carcinomas.

Pure red cell aplasia is a rare cause of anemia, caused by the absence of RBC precursors in the bone marrow. Causes of pure red cell aplasia include:

  • Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia
  • Drug exposure - phenytoin, azathioprine, and isoniazid

Factors that cause coagulopathy include:

  • Secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines - interleukin-1b (IL-1b) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)

Acanthosis nigricans is a disorder characterized by gray-black patches of thickened, hyperkeratotic skin with a velvety appearance. The causal mechanism is immunologic due to the secretion of epidermal growth factor.

Acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with:

  • Gastric carcinoma
  • Lung carcinoma
  • Gynecological cancers

question: A 48-year-old obese female presents with skin changes in her axilla and neck as shown in the image. Which of the following tumors is not associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history and laboratory investigations are suggestive of polycythemia which is not seen in melanoma as a paraneoplastic manifestation.

Polycythemia, as a paraneoplastic syndrome, is mediated by erythropoietin (EPO). EPO is a glycoprotein that induces differentiation of erythrocyte colony-forming units in the bone marrow to promote red blood cell production.

Under normal physiological conditions, EPO is produced by peritubular renal interstitial cells in response to local tissue hypoxia. However, in tumors, EPO production occurs in the neoplastic cells themselves.

question: Which of these paraneoplastic syndromes is associated with small-cell carcinoma lung?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation is suggestive of migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), and it is not associated with bladder carcinoma.

Trousseau syndrome is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state characterized by recurrent, migratory, superficial thrombophlebitis. It presents as tender, red nodules that follow superficial veins, often appearing and resolving spontaneously in different areas of the body. This condition is most commonly associated with deep-seated malignancies, particularly pancreatic and lung carcinomas. The underlying cause is tumor-induced hypercoagulability, leading to repeated venous thromboembolic events.

Malignant brain tumors, hematological malignancies, and adenocarcinomas of the pancreas, stomach, ovary, uterus, lungs, and kidneys are at the highest risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) development.

Advanced, metastatic cancer is associated with an increased risk of VTE compared with localized tumors.

question: A 60-year-old patient notices spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules in different parts of the body. Which of the following malignancies is not associated with this clinical presentation?

explanationHtml:
The serum levels of catecholamines are elevated in malignant pheochromocytoma. Extra-adrenal location is the only criteria for malignancy in pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine-secreting tumor that may precipitate life-threatening hypertension. It is classically associated with three syndromes:

  • Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
  • Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2)
  • von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome

Catecholamines produced by pheochromocytomas are metabolized within chromaffin cells, leading to the formation of normetanephrine from norepinephrine and metanephrine from epinephrine. Therefore, pheochromocytomas are best diagnosed by the measurement of these metabolites, rather than by the measurement of the parent catecholamines.

question: A 24-year-old patient with paroxysmal hypertension is suspected to have malignant pheochromocytoma. Which of the following tumor markers will help you confirm your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) are oncofetal antigens.

Alpha-fetoprotein is a valuable clinical aid in the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of the following tumors:

  • Primary hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Hepatoblastoma
  • Non-seminomatous testicular germ cell tumors
  • Embryonal carcinoma
  • Teratomas
  • Choriocarcinoma
  • Yolk sac carcinoma
  • Germ cell tumors of the ovary and extragonadal germ cell tumors

Regenerated hepatic tissue following liver damage due to viral hepatitis, chemically induced necrosis, and liver surgery is associated with moderately raised serum AFP levels.

Carcinoembryonic antigen is normally detected in the glycocalyx of fetal epithelial cells. It is useful in the detection, assessment of recurrence, and prognosis of the following tumors:

  • Adenocarcinoma of the lung
  • Colorectal carcinoma

CEA levels greater than 5 ng/dL are noted in ascites fluid associated with malignancy. The canalicular pattern for polyclonal CEA is more sensitive for detecting hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, but less sensitive for metastases in bile duct adenoma.

Elevated levels are also present in the following non-neoplastic conditions:

  • Cirrhosis
  • Biliary obstruction
  • Hepatitis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Smokers
  • Post-surgical bowel sequestration
  • Mucocele
  • Benign cysts may be positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

question: A 42-year-old patient is diagnosed with breast cancer. Which of the following glycoproteins is expected to be elevated in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of small cell carcinoma of the lung (SCLC) in which levels of neuron-specific enolase (NSE) are elevated.

Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is a neuroendocrine tumor. As a result, it commonly expresses neuroendocrine markers, including neuron-specific enolase (NSE), chromogranin A, and synaptophysin, which are useful for diagnosis and disease monitoring.

NSE is also called gamma enolase or enolase 2 (ENO2) and is encoded by the ENO2 gene. It is a phosphopyruvate hydratase that is produced by small-cell lung carcinomas, which are neuroendocrine in origin. Their levels have been implicated as a prognostic factor for patients with small-cell lung cancer.

question: A 51-year-old male patient who is a chronic smoker presents with dry persistent cough and progressive dyspnea. You are suspecting small cell carcinoma of lung. Which of the following tumor markers is likely to be elevated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
NRG-1 (Neuregulin-1) is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs).

GIST are the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, the stomach being the most common site. They arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the GIT. GIST is seen in the 5th to 6th decade of life and has an equal preponderance among males and females. Most patients present with haematemesis, melena, or vague abdominal pain. The most common indications for surgery include bleeding and obstruction.

The GIST may occur in a sporadic form or as part of familial syndromes. In sporadic GIST, the most common mutations seen are gain-of-function mutation in KIT (75-80%) and PDGFRA mutation (8%). Microscopically, GIST has elongated spindle cells or plumper epithelioid cells, or a mixed pattern.

The below image shows the microscopy of GIST composed of bundles, or fascicles, of spindle-shaped tumor cells.

[[figure-1]]

Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient GIST is a subset of wild-type GIST seen with Carney triad or Carney-Stratakis syndrome.

Imatinib can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) - deficient GIST is imatinib-resistant, so sunitinib, sorafenib, or regorafenib can be used instead.

During surgical resection of GIST, care must be taken to prevent capsule rupture, which causes seeding of nearby tissues, leading to relapse in 100% of the cases. If capsule rupture occurs, adjuvant therapy with imatinib is indicated regardless of tumor extent.

Other options:

Option A: KIT (CD117): This is the most well-known marker for GISTs. About 85% of GISTs show mutations in the KIT gene, leading to the expression of the KIT protein on the cell surface. KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and its activation is a key driver in the pathogenesis of GISTs.

Option B: SDH (Succinate Dehydrogenase): SDH mutations are associated with a subset of GISTs, particularly those that are KIT and PDGFRA wild-type. Loss of SDH function is characteristic of this subgroup, and SDH deficiency can be demonstrated through immunohistochemistry.

Option C: PDGFRA (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor Alpha): Mutations in the PDGFRA gene account for approximately 5-10% of GISTs. Similar to KIT, PDGFRA is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and mutations in this gene can lead to the development of GISTs.
