question: Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors?

explanationHtml:
B cell is not a component of innate immunity. It is a component of adaptive immunity.

Innate immunity refers to the body’s natural immunity. It is a built-in defence system that is present since birth. It differs from adaptive immunity in that it does not require any prior sensitization to an antigen.

The major components of innate immunity are as follows:

  • Epithelial barriers that block the entry of microbes
  • Phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages)
  • Natural killer (NK) cells
  • Dendritic cell
  • Cells that can sense and react to microbes - mast cells, epithelial, and endothelial cells
  • Plasma proteins - complement system factors, mannose-binding lectin, and C-reactive protein
  • Innate lymphoid cells
  • Lung surfactant

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following is not a component of innate immunity?

correctAnswer: C. NFκB mediated transcription of nuclear factor
explanationHtml:
Toll-like receptors (TLRs) stimulate immune response by NFκB-mediated transcription of nuclear factors.

TLRs are pattern recognition receptors that activate two sets of transcription factors:

  • NF-κB - stimulates the synthesis and secretion of cytokines and the expression of adhesion molecules. Both are critical for the recruitment and activation of leukocytes.
  • Interferon regulatory factors - stimulate the production of the antiviral cytokines such as type I interferons

The image given below shows a toll-like receptor:

[[figure-1]]

The various classes of innate immune receptors are as follows:

Receptors Location Function
Toll-like receptors Plasma membrane and endosomal vesicles

Important TLRs and molecules recognised:

  • TLR2 - peptidoglycan of gram + bacteria, lipopolysaccharide of Leptospira
  • TLR3 - dsRNA viruses
  • TLR4Q - Chlamydia and lipopolysaccharide
NOD-like receptors Cytosol of immune cells and epithelial cells
  • Recognise substances from necrotic cells and microbial products
  • activates caspase and IL-1 through inflammasome signalling.
C-type lectin receptors Plasma membrane of macrophages and dendritic cells
  • Detect fungal glycans and elicit inflammatory reactions to fungi
RIG-like receptors Cytosol of most cell types
  • recognize nucleic acids of viruses
  • Stimulate the production of antiviral cytokines
  • Recognize short bacterial peptides containing N-formyl methionyl residues and stimulate chemotaxis
Mannose receptors Plasma membrane of macrophages, immature dendritic cells, and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells
  • Recognizes microbial sugars that contain terminal mannose residues and induce phagocytosis.

Mannose receptor is a soluble pattern-recognition receptor. All the others are surface pattern-recognition receptors.

options.text: NFκB mediated transcription of nuclear factor

question: What is the mechanism by which toll-like receptors stimulate immune response against bacterial products?

correctAnswer: C. NK cells, neutrophils and eosinophils
explanationHtml:
Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is mediated by NK cells, neutrophils and eosinophils (killing certain parasitic worms like helminths via IgE antibodies).

In ADCC, cells/ antigens are coated with IgG antibodies. These are killed by effector cells like NK cells and macrophages. These effector cells bind to the target by their receptors for the Fc fragment of IgG and cell lysis proceeds without phagocytosis.
question: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is seen with:

explanationHtml:
The gain-of-function mutations in NOD-like receptors (NLRs) result in periodic fever syndromes, also known as autoinflammatory syndromes.

They are a group of clinical conditions characterised by recurrent inflammatory episodes. This disorder is characterized by abnormally increased inflammation, primarily mediated by cells and molecules of the innate immune system, with a significant predisposition in the host.

NOD-like receptors are cytosolic receptors that signal via a cytosolic multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. This activates caspase-1, which generates a biologically active form of interleukin-1 (IL-1). IL-1 is a mediator of inflammation that recruits leukocytes and induces fever. The autoinflammatory syndromes respond very well to treatment with IL-1 antagonists.

Note: Autoimmune diseases result from T and B-lymphocyte reactions against self-antigens.
question: Which of the following occurs due to gain-of-function mutations in NOD-Like receptors?

explanationHtml:
Normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio is 2:1. Approximately 60% of mature T cells are CD4+ and about 30% are CD8+.

T-lymphocytes (thymus-derived cells) constitute 60–70% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. T-cell progenitors are derived from the bone marrow, but travel to the thymus, where they mature. T cells can be divided into three main subtypes:

Type of T cell

Function

Helper T cell (CD4+)

Helps B lymphocytes to make antibodies and activate other leukocytes to destroy microbes

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs or CD8+)

Kill infected cells

Regulatory T cells

Limit immune responses and prevent reactions against self-antigens.

They are located in the paracortical areas of lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen. They have antigen-specific T-cell receptors (TCR), which have alpha/beta polypeptide chains. Demonstration of TCR gene rearrangement by Southern blot is a molecular marker of T-cell lineage.

The CD molecules present on T cells are CD1, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, and CD28. CD3 is involved in signal transduction and is also called a pan-T-cell marker. CD40 ligand on the surface is required for B-cell activation and induction of immunoglobulin.
question: What is the normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio?

explanationHtml:
CD86 is a protein expressed on antigen-presenting cells, and not B-cell receptor complex. This protein provides costimulatory signals necessary for T-cell activation and survival.

B-cell receptor complex expresses the following:

  • CD79a and CD79b - essential for signal transduction through the antigen receptor
  • CD21 or CR2 - complement receptor (recognize complement products during innate immune response) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) receptor
  • CD40 - receives signals from helper T cells

Other B cell-associated markers are CD10 (CALLA), CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23.
question: Which of the following is not expressed in the B-cell receptor complex?

explanationHtml:
Dendritic cells or interdigitating dendritic cells are the most important antigen-presenting cells. They initiate T-cell responses against protein antigens.

They are located in the epithelium and interstitium. They express many receptors for capturing and responding to microbes (and other antigens), including toll-like receptors (TLRs) and lectins. They also express high levels of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) for presenting antigens to and activating T cells.

In response to microbes, dendritic cells are recruited to the T-cell zones of lymphoid organs. Here, they present antigens to T cells with the help of MHC.

Similar cells with dendritic morphology in the germinal centers of lymphoid follicles in the spleen and lymph nodes are follicular dendritic cells. They bear Fc receptors for IgG and receptors for C3b. Immature dendritic cells within the epidermis are called Langerhans cells.

Note:

  • Agretope - part of the antigen associated with the MHC molecule on the antigen-presenting cell
  • Epitope - antigenic part of contact with the T-cell receptor
question: Which of the following are the most important antigen-presenting cells?

correctAnswer: D. It is a component of innate immunity only
explanationHtml:
Macrophages are components of both innate and acquired immunity.

They phagocytose microbes and protein antigens. They process the antigens and present the peptide fragments to T cells. Thus, macrophages function as antigen-presenting cells in T-cell activation.

They also participate in the effector phase of humoral immunity. Macrophages efficiently phagocytose and destroy microbes that are opsonized (coated) with IgG or C3b.

They are key effector cells in certain forms of cell-mediated immunity to eliminate intracellular microbes. In this type of response, T cells activate macrophages and enhance their ability to kill ingested microbes.

options.text: It acts as an antigen presenting cell
It plays a role in humoral immunity
It plays a role in cell-mediated immunity
It is a component of innate immunity only

question: Which of the following statements is false about macrophages?

correctAnswer: C. IL-12 stimulates the proliferation of NK cells
explanationHtml:
IL-2 and IL-15 stimulate the proliferation of NK cells. On the other hand, IL-12 activates the killing of target cells and secretion of IFN-γ.

NK cells are large granular lymphocytes, which constitute 5% to 10% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules.

Functions of NK cells:

  • Killing of a variety of virus-infected cells and tumor cells, without prior exposure to or activation by these microbes or tumors
  • Secretion of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), which activates macrophages to destroy ingested microbes
  • Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) - NK cells express CD16, which is a receptor for IgG Fc tails. Hence, these cells can lyse IgG-coated target cells.

ADCC is also seen in immune responses involving neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, etc.

The image given below shows activating and inhibitory receptors of natural killer (NK) cells:

[[figure-1]]

Note: A new group of T cells has been discovered called NK-T cells. These are T cells that contain markers of NK cells. These are important defence mechanisms against microorganisms like Listeria monocytogenes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

options.text: CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules
They are involved in antibody-dependant cytotoxic killing
IL-12 stimulates the proliferation of NK cells
They activate macrophages by secreting IFN-γ

question: Which of the following is false about natural killer cells?

explanationHtml:
Both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells are effective against virus-infected cells.

The NK cells have different mechanisms of action while killing target cells.

NK cells have a CD16 receptor which binds to the Fc tail of IgG and kills IgG-coated target cells. This phenomenon is known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

Target cell destruction by NK cells is also mediated through two other receptors - activating receptors and inhibitory receptors.

The activating receptors enable NK cells to recognize infected and stressed cells. The inhibitory receptors recognize self-class-I MHC molecules, which are expressed on all healthy cells, thereby preventing NK cells from killing normal cells. Virus infection / neoplastic transformation overexpresses the activating receptors and simultaneously reduces the expression of class-I MHC molecules. As a result, NK cells are activated and the infected cells are killed.

NK cells also activate macrophages to destroy ingested microbes by secreting cytokines like interferon-γ (IFN-γ).

CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes directly kill damaged cells.

The differences between NK cells and cytotoxic T-cells are:

Natural killer (NK) cell Cytotoxic T-cells
Does not require priming - rapid response in hours require priming - takes days to respond
MHC unrestricted MHC restricted

Antibody-mediated and non-antibody-mediated killing

Non-antibody mediated killing / direct cytotoxicity

Kills virus-infected and neoplastic cells by apoptosis

Kills virus-infected, neoplastic, and donor graft cells by apoptosis
Antigen non-specific Antigen-specific
Memory is absent Memory is present

options.text: They are MHC l restricted cells
Require antibodies to be present for action

question: Which of these is common to both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells?

explanationHtml:
CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) are the costimulatory molecules present on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). They bind to CD28 protein present on T cells. This promotes the expansion of antigen-stimulated T cells and their differentiation into effector and memory cells.

T-cell activation requires two signals that are delivered by APCs. They include:

  1. Antigens displayed by APCs in the form of peptides bound to MHC molecules, that are recognised by T-cell receptors
  2. Costimulatory signal (as it stimulates T cells in conjunction with antigen) provided by molecules on APCs that engage particular costimulatory receptors on T cells

In the absence of costimulation, T cells that recognize antigen either fail to respond and die or enter a state of unresponsiveness known as anergy. Thus, costimulation is a key determinant of the outcome of a T-cell encounter with an antigen.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following markers on antigen-presenting cells function as costimulatory molecules for T cells?

explanationHtml:
IL-4 induces T helper 2 cells.

Mechanism of cell-mediated immunity:

  • Antigen-presenting cells → recognized by naive CD4+ T cells → IL-2 secretion → T-cell proliferation and differentiation → activated CD4+ T helper cells
  • Activated CD4+ T cells further differentiate into effector cells that secrete different sets of cytokines and perform different functions
question: Which of the following cytokines induces T-helper type 2 cells?

explanationHtml: IL-4 stimulates B-cells to differentiate into IgE secreting plasma cells.
question: B-cells are induced to produce IgE by which of the following:

explanationHtml:
Polysaccharides and lipids stimulate the secretion of mainly IgM antibodies.

B lymphocytes use their antigen receptors to recognize various types of antigens:

  • Proteins (through CD40L and cytokine-mediated helper T-cell actions) - induce production of IgG, IgA, and IgE
  • Polysaccharides and lipids - induce the production of IgM mainly

Helper T cells also help in antibody production by the following mechanisms:

  • Stimulate the formation of germinal centers, which consist of proliferating B cells
  • Induce isotype switching through cytokines IFN-γ and IL-4
  • Affinity maturation - stimulates the production of antigen-specific antibodies

Isotype switching and affinity maturation occur mainly in germinal centers.
question: Production of which of the following antibodies is induced by polysaccharides and lipids?

explanationHtml:
When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments.

Papain is a proteolytic enzyme that cleaves immunoglobulin (Ig) molecules (typically IgG) above the hinge region, resulting in: 1 Fc and 2 Fab

If an antibody molecule is digested with papain, cleavage occurs above the disulfide bonds that hold the heavy chains together. This generates 3 separate fragments, two of which are called Fab (fragment antigen binding), and one of which is called Fc (fragment crystallizable).

The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by papain:

[[figure-1]]

Cleavage of the antibody molecule with pepsin generates one large fragment called F(ab´)2 and a digested Fc fragment.

The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by pepsin.

question: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, which of the following are the end products?

explanationHtml:
Lymphocyte recirculation is seen in T lymphocytes.

Migration of the lymphocytes between the blood and lymphoid organs is called recirculation. Naive lymphocytes traverse the peripheral lymphoid organs, where immune responses are initiated. When antigen-presenting cells activate them, the effector lymphocytes migrate to sites of infection and inflammation.

In contrast, plasma cells remain in lymphoid organs and the bone marrow. They do not need to migrate to sites of infection because they secrete antibodies that are carried to distant tissues.

options.text: Both plasma cells and T lymphocytes
Both B lymphocytes and plasma cells

question: In which of the following cells is recirculation seen?

correctAnswer: B. Need antigen processing and presentation for their recognition
explanationHtml:
γ𝛿 T-cells do not need antigen processing and presentation for their recognition.

There are two types of T cells: γ𝛿 T-cells and αβ T-cells.

The functions of γ𝛿 T-cells:

  • Protect against mycobacteria by direct killing of infected macrophages
  • Kills extracellular bacteria with granulysin and perforin
  • Plays a role in maintaining self-tolerance
  • Capable of recognising and lysing diverse cancers in an MHC-unrestricted manner

αβ T-cells have MHC-restricted action.

options.text: Kills extracellular bacteria by granulysin and perforin
Need antigen processing and presentation for their recognition

question: Which of the following about γ𝛿 T-cells is incorrect:

explanationHtml:
Basophils are activated by IL-5 and IL-3.

Note: IL-5 primarily activates eosinophils.
question: Basophils are activated by:

correctAnswer: C. B cells, dendritic cells, mononuclear phagocytes
explanationHtml:
Class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules are mainly expressed on macrophages, B lymphocytes, and dendritic cells. These cells present ingested antigens to T-cells.

The function of MHC molecules is to display peptide fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells. In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens (HLA) because they were initially detected on leukocytes by the binding of antibodies. The combination of HLA alleles in each individual is called the HLA haplotype.

The genes encoding HLA molecules are clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6.

Uses of MHC/ HLA typing include:

  • Anthropology
  • Transfusion
  • Paternity testing
  • Forensic science
  • Transplantation
  • Disease correlation

options.text: B cells, dendritic cells, mononuclear phagocytes

question: Among the following, which cells have MHC class II?

explanationHtml:
β2 microglobulin associated cell surface molecules are encoded by MHC class I and not class III.

Class III MHC molecules include:

  • Complement proteins (such as C2, C4, and B factor)
  • Cytokines (such as TNF-α, LTA, and LTB)
  • Properdin factor BQ of alternate pathway
  • Enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase
  • Heat-shock proteins

Class III molecules are encoded by genes located between those that encode class I and class II molecules.
question: Which of the following is not encoded by MHC class III genes?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of anaphylaxis following a bee sting. This is an example of an IgE-mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity.

Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions. There are four types of hypersensitivity reactions.

Immediate (Type 1) hypersensitivity is also called an allergic reaction. They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals.

IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg. Reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators. The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents like prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines.

It occurs in two phases: the immediate phase and the late phase. The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation). The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

question: A child, upon disturbing a beehive, had several stings. After a few minutes, he developed shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. What is the pathogenesis of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Arthus reaction is characterized by a localized area of tissue necrosis due to immune-complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity reaction) vasculitis in the skin.

This reaction can be produced experimentally by intracutaneous injection of antigen in a previously immunised animal that contains circulating antibodies against the antigen. As the antigen diffuses into the vessel wall, it binds with the preformed antibody, and immune complexes are formed locally. These complexes precipitate in the vessel walls and cause fibrinoid necrosis.
question: Arthus reaction is caused by which of the following process?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis. It is an example of a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder typically associated with autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. It is an example of a Type II hypersensitivity reaction, in which antibodies target antigens present on cell surfaces or within the extracellular matrix. These antibodies can lead to cell destruction, inflammation, or interference with normal physiological functions, depending on the nature of the antigen and the immune response involved.s.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephritic syndrome due to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. This is an example of a type III hypersensitivity reaction.

In type III hypersensitivity, immune complexes may deposit in tissues or blood vessels and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement. The pathogenesis of systemic immune complex disease can be divided into three phases:

  • Formation of immune complexes
  • Deposition of immune complexes
  • Inflammation and tissue injury

This results in various manifestations like vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, and arthritis.

Examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions:

  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Reactive arthritis
  • Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Serum sickness
  • Arthus reaction
  • Farmer’s lung
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  • Type II lepra reaction

question: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and smoky, cola-colored urine 2 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. He is found to have periorbital edema and mild hypertension. Urine examination shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts in the urine with mild proteinuria. Which type of hypersensitivity is responsible for this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario shows a positive tuberculin test. It is a classical example of type IV or delayed or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.

Tuberculin test involves intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD, also called tuberculin), a protein-containing antigen of the tubercle bacillus. In a previously sensitized individual, reddening and induration of the site appear in 8 to 12 hours, reach a peak in 24 to 72 hours, and thereafter slowly subside.

Morphologically, delayed-type hypersensitivity is characterized by the accumulation of mononuclear cells, mainly CD4+ T cells and macrophages, around venules. The cell-mediated type of hypersensitivity is caused by inflammation resulting from cytokines produced by CD4+ T cells and cell killing by CD8+ T cells.

explanationHtml:
Anaphylactoid reactions are those reactions that are similar to the anaphylactic reactions but are not IgE-mediated. These reactions are caused by direct degranulation of the mast cells or basophils, which causes the release of mediators.

An anaphylactoid reaction (non-IgE-mediated anaphylaxis) resembles anaphylaxis clinically but differs mechanistically.

Unlike classic anaphylaxis, which occurs on re-exposure to the allergen, the anaphylactoid reaction can occur even on the first exposure. The most common agents that can cause an anaphylactoid reaction include NSAIDs and radiocontrast media.

In 2014, the World Allergy Organisation introduced two new terms:

  • Immunologic anaphylaxis - It includes anaphylactic reactions mediated by IgE, IgG (in animals), and immune complex/ complement-mediated reactions.
  • Non-immunologic anaphylaxis (formerly anaphylactoid reaction) - occurs due to excessive degranulation of mast cells/basophils. Immunoglobulins are usually not involved.

explanationHtml:
The PTPN22 gene is most commonly associated with autoimmunity.

PTPN22, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase, is associated with the following conditions:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
  • Type 1 diabetes

Because these disorders have a relatively high prevalence, PTPN22 is considered the gene most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.

Other options:

Option A: Mutations in FOXP3 cause a systemic autoimmune disease called IPEX (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked).

Option C: Polymorphisms in the gene encoding for NOD2 are associated with Crohn's disease.

explanationHtml:
The above process is called central tolerance, and the AIRE (AutoImmune REgulator) protein is necessary for this process.

Immature self-reactive T and B lymphocyte clones recognize self-antigens during their maturation in the central lymphoid organs (thymus for T cells, bone marrow for B cells). They are killed or rendered harmless.

The removal of self-reacting T lymphocytes in the thymus is called negative selection/ deletion. For this process, the AIRE protein is needed. Mutations in the AIRE gene result in autoimmune disorders (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy).

B cells undergo a process called receptor editing. When developing B cells encounter an antigen, it forms a change in the receptor that makes the antigen unrecognizable. Self-reacting B cells can also undergo apoptosis.
question: During development, thymic cells recognizing self-antigens are removed to prevent autoimmunity. Which gene among the following is involved in the process?

explanationHtml:
Autoimmunity in Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection is the result of polyclonal B cell activation.

Microbes may induce other abnormalities that promote autoimmune reactions. Some viruses, such as EBV and HIV, cause polyclonal B-cell activation, which may result in the production of autoantibodies.

The role of infections in autoimmunity is exemplified by the following:

  1. Molecular mimicry of antigenic cross-reactivity: The structural similarity of the microbial antigens and self-antigens. Rheumatic heart disease is an example in which streptococcal proteins cross-react with myocardial proteins, causing myocarditis.
  2. Upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules by infectious organisms.
  3. Polyclonal B cell activation: Caused by EBV and HIV, resulting in the production of autoantibodies.
  4. Alteration of tissue antigens: Infections may alter tissue self-antigens so that they activate T cells and lose the property of self-tolerance.

Homogeneous or diffuse nuclear staining does not reflect antibodies to RNA. The nucleolar pattern of staining represents antibodies to RNA.

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are directed against antibodies to:

  • DNA
  • Histones

The most widely used method for detecting ANAs is indirect immunofluorescence. The pattern of nuclear fluorescence suggests the type of antibody present in the patient’s serum.

explanationHtml:
The lupus erythematosus (LE) cell is a phagocytic neutrophil or macrophage.

Nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous to produce LE bodies or hematoxylin bodies. Phagocytic neutrophils or macrophages engulf the denatured nucleus of an injured cell. Demonstration of LE cells in vitro was used in the past for the diagnosis of SLE.

question: What type of cell is the lupus erythematosus cell?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In this condition, lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary gland is not seen. However, this finding is seen in Sjogren's syndrome.

If cell nuclei are exposed to anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs), they can bind to them. The nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous. They are called lupus erythematosus (LE) bodies or hematoxylin bodies.

An acute necrotizing vasculitis involving capillaries, small arteries, and arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis is seen in SLE. Central penicilliary arteries in the spleen may show concentric intimal and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia, producing so-called onion-skin lesions.

Celiac disease is not an IgG4-related disease.

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a newly recognized constellation of disorders characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibody-producing plasma cells and lymphocytes, particularly T cells, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and usually increased serum IgG4.

IgG4-RD spectrum includes:

  • Mikulicz syndrome - enlargement and fibrosis of salivary and lacrimal glands
  • Riedel thyroiditis
  • Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis
  • Inflammatory pseudotumors of the orbit, lungs, and kidney

explanationHtml:
Leukocyte-adhesion deficiency (LAD) type 2 is due to the absence of Sialyl-Lewis X.

Physiologically, Sialyl-Lewis X has the necessary ligand for the selectins, which bind to leukocytes.

Inherited defects in leukocyte adhesion:

  • Type 1 - defect in the biosynthesis of the β2 chain shared by the LFA-1 and Mac-1 integrins
  • Type 2 - absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose-containing ligand for E- and P-selectins. It is due to a defect in the fucosyltransferase, the enzyme that attaches fucose moieties to protein backbones.

The major clinical problem in both conditions is recurrent bacterial infections due to inadequate granulocyte function.

question: Leukocyte-adhesion deficiency type 2 is due to the absence of which of the following?

correctAnswer: D. Granules are absent in white blood cells
explanationHtml:
Leukocytes contain giant granules in Chédiak–Higashi syndrome as seen in peripheral blood smears. They are due to aberrant phagolysosome fusion.

The image shows giant granules in a neutrophil in Chédiak–Higashi syndrome:

Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. The defective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes results in defective phagocytes function and susceptibility to infections.

The abnormalities are neutropenia, defective degranulation, and delayed microbial killing, causing:

  • Albinism - melanocytes
  • Nerve defects - nervous system cells
  • Bleeding disorders - platelets

The gene associated with this disorder encodes a large cytosolic protein called LYST, which is believed to regulate lysosomal trafficking.

question: Which of the following statements is false about Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?

correctAnswer: D. Due to lymphocytic inflammatory reaction
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests chronic granulomatous disease. It is due to a macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction, not lymphocytic.

Chronic granulomatous disease is a defect in bacterial killing and renders patients susceptible to recurrent bacterial infections. The name of this disease comes from the macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction that tries to control the infection when the initial neutrophil defense is inadequate. This often leads to collections of activated macrophages that wall off the microbes, forming granulomas.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hereditary angioneurotic edema. It is due to the deficiency of C1 inhibitors.

Hereditary angioneurotic edema is an autosomal dominant disorder that is more common than complement deficiency states.

Targets of C1 inhibitors are proteases, specifically C1r and C1s of the complement cascade, factor XII of the coagulation pathway, and the kallikrein system. Deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein. This increases the production of vasoactive peptides such as bradykinin.

It causes episodes of edema affecting the skin and mucosal surfaces, such as the larynx and the gastrointestinal tract. This may result in life-threatening asphyxia or nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea after minor trauma or emotional stress.
question: A patient presents with recurrent swelling of the face and lips as shown with vomiting and diarrhea when emotionally stressed. What is the most likely deficiency?

correctAnswer: C. It is due to defect only in cell mediated immune response
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The biopsy of the thymus showing remnants of Hassall's corpuscles indicates it is due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. SCID is a defect in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Usually, the defect lies in the T-cell compartment with secondary impairment in humoral immunity.

Affected infants present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive. Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus, causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:

  • Candida albicans
  • Pneumocystis jiroveci
  • Pseudomonas
  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Varicella

There are 2 types of SCID based on inheritance:

1. X-linked SCID is the most common form, and hence it is more common in boys than in girls. The genetic defect is the mutation in the common γ-chain (γc) subunit of cytokine receptors. T-cell numbers are greatly reduced, and although B cells may be normal in number, antibody synthesis is impaired because of the lack of T-cell help. The thymus contains lobules of undifferentiated epithelial cells resembling fetal thymus.

2. Autosomal recessive is most commonly caused by a deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). The deficiency of ADA leads to the accumulation of deoxyadenosine and its derivatives (e.g., deoxy-ATP). They are toxic to rapidly dividing immature lymphocytes, especially those of the T-cell lineage. Hence, there may be a greater reduction in the number of T lymphocytes.

In the two most common forms (γc mutation and ADA deficiency), the thymus is small and devoid of lymphoid cells. In SCID caused by ADA deficiency, remnants of Hassall’s corpuscles can be found.

Note: X-linked SCID is the first human disease in which gene therapy has been successful.

options.text: It is due to defect only in cell mediated immune response
B cell count can be normal

question: A 4-month-old baby was brought with severe diaper rash. The parents gave a history of recurrent infections in the past 4 months which required frequent hospitalization.  On examination white patches were present in oral mucosa which could be scraped easily. The biopsy of the thymus showed remnants of Hassall's corpuscles. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

explanationHtml:
BTK mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia and not SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency).

Severe combined immunodeficiency is a defect in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. In this condition, the following genes are involved:

  • JAK3
  • RAG1
  • IL-7Rα

Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:

  • Candida albicans
  • Pneumocystis jiroveci
  • Pseudomonas
  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Varicella
question: Which gene is not involved in SCID?

correctAnswer: D. Not associated with autoimmune disease
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Bruton agammaglobulinemia/ X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA). Even though it is an immunodeficiency disease, it is paradoxically associated with autoimmune diseases such as arthritis and dermatomyositis in 35% of individuals.

The classic form of this disease has the following characteristics:

  • B cells are absent or markedly decreased and the serum levels of all classes of immunoglobulins are decreased
  • T-cell mediated reactions are normal
  • Germinal centers of lymph nodes, Peyer’s patches, the appendix, and tonsils are underdeveloped
  • Plasma cells are absent throughout the body

XLA is characterized by the failure of B-cell precursors (pro-B cells and pre-B cells) to develop into mature B cells. It is associated with mutations in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase called Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk).

The related gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome. This X-linked disease is seen almost entirely in males. The disease usually does not become apparent until about 6 months of age, when maternal immunoglobulins are depleted.

Affected individuals are susceptible to infections with:

  • Bacteria that are normally opsonized by antibodies and cleared by phagocytosis
    • Haemophilus influenzae
    • Streptococcus pneumonia
    • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Giardia lamblia - intestinal protozoan that is normally resisted by secreted IgA, causes persistent infections
  • Enteroviruses
    • Echovirus
    • Poliovirus
    • Coxsackievirus

options.text: Germinal centres of lymph nodes are underdeveloped
Manifestation is seen usually after 6 months of age

question: A 9-month-old baby was brought with a cough and difficulty in breathing. The baby was admitted with similar complaints in the past. On auscultation, coarse crepitations were heard. Quantitative serum immunoglobulin analysis was done and serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were low. His cellular immunity was found to be normal. Which of the following is false about his condition?

correctAnswer: D. Failure of development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with the image suggests DiGeorge syndrome. It results from the failure of the development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches. They give rise to the thymus, the parathyroids, some of the C cells of the thyroid, and the ultimobranchial body.

The absence of cell-mediated immunity causes poor defense against certain fungal and viral infections. The T-cell zones of lymphoid organs, i.e. paracortical areas of the lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen, are depleted. Ig levels may be normal or reduced, depending on the severity of the T-cell deficiency.

options.text: It is associated with T cell deficiency
Thymic hypoplasia is a prominent feature
Failure of development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches

question: A 2-year-old boy was brought to the OPD with delayed development. On examination, he had the following appearance. Further workup revealed hypocalcemia and an atrial septal defect.  Chromosomal studies showed deletion of 22q11. All are true about this syndrome except:

correctAnswer: B. They have normal serum IgG levels
explanationHtml:
The serum of patients with Hyper-IgM syndrome contains extremely low levels of IgG.

In Hyper-IgM syndrome, production of IgM antibodies is normal, but the ability to produce IgG, IgA, and IgE antibodies is deficient. It affects the ability of helper T cells to deliver activating signals to B cells and macrophages. However, the B-cell and T-cell amounts remain unchanged.

It is mostly an X-linked disease that has mutations in the gene encoding CD40L located on Xq26. In an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, there are CD40 or the enzyme called activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) loss-of-function mutations

Those with CD40L mutations are also susceptible to pneumonia caused by the intracellular organism Pneumocystis jiroveci. This is due to CD40L-mediated macrophage activation, a key reaction of cell-mediated immunity, being defective. Recurrent pyogenic infection occurs because the level of opsonizing IgG antibodies is low.

Occasionally, the IgM antibodies react with blood cells, giving rise to autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. In older patients, the proliferation of IgM-producing plasma cells that infiltrate the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract is seen.

options.text: It has X-linked mode of inheritance
They have normal serum IgG levels
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia can be seen
They have normal B-cell and T-cell numbers

question: Which of the following is least likely to be a feature in a patient with Hyper-IgM syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The deficiency of CD40 and its absence in B cells interfere with class switching and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to antigens is unaffected, accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies. Hence, the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome.

The given clinical scenario and the flow cytometry are suggestive of Hyper IgM syndrome. The flow cytometry shows the following findings:

    Gating of B cells means selecting a cell during a flow cytometry experiment for further analysis or data presentation.CD 19 is widely expressed on B cells. Hence, the graph shows B-cell gating. Side scatter measurement provides information about the granularity of a cell.
  • In comparison of image 4 to 2, where CD 40 is plotted against CD 19: B cells are present only in quadrant 4, which means that there is a CD 40 deficiency.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. The flow cytometry analysis of the boy (Boxes 3& 4) is shown below (Boxes 1 & 2 are normal). What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Isolated IgA deficiency is associated with deficiency of IgG subtypes IgG2 and IgG4.

IgA-deficient individuals have extremely low levels of both serum and secretory IgA. It may be familial or acquired in association with toxoplasmosis, measles, or some other viral infection.

Because IgA is the major antibody in external secretions, mucosal defenses are weakened, and infections are more likely to occur in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts. Symptomatic patients commonly have recurrent sinopulmonary infections and diarrhea.

IgA-deficient patients have a high frequency of respiratory tract allergy and a variety of autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis.
question: Patients with isolated Ig A deficiency would have associated deficiency of which of the following IgG subtypes?

explanationHtml:
The X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome is due to mutations in the gene encoding an adaptor molecule called SLAM-associated protein (SAP).

It is characterized by an inability to eliminate Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), eventually leading to fulminant infectious mononucleosis and the development of B-cell tumors.

In approximately 80% of cases, the disease is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the adaptor molecule SAP. Defects in SAP contribute to attenuated NK cell and T-cell activation, resulting in increased susceptibility to viral infections.

Other options:

Option B: The LYST gene is associated with Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

Option C: The BTK gene is associated with Isolated growth hormone deficiency type III and Bruton's (X-Linked) Agammaglobulinemia.

Option D: The TBX1 gene is associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
question: Which of the following are mutated in X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Normal B-cell count is most commonly seen in the lymphoid tissues of individuals with common variable hypogammaglobulinemia.

It is a heterogeneous group of disorders in which the common feature is hypogammaglobulinemia, generally affecting all the antibody classes, but sometimes only IgG.

In contrast to X-linked agammaglobulinemia, most individuals with common variable immunodeficiency have normal or near-normal numbers of B-cells in the blood and lymphoid tissues. These B cells, however, are not able to differentiate into plasma cells.

FDA approved XEMBIFY in 2019, a 20% immunoglobulin solution for subcutaneous injection. It is indicated for the use of primary humoral immunodeficiency disorders in patients 2 years of age and older.
question: Which of the following lymphoid tissue findings is seen most commonly in patients with common variable hypogammaglobulinemia?

explanationHtml:
The given history with eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia points towards Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. In this condition, IgM levels in the serum are low.

Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP), which is located on Xp11.23. The X-linked disease is characterized by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and a marked vulnerability to recurrent infection, resulting in early death.

Platelets are small in size. The thymus is morphologically normal, at least early in the course of the disease, but there is a progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood and in the T-cell zones (paracortical areas) of the lymph nodes, with variable defects in cellular immunity.

Patients do not make antibodies to polysaccharide antigens, and the response to protein antigens is poor. IgM levels are low, IgG is usually normal, while the levels of IgA and IgE are often elevated. Patients are prone to developing B-cell lymphomas.
question: A 3-year-old boy is brought with complaints of red rashes over his skin. His mother says that the child will be constantly scratching the rashes. On asking any previous history she says the child keeps getting recurrent infections which mostly require hospitalization. Blood investigations showed a low platelet count. Which of the following is false regarding this syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario and image showing telangiectasia are diagnostic of ataxia-telangiectasia. It is an autosomal-recessive disorder, not autosomal dominant.

The most prominent humoral immune abnormalities are defective production of IgA and IgG2. The gene responsible for this disorder is located on chromosome 11 and encodes a protein called ATM. The ATM protein is a sensor of DNA damage (double-strand breaks), and it activates p53 by phosphorylation.

Ataxia-telangiectasia is characterized by abnormal gait (ataxia), vascular malformations (telangiectases), neurologic deficits, increased incidence of tumors, and immunodeficiency. It may affect both B and T cells.

There is a high incidence of lymphomas and leukemias.

options.text: There is defective production of IgA and IgG2
Affected gene is located on chromosome 11
There is increased risk of malignancy

question: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the OPD with complaints of repeated falls while walking for the past 1 year. She had difficulty in eating, gripping, or holding things. On examination, hand mouth incoordination and slurring of speech were noted.  On ocular examination, the following finding was seen. All are true about this condition except:

explanationHtml:
The CD4 cells are affected by HIV due to their interaction with gp120.

HIV-1 virion is spherical and contains an electron-dense, cone-shaped core surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from the host cell membrane. Target cells of HIV include CD4+ helper T cells (worst affected), monocyte-macrophages, and dendritic cells.

The virus core contains:

  • Major capsid protein p24
  • Nucleocapsid protein p7/p9
  • Two copies of viral genomic RNA
  • The three viral enzymes (protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase)

The viral core is surrounded by a matrix protein called p17, which lies underneath the virion envelope. The viral envelope is studded with two viral glycoproteins, gp120 and gp41, which are critical for HIV infection of cells.

Viral glycoprotein gp120 binds to CD4+ cells in the host. CXCR4 and CCR5 function as coreceptors for HIV-1 entry into CD4+ cells. This binding leads to a conformational change in gp41, causing exposure of a hydrophobic region called the fusion peptide at the tip of gp41. This peptide inserts into the cell membrane of the target cells (e.g., T cells or macrophages), leading to the fusion of the virus with the host cell.

question: Human immunodeficiency virus affects CD4 cells due to their interaction with which protein?

explanationHtml:
The neutrophil is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

HIV enters the body and affects T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Particularly, memory and activated T cells are infected, but it is inefficient at productively infecting naive (unactivated) T cells.

Completion of the viral life cycle in latently infected cells occurs only after cell activation, and in the case of most CD4+ T cells, virus activation results in cell lysis.

question: Which of the following cell types is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of HIV infection?

explanationHtml:
The most common central nervous system (CNS) neoplasm in patients with HIV infection is primary CNS lymphoma.

Lymphomas are the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppressed individuals, including those with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and immunosuppression after transplantation. They are associated with latent infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). The vast majority of primary brain lymphomas are of B-cell origin.

At least two mechanisms appear to underlie the increased risk of B-cell tumors in HIV-infected individuals. They are:

  • The unchecked proliferation of B cells infected with oncogenic herpes viruses in the setting of profound T-cell depletion (AIDS).
  • Germinal center B-cell hyperplasia in the setting of early HIV infection.

Note: The most common site for lymphoma in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is the central nervous system (CNS).

explanationHtml:
Amyloid can be best described as a misfolded protein.

Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of fibrillar proteins.

Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans (heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate), and plasma proteins (serum amyloid P component).

The abundant charged sugar groups in these adsorbed proteins give the deposits staining characteristics that resemble starch (amylose). Therefore, these deposits are called amyloid.

Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

In inflammatory states, there is a release of IL-1 and IL-6, which act on the liver cells. The liver increases the production of SAA (serum amyloid-associated) proteins, which circulate bound to high-density lipoproteins. This gives rise to AA proteins, which get deposited in tissues, causing reactive systemic amyloidosis or secondary amyloidosis.

The most common sites are the kidney and heart.

It is usually seen secondary to:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (most common)
  • Tuberculosis
  • Bronchiectasis

explanationHtml:
Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP) is associated with the deposition of mutant transthyretin protein (TTR).

FAP is an autosomal dominant condition. The deposition occurs as amyloid fibrils in peripheral and autonomic nerves. Mutated TTR is prone to misfolding and aggregation, and shows resistance to proteolysis.

Systemic senile amyloidosis (amyloid of aging) refers to the systemic deposition of normal TTR amyloid in elderly patients. Symptomatic patients present with restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. Another rare form affecting predominantly the heart results from the deposition of a mutant form of TTR.

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive condition seen in individuals of Mediterranean descent (Armenian, Sephardic Jewish, and Arabic). The affected gene encodes a protein called pyrin, which is involved in cytokine production. The amyloid fibril proteins in this condition are made up of AA proteins. It presents with attacks of fever and serositis.

Isolated atrial amyloidosis is associated with AANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) amyloid deposition.

explanationHtml:
In suspected systemic amyloidosis, the initial investigation of choice is abdominal fat aspirate staining.

Diagnosis of amyloidosis involves the following:

  • Localized amyloidosis - biopsy the organ involved. e.g., kidney
  • Systemic amyloidosis - deposits can be found in any tissue of the body
    • Initial test - non-invasive test on easily accessible tissue (eg, abdominal fat) which is positive in >80% of cases
    • If this is negative, more invasive biopsies of the kidney, heart, lung, or GI tract (rectal biopsy) are required.
  • Suspected AL amyloidosis - serum and urine electrophoresis and immunoelectrophoresis

The histological examination of the biopsy material is the commonest confirmatory method for the diagnosis in a suspected case of amyloidosis. The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis employing mass spectrometry.

Scintigraphy with radiolabeled serum amyloid P component is a rapid and specific test that gives the extent of the disease. It can be used to follow up on patients undergoing treatment.

question: A pathologist is examining a sample from a patient with amyloidosis. Which of the following is false about the specimen's appearance?

explanationHtml:
Macrophages present foreign graft antigens to the T-cells, but are not directly involved in graft rejection.

Graft rejection is both humoral and cell-mediated in nature. It is a process in which T-cells and antibodies produced against graft antigens react against tissue grafts and destroy them.

The major antigenic differences that result in the rejection of transplants are differences in HLA alleles. The recipient T-cells are involved in the recognition of the donor MHC molecules and mount an immune response. Depending on the antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that are involved in T-cell activation, there are 2 pathways:

  • Direct pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the APCs in the graft
  • Indirect pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the recipient’s own APCs (e.g., macrophages)

The early activation of NK cells kills allogeneic target cells directly or via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and releases various chemokines and immunomodulatory cytokines.

question: A man is receiving a matched blood group kidney allograft. While closing the abdomen, the surgeon notices a sudden color change to pale-white in the transplanted kidney. He decides to remove it. Which of the following is responsible for graft rejection in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history and the biopsy findings of endotheliitis suggest a diagnosis of acute cell-mediated graft rejection.

In acute cell-mediated graft rejection, CD8+ CTLs directly destroy graft cells or CD4+ cells secrete cytokines that damage the graft.

On histopathology, it produces two different patterns of injury in the graft:

  • Tubulointerstitial pattern (type I): extensive interstitial and tubular inflammation associated with focal tubular injury
  • Vascular pattern - Inflammation (type II) and necrosis (type III), endotheliitis (swollen endothelial cells with lymphocytes between endothelium and vessel wall)

Note: Immunosuppressive therapy aims to prevent and reduce acute rejection by blocking the activation of alloreactive T cells. In the absence of humoral rejection, patients respond well to immunosuppressive therapy.

explanationHtml:
The lung is least likely to be affected in acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients. The transferred cells recognize alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues.

It is seen most commonly in the setting of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation. Rarely, it may occur following transplantation of solid organs rich in lymphoid cells (e.g., the liver) or transfusion of unirradiated blood.

It is of two types, acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD develops within days to weeks. There is the involvement of the immune system and epithelium of the skin, liver, and intestines. It presents with:

  • Generalized rash
  • Jaundice
  • Bloody diarrhea due to mucosal ulceration
  • Non-infectious pulmonary infiltrates (rarely), the outcome is generally poor

Chronic GVHD may follow the acute syndrome or occur insidiously. It presents with:

  • Skin - extensive cutaneous injury, with the destruction of skin appendages and dermal fibrosis (may resemble systemic sclerosis)
  • Liver - chronic liver disease, manifested as cholestatic jaundice
  • GIT - esophageal strictures
  • Immune system involvement - involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes

GVHD is mediated by T lymphocytes contained in the transplanted donor cells. Therefore, depletion of donor T cells before transfusion virtually eliminates the disease.

explanationHtml:
Most of the functional iron (80%) in the body is found in hemoglobin.

The total body iron content can be divided into functional (80-85% of total) and storage (15-20% of total) compartments. About 80% of the functional iron is found in hemoglobin; the rest is in myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes such as catalase and cytochromes. The storage pool is represented by hemosiderin and ferritin.

explanationHtml:
DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte.

Dietary iron is mostly in Fe3+ (ferric state) and must be reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous state) by ferrireductases for absorption. Once reduced to Fe2+, it is transported across the apical membrane of intestinal cells by DMT1. Fe2+ iron destined for circulation is transported from the cytoplasm of intestinal cells across the basolateral enterocyte membrane by ferroportin 1. Hephaestin and ceruloplasmin are iron oxidases that convert absorbed Fe2+ to Fe3+, which can now bind to transferrin to be transported to the target sites.

question: Which transporter is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte?

explanationHtml:
Ceruloplasmin is involved in iron metabolism.

Ceruloplasmin and hephaestin help in the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ at the basolateral border of enterocytes. This is coupled with transport through ferroportin. In plasma, iron is transported by transferrin.

question: Which of the following is involved in iron metabolism?

explanationHtml:
Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.

Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.

Transcription of hepcidin is increased by the following factors:

  • Increased levels of iron
  • Inflammatory cytokines

Transcription of hepcidin is decreased by the following factors:

  • Iron deficiency
  • Hypoxia
  • Ineffective erythropoiesis

Hepcidin is encoded by the HAMP gene and its mutations are associated with hereditary hemochromatosis.

Absorption of iron mainly occurs in the proximal duodenum.

This is the reason why celiac disease leads to iron deficiency. Celiac disease causes the most severe damage to the duodenum, which is the primary site for absorbing dietary iron.
question: What is the main site of iron absorption?

correctAnswer: B. Transferrin receptor 1 iron-responsive elements increases transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis
explanationHtml:
In iron deficiency anaemia, there is an increase in transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis.

In iron deficiency, iron regulatory proteins (IRPs), which are the sensors of iron levels, bind to the iron-responsive elements (IREs) in the transferrin receptor-1 (TfR1) mRNA. This binding stabilizes the TfR1 mRNA, preventing its degradation and allowing more TfR1 protein to be produced. More TfR1 protein on the cell surface means the cell can bind more transferrin-bound iron, increasing iron uptake into the cell.

Iron absorbed through the diet or which is released from circulation is bound to transferrin (iron transfer protein). When erythropoiesis is stimulated, iron-transferrin complexes interact with transferrin receptors on the surface of bone marrow erythroid cells. Through receptor-mediated endocytosis, this complex is internalised.

This iron is then made available for heme synthesis while the transferrin-receptor complex is recycled to the surface of the cell, from where the transferrin is released back into circulation and the transferrin receptor re-anchors into the cell membrane. The excess iron after hemoglobin synthesis binds to apoferritin (storage protein), forming ferritin.

Senescent RBCs undergo phagocytosis in the cells of the reticuloendothelial system. The hemoglobin is broken down, the globin and other proteins are returned to the amino acid pool, and the iron is shuttled back to the surface of the reticuloendothelial cell, where it is taken up by transferrin via ferroportin (iron export channel).

There is no regulated excretory pathway for iron, and the only mechanisms by which iron is lost are blood loss (via gastrointestinal bleeding, menstruation, or other forms of bleeding) and the loss of epithelial cells from the skin, gut, and genitourinary tract. The normal daily iron loss from the body is 1-2 mg.

Transferrin receptor synthesis ↑ ↓
Transferrin receptor mRNA concentration ↑ ↓
Iron storage ↓ ↑
Ferritin synthesis ↓ ↑
Ferritin mRNA concentration No change No change

explanationHtml:
Ileal resection for Crohn's disease can cause megaloblastic anaemia due to the decrease in cubulin receptors. They are the vitamin B12 receptors on the ileum.

Absorption of vitamin B12 involves the following steps:

  • Pepsin in the stomach releases vitamin B12 from the binding proteins in the food
  • Released B12 binds to haptocorrin (R-protein), which is a salivary protein
  • In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases release B12 from haptocorrin
  • B12 binds to intrinsic factor to form the IF-B12 complex
  • In the ileum, ileal enterocytes that contain cubulin receptors (IF receptor) endocytose the complex
  • In the ileal cells, B12 is associated with transcobalamin II, which is a carrier protein
  • B12 is delivered to the liver, bone marrow, and GIT

question: A 40-year-old man with a history of bowel resection for Crohn's disease develops megaloblastic anaemia. Which component of the vitamin B12 metabolism is likely to be affected in this patient?

correctAnswer: D. A 23-year-old woman on phenytoin therapy
explanationHtml:
Phenytoin therapy causes folate deficiency leading to megaloblastic anaemia. It does not cause vitamin B12 deficiency.

Dietary folate is in polyglutamate form, which is then converted into monoglutamates by the intestinal conjugase. Phenytoin acts by inhibiting this enzyme, thereby causing folate deficiency, and thus megaloblastic anaemia.

Other options:

question: In which of the following patients would you not suspect megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Skin hyperpigmentation especially on the dorsum of hands involving the knuckles is seen in cyanocobalamin or vitamin B12 deficiency which is a causative factor of megaloblastic anaemia.

In megaloblastic anaemia, there is impairment of DNA synthesis that leads to ineffective hematopoiesis. It also causes distinctive morphologic changes, including abnormally large erythroid precursors and red cells.

Clinical features of megaloblastic anaemia (cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency) include:

System Clinical features
Oral

Glossitis

Angular cheilosis
Gastrointestinal

Anorexia

Weight loss

Diarrhea

Constipation
Skin Hyperpigmentation (reversible)
Hematological

Thrombocytopenia

Leucopenia

Ineffective erythropoiesis and unconjugated jaundice
Cardiovascular

Atherosclerosis leading to PVD, CAD (due to elevated homocysteine)
Neurological (only B12)

Peripheral neuropathy

Subacute combined degeneration (degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord)
Pregnancy (only folate)

Recurrent fetal loss

Neural tube defects
Others

Mild fever in severe cases

Psychiatric disturbances

Peripheral smear findings:

  • Macro-ovalocytes
  • Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.
  • Reticulocyte count is low
  • Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anaemia is severe
  • Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, having five or more nuclear lobules

The image given below shows hypersegmented neutrophils seen in megaloblastic anaemia.

[[figure-1]]

Bone marrow findings:

  • Markedly hypercellular as a result of increased hematopoietic precursors.
  • Sieve-like pattern of chromatin of immature precursors (Megaloblasts)
  • Granulocytic precursors also display dysmaturation in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms
  • Megakaryocytes can be abnormally large and have bizarre, multilobate nuclei
  • The derangement in DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow (ineffective hematopoiesis) and leads to pancytopenia

The reticulocyte count is low in cases of megaloblastic anemia because of ineffective erythropoiesis, where defective red blood cell precursors are destroyed within the bone marrow before they can mature and be released.

explanationHtml:
Type III antibodies are not against haptocorrin. They recognize the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pumps.

Pernicious anaemia is a specific form of megaloblastic anaemia caused by autoimmune gastritis. It impairs the production of intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 uptake from the gut.

Types of antibodies in pernicious anaemia are:

  • Type I antibodies - block the binding of vitamin B12 to intrinsic factor. They are found in both plasma and gastric juice
  • Type II antibodies - prevent binding of the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 (IF-B12) complex to its ileal receptor. They are also found in both plasma and gastric juice
  • Type III antibodies - recognize the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump of parietal cells

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the antibodies of pernicious anaemia?

correctAnswer: B. Anemia can be normocytic and normochromic
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of anaemia of chronic disease (ACD). In this condition, the anaemia initially can be normocytic normochromic. If the chronic inflammation persists for a very long time, the anemia can eventually progress to a microcytic, hypochromic state.

ACD occurs in the setting of persistent systemic inflammation, such as in diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. It is associated with

  • Low serum iron
  • Reduced total iron-binding capacity
  • Abundant stored iron in tissue macrophages

Inflammatory mediators like IL-6 stimulate an increase in the production of hepcidin. This inhibits ferroportin function in the macrophages and reduces the transfer of iron from the storage pool to developing erythroid precursors in the marrow. As a result, erythroid precursors are starved for iron despite the availability of plenty of iron in tissue macrophages.

Also, inflammatory cytokines are believed to suppress erythropoietin production, leading to inadequate proliferation of RBC progenitors.

question: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and chronic fatigue. Physical examination reveals a hard nodule of about 1cm in the prostate. His lab reports reveal low Hb and elevated PSA. Peripheral blood smear shows a normocytic normochromic picture. There are some occasional myelocytes, a few tear-drop cells and 2 nucleated RBCs per 100 white cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given findings are suggestive of pernicious anemia, which is associated with atrophic gastritis and vitamin B12 deficiency.

Anemic patient with a peripheral smear showing macrocytic RBCs and hypersegmented neutrophils are important characteristic features of megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency are the main causes of megaloblastic anemia.

Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies which impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF). This is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The action of each of these include:

  • Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intinsic factor (IF).
  • Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
  • Autoantibody type III acts against the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.

These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.

explanationHtml:
The patient's clinical presentation points to a congenital hemolytic anemia. Enzyme deficiency in the glycolytic pathway can cause hemolysis.

RBCs do not have mitochondria, so they cannot perform aerobic respiration. This leaves anaerobic glycolysis as the only pathway for an RBC to generate the ATP it needs to survive. A congenital deficiency in a glycolytic enzyme, such as pyruvate kinase, leads to ATP depletion. The resulting ATP depletion causes the ion pumps to fail, leading to an influx of water, cell swelling, and loss of membrane integrity. These rigid, fragile cells are easily destroyed as they pass through the narrow capillaries of the spleen, leading to hemolysis.

The following enzyme deficiencies can cause hemolysis:

In the glycolytic pathway:

  • Pyruvate kinase deficiency
  • Hexokinase deficiency

In the HMP shunt pathway:

  • G6PD deficiency
  • Glutathione synthetase deficiency

Note: Orotic aciduria causes megaloblastic anaemia.

explanationHtml:
Reticulocytes are red cell precursors, which are non-nucleated.

They have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA. They can be visualized using supravital stains like methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue, which stain the ribosomal RNA.

Normal reticulocyte count is 0.5–1.5% of total red cells.

Reticulocytosis (increased reticulocytes) indicates effective erythropoiesis i.e. good bone marrow response to anaemia. It is seen in:

  • Hemolytic anaemias
  • Acute blood loss

Reticulocytopenia (decreased reticulocytes) indicates ineffective erythropoiesis i.e. poor bone marrow response to anaemia. It is seen in:

  • Chemotherapy
  • Aplastic anaemia
  • Bone marrow malignancy
  • Anaemia of chronic disease
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia
  • Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency

question: Which of the following statements is false about reticulocytes?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the corrected reticulocyte count is 3.

It is given by the following formula:

Corrected reticulocyte count = Reticulocyte count × (patient's hemoglobin or hematocrit ⁄ standard hemoglobin or hematocrit)

So, in this case, the corrected reticulocyte count = 9× (5/15) = 9/3 = 3

This formula corrects for hemoglobin. It will show you if the patient is making enough reticulocytes for the degree of anemia present. As the hemoglobin drops, reticulocytes increase from the normal range of 0.5–2.0%.

The standard reference range of hemoglobin concentration in females is 12-15 g/dl. Accordingly, in this scenario, the corrected reticulocyte count would range between 3-3.75%. So, the best answer to this question remains option C.

Absolute reticulocyte count is the percentage of red cells that are reticulocytes (normal is about 0.5 – 2.0%). However, it does not reflect the fact that, as the hemoglobin drops, there should be more reticulocytes, percentage-wise (for example, at a hemoglobin of 5, you should have a much higher percentage of reticulocytes than you should at a hemoglobin of 10). To take this into account, we use the corrected reticulocyte count.

Reticulocyte Index = Corrected reticulocyte count/maturation factor

This corrects for the longer life span of prematurely released reticulocytes in the blood, which is a phenomenon of increased red blood cell production.

Hematocrit Maturation factor
≥ 35% 1.0
35% > Hct ≥ 25% 1.5
25% > Hct ≥ 20% 2.0
< 20% 2.5

Types of hemolysis based on location:

  • Intravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs mainly within the blood vessels
  • Extravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs via macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lymph nodes

explanationHtml:
Thalassemia causes extravascular hemolysis.

The red cells in thalassemia usually have membrane defects and inclusions, which make them susceptible to sequestration in the spleen and the eventual extravascular hemolysis.

Causes of intravascular hemolysis:

  • Mechanical injury
    • Trauma caused by cardiac valves
    • Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia (Eg, DIC, TTP, HUS)
    • Repetitive physical trauma
  • Complement fixation (antibody-mediated destruction)
    • Hemolytic disease of the newborn
    • Transfusion reaction
    • Drug-induced
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  • Infections of red blood cells
    • Malaria
    • Babesiosis
  • Exogenous toxic factors - Clostridial sepsis.

  • Hereditary spherocytosis

question: Which of the following does not cause intravascular hemolysis?

explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a disease that results from acquired mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA).

This gene codes for an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of certain membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. It is the only hemolytic anaemia caused by an acquired genetic defect.

PNH blood cells are deficient in 3 GPI-linked proteins that regulate complement activity:

  • Decay Accelerating Factor or CD55
  • Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis or CD59
  • C8-binding protein

CD59, a potent inhibitor of C3 convertase, prevents the spontaneous activation of the alternative complement pathway. Red cells deficient in these GPI-linked factors are abnormally susceptible to lysis or injury by C5b-C9 membrane attack complex of the complement system.

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following pairs of mutation and involved genes describes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

explanationHtml:
All three cell lines, RBCs, WBCs, and platelets are affected in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

PNH occurs from acquired mutations in the gene PIGA which affect GPI-linked proteins. These causative mutations occur in a hematopoietic stem cell. Hence, all of its clonal progeny, i.e., red cells, white cells, and platelets, are deficient in GPI-linked proteins.

Clinical features of PNH include:

  • Intravascular hemoglobinuria - cola-colored urine
  • Pancytopenia + hypercellular bone marrow
  • Thrombosis (if hepatic vein involved → Budd–Chiari syndrome)

LAP score is obtained by assessing the staining intensity in 100 consecutive neutrophils, with each neutrophil scored on a scale of 1–4. Conditions that result in an increase in leukocytes in all stages of maturity will reflect a corresponding increase in LAP.

question: A 23-year-old man with pancytopenia is suspected to have PNH. Which of the following findings is inconsistent with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, Budd-Chiari Syndrome is the most likely cause of death in a patient with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

Thrombosis (particularly venous thrombosis) is the leading cause of disease-related death in patients with PNH. 40% of PNH patients suffer from venous thrombosis, which commonly affects the hepatic, portal, or cerebral veins.

The pathophysiology of thrombosis in PNH is not completely understood, but two main mechanisms may be responsible:

  • Nitric oxide (NO) is absorbed by free hemoglobin (which is released during hemolysis).
  • Endothelial damage caused by the C5-9 membrane attack complex (due to deficiency of CD59).

explanationHtml:
The deficiency of GPI-linked proteins on blood cells is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Cryoglobulinemia is not a complication of this condition.

Thrombosis is the leading cause of disease-related death in individuals with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). About 5% to 10% of patients eventually develop acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndrome.

explanationHtml:
The gold standard for the diagnosis of PNH is flow cytometry. It provides a sensitive means for detecting red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.

Investigations in PNH include:

  • Flow cytometry (gold standard) - deficiency of CD59 and CD55
  • Ham test (acidified serum lysis) - lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH due to complement fixation
  • Bone marrow biopsy -
    • Hypercellularity with erythroid hyperplasia is seen in classical presentations
    • Patients who develop pancytopenia will have hypocellular bone marrow
  • Imaging - to evaluate venous thrombosis

question: What is the gold standard for the diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria). The only curative therapy for this condition is a hematopoietic stem cell transplant. By replacing the defective stem cell, transplant provides a permanent cure, which drugs cannot achieve.

Pancytopenia is seen in this condition. Flow cytometry shows 2 populations of red cells:

  • Marked red in the left lower quadrant - deficient in both CD55 and CD59, characteristic of PNH.
  • Marked black in the right upper quadrant - CD55+ and CD59+ cells from the residual normal hematopoietic cells

Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that can be used in PNH. It prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a and reduces hemolysis.
Immunosuppressive drugs are sometimes beneficial for those with evidence of marrow aplasia.

Note: FDA has approved the following drugs for treatment of adults with PNH:

  • Ravulizumab injection, a long-acting C-5 complement inhibitor
  • Pegcetacoplan, which acts by binding to complement protein C3 and increasing hemoglobin concentration

explanationHtml:
α chains are coded by 4 genes, i.e., two pairs of genes located on chromosome 16.

Other options:

Option A: Free β and γ chains are more soluble than free α chains. They also form more stable homotetramers. Hence, hemolysis and dyserythropoiesis in α thalassemia are less severe when compared to β thalassemia.

Option B: In HbH disease, excess β-globin chains form β4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with α-thalassemia.

Hb Barts has a higher affinity for oxygen. This leads to intrauterine hypoxia, eventually leading to stillbirth.
