explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of extravascular hemolysis (jaundice and splenomegaly) and peripheral smear showing golf ball cells is suggestive of HBH disease. It is a type of α thalassemia where the HbH is composed of tetramers of β chains (β4).

Hb-H disease is one type of alpha-thalassaemia with inactivation of 3 of the 4 alleles. It is more common in the Asian population. It usually manifests in the 1st year of life. It causes acute episodes of hemolysis when triggered by infections or oxidant drugs.

The decreased α chain production leads to a relative excess of β chains. This leads to the formation of HbH which has a high affinity for oxygen. Such RBCs are more prone to oxidation which causes precipitation of HbH to form golf ball inclusion bodies. This leads to increased sequestration and phagocytosis in the spleen.

The given peripheral smear showing spherocytes, along with the history, is suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis. Inheritance of this condition is mainly autosomal dominant.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a structural RBC disorder making the RBCs more spheroid. The RBCs are less deformable and more vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction. This decreases the lifespan of RBCs.
question: A 25-year old man presents with chronic anemia and gall stones. His family history is significant for a similar illness. His peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the mode of the inheritance of the given clinical condition?

explanationHtml:
Ankyrin is the most common protein deficiency associated with hereditary spherocytosis (HS).

The chief protein component of the RBC membrane skeleton is spectrin. It consists of two polypeptide chains, alpha and beta. These dimers associate with actin oligomers. The spectrin–actin skeleton is then connected to the cell membrane by two distinct interactions:

  • Ankyrin and band 4.2 bind spectrin to the transmembrane ion transporter, band 3
  • Protein 4.1 binds the tail of spectrin to the transmembrane protein glycophorin A

Defect in any of the components of the red cell membrane skeleton results in hereditary spherocytosis. The image given below shows the pathogenesis of this condition:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Few one-liners on membrane skeleton -

  • Most abundant integral proteins - glycophorin, band 3
  • Responsible for biconcave shape of RBC - spectrin
  • Most severe deficiency - spectrin
  • Hereditary elliptocytosis is due to deficiency of alpha spectrin
  • Mushroom cells appearance due to deficiency of band 3
  • Never involved in HS - glycophorin

question: The peripheral smear of a patient with anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly shows pincer cells. Which protein deficiency is responsible for this finding?

explanationHtml:
Hemoglobinuria is not seen in hereditary spherocytosis where extravascular hemolysis occurs. It is a feature of intravascular hemolysis. Pigment gallstones, pallor and splenomegaly can be seen in this condition.

Cinical features of extravascular hemolysis include:

  • Anaemia
  • Jaundice
  • Splenomegaly

Causes of extravascular hemolysis:

  • Hereditary spherocytosis
  • Thalassemia
  • Sickle cell anaemia

Note: G6PD deficiency and autoimmune hemolytic anaemia can cause both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.
question: Which of the following features would you least expect to see in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis?

explanationHtml: The life span of affected red cells in hereditary spherocytosis is 10 to 20 days. The normal life span of RBC is 120 days.
question: What is the life span of affected red cells in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?

explanationHtml:
Increased MCHC in hereditary spherocytosis is due to dehydration caused by the loss of K+ and H2O.

MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) is given by the formula hemoglobin / PCV (g/dL). It indicates the amount of hemoglobin per unit volume.

Note:

  • MCV (mean corpuscular volume) is given by the formula PCV / RBC (fL). It denotes the size of the RBCs.
  • MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) is given by the formula hemoglobin / RBC (pg). It quantifies the hemoglobin in the RBCs.
question: In a patient with hereditary spherocytosis, MCHC of 38 g/dL was noted. What could be the probable reason for this finding?

explanationHtml:
Osmotic fragility curve shifts to the right in hereditary spherocytosis.

In hereditary spherocytosis, the cells are spherocytic in normal plasma (0.9% NaCl) and hemolyse readily at higher concentrations than normal discoid red cells do, hence shifting the curve to the right.

Osmotic fragility is the susceptibility of the RBC to rupture under osmotic stress. In hypotonic solutions, RBCs swell to become spherical and eventually hemolyse. In the graph, the x-axis represents the saline concentration, while the y-axis represents the percentage of red cells that have undergone hemolysis. When osmotic fragility is normal, red cells begin to hemolyse at 0.5% saline, with 50% of hemolysis occurring at 0.40-0.42% saline and complete hemolysis occurring at 0.35% saline as represented in the curve.

In thalassemia and sickle cell anemia on the other hand, the cells are resistant to hemolysis and don’t hemolyse unless the concentration of saline is very low, shifting the graph to the left.

[[figure-1]]
question: In the following osmotic fragility curve, A occurs in _________.

explanationHtml:
A hemogram showing pancytopenia and spherocytes on a peripheral smear in a patient with underlying hereditary spherocytosis is suggestive of an aplastic crisis. This clinical scenario is typically triggered by a parvovirus B19 infection.

Parvovirus destroys red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow. This causes a transient arrest of erythropoiesis, called aplastic crisis. While the primary effect is red cell aplasia, a transient pancytopenia can also be observed due to a temporary arrest of general hematopoiesis or virus-associated hemophagocytosis.

The body's immune response clears the virus in one to two weeks. Blood transfusions may be necessary during the acute phases of the disease.

Pancytopenia can be seen in both parvovirus and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infections. However, the classic presentation of acute onset of fever, jaundice, and anemia in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis, is a hallmark of parvovirus B19 infection. This should be clinically distinguished from other causes like EBV infection, which most commonly presents with infectious mononucleosis characterized by generalized lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and pharyngitis.
question:
A 7-year-old girl presents with fever and jaundice for 5 days. On examination, splenomegaly is noted. Her lab reports are given below. What is the likely trigger to have caused this condition?

Hb - 5 g%

WBC - 1000 /mm3

Platelets - 45,000 /mm3

Peripheral smear shows spherocytes

explanationHtml:
Glutamate lies at the 6th position of the beta chain of hemoglobin.

Sickle-cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the sixth codon of β-globin. This leads to the replacement of a glutamate residue with a valine residue.

Note: Standard Biochemical Nomenclature counts from the first amino acid of the mature beta-globin protein. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 6. Genomic Convention (as stated in Harrison 21E) includes the initiating methionine (AUG) from the translation start site, even though it is cleaved off in the mature protein. This shifts the numbering by +1, making Glu6 → Val become Glu7 → Val. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 7.
question: Which amino acid lies at the sixth position of the beta chain of hemoglobin?

explanationHtml:
Solubility can be used to differentiate as HbS is less soluble than HbA. The function, stability and affinity of HbS are similar to that of HbA.

In HbS, glutamic acid, which is a polar amino acid, is replaced by a non-polar amino acid valine at the 6th position. HbS molecules have the tendency to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. This process converts the red cell cytosol from a free-flowing liquid into a viscous gel. This causes a change in the solubility of the hemoglobin.

The major pathologic manifestations of decreased solubility and polymerisation of HbS are chronic hemolysis, microvascular occlusions, and tissue damage.

Note: Standard Biochemical Nomenclature counts from the first amino acid of the mature beta-globin protein. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 6. Genomic Convention (as stated in Harrison 21E) includes the initiating methionine (AUG) from the translation start site, even though it is cleaved off in the mature protein. This shifts the numbering by +1, making Glu6 → Val become Glu7 → Val. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 7.
question: A blood sample is taken from a suspected case of sickle cell anaemia. Which of the following properties can be used to differentiate HbS from HbA?

explanationHtml:
In heterozygotes with sickle-cell trait, about 40% of the hemoglobin is HbS. The rest of hemoglobin (60%) is HbA.

Sickle cell trait is a largely asymptomatic condition characterised by heterozygosity seen for HbS (sickle hemoglobin). As only a fraction of the Hb are HbS, polymerization leading to sickling only occurs in severe and prolonged hypoxia. Offsprings of 2 heterozygotes have a 1 in 4 chance of having sickle cell disease.

In HbSC heterozygotes, HbS is 50% and HbC is 50%.
question: A 35-year-old man was diagnosed to have heterozygous sickle cell trait. What will be the approximate percentage of HbS in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, the heterozygous combination of HbS and HbC causes a more severe form of the disease. Overall severity is more in homozygous HbS.

Severity sequence is HbSS > HbSC > HbSA > HbSF.

In HbC, lysine is substituted for glutamate in the sixth amino acid residue of β-globin. The percentage of HbS is 50% in HbSC red cells and 40% in HbAS cells. Moreover, HbSC cells have a tendency to lose salt and water, leading to dehydration. This process results in an increased intracellular concentration of HbS. As a result, a milder symptomatic sickling disorder variant, termed as HbSC disease is seen in people having both, HbS and HbC.

HbF inhibits the polymerization of HbS even more than HbA. Hence, infants do not become symptomatic until they reach 5 or 6 months of age when the level of HbF normally falls.
question: Patients with which of the following combinations of beta-globin chains tend to have a more severe sickle cell disease?

explanationHtml:
HbC promotes the sickling of RBC, whereas HbF opposes it.

Factors that promote sickling are:

  • Increased MCHC
  • HbC
  • Acidic pH
  • Hypoxia

HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen than other hemoglobins. Hence, high oxygen content prevents sickling. HbF inhibits the polymerization of HbS. So the infants do not become symptomatic until they reach 5 or 6 months of age, when the level of HbF normally falls.
question: In patients with sickle cell anaemia, which of the following factors promote sickling of RBC?

explanationHtml:
The reagent used for the sickling test is sodium metabisulfite. It is an oxygen-consuming reagent, which induces the sickling of red cells in the presence of HbS.

The sickling test is a diagnostic test used to detect the presence of sickle-shaped red blood cells in conditions like sickle cell anemia.
question: Which of the following reagents is used for sickling test?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of sickle cell anaemia. HbS gives protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of the hands and feet is a severe acute inflammatory response seen in sickle cell anaemia. It is caused by vaso-occlusive episodes leading to ischemia and finally infarction of the distal portions of the extremities.

Sickle cells impair the formation of membrane knobs containing a protein made by P. falciparum called PfEMP-1. This decreases the adherence of infected red cells to the endothelium.

Individuals with sickle cell trait are significantly less likely to have severe disease or to die from malaria. It is because of the increased phagocytosis of sickled cells in the spleen, which keeps the parasite load down.

question: A 12-year-old girl presents with fever and severe pain in her hands and feet. There is no history of trauma. Her lab reports reveal Hb to be 8.2 g/dL and peripheral smear as shown below. Which of the following parasitic infections is this condition protective against?

explanationHtml:
The concurrence of sickle cell anaemia and α-thalassemia results in less severe hemolytic anaemia.

Sickle cell anaemia is caused by point mutations in β-globin synthesis, leading to defective HbS synthesis. When these RBCs release oxygen, the HbS polymerises, leading to membrane distortion.

Thalassemia is due to germline mutations causing decreased globin chain synthesis (α or β). Since these diseases have different pathogeneses, they can occur concurrently.

In alpha-thalassemia, the concentration of hemoglobin is decreased. Therefore, the concentration of HbS in sickle cell anaemia is also decreased. Since HbS molecules should be close to each other for polymerization to occur. Since there is a decreased concentration of HbS in alpha-thalassemia, the HbS molecules are far apart. So there is a decreased polymerization of HbS and therefore less severity of the disease.
question: What happens to the severity of hemolytic anaemia in concurrent sickle cell anaemia and α-thalassemia?

explanationHtml:
Aplastic crisis in sickle cell anaemia is caused by parvovirus B19. It is a transient arrest of erythropoiesis, usually triggered by an acute parvovirus infection. Parvovirus infects and kills red cell precursors. It occurs in sickle cell disease and other hemolytic anaemias.

Vaso-occlusive crises (pain crises) are episodes of hypoxic injury and infarction that cause severe pain in the affected region. The most commonly involved sites are the bones, lungs, liver, brain, spleen, and penis. Acute chest syndrome is a type of vaso-occlusive crisis involving the lungs. It typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates. Pulmonary inflammation may cause blood flow to become sluggish and “spleenlike,” leading to sickling and vaso-occlusion.

Sequestration crises occur in children with intact spleens. Massive entrapment of sickle red cells leads to rapid splenic enlargement, hypovolemia, and sometimes shock. Both sequestration crises and acute chest syndrome may be fatal and sometimes require prompt treatment with exchange transfusions.
question: A 23-year-old patient with sickle cell anaemia presents with fever and malaise. IgM ELISA confirms a parvovirus B19 infection. Which of the following crises will you expect to see in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Non-visualisation of the spleen on routine USG is suggestive of autosplenectomy, which is seen in sickle cell anemia. Splenomegaly is seen in thalassemia and hereditary spherocytosis.

In children with sickle cell anaemia, there is moderate splenomegaly. This is due to red pulp congestion caused by the entrapment of sickled red cells. As age advances, chronic erythrostasis produces hypoxic damage and infarcts. By adulthood, the spleen is reduced to a band of fibrous tissue. This process is called autosplenectomy.
question: During USG examination in a patient with hemolytic anemia, the spleen was not visualized. There is no past history of trauma or surgery. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history, suggestive of hemolysis after the antimalarial (primaquine) and Heinz bodies on PBF, points to a diagnosis of G6PD deficiency (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency). It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait.

G6PD is an enzyme belonging to the hexose monophosphate shunt (HMP) pathway. Deficiency of enzymes of this pathway causes hemolysis as the protective ability of RBCs from oxidative stress is impaired.

The image given below shows the Heinz bodies seen on peripheral smear:

question: A 29-year-old African American man receives primaquine chemoprophylaxis before traveling for a business trip. Four days later, he presents with jaundice and dark urine. Laboratory investigations show anemia, reticulocytosis, and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral blood smear shows the presence of Heinz bodies. What is the most likely mode of inheritance of the given clinical condition?

explanationHtml:
The most common trigger for hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is infection. Viral hepatitis, pneumonia, and typhoid are the common infections that trigger hemolysis.

Episodic hemolysis (both intravascular and extravascular) is seen in G6PD deficiency. It is due to exposures that cause oxidative stress. The triggers include:

  • Infections - oxygen-derived free radicals produced by activated leukocytes
  • Drugs
    • Antimalarials - primaquine and chloroquine
    • Sulfonamides
    • Nitrofurantoin
  • Diet - fava bean

question: Which of the following is the most common trigger for hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency?

correctAnswer: D. They do not cause intravascular hemolysis
explanationHtml:
The given peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies, which are dark-stained inclusion bodies in red cells. They can cause intravascular as well as extravascular hemolysis.

In G6PD deficiency, the RBCs are exposed to high levels of oxidants. This causes cross-linking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains. The globin chains become denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These can be detected by supravital staining.

Heinz bodies can damage the membrane sufficiently to cause intravascular hemolysis.

As RBCs with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen, the macrophages pluck out the Heinz bodies. As a result, some of these partially devoured cells retain an abnormal shape, i.e., as if a bite was taken out of them. Such cells are called bite cells. Bite cells are trapped in splenic cords and removed by phagocytes, leading to extravascular hemolysis.

The images given below show Heinz bodies and bite cells seen in G6PD deficiency:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

question: Peripheral smear of a patient with viral hepatitis is given below. Which of the following statements is false about this finding?

explanationHtml:
Acute hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is intravascular. This is marked by anaemia, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria.

These usually begin 2 to 3 days following exposure of G6PD-deficient individuals to environmental triggers and are self-limited and intermittent. Reticulocytosis occurs during the recovery phase. Hence, features related to chronic hemolysis (e.g., splenomegaly, cholelithiasis) are absent.

A patient with G6PD deficiency was suspected to have acute hemolytic episode. Which of the following features would you expect to see in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The peripheral smear shows RBCs with anisopoikilocytosis with polychromasia and many bite cells (arrows) suggestive of G6PD deficiency. This condition is protective against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Malarial parasites preferentially invade RBCs, which are rich in G6PD. G6PD deficiency causes oxidative stress and hemolysis, preferably in the older RBCs. Reticulocytes and young erythrocytes have much higher G6PD activities and are less susceptible to oxidant damage.

P. falciparum can invade erythrocytes of all ages. P. vivax and P. ovale invade reticulocytes (immature erythrocytes) preferentially. Hence, a low G6PD level in older RBC is protective against P. falciparum malaria.

Episodic hemolysis in this condition can be triggered by fava beans, which are a staple in Egyptian cuisine.

question: A 23-year-old food blogger presents with complaints of icterus and abdominal fullness. She returned yesterday from a vacation in Egypt where she tried fava beans. Her peripheral smear is given below. This condition is protective against which of the following malarial parasites?

correctAnswer: D. Hemolysis continues as long as there is exposure to oxidant drugs
explanationHtml:
Hemolysis in G6PD-deficiency anemia does not continue for the entire period that the patient takes the offending drug. It stops after a few days.

Two variants of G6PD, designated as G6PD– and G6PD Mediterranean, cause most of the clinically significant hemolytic anemias. The half-life of G6PD- is moderately reduced, whereas that of G6PD Mediterranean is markedly reduced; hence, the severity of deficiency is greater with the Mediterranean variant. The most common normal variant is G6PD B.

The hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis. The damaged red cells are sequestered in the spleen and killed by macrophages, causing extravascular hemolysis. The oxidative stresses can denature hemoglobin, resulting in intravascular hemolysis.

In individuals with G6PD deficiency, acute intravascular hemolysis begins 2 to 3 days after exposure to oxidants. Only older RBCs are at risk for lysis. The hemolytic episode is self-limited because hemolysis stops when only younger G6PD-replete red cells remain, even if the patient continues to take the offending drug.

Immunohemolytic anaemia is caused by antibodies that cause premature destruction of the red cells. Based on the temperature at which the different types of antibodies bind to the RBCs stably, they are classified as:

  • Warm antibody type - most common
  • Cold agglutinin type
  • Cold hemolysin type

question: What class of antibodies are involved in the most common form of immunohemolytic anaemia?

explanationHtml:
The types of hemolysis seen in the different immunohemolytic anemias are:

Type Hemolysis
Warm antibody Extravascular
Cold agglutinin Extravascular and intravascular
Cold hemolysin Intravascular

Autoimmune hemolytic anemias (AIHA) cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis.

In the warm antibody type, hemolysis is extravascular. IgG-coated red cells are phagocytosed and destroyed in the spleen.

In cold agglutinin type, hemolysis is extravascular and intravascular. In the peripheral vascular bed (low temperature), IgM binds to the red cells. This causes agglutination and complement-fixing. They are unbound when they reach the general circulation. However, the IgM interaction causes deposition of sublytic quantities of C3b. It is an excellent opsonin, which leads to the removal of RBCs by phagocytes in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

Cold hemolysin type is a rare subtype of AIHA. Hemolysis is intravascular. IgG binds to the P blood group antigen on the red cells, which leads to complement-mediated lysis.

Two different mechanisms for drug-induced immune hemolytic anemias are:

Antigenic drugs:

  • Anemia occurs 1-2 weeks after initiation of a large IV dose of the offending drug
  • These drugs bind to the red cell membrane and are recognised by anti-drug antibodies
  • They can cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis
  • E.g., penicillin, cephalosporins, quinidine

Tolerance-breaking drugs:

  • Antibodies are produced against red cell antigens, particularly Rh antigens
  • E.g. alpha-methyl dopa

In paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), antibodies are directed against the P blood group antigen.

PCH is a cold hemolysin type of hemolysis caused by IgG autoantibodies, classically. They are also called Donath-Landsteiner antibodies and are often produced in response to a viral infection. This antibody is a biphasic hemolysin. i.e., the antibody binds to RBC at colder temperatures, but hemolysis occurs at core temperature 37°C.

This can cause substantial, sometimes fatal, intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children following viral infections and usually recover within 1 month.

Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia is most commonly seen with disseminated intravascular coagulation.

It occurs in the following conditions:

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
  • Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)

A common pathogenic feature in these disorders is a microvascular lesion. Deposition of fibrin and platelets results in luminal narrowing. These vascular changes produce shear stresses. These changes mechanically injure the passing red cells, producing schistocytes or helmet cells on the peripheral smear.

Components Value

The steps involved in platelet count are:

I - Filling the pipette

  • Diluting fluid is drawn to mark 1 of the RBC pipette and expelled
  • Blood is aspirated to 0.5 mark of the RBCs diluting pipette
  • Diluting fluid is aspirated to 101 mark
  • Blood and diluting fluid are mixed mechanically for 5 min

II - Filling the counting chamber

  • Allow the counting chamber to stand for 20-30 minutes to allow the platelets to settle.
  • To prevent drying out of the preparation, it should be kept in a moist atmosphere, this is most easily arranged by placing the filled counting chamber in the bottom of a clean Petri dish, alongside which arrange a small piece of cotton wool which has been soaked in water and squeezed out. Petri dish lid is additionally put over the dish.
  • After 20-30minutes, the counting chamber can be removed and carefully transferred to the microscope stage.

III - Counting the number of platelets

  • Focus on the surface of the hemocytometer chamber with a high power dry objective. Dim the light to make the thrombocytes visible, and count all of the thrombocytes in the entire center 1 mm² (erythrocyte counting area) of both sides of the hemocytometer. This gives the number of thrombocytes in 0.2 l of 1: 200 dilution of blood.
  • The number of thrombocytes counted X 1000 = number of thrombocytes/l of undiluted blood.

explanationHtml:
Spontaneous bleeding (non-traumatic) is associated with platelet values below 20,000 platelets/µL.

It most often involves small vessels. The common sites for such hemorrhages are:

  • Skin
  • Mucosa of gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts
  • Intracranial bleeding - most feared site of bleeding

The production of the platelets is regulated by the hormone thrombopoietin produced in the liver. The platelet synthesis is also specifically increased by interleukin 6. The average lifespan of the platelets is 7–10 days. The normal platelet count is 1,50,000 - 4,00,000 /µL.

Controversial - According to Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition, spontaneous bleeding may be seen in patients with <5,000-10,000/µL. There is a lack of consensus among other references. However, this question is in alignment with the 10th edition of Robbin and Cotran’s Pathologic Basis of Disease, which states that a platelet count of <20,000/µL can lead to spontaneous bleeding.
question: A 12-year-old girl with dengue hemorrhagic fever is being monitored by measuring platelet count. Spontaneous bleeding is associated with platelet values below _______ /µL.

correctAnswer: B. Normal platelet count and increased bleeding time
explanationHtml:
Functional platelet disorders have a normal platelet count and increased bleeding time.

Functional platelet disorders refer to conditions where the number of platelets is normal, but their function is defective

Classification of platelet functional disorders:

  • Defect in platelet-vessel wall interaction (disorders of adhesion)
    • Von Willebrand disease - deficiency or defect in plasma vWF
    • Bernard–Soulier syndrome - deficiency or defect in GP Ib IX
  • Defects in platelet-platelet interaction (disorders of aggregation)
    • Congenital afibrinogenemia - deficiency of plasma fibrinogen
    • Glanzmann thrombasthenia - deficiency or defect in GPIIb-IIIa
  • Disorders of platelet secretion and signal transduction
    • Storage pool deficiency - α-Granule deficiency and gamma-Granule deficiency
    • Quebec platelet disorder
    • Chediak–Higashi syndrome
    • Gray platelet syndrome
    • Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome
  • Disorders of platelet coagulation-protein interaction
    • Scott syndrome - a defect in factor Va-Xa interaction on platelets

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding functional platelet disorders?

correctAnswer: A. It is synthesized by hepatocytes
explanationHtml:
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is not synthesized by hepatocytes. They are produced by the endothelial cells of the liver and megakaryocytes. It is also found in:

  • Platelet granules - fewer compared to endothelial cells
  • Endothelial cells within cytoplasmic vesicles called Weibel-Palade bodies
  • Subendothelium - binds to collagen

It mediates the adhesion of platelets to sites of vascular injury (subendothelium). It links the exposed collagen to platelets. It facilitates platelet-to-platelet interaction and also stabilizes the hemostatic plug against shear forces.

It is a carrier protein for factor VIII and also protects it from proteolytic degradation and stabilizes it. The half-life of factor VIII is about 2.4 hours when free and 12 hours when bound to vWF in the circulation.

Since vWF stabilizes factor VIII, a deficiency of vWF gives rise to a secondary decrease in factor VIII levels. This may be reflected by a prolongation of the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) in von Willebrand disease types 1 and 3.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Its deficiency can also cause factor VIII defect

It serves as a carrier for factor VIII

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand disease (vWD). Type 3 vWD is inherited as an autosomal recessive disease.

The characteristics of different subtypes of vWD are:

Subtype

Description

Inheritance

Type 1 is the most common subtype of vWD. In Type 2, vWF is expressed in normal amounts, but missense mutations are present that lead to defective multimer assembly. This type has several subtypes, of which type 2A is the most common.

Laboratory findings in vWD:

  • Prolonged bleeding time
  • Normal platelet count
  • Hess test - positive tourniquet test due to defective platelet adhesion
  • Ristocetin-induced aggregation is defective and diagnostic of this disease
  • Platelet aggregation with ADP, collagen, and thrombin - normal
  • Increased aPTT

Though the synthesis of factor VIII remains normal, the half-life of VIII in plasma decreases due to reduced vWF (carrier) levels. This leads to secondary VIIIC deficiency in plasma. So, the intrinsic pathway of coagulation is affected. Hence, aPTT is increased in these patients.

explanationHtml:

The receptor for vWF, i.e., Ib-IX, is essential for normal platelet adhesion to the subendothelial extracellular matrix. In this condition, there is a deficiency of Gp Ib/ IX. Clinical manifestations include epistaxis, ecchymoses, menorrhagia, gingival bleeding, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

It is an abnormality of platelet GPIIb-IIIa (fibrinogen receptor). Platelets are unable to adhere to each other and to the underlying tissue of the damaged blood vessels. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The symptoms include mucocutaneous bleeding in the neonatal period, menorrhagia, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and gingival hemorrhage.

Types of Glanzmann thrombasthenia include:

  • Type 1: Absence of GPIIb-IIIa
  • Type 2: Reduced surface expression of GPIIb-IIIa/ Essentialis athrombia - clot retraction is normal
  • Type 3: Dysfunction of GPIIb-IIIa

Laboratory features of Glanzmann thrombasthenia:

  • Normal platelet count and morphology
  • Platelet aggregation occurs in response to ristocetin, but not to other agonists (such as ADP, thrombin, collagen or epinephrine)
  • Clot retraction is absent

question: A 1-year-old boy is brought with a history of recurrent impetigo. Physical examination findings are given below. Platelet counts are low and peripheral smear shows abnormally small-sized platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Autoantibodies seen in ITP are most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX. It is a diagnosis of exclusion due to the following findings:

  • Bleeding tendency - petechiae
  • Low platelet count, elevated bleeding time
  • Presence of megathrombocytes in the peripheral smear - a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis
  • Female preponderance
  • Absence of splenomegaly

Note: Prothrombin time (PT) is normal in ITP.
question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with epistaxis, easy bruising and menorrhagia. There is no history of drug intake. Physical examination shows scattered petechiae and a normal-sized spleen. Her lab investigations are given below. Antibodies against which of the following can lead to this condition?

Platelet count - 37,000/μL

Bleeding time - 16 minutes

PT - 13 seconds

aPTT - 30 seconds

explanationHtml:
IgG type of antiplatelet antibodies are mainly seen in chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

Autoantibodies are formed most commonly against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX which can be demonstrated in the plasma or bound to the platelet surface in about 80% of patients.
question: Which class of antiplatelet antibodies are seen in patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura?

explanationHtml:
Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are uncommon in idiopathic (primary) ITP. They are seen in secondary ITP.

Chronic ITP occurs most commonly in adult women younger than 40 years of age. The female-to-male ratio is 3:1. It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction. It is of 2 types:

  • Primary or idiopathic - without any risk factors
  • Secondary - presence of predisposing conditions like SLE, HIV, CLL

Signs of accelerated thrombopoiesis that are seen in this condition are:

  • Megakaryocytes in bone marrow
  • Megathrombocytes (abnormally large platelets) in peripheral blood

The image given below shows 2 megakaryocytes seen in bone marrow aspirate (Wright's stain):

[[figure-1]]

Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood. It occurs with equal frequency in both sexes, mostly after a viral illness. It is a self-limited condition that resolves within 6 months.
question: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed to have idiopathic ITP. Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in her?

explanationHtml:
Systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis can predispose to the development of secondary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

The predisposing conditions of secondary chronic ITP include:

  • Autoimmune conditions

    • Evans syndrome

  • Lymphoproliferative diseases

Terlipressin does not cause drug-induced thrombocytopenia.

Drug-induced thrombocytopenia (DITP) is a condition in which certain drugs cause a decrease in platelet count, often through immune-mediated destruction of platelets.

Drug-induced thrombocytopenia can be caused by:

  • Vancomycin

explanationHtml:

ADAMTS13 is also called vWF metalloprotease, which degrades very high-molecular-weight multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Its deficiency causes accumulation of these multimers in the plasma and promotes platelet activation and aggregation.

TTP is a part of a spectrum of clinical syndromes called thrombotic microangiopathy. They are caused by insults that lead to excessive activation of platelets, which deposit as thrombi in small blood vessels.

Features of TTP include:

  • Fever
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia
  • Transient neurologic deficits
  • Renal failure

question: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of hematuria and melena for 10 days. Laboratory investigations reveal mild thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation tests. Peripheral smear is given below. Which organism is most frequently involved in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome is not associated with a deficiency of CD59.

It is associated with a deficiency of the following components:

  • Complement factor H
  • Membrane cofactor protein (CD46)
  • Complement factor I

These three proteins prevent excessive activation of the alternative complement pathway.

Inherited defects or acquired inhibitory autoantibodies can cause deficiencies of these proteins. The disease may be associated with a remitting, relapsing course.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) are nonimmunogenic causes. Hence, the Coombs test is negative in these conditions.

question: Coombs test is found to be positive in a patient with thrombocytopenia. Which of the following conditions could be a likely cause?

explanationHtml:
Weber–Osler–Rendu syndrome is a disorder of the blood vessels.

It is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations that modulate TGF-β signalling. It is also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

This condition is characterized by dilated, tortuous blood vessels with thin walls that bleed readily. Bleeding is most common in the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis), tongue, mouth, and eyes, and throughout the gastrointestinal tract.

Platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) are normal.

Clinical conditions in which abnormalities of the vessel wall cause bleeding include:

  • Infections - meningococcemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses
  • Collagen defects - Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, scurvy, and Cushing's syndrome
  • Perivascular amyloidosis - most common with amyloid light-chain (AL) amyloidosis
  • Henoch–Schönlein purpura
  • Drug reactions

explanationHtml:

question: What is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario showing hemarthrosis and elevated aPTT is suggestive of hemophilia.

Specific tests for measuring levels of factor VIII and factor IX can determine whether it is hemophilia A or hemophilia B, respectively.

Clinical features of hemophilia:

  • Hemarthroses - joint hemorrhages, later causing progressive deformities
  • Recurrent bleeding
  • Pseudotumour syndrome - fascial hemorrhages that occur as blood-filled cysts with calcification and proliferation of fibroblasts, giving the appearance of a tumor

It is associated with elevated aPTT and normal platelet count, bleeding time, and PT.

Other options:

Option A: In ITP, the platelet count is low, and the bleeding time is prolonged.

Option B: In functional platelet disorders, like Bernard Soulier syndrome, the platelet count is normal, and bleeding time is prolonged.

Option D: In vitamin K deficiency, both PT and aPTT are prolonged. PT is relatively more prolonged than is the aPTT.

question: A 7-year-old boy was found to have excessive bleeding following tooth extraction. Lab investigations revealed prolonged aPTT, decreased serum factor VIII levels and normal VwF activity. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Hemophilia B never affects females
explanationHtml:
Hemophilia A and B mostly affect males, but they can also affect females, although it is rare.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, affecting mainly males and homozygous females. Rarely, excessive bleeding occurs in heterozygous females. It is due to the inactivation of the X chromosome bearing the normal factor VIII allele by chance in most cells (unfavourable lyonization). About 30% of patients have no family history, and the disorder is caused by new mutations.

Hemophilia B is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. There is a deficiency of factor IX.

Hemophilia C is an autosomal recessive condition and hence can occur in females. There is a deficiency of factor XI.

Reptilase is a thrombin agonist which is used to differentiate heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and afibrinogenemia. It is resistant to the action of heparin.

The differential diagnosis for normal platelet count with elevated PT, aPTT and TT are HIT and afibrinogenemia. After adding reptilase, if the TT is corrected, it points to HIT. In afibrinogenemia, since there is an absence of fibrin, there is no change in the TT.

explanationHtml:
Kasabach–Merritt syndrome is associated with DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). This syndrome is characterised by the following features:

  • Rapidly growing vascular tumour
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
  • Consumptive coagulopathy

An unusual form of DIC occurs in association with giant hemangiomas. In this type, stasis and recurrent trauma to the fragile blood vessels cause thrombi to form within the neoplasm.

The image given below shows a reddish-blue lesion covering the lower part of the abdomen. It is a cavernous-capillary haemangioma seen in Kasabach–Merritt syndrome:

[[figure-1]]
question: A 1-year-old child was diagnosed to have Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. What is this condition associated with?

explanationHtml:
Factor XII deficiency will not affect the clotting in vivo.

Unlike the clotting cascade in the lab (in vitro), the cascade in the body (in vivo) differs slightly, as tissue factor (TF) is the major initiator of the cascade. The TF/VIIa complex is the most important activator of factor IX, and the factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X. Factor V is involved in both pathways, as shown in the image below.

The coagulation cascade in the laboratory:

  • Extrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube): Tissue factor → Factor VII → Factor X.
  • Intrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube): Factor XII → Factor XI → Factor IX → Factor X

Laboratory methods to initiate clotting include:

  • Intrinsic pathway - adding phospholipids, calcium, and either a negatively charged substance, such as glass beads
  • Extrinsic pathway - a source of tissue factor

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following clotting factor deficiency will not affect clotting in vivo?

explanationHtml:
Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation.

PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin). This indicates the overall efficiency of the extrinsic clotting system.

Causes of prolonged PT:

  • Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs - vitamin K antagonists
  • Liver disease - obstructive jaundice
  • Vitamin K deficiency
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect (rare)

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) measures the clotting time of plasma after the activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and CaCl2, but without added tissue thromboplastin. It indicates the overall efficiency of the intrinsic pathway.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Liver disease
  • Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
  • Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
  • A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
  • Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII
  • Intake of oral anticoagulant drugs
  • Vitamin K deficiency

explanationHtml:

explanationHtml:
Blood received from the blood bank should be completely transfused within 4 hours of receiving.

Principles of blood administration:

  • All blood products should be given through an appropriate blood administration set containing a filter.
  • A careful aseptic technique should be practised at all times.
  • Vital signs should be documented before and after transfusion and as clinically required. For the first 15 minutes after the infusion has begun, the patient should be kept under close observation to detect any signs of a serious transfusion reaction. If none is observed, the infusion rate may be increased.
  • One unit of red cells is often given in 1 to 4 hours, depending on the amount to be transfused and on the patient’s cardiovascular status. Infusion of a unit for longer than 4 hours is not recommended, as there is a risk of bacterial proliferation because the opened unit is at room temperature.
  • No other solution and no medication should be added to or infused through the same tubing as a blood product.
  • Ringer’s lactate or other solutions containing calcium must never be added to a blood product because the calcium present leads to coagulation.
  • After the transfusion has been completed, the transfusion tag or record should become part of the patient’s chart.

Platelets (unlike red cells) must be stored at room temperature. This is a condition that is favourable for bacterial proliferation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started while waiting for the culture reports.

The blood components that are preferred for the other conditions are:

These antibodies recognize foreign protein red cell antigens in a previously sensitized recipient (through a prior blood transfusion). They present with laboratory features of hemolysis, such as low haptoglobin levels and elevated LDH.

Acute hemolytic reactions are usually caused by preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells that fix complement. The direct Coombs test is usually positive.

correctAnswer: C. Symptoms develop after 2 days of transfusion
explanationHtml:
Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is sudden-onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after the transfusion. It occurs within 6 hours, and not after 2 days following transfusion.

TRALI is a severe, fatal complication of blood transfusion. The incidence of TRALI is low (1 per 10,000 transfusions). However, it may occur more frequently in patients with preexisting lung disease.

The pathogenesis involves a two-hit hypothesis:

  • Priming event - increased sequestration and sensitization of neutrophils in the microvasculature of the lung
  • Second hit - the factor (most commonly MHC class II antigens) present in the transfused blood product activates the primed neutrophils

TRALI can occur in transfusions with all plasma-containing blood products. However, it is more likely to occur following the transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and platelets. This is because these products contain high levels of donor antibodies.

Note: TRALI is important to recognize because donor products that induce complications in one patient are much more likely to do so in a second. Indeed, recent measures to exclude multiparous women from plasma donation have resulted in reduced incidence of TRALI.

question: A patient who was admitted for blood transfusion developed transfusion-related acute lung injury. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

Features of TRALI are:

  • Fever
  • Hypotension
  • Hypoxemia
  • Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates - not responsive to diuretics

Treatment is mainly supportive, and blood transfusions are discontinued. The mortality rate in this condition is 5-10%.

question: A 33-year-old man is receiving massive blood transfusion following a fall from height. 4 hours after transfusion, he becomes breathless and oxygen saturation decreases. Chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO).

TACO is caused by rapid or excessive transfusion of red cell preparations or plasma products. This condition is characterized by:

  • Dyspnea with O2% <90 at room air
  • Bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray
  • Systolic hypertension
  • Elevation of brain natriuretic peptide, 1.5 times that of pre-transfusion levels

It can be prevented by administering the transfusion slowly, at the rate of 1 to 2 ml of blood/kg of body weight per hour. Diuretics are also used if necessary.
question: A CKD patient had to undergo dialysis and his Hb was 5.2gm/dL. So two blood transfusions were to be given. The first bag was completed in 2 hours. FNHTR may occur due to the following:

Note: Luspatercept is an erythroid maturation agent, a receptor fusion protein consisting of a modified extracellular domain of human activin receptor type-2B linked to the human Ig-G1 Fc domain. The drug was recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of transfusion-dependent thalassemia.
question: A patient who receives recurrent transfusions for thalassemia develops fever and chills during this time. There is no evidence of hemolysis. Which of the following measures can decrease the rate of transfusion reactions?

explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is not a preleukemic condition.

Pre-leukemic conditions are disorders that carry a risk of transformation into acute leukemia.

It is an autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to IgG autoantibodies that bind to the P blood group antigen and cause intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children and show recovery within a month.

Other options:

Option A: Few patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) develop acute non-lymphocytic leukemia. This is thought to arise from the injured marrow as a secondary hematopoietic disorder.

Option B: Bone marrow aplasia preceding acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a rare condition that usually affects children. It generally follows the recovery of normal blood counts and most commonly occurs within 6 months of the onset of aplasia.

Option C: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 10% to 40% of individuals with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). It is usually accompanied by the appearance of additional cytogenetic abnormalities.

question: A 10-year-old boy with fever, weight loss came to the hospital. On examination, he was pale and had significant lymphadenopathy. The bone marrow histology of the person is as given below. Your diagnosis is?

Clinical features of ALL include:

  • Bone marrow failure - anemia, fever, infections, bleeding
  • Mass effects due to neoplastic infiltration - bone pain, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and testicular enlargement
  • CNS manifestations - headache, vomiting, and nerve palsies

question: An adolescent male patient presents with fatigue. His total leucocyte count is 138 x 10^9 / L with 80% blasts on the peripheral smear. Chest X-ray shows a large mediastinal mass. The bone marrow aspirate is as shown below. What would the immunophenotyping of this patient’s blasts most likely demonstrate?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) based on immunophenotyping.

CD10 and CD19 are markers for the B-cell lineage, and this patient most probably has B-ALL. Although CD13 and CD33 are myeloid antigens, their expression does not exclude the diagnosis of B-ALL.

Option B: The diagnosis of mixed phenotypic acute leukemia (MPAL)/ acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage (ALAL) (previously known as biphenotypic leukemia) requires a demonstration of multiple lineages in blast cells. According to the WHO's latest update (2022), the requirements for assigning more than one lineage to blast cells are :

B cell lineage
  • CD19 strong:

    ≥1 expressed CD10, CD22, CD79a

  • CD 19 weak:

    ≥ 2 or more strongly expressed CD10, CD22, CD79a
T cell lineage CD3 positive
Myeloid lineage

Myeloperoxidase (MPO)

OR

Monocyte differentiation (non-specific esterase, CD11c, CD14, CD64, lysozyme)

In the absence of MPO or evidence of monocytic differentiation, expression of CD13 and CD33 is not sufficient for a diagnosis of MPAL. Hence, biphenotypic leukemia is not the answer here.

Myeloid proliferations of Down's syndrome are usually megakaryoblastic. It includes:

  • Transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM) - occurs at birth or within days of birth and resolves in 1 to 2 months
  • Myeloid leukemia associated with Down syndrome - occurs later, but usually in the first 3 years of life.

question: What is the most common subtype of acute myeloid leukemia seen in patients with Down's syndrome?

explanationHtml:

AML is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. It occurs at all ages, but the incidence rises throughout life, peaking after 60 years of age.

The peripheral smear shows blasts with abundant cytoplasm, fine azurophilic granules, Auer rods, and delicate nuclear chromatin with 1-4 prominent nucleoli. The blasts are positive for CD33. Occasionally, blasts are absent from the blood (aleukemic leukemia). Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukemia in pancytopenic patients.

question: Peripheral smear of a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia shows myeloblasts with the following finding. What are these made of?

question:

  2. Acute monocytic leukemia
  3. Myelodysplasia

explanationHtml:
The given cell shows multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell, resembling a bundle of sticks. Such cells have been termed as faggot cells (faggot in French means bundle of sticks).

Since the question specifically asks about the cell, the best answer is faggot cell (not Auer rods).

Other options:

Option A: Auer rods are distinctive needle-like azurophilic granules present in many cases but particularly numerous in AML with the t(15;17) aberration (acute promyelocytic leukemia).

Option B: The term flaming promyelocyte refers to cells that appear to be breaking apart, taking on a vibrant reddish-purple hue with the apparent liberation of granules into the surrounding cellular matrix.

Option D: Promyelocytes containing fine granules appear dusky or hazy and are referred to as dusky promyelocytes.
question: A 20-year-old male patient is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. The peripheral blood smear picture is given in the image. The cell indicated by the arrow is best described as:

question: Bone marrow aspirate of a patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia shows the presence of faggot cells. What is the most likely subtype of acute myeloid leukemia that the patient is suffering from?

explanationHtml:
The patient shows features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). It is most likely to be associated with acute myeloid leukemia - M3 or acute promyelocytic leukemia. The pathogenesis behind this is t(15,17) or PML-RARA fusion gene.

Other options:

question:
A patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia presents with a one-day history of bleeding gums, subconjunctival bleed, and purpuric rash. Investigations done are given below. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely to be detected?

explanationHtml:
AML M0 is negative for myeloperoxidase (MPO). AML-M5 (monocytic), AML-M6 (erythroid), and AML-M7 (megakaryocytic) are also negative for MPO.

Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is located in the primary granules of neutrophils and their precursors, in eosinophil granules, and in the azurophilic granules of monocytes.

The most primitive myeloblasts are negative, with granular positivity appearing progressively as they mature toward the promyelocyte stage. Promyelocytes and myelocytes are the most strongly staining cells in the granulocyte series. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive.

AML-M4 shows both myelocytic and monocytic differentiation. Hence, it shows both MPO and non-specific esterase (marker for monocytes) positivity.
question: Which type of acute myeloid leukemia is myeloperoxidase-negative?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with myeloblasts that stain positive for CD61 is suggestive of acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AML-M7).

AML M7 is the least common type of AML. Blasts of megakaryocytic lineage predominate and are associated with marrow fibrosis. There is also frequent budding of cytoplasmic margins.

They are CD41+ and CD61+. They stain negatively with Sudan black B (SBB) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). Blasts are reactive with PAS and acid phosphatase.

The prognosis for this type of acute leukemia is poor.
question: A patient with fatigue and recurrent infections undergoes bone marrow evaluation. It shows > 20% myeloblasts, which stain positive for CD61. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows leukemia cutis. It is seen in acute myeloid leukemia - M4 and acute myeloid leukemia - M5. It refers to leukemic cells infiltrating the skin.

All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML), which is associated with the PML-RARA fusion gene.

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) is associated with a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17, producing a PML-RARA fusion gene. This fusion gene encodes for a chimeric protein, which consists of a part of the PML protein and a part of the retinoic acid receptor-α (RARα).

The normal RARα binds to the DNA and activates the transcription in the presence of retinoids. However, the chimeric protein produced by PML-RARA has reduced affinity for retinoids. This causes inhibition of transcription, thereby preventing gene expression for cellular differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of myeloid progenitor cells.

The condition is treated with all-trans retinoic acid. It binds to the PML-RARA chimeric protein. This causes conformational change such that the protein regains its normal function and activates DNA transcription.

The peripheral smear shows smudge cells and increased lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm, round to slightly irregular nuclei containing clumped chromatin. This large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes is often described as a "convent-girl" appearance.

[[figure-1]]

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) / Small lymphocytic lymphoma(SLL) is the most common leukemia among adults in the Western world.

The differentiating point between CLL and SLL is that in CLL, the absolute lymphocyte count is >5000 per mm³, and in SLL, it is <5000 per mm³.

It is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are typically seen.

  • Total blood count:
    • The total leukocyte count is highly variable; leukopenia is typically seen when the marrow is involved.
    • Hypogammaglobulinemia is common and contributes to increased susceptibility to infections.
    • 10% to 15% of patients develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by nonneoplastic B cells.
  • Peripheral smear:
    • Predominantly shows small lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm
    • Smudge cells, basket cells, or parachute cells - artifacts of the lymphocytes that are disrupted during the process of making smears.
    • Contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.
    • Spherocytes (due to coexisting autoimmune hemolytic anemia) and nucleated RBCs (due to premature release of progenitors in the face of severe anemia, marrow infiltration by the tumor, or both)
  • Lymph node biopsy:
    • Diffuse effacement composed of small lymphocytes admixed with variable numbers of larger activated lymphocytes that often gather in loose aggregates
    • Referred to as proliferation centers, which contain mitotically active cells. Proliferation centers are pathognomonic for CLL / SLL.

The chromosomal defects:

  • Deletion of 11q
  • Trisomy 12q
  • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis).
