B-cell lymphoma results in malignant proliferation within the lymph node, not follicular hyperplasia.

Follicular hyperplasia is a benign condition caused by stimuli that activate humoral immune responses. It may occur in:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Toxoplasmosis
  • Early stages of HIV infection

It is defined by the presence of large oblong germinal centres (secondary follicles), which are surrounded by a collar of small, resting naive B cells (mantle zone).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following does not cause follicular hyperplasia of the lymph nodes?

correctAnswer: C. No variation in shape and size of the follicles
explanationHtml:
In reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, there is marked variation in the shape and size of follicles.

Features favoring reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, which are absent in neoplastic follicles are:

  • Preservation of the lymph node architecture, including the interfollicular T-cell zones and the sinusoids
  • Follicles are enlarged and show variation in shape and size
  • Presence of numerous mitotic figures
  • Phagocytic macrophages (called tingible body macrophages) are numerous
  • Recognizable light (germinal center) and dark (mantle zone) zones

options.text: No variation in shape and size of the follicles

question: Which of the following is not a feature of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia?

explanationHtml:
Tingible-body macrophages are found in lymph nodes.

A tingible-body macrophage is a type of macrophage predominantly found in germinal centers containing many phagocytosed apoptotic cell debris. This debris is referred to as tingible bodies (tingible meaning stainable). The presence of these macrophages suggests non-neoplastic reactive hyperplasia of the lymph node, or can be seen as the stars in the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: In which of the following organs are tingible body macrophages found?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. Acute viral infections, like infectious mononucleosis, produce paracortical hyperplasia.

There are three types of lymph node hyperplasia. They are:

  • Follicular hyperplasia
  • Paracortical hyperplasia
  • Sinus histiocytosis (reticular hyperplasia)

Paracortical hyperplasia is seen in the T-cell-containing paracortical region of the lymph node. It is caused by stimuli that trigger T-cell–mediated immune responses. The involved regions typically contain:

  • Immunoblasts
  • Activated T-cells 3-4 times the size of resting lymphocytes t
    • Round nuclei
    • Open chromatin
    • Several prominent nucleoli
    • Moderate amounts of pale cytoplasm
  • Hypertrophy of sinusoidal and vascular endothelial cells, with infiltrating macrophages and eosinophils
question: A 16-year-old boy presented with complaints of fever, sore throat, and enlarged lymph nodes. Paul Bunnell's test was done and found to be positive. What type of lymphoid hyperplasia is seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
In the case of lymph node metastases, there is prominent reticular hyperplasia.

Reticular hyperplasia or sinus histiocytosis refers to an increase in the number and size of the cells that line lymphatic sinusoids. Although nonspecific, this form of hyperplasia may be particularly prominent in lymph nodes draining cancers such as carcinoma of the breast.

The lining lymphatic endothelial cells are markedly hypertrophied and macrophages are greatly increased in numbers, resulting in the expansion and distension of the sinuses.

The image given below shows reticular hyperplasia in the lymph node.

[[figure-1]]
question: In patients with breast cancer with lymph node metastases, which of the following changes is seen in affected lymph nodes?

correctAnswer: D. Hemophagocytosis seen in bone marrow is sufficient for diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Bone marrow examination may show hemophagocytosis, but it is not required for the diagnosis of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).

HLH is a reactive condition also known as macrophage-activation syndrome. The common feature of all forms of HLH is the systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T-cells.

An infection, especially with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), is the most common trigger for Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). It is characterized by acute febrile illness associated with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and cytopenias.

options.text: There is systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T cells
The most common trigger is infection with Epstein-Barr virus
It presents as an acute febrile illness with hepatosplenomegaly
Hemophagocytosis seen in bone marrow is sufficient for diagnosis

question: Which of the following statements about hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is false?

explanationHtml:
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is associated with very high serum ferritin levels.

Laboratory findings in HLH include:

  • Anemia
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • High serum ferritin
  • High plasma IL2 receptor levels
  • Elevated liver enzyme levels
  • High triglyceride levels
  • Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
question: Which of the following is not a feature in patients with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis?

explanationHtml:
Vascular injury results in intimal thickening due to smooth muscle proliferation.

Vascular injury stimulates the migration of smooth muscle cells of the tunica media to the tunica intima. These smooth muscle cells proliferate and also synthesize extracellular matrix, leading to intimal thickening. This is the stereotypical response of the vessel wall to an injury, regardless of the cause of injury.

The image below shows intimal thickening occurring in response to vascular injury:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Endothelial cell hyperplasia is a benign reactive process that usually occurs, causing Intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia, also known as Masson tumour.

Option C & D: Thickening of the basement membrane and deposition of hyaline material are characteristic features of diabetic microangiopathic changes.
question: Vascular injury causes intimal thickening by which of the following mechanisms?

explanationHtml:
Endothelial dysfunction is not implicated in aneurysm formation. An aneurysm occurs due to the pathology of connective tissue within the vascular wall.

Endothelial dysfunction is the pathological alteration of the endothelium such that it becomes pro-inflammatory and prothrombogenic. It is caused by various injuries to endothelial cells:

  • Hemodynamic stresses - responsible for vascular pathology in hypertension.
  • Lipid products - leading to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.
  • Advanced glycation end-products (AGE) - responsible for diabetic microangiopathy.
  • Viruses, bacterial products, cytokines, and complement components.
question: Endothelial dysfunction is implicated in all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
The given image shows arteriosclerosis and calcification in the tunica media, that does not encroach on the vessel lumen. This is suggestive of Monckeberg's medial sclerosis.

Monckeberg's medial sclerosis affects medium-sized muscular arteries and is characterized by calcification of the medial walls of the affected arteries. Adults aged over 50 years are usually affected.

[[figure-1]]

Arteriosclerosis refers to the thickening of the arterial wall and loss of elasticity. There are four patterns of arteriosclerosis:

  • Small vessel arteriosclerosis - involves small arteries and arterioles
    • It has two variants - hyaline arteriosclerosis, and hyperplastic arteriosclerosis
  • Monckeberg medial sclerosis - involves calcification of the walls of muscular arteries
  • Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia- usually a healing response to inflammation (eg: arteritis) or mechanical injury (eg: stent insertion)
  • Atherosclerosis - mainly involves elastic and muscular arteries
question: Identify the condition:

correctAnswer: A. It involves the internal elastic lamina
explanationHtml:
The given radiograph shows extensive calcification of the femoral arteries which is suggestive of Monckeberg medial sclerosis. It is characterized by the calcification of the walls of muscular arteries, typically starting along the internal elastic lamina and involves the media of the arteries.

It occurs in people aged 50 years and above as a part of senile degeneration. It is not associated with hypertension or diabetes. It is usually an incidental finding.

options.text: It involves the internal elastic lamina
It involves the external elastic lamina

question: The following incidental finding is seen on a radiograph of a 60-year-old man. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hypertension results in hyaline arteriolosclerosis of the small vessels.

Hypertension leads to a variety of vascular pathologies. In small blood vessels, hypertension may lead to arteriosclerosis, which is the thickening of the vessel wall. It has two variants, which are hyaline arteriosclerosis and hyperplastic arteriosclerosis.

In large and medium-sized arteries, hypertension leads to degenerative changes in the vessel walls, leading to:

  • Dissection
  • Aneurysm formation
  • Cerebrovascular hemorrhage
  • Acceleration of atherosclerosis
question: Which of the following pathological changes occurs in the small vessels of patients suffering from hypertension?

explanationHtml:
The arteriolar wall thickening in hyaline arteriosclerosis occurs as a result of plasma protein deposition.

Hyaline arteriosclerosis occurs due to injury to the endothelial cells. This allows plasma protein leakage into the arteriolar wall. The endothelial injury also stimulates increased matrix synthesis by the smooth muscle cells. These lead to the deposition of homogenous pink hyaline material, causing the thickening of arteriolar walls.

Other options:

Option B: Immune complex deposition is seen in fibrinoid necrosis, where plasma proteins leak out together and form a pink and amorphous appearance.

Option C: Amyloid deposition is due to abnormal folding of proteins, which aggregate and deposit as fibrils in extracellular tissue.

Option D: Vascular injury stimulates the migration of smooth muscle cells of the tunica media to the tunica intima. These smooth muscle cells proliferate to cause intimal thickening.
question: Which of the following is responsible for arteriolar wall thickening in hyaline arteriosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows hyaline arteriosclerosis, which is less likely to be seen in severe hypertension.

Severe hypertension presents with hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, where the vessels exhibit concentric, laminated thickening of the walls with luminal narrowing. The characteristic onion skin appearance can be seen in the image below:

[[figure-1]]

Hyaline arteriolosclerosis refers to arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity associated with plasma protein leakage and smooth muscle cell matrix synthesis in response to chronic hemodynamic pressures.

It occurs in the following conditions:

  • Elderly patients who are normotensive
  • Benign hypertension: due to chronic hemodynamic stresses
  • Diabetes mellitus: due to hyperglycemia-induced endothelial dysfunction

Hyaline arteriosclerosis with a narrowed lumen can be visualized below:

[[figure-2]]
question: A pathology resident is studying a vascular biopsy sample. This vascular lesion is less likely seen in which of the following conditions

explanationHtml:
The given image shows hyperplastic arteriosclerosis, as noted by the onion-skin appearance of the arteriole. This is seen in malignant nephrosclerosis.

Nephrosclerosis is caused by sclerosis of the small arteries and the arterioles of the kidney, leading to diffuse impairment of renal blood supply. It is of 2 types:

Benign nephrosclerosis Malignant nephrosclerosis
Seen in benign hypertension Seen in malignant hypertension
Causes hyaline arteriosclerosis Causes hyperplastic arteriosclerosis and fibrinoid necrosis of the arterioles.

The features of malignant nephrosclerosis can be visualized below:

[[figure-1]]

The characteristic flea-bitten appearance of the kidney is seen in malignant nephrosclerosis (shown below). This is due to small petechial hemorrhages resulting from the rupture of arterioles.

[[figure-2]]
question: The renal biopsy of a 50-year-old chronic hypertensive patient is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing occlusion of the left circumflex coronary artery are suggestive of atherosclerosis. It progresses in the following sequence:

  1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction
  2. Accumulation of lipoproteins in the vessel wall
  3. Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium
  4. Platelet adhesion
  5. Factor release from activated platelets, macrophages, and vascular wall cells
  6. Smooth muscle cell proliferation, extracellular matrix production, and recruitment of T cells
  7. Lipid accumulation both extracellularly and within cells
  8. Calcification of the extracellular matrix and necrotic debris late in the pathogenesis

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. The two most important causes of endothelial injury leading to atherosclerosis are hemodynamic disturbances and hypercholesterolemia.

The images below show partial occlusion of the left circumflex coronary artery and arterial wall changes in response to endothelial injury:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question:
A 65-year-old man presented with chest pain. Past history is significant for dyslipidemia and an ischemic stroke 2 years ago. Coronary angiography was performed and showed the following. What is the correct sequence of events leading to this condition?

  1. Platelet adhesion
  2. Accumulation of lipoproteins in vessel wall
  3. Endothelial injury and dysfunction
  4. Monocyte adhesion to endothelium

explanationHtml:
The most important independent non-modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis is family history.

The familial predisposition to atherosclerosis is usually polygenic. It is related to the familial clustering of other established risk factors, such as hypertension or diabetes. It may also be due to inherited variations in pathophysiologic processes such as inflammation.

Hyperlipidemia (specifically hypercholesterolemia) is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis. Even in the absence of other risk factors, hypercholesterolemia is sufficient to initiate lesion development.

The following pearl describes the risk factors for atherosclerosis:
question: What is the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common site of atherosclerosis is the lower abdominal aorta.

In descending order, the most extensively involved vessels in atherosclerosis are:

  • Lower abdominal aorta
  • Coronary arteries
  • Popliteal arteries
  • Internal carotid arteries
  • Arteries of the circle of Willis
question: Which of the following is the most common site of atherosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The above image shows yellow spots on the inner surface of the aorta, which represent fatty streaks. They indicate a collection of foamy macrophages in the intima of the vessel wall.

Although not always indicative of atherosclerosis, presence of fatty streaks has been seen in the aorta of infants, virtually all adolescents, and even individuals without known risk factors. Eventually, some of them may develop into atheromatous plaques later in life by smooth muscle proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition.

The following image shows ruptured atheromatous plaques of the aorta:

[[figure-1]]
question: The autopsy of a 14-year-old boy who died in a motor vehicle accident showed the following lesions on the inner surface of the aorta. What do these lesions indicate?

explanationHtml:
The cells marked in the image above are the foam cells in atheromatous plaques. They refer to lipid-laden monocytes/macrophages or smooth muscle cells within the plaques.

These cells ingest lipoproteins accumulated within the intima of the vessel wall. Since these lipoproteins are modified due to the action of inflammatory mediators, they cannot be degraded further within these cells. This leads to the accumulation of modified lipids within these cells, converting them to foam cells.
question: Where are the following cells in an atheromatous plaque derived from?

explanationHtml:
T-cells and macrophages are in abundance in the shoulder of an atheromatous plaque.

Structure of an atherosclerotic plaque:

  • Superficial fibrous cap - made up of smooth muscle cells and connective tissue, especially collagen. It also contains macrophages, foam cells, and lymphocytes. It determines the stability of plaque.
  • Necrotic core - contains lipid (cholesterol and cholesterol esters), debris from dead cells, calcium, and foam cells.
  • Shoulder - a more cellular area containing macrophages, T-cells, and smooth muscle cells.
  • Periphery - shows neovascularization/proliferation of small blood vessels.

The image below shows the structure of an atherosclerotic plaque:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: In which part of the atheromatous plaque are the T-cells and macrophages in abundance?

explanationHtml:
A stable atherosclerotic plaque has abundant smooth muscle cells.

These cells synthesize collagen, which stabilizes the plaque. Both these features contribute to a thick fibrous cap that prevents the easy rupture of a plaque.

Stable plaque Vulnerable plaque
Dense collagen Less collagen
Thick fibrous cap Thin fibrous cap
Minimal inflammation Increased inflammation
Less extracellular lipid Abundant extracellular lipid
Abundant smooth muscle cells A few smooth muscle cells
Few foam cells Abundant foam cells
question: Which of the following is true regarding a stable atherosclerotic plaque?

explanationHtml:
The patient is likely to have atherosclerosis. Dissection is associated with hypertension.

An atherosclerotic plaque may undergo pathological changes such as:

  • Thrombus formation - due to rupture, ulceration, erosion
  • Increase in plaque size - due to hemorrhage into the plaque

These consequences occlude the lumen of the vessel and impair the blood supply. Impaired blood supply may lead to claudication, ischemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, or even gangrene.

The thrombus may dislodge and cause an embolism. Atherosclerotic debris released due to plaque rupture may produce microemboli, known as atheroembolism.

Atherosclerotic plaques also cause ischemic atrophy of the underlying media. This causes weakness of the vessel wall, leading to aneurysm formation.

The image below depicts the late complications of atherosclerosis:

[[figure-1]]
question: In a 50-year-old normotensive patient with a 10-year history of dyslipidemia, which of the following complications is he at the least risk of developing?

explanationHtml:
This symptomatic patient likely has >70% occlusion of his coronary arteries. This is known as critical stenosis.

It refers to the stage at which the occlusion is sufficiently severe to produce tissue ischemia. This leads to clinical manifestations of ischemia, such as:

  • Stable angina
  • Bowel ischemia
  • Intermittent claudication
question: A patient with anginal chest pain is planned for coronary angiography. What level of stenosis would you expect to see in the affected artery?

explanationHtml:
Elevated plasminogen levels are not associated with stroke. Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of plasmin, which is responsible for fibrinolysis. Elevated levels of the following are predictors of stroke:

  • C-reactive protein is an acute phase reactant that also indicates risk for Myocardial infarction(MI), peripheral arterial disease(PAD), and is used to monitor the effectiveness of risk reduction measures like exercise and weight loss.
  • Homocysteine is responsible for endothelial injury and has prothrombotic effects and correlates with cerebral infarction, MI, PAD, venous thrombosis, and premature vascular disease.
  • Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 limits fibrinolysis and acts as a marker of hemostatic and/or fibrinolytic function, and also predicts risk of MI.
question: Elevated levels of which of the following is not a predictor for stroke?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of an early failure of a small-diameter venous graft (≤8 mm). The likely mechanism for graft failure within the 1st month is acute thrombosis.

Based on the diameter of the synthetic or autologous vascular graft, it can be classified as:

  • Large diameter graft (12-18mm) -
    • Used in high-flow locations such as the aorta
  • Small diameter graft (≤8 mm) -
    • Includes the saphenous vein or left internal mammary artery
    • Used in coronary bypass surgeries

Other options:

Option A, B and D: Atherosclerotic plaque, neointimal hyperplasia and aneurysms are all late complications of graft failure taking months or years to manifest.
question: A patient presented with symptoms of heart failure. He had undergone a coronary bypass procedure with a small-diameter graft 3 weeks ago.  What is the likely cause for his presentation?

correctAnswer: B. Turns on inflammatory gene transcription
explanationHtml:
Kruppel-like factor-2 (KLF-2) is responsible for turning off the inflammatory gene transcription.

KLF-2 production is induced by laminar blood flow, which is seen in normal endothelium. This transcription factor activates the atheroprotective genes and turns off inflammatory gene transcription. Statins upregulate KLF-2 expression in endothelial cells, and this activity is associated with an anti-inflammatory phenotype.

Up-regulation of the KLF-2 gene expression may be a novel strategy for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

options.text: Production is induced by laminar blood flow
Responsible for the atheroprotective role of statins

question: Which of the following is false regarding the KLF-2 transcription factor?

explanationHtml:
Pulsating hematoma is associated with a false aneurysm. It is also known as a pseudoaneurysm, and is caused by a defect in the vascular wall leading to extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space.

An aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart. There are 2 types:

  • True aneurysm
    • Due to a weakened and thinned, but intact, arterial wall
  • False aneurysm
    • Due to a defect in the vascular wall
    • Results in an extravascular hematoma that communicates with the intravascular space
    • Causes transmission of arterial pulsations to the hematoma (pulsating hematoma)

Saccular aneurysm are spherical outpouchings involving a portion of the vessel wall. They are the most common type of intracranial aneurysm (also known as berry aneurysms) and cause spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Dissection occurs when blood enters a defect in the arterial wall and tunnels/dissects between its layers.

False aneurysm Dissection
Defect across all the layers of the vessel wall Defect is usually an intimal tear

Hematoma is extravascular (outside the vessel wall)

 Hematoma is within the layers of the vessel wall
Hematoma is lined by extravascular connective tissue Hematoma is lined by the layers of the vessel wall

Fusiform aneurysm involve diffuse, circumferential dilation of a long vascular segment, usually involving extensive portions of the aortic arch, abdominal aorta, or the iliac arteries.

The image below shows a pseudo/false aneurysm of the left ventricle:

[[figure-1]]
question: Pulsating hematoma is associated with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in a hypertensive patient. It may occur due to the rupture of Berry aneurysms, which are saccular aneurysms.

Other options:

Option B: Fusiform aneurysms are diffuse, circumferential dilations involving long vascular segments and usually involve extensive portions of the aortic arch, abdominal aorta, or the iliac arteries.

Option C: False aneurysm, also known as pseudoaneurysm, is a defect in the vascular wall leading to extravascular hematoma that freely communicates with the intravascular space.

Option D: A Dissecting aneurysm is produced when a dissection leads to an aneurysm.

The image below shows the CT appearance of a SAH:

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient presented with a severe headache and transient loss of consciousness. On examination, neck rigidity was present and blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg. A CT brain was done as shown below.  Which type of aneurysm could have been involved in causing this condition?

explanationHtml:
The likely underlying pathophysiology causing abdominal aortic aneurysm is increased metalloproteinase expression, which degrades the extracellular matrix and weakens the vessel wall.

The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are atherosclerosis and hypertension. Aneurysms that occur as a consequence of atherosclerosis most commonly occur in the abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries.

Other options:

Option A: Obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum occurs in late-stage syphilis and can contribute to aneurysms.

Option D: Medial hypertrophy of vasa vasorum occurs in hypertension, which is associated most commonly with ascending aortic aneurysms.
question: A patient who is a known case of hypertension was diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is the likely underlying pathophysiology causing this condition?

explanationHtml:
Cystic medial degeneration leading to aneurysms is a feature of Marfan syndrome.

Cystic medial degeneration refers to the degenerative changes in the media of the vessel wall that lead to aneurysm formation. These include:

  • Loss of smooth muscle cells
  • Loss of elastic fibers
  • Inadequate extracellular matrix synthesis
  • Increased production of glycosaminoglycan

It can be caused due to:

  • Medial ischemia - atherosclerosis, hypertension
  • Defective connective tissue - Marfan syndrome, scurvy

The image below (Movat stain) shows a cross-section of the aortic media from a patient with Marfan's syndrome showing elastin fragmentation (stained black) and loss of smooth muscle cells (cells stained red and nuclei stained violet):

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option B: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 9q13. It is commonly associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which mainly contributes to mortality

Option C: Down syndrome is due to trisomy 21 and is associated with congenital heart diseases most commonly atrioventricular septal defects and tetralogy of fallot.

Option D: Kawasaki syndrome causes medium sized vessel arteritis and is associated with coronary artery involvement causing myocardial infarction.
question: Arterial aneurysms due to underlying cystic medial degeneration are seen in patients with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Loeys–Dietz syndrome leads to aneurysm formation due to defective elastin (due to a defect in the TGF-β signalling pathway).

Aneurysms are caused due to structural or functional defects in the connective tissue of the vascular wall. The following conditions cause intrinsic defects in connective tissue, leading to aneurysm formation:

Syndrome Defect in
Loeys–Dietz syndrome Synthesis of elastin and collagens I and III
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome Synthesis of type III collagen in some subtypes
Marfan syndrome Synthesis of the protein fibrillin causes weakening of the elastic tissue
Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) Hydroxylation of procollagen
question: Which of the following causes aneurysm formation due to defective elastin?

explanationHtml:
Syphilitic aneurysms most commonly involve the ascending aorta.

Late-stage syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the aorta. This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media, resulting in aneurysmal dilation.

Other options:

Option B: Circle of Willis is generally affected by saccular or berry aneurysm, which occur sporadically and may have a genetic component.

Option C & D: Iliac artery and abdominal artery aneurysms usually occur as a consequence of atherosclerosis.
question: What is the most common site of syphilitic aneurysms?

explanationHtml:
Dyslipidemia is not a direct risk factor for deep vein thrombosis.

Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and its complications, including abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). AAA can also be associated with smaller aneurysms of the iliac arteries. Patients with AAA are also likely to have atherosclerotic lesions in other vascular beds that may lead to ischemic heart disease or stroke.
question: A 55-year-old normotensive patient with dyslipidemia is undergoing a regular check-up. He is at an increased risk of developing all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
Anterior transmural infarcts are involved in causing aneurysm as a post-MI complication.

Other options:

Option A: Subendocardial infarcts result from prolonged global hypotension and are not associated with aneurysm formation.

Option C: Posterior transmural infarcts result in papillary muscle rupture, mitral regurgitation, and arrhythmias commonly.

Option D: Inferior wall infarcts are more likely to be complicated by conduction blocks, right ventricular involvement, hypotension, and cardiogenic shock.
question: Which of the following myocardial infarcts cause aneurysm as a post-MI complication?

explanationHtml:
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) of size ≤ 4 cm with slow growth have no risk of rupture.

The risk of rupture for AAA is directly related to the size of the aneurysm:

  • ≤4 cm - nil
  • 4–5 cm - 1% per year
  • 5–6 cm - 11% per year
  • >6 cm - 25% per year

Most aneurysms expand at a rate of 0.2 to 0.3 cm/year. The risk of rupture increases when there is a growth of > 0.5 cm/6 months, as well as in active smokers.
question: A patient was diagnosed with an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm of a diameter of 3.6cm. On a follow-up visit 1 year later, the diameter was noted to be 3.8cm. What is the risk of rupture of the aneurysm in this patient at present?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with the CT finding of a second column of blood after an intimal tear is the classic presentation of an aortic dissection. The major risk factor for aortic dissection is hypertension.

Dissection occurs when blood enters the media to form a blood-filled channel between the laminar planes of the media. It usually occurs due to a tear in the intima, which allows blood in the lumen to flow into the media. It may also occur due to the rupture of vasa vasorum.

It occurs due to:

  • Hypertension
  • Connective tissue defects like Marfan syndrome
  • Iatrogenic trauma during coronary catheterization or cardiopulmonary bypass
question: A 55-year-old man presents with sudden onset chest pain radiating to the back between the scapulae. The CT of this patient is given below. What is the major risk factor for developing this condition?

correctAnswer: B. It is a severe type of dissection
explanationHtml:
The above image shows a double-barreled aorta with a superior and inferior lumen. It is a less severe type of dissection because it is less likely to cause hemorrhage.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

A double-barreled aorta is seen there with two intimal tears. Hence, the hematoma enters the media through an intimal tear but re-enters the lumen through another intimal tear present distally. As the blood enters the lumen back, this type of dissection does not progress, thus averting hemorrhage.

This creates a false vascular channel in the blood vessel, which, over time, can be endothelialized to become chronic dissections.

options.text: It is a severe type of dissection

question: A 2D echocardiography of a patient who presented with chest pain showed the following appearance of the aorta on suprasternal parasagittal view. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis. It is a chronic granulomatous inflammation of the large arteries, usually in the head. It can present with unilateral headaches, jaw pain, and could lead to blindness by involving the ophthalmic artery.

Other options:

Option B: Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis that generally occurs in children with fever. It preferentially affects the coronary arteries and can result in aneurysm or even myocardial infarction.

Option C: IgA vasculitis, also known as Henoch-Schonlein purpura, is an immune-mediated small vessel vasculitis that usually follows a recent upper respiratory tract infection. It occurs commonly in children with purpuric skin lesions, hematuria, and melena.

Option D: Polyarteritis nodosa is a small or medium vessel vasculitis that usually affects the renal and visceral vessels, sparing the pulmonary circulation. It is highly associated with Hepatitis B.

The following pearl classifies the types of vasculitis:
question: Which of the following is a large vessel vasculitis?

explanationHtml:
Giant cell arteritis does not involve the veins.

Other options:

Option A: Thrombangiitis obliterans, also known as Buerger disease, is a medium vessel vasculitis that causes segmental thrombosis with vein and nerve involvement. Increased risk is associated with smoking.

Option B: Behcet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels. It classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. It is also associated with venular involvement and aneurysm.

Option C: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is an acute necrotizing vasculitis of the small and large vessels, which is caused by immune complex formation. It can produce purpura, cutaneous ulcer, and nail bed infarction. It is associated with the involvement of the veins.
question: All of the following vasculitides involves veins except?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of giant cell arteritis.

Giant cell / temporal arteritis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of large to small-sized arteries that primarily affects the temporal arteries. It is seen in people over 50 years of age. It usually presents with facial pain or headache along the course of the superficial temporal artery.

It can also affect:

  • Ophthalmic arteries - leading to a sudden onset of diplopia or blindness
  • Aorta - leading to giant-cell aortitis
  • Vertebral arteries

A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Giant cell arteritis needs to be promptly diagnosed and treated with steroids to prevent permanent blindness.

Other options:

Option A: Thromboangiitis obliterans, also known as Buerger disease, is a medium vessel vasculitis causing segmental thrombosis. It is commonly seen in male smokers.

Option B: Granulomatosis with polyangitis is a small vessel vasculitis causing necrotizing granulomas. It is also called Wegener's granulomatosis. It is commonly associated with lung and kidney involvement.

Option C: Takayasu arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis that is common in women. It is also called pulseless disease due to a weak or absent pulse in the upper extremities. It presents with granulomas in the aortic arch.
question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset blindness. He gives a history of frequent headaches along the sides of his scalp. What is the most probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. A negative biopsy excludes the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
A negative biopsy cannot exclude the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis. It is because the lesions are focally distributed. A biopsy sample may be taken from the normal part of the artery, leading to a false-negative report. An adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment.

Biopsy findings:

  • Giant cell arteritis is primarily medial granulomatous inflammation.
  • These lesions involve the internal elastic lamina, leading to elastic lamina fragmentation.
  • There is intimal thickening that reduces the luminal diameter.

Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, infiltrate of T cells (CD4+ >CD8+), and macrophages.

The following histological image is of giant-cell arteritis with intimal thickening and internal elastic lamina fragmentation:

[[figure-1]]


Note: According to the 21st edition of Harrison's Medicine, as involvement of the vessel may be segmental, getting a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens would help to increase a positive yield.

options.text: A negative biopsy excludes the diagnosis
The classic lesions are medial granulomas
Fragmentation is seen in internal elastic lamina

question: An elderly patient presented with temporal headache and jaw claudication. She was diagnosed to be a case of Giant cell arteritis. Which of the following statements about giant cell arteritis is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and radiological findings are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis.

Takayasu's arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis affecting medium and large-sized arteries, in this case, the aortic arch and its branches. Clinical manifestations include vision disturbances and profound weakening of the pulses, especially in the upper extremities.

Histopathology:

  • Irregular thickening of the vessel wall is seen with associated intimal hyperplasia.
  • Characteristic granulomatous inflammation, with the presence of giant cells and patchy medial necrosis.
  • Disease progression is associated with collagenous scarring and chronic inflammatory infiltrates across all layers of the vessel wall.

Other options:

Option A: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, is an inflammation of medium and large-sized vessels. It is more common in women and people aged >50 years.
The clinical features include headache associated with scalp pain and jaw claudication, fever, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss.

Half of the patients have temporal artery abnormalities such as enlargement, tenderness, nodular swelling, and loss of pulse of the temporal artery, either unilateral or bilateral. Gentle pressure on the scalp may elicit focal or generalised tenderness.

Though the arch of the aorta may also be involved in giant cell arteritis (known as giant cell aortitis), it is seen in people more than 50 years of age. Whereas, Takayasu arteritis is seen more commonly in adolescents and young women.

Option C: Thromboangitis obliterans, also known as Buerger's disease, is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder involving medium- and small-sized vessels in the distal extremities. It is most frequently seen in male smokers less than 40 years of age.

Option D: Behcet's disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations, with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms.
question: A 30-year-old lady presents with weakness of the left upper limb. On examination, the blood pressure recorded on the left upper limb was found to be lower than that of the right upper limb. Her aortic arch angiogram showed narrowing of the arch of the aorta and subclavian artery. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most commonly involved blood vessel in Takayasu arteritis is the subclavian artery.

Takayasu arteritis is an inflammatory and stenotic disease of medium and large-sized arteries characterized by a strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches. It is also known as aortic arch syndrome.

The order of arteries affected in Takayasu arteritis is subclavian artery > common carotid artery > abdominal aorta > renal artery > aortic arch = vertebral > coeliac axis > iliac > pulmonary > coronary artery.

Takayasu arteritis causes irregular thickening of the vessel wall with intimal hyperplasia, leading to narrowing of the lumen and organ ischemia.

It may have various clinical presentations depending on the vessel involved:

  • Arch of the aorta and its branches:
    • Subclavian artery- leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities. Hence, it is also known as pulseless disease
    • Carotid arteries- leads to weak pulses, blindness, neurological deficits
  • Distal aorta- leads to claudication of the legs
  • Pulmonary artery- leads to pulmonary hypertension
  • Coronary arteries- leads to myocardial infarction
  • Renal arteries- leads to systemic hypertension
question: A young girl with bilaterally unequal pulses is diagnosed with Takayasu Arteritis. Which of the following is the most commonly involved site in Takayasu arteritis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are suggestive of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).

PAN affects small or medium-sized muscular arteries. It typically affects young adults. The patient may present with rapidly accelerating hypertension due to renal artery involvement (most common) or abdominal pain and bloody stools caused by involvement of gastrointestinal vessels.

Option A: Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis is a vascular pathology seen in severe hypertension.

Option B: Cystic medial degeneration leads to dissecting aortic aneurysm.

Option C: Mönckeberg’s arteriosclerosis does not cause infarction.
question: A young male presents to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain. The small bowel is found to have a small infarcted area which is surgically removed. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen is given below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the small bowel infarction?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Kawasaki disease or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.

Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness associated with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels. It is commonly seen in infants and children <4 years of age.

Clinical features include:

  • Fever
  • Conjunctival and oral erythema
  • Blistering, edema of hands and feet
  • Erythema of palms and soles
  • Desquamative rash
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy

The disease is usually self-limiting. In some cases, the disease may involve the coronary artery, leading to thrombosis and acute myocardial infarction. Intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin may be given to reduce the risk of coronary artery disease.

Other options:

Option B: Rubella is caused by an enveloped Togaviridae RNA virus . It characteristically presents with Forchheimer spots, which are tiny rose-colored lesions on the soft palate. The rash in rubella begins on the face and spreads to the trunk.

Option C: Scarlet fever is caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, the rash is characteristically sandpaper-like in texture and would have a history of tonsillitis

Option D: Henoch-Scholein purpura is an IgA immune complex-mediated vasculitis and is the most common systemic vasculitis in children, but presents commonly with renal involvement and palpable purpura.
question: A 3-year-old child was brought to the hospital with complaints of fever, rash and swelling of her hands and feet since past 5 days.  There is desquamative skin rash, oedema of hands and feet, erythema of palms and soles, oral erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the likely condition?

explanationHtml:
Antibodies to endothelial cells are associated with vasculitis in Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease, also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is an acute febrile illness associated with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels. It is commonly seen in infants and children <4 years of age.

Other options:

Option A: Immune complex deposition is characteristic of vasculitis due to systemic immunologic disorders such as SLE.

Option B: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic bodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis is seen in conditions such as microscopic polyangiitis, Churg–Strauss syndrome, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Option D: Autoreactive T cells are seen in giant cell arteritis.

Note: Reports have been described in children with a multisystem inflammatory condition (MIS-C) linked to COVID-19 infection with some features similar to Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome. Although shock is rarely associated with Kawasaki disease, many children with the inflammatory syndrome related to COVID show signs of shock.
question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother, who reports that he has had a fever and rash for the past week. Upon examination, a rash is observed on the boy's hands, feet, and trunk, along with enlarged lymph nodes in his neck and conjunctival injection. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of the child's condition?

explanationHtml:
Pulmonary artery hypertension is not a complication of polyarteritis nodosa.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic vasculitis of the small and medium-sized muscular arteries, typically involving renal and visceral vessels, but sparing the pulmonary arteries.

The vascular lesion in PAN is a segmental transmural necrotizing inflammation, which tends to involve bifurcations and branching of arteries. Fibrinoid necrosis ensues with compromise of the lumen, thrombosis, and infarction of the tissues supplied by the vessel. Granulomas are not observed.

30% of patients with PAN have chronic hepatitis B and deposits containing HBsAg-HBsAb complexes in the affected vessels.

Non-specific symptoms like fever, weight loss, and malaise are present in over one-half of cases.

Specific complaints related to a particular organ system may also dominate the clinical picture:

  • Renal - renal failure, hypertension
  • Musculoskeletal - arthritis, arthralgia, myalgia
  • Peripheral nervous system - Peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex
  • Gastrointestinal tract - Abdominal pain, bleeding, bowel infarction, and perforation
  • Skin - rash, purpura, cutaneous infarcts, livedo reticularis, Raynaud's phenomenon
  • Cardiac - Congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, pericarditis
  • Genitourinary - Testicular, ovarian, or epididymal pain
  • Central nervous system - Cerebral vascular accident, seizure, altered mental status

Diagnosis: The diagnosis is based on the demonstration of characteristic findings of vasculitis on biopsy material. An elevated ESR is almost always present. All patients should be screened for hepatitis B and C.

Treatment: Prednisolone and cyclophosphamide have shown favorable results. In patients with hepatitis B, antiviral therapy is used in combination with glucocorticoids and plasma exchange.
question: A young male presents with symptoms of arthralgia, weight loss, malaise, and new-onset headache. Upon examination, his blood pressure is 190/120 mm Hg. Following thorough evaluation, a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa is established. Which of the following complications would not be expected in this disease condition?

correctAnswer: C. It is triggered by infections
explanationHtml:
Anti-proteinase-3/PR3-ANCA/ c-ANCA is triggered by certain infections, as proteinase 3 shares similarities with many microbial peptides. This is the major antibody responsible for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA).

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are a heterogeneous group of autoantibodies directed against the constituents of neutrophils or monocytes. Many patients with vasculitis have circulating antibodies that react with neutrophil cytoplasmic antigens.

The two most important ANCAs related to vasculitis are:

  • Anti-proteinase-3/PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA - Directed against PR3, which is a neutrophil azurophilic granule constituent.
  • Anti-myeloperoxidase/MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA - Directed against MPO, which is a lysosomal granule constituent involved in oxygen-free radical generation. MPO-ANCAs are induced by several therapeutic agents, particularly propylthiouracil.

options.text: It is also known as p-ANCA
It shows perinuclear staining on immunofluorescence

question: A 43 year-old-male patient came to the clinic with complaints of occasional hematuria and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Examination revealed tiny petechial hemorrhages over his lower limbs. The patient tests positive for the anti-proteinase-3 antibody. Which of the following is true about this major antibody?

explanationHtml:
Type III or pauci-immune-type of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) may be a component of systemic vasculitis such as Wegener granulomatosis or microscopic polyangiitis.

It presents with crescentic glomerulonephritis, which comprises macrophages and fibrins, and doesn't show few or no immune deposits in glomeruli, hence is called pauci-immune type.

Other options:

Option A: Lupus nephritis is divided into six classes based on the histological features, with class IV being the most common and severe form, causing diffuse lupus nephritis, which can progress into type 2 RPGN.

Option C: IgA nephropathy, also called Berger's disease, is associated with mesangial deposition of IgA. It usually presents with hematuria and low-grade fever following a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection.

Option D: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by a type 2 hypersensitivity reaction against type 4 collagen, leading to destruction of the basement membrane in renal glomeruli. It causes type 1 RPGN, which shows linear immunofluorescence.
question: Which of the following is a pauci-immune rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis?

correctAnswer: D. Lesions of different stages of activity coexist in the same vessel
explanationHtml:
All lesions of microscopic polyangiitis tend to be of the same age in any given patient, unlike polyarteritis nodosa, where all stages of activity from early to late may coexist in different vessels or even within the same vessel.

Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that affects capillaries, small arterioles, and venules. It is associated with MPO-ANCA. It is also called leukocytoclastic vasculitis because of apoptotic neutrophils.

It may involve the skin, mucous membranes, lungs, brain, heart, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and muscles. Therefore, the patient may present with hemoptysis, hematuria, proteinuria, bowel pain or bleeding, muscle pain or weakness, and palpable cutaneous purpura. Necrotizing glomerulonephritis (90% of patients) and pulmonary capillaritis are particularly common.

options.text: It affects capillaries, small arterioles, and venules
It is also known as leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Lesions of different stages of activity coexist in the same vessel

question: Which of the following statements about microscopic polyangiitis is not true?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the lab findings are suggestive of Churg–Strauss syndrome.

Churg-Strauss Syndrome/Allergic granulomatosis and angiitis is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically associated with:

  • Asthma
  • Allergic rhinitis
  • Asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex
  • Lung infiltrates
  • Peripheral hypereosinophilia
  • Extravascular necrotizing granulomata.

It is a multisystem disease with cutaneous involvement(palpable purpura), gastrointestinal tract bleeding, and renal disease. Eosinophilic infiltrates may also be observed in the myocardium, leading to cardiomyopathy.

p- ANCA (MPO-ANCA) is positive in about 50% of cases. Histological features are similar to those observed in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) or microscopic polyangiitis but are characteristically accompanied by granulomas and eosinophils.

A histopathological image of eosinophilic vasculitis seen in Churg-Strauss syndrome is shown below:

[[figure-1]]
question: A 21-year-old boy, who is a known case of asthma, presents with wheezing and rhinitis. Laboratory results show peripheral eosinophilia and antibodies against neutrophil myeloperoxidase. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Associated predominantly with MPO- ANCA
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of Wegener's granulomatosis. It is associated with predominantly PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in about 65-75% of cases and is also associated with MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) in the other 25% of cases.

Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis/Wegener granulomatosis is a necrotizing vasculitis characterized by a triad of necrotizing inflammation:

  • Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract or the lung
  • Necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels, most prominently in the lungs
  • Focal necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis

Males are affected more often than females. The most common clinical features include persistent pneumonitis with bilateral nodular and cavitary infiltrates, chronic sinusitis, mucosal ulcerations of the nasopharynx, and evidence of renal disease.

The following chest radiograph image shows pulmonary granulomatosis:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Negative ANCA does not exclude GPA and can occur in 10-20% of cases. Tissue biopsy and clinical evaluation are required in such cases.

options.text: Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract

question: A 45-year-old man presents with hematuria, intermittent hemoptysis and chronic sinusitis. His chest radiograph shows multiple opacities and cavities. Renal biopsy suggests focal necrotizing glomerulonephritis. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Behçet disease. Nail fold capillary abnormalities are typically seen in systemic sclerosis and Raynaud's phenomenon.

Behçet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels, classically presenting as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Other skin findings include erythema nodosa (red tender nodules on legs) and positive pathergy test (pustular reaction 24-48 hrs after sterile needle puncture or normal saline injection).

There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations, with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms. Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation in children. Pulmonary aneurysms are the most severe feature of pediatric BD.

It is associated with HLA subtype B51. T helper 17 (Th17) cells make an important contribution to the recruitment of neutrophils, which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.

Note: Nail-fold capillaroscopy is a non-invasive, easy, and safe diagnostic technique designed to evaluate the general architecture of capillary rows and fine details of small vessels of the microcirculation in the nail fold.
question: A 15-year old boy comes to the clinic complaining about recurrent painful oral ulcers. He also experiences repeated episodes of eye redness and pain which subside with medication. On examination, ulcers are seen on his genitals. Which of the following features would you not expect to see in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder, commonly seen in children aged 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features:

  • Skin lesions- characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and also the buttocks
  • Abdominal manifestations- include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding.
  • Renal manifestations- include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults.

It is strongly associated with atopy in a few patients, and the onset often follows an upper respiratory infection. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy.

Other options:

Option B: Wegener's granulomatosis, also known as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, is a granulomatous and necrotizing vasculitis of the small arteries and veins that mainly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing sinusitis, otitis media, chronic sinusitis, and serous otitis media. Lung involvement typically appears as multiple, bilateral nodular cavitary infiltrates. It can also cause focal or segmental glomerulonephritis, and if left untreated, it can lead to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Skin lesions such as palpable purpura or subcutaneous nodules may also manifest.

Option C: Kawasaki’s disease is an autoimmune condition that damages vessels and causes neutrophilic arteritis in Kawasaki disease, which is responsible for vessel wall inflammation and the formation of coronary artery aneurysms. It typically presents with fever, mucocutaneous rash, conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, and changes in the extremities.

Option D: Goodpasture syndrome is characterized by pulmonary hemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and elevated anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody levels and is commonly seen in young adult males. It doesn't present with notable skin manifestations.
question: A 5-year-old child presents with colicky abdominal pain and purpuric skin lesions on the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs. Urine analysis reveals hematuria and mild proteinuria. The most probable diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is thromboangiitis obliterans/Buerger disease.

It is the segmental, thrombosing, acute, and chronic inflammation of medium-sized and small arteries. It principally involves the tibial and radial arteries.

It is seen in smokers, usually before the age of 35 years. HLA-A-9 and HLA-B-5 are associated with a high risk of TAO.

The patients present with intermittent claudication, chronic ulcerations of the extremity, and later progress to frank gangrene. The microscopy findings include luminal thrombosis (thrombangiitis), which is thrombus containing microabscesses that occlude the lumen (obliterans). They contain small microabscesses composed of neutrophils.

Other options:

Option B: Churg-Strauss syndrome is a small vessel vasculitis with necrotising granulomatous inflammation and eosinophils. It presents with fever, hematuria, hemoptysis, chronic rhinosinusitis, and asthma.

Option C: Wegener's granulomatosis is a granulomatous and necrotizing vasculitis of the small arteries and veins that mainly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.

Option D: Berger disease refers to IgA nephropathy. It is seen within 3-5 days of a sore throat and is associated with purpuric rash in the lower limbs.
question: A 32-year-old male smoker presents with intermittent claudication and gangrene of the lower extremities. Biopsy of the blood vessels supplying this area shows acute and chronic inflammation, with luminal thrombosis containing small neutrophilic microabscesses. Granulomatous inflammation appears to extend into the contiguous veins and nerves. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Luminal thrombosis containing small microabscesses composed of neutrophils is seen in thromboangiitis obliterans or Buerger disease.

Option A: Adventitial mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasa vasorum have been described in Takayasu arteritis.

Option B: Fragmented neutrophils undergoing apoptosis and infiltrating blood vessels are together termed as leukocytoclastic vasculitis and are seen in small vessel vasculitides.

Option D: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels and is seen in immunologically mediated vasculitis syndromes.

options.text: Mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasavasorum

question: Which of the following histologic findings would be most suggestive of Buerger’s disease in a patient?

explanationHtml:
Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm. It is a vascular tumor arising from the endothelial cells.

Benign vascular tumors are characterized by well-formed vascular channels lined by normal endothelial cells. Whereas malignant vascular tumors are characterized by poorly formed vessels with cellular atypia.
question: Which of the following best describes angiosarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Hemangiopericytoma is not derived from endothelial cells. It is a malignant vascular tumor derived from supporting cells of the blood vessels.

Vascular tumors derived from endothelial cells are:

  • Hemangioma
  • Lymphangioma
  • Angiosarcoma

The endothelial origin of vascular neoplasms can be confirmed using endothelial cell-specific markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.

Other options:

Option A: Hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors that are characterized by well-formed vascular channels lined by normal endothelial cells. They can increase in size and may regress spontaneously. They are typically present over the skin around the head, neck, and thorax, but can also occur internally in the liver. Extensive formations are called angiomatosis.

Option C: Lymphangiomas are benign lymphatic counterparts of hemangiomas. They can be simple capillary lymphangiomas or cavernous (cystic hygromas), which are found in the neck and axilla of children.

Option D: Angiosarcomas are malignant neoplasms that arise from the endothelial cells and are characterized by poorly formed vessels with cellular atypia.

The following pearl shows the classification of vascular tumors:
question: Which of the following vascular tumors are not derived from endothelial cells?

explanationHtml:
The most common form of vascular ectasia is nevus flammeus.

Vascular ectasias are conditions involving the dilatation of blood vessels. They can be congenital or acquired malformations or hamartomas.

Nevus flammeus (birthmark) is a Pink/purple flat lesion on the head or neck. They regress spontaneously. An image showing nevus flammeus in a newborn is given below:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option B: Spider telangiectasias are pulsatile and blanch with pressure. These are permanent dilations of small blood vessels. They lead to red lesions in the skin or mucous membranes. These commonly occur on the face, neck, or upper chest. They are associated with hyperestrogenic states, such as pregnancy or liver cirrhosis. An image showing spider telangiectasia is given below:

[[figure-2]]

Option C: Port-wine stain is a special form of nevus flammeus. It thickens the skin surface. It develops during childhood and persists over time. An Image showing a port-wine stain in a child is given below:

[[figure-3]]

Option D: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu disease) is caused by mutations in genes related to the TGF-β signaling pathway. It is characterized by dilated blood vessels with thin walls that bleed easily. There can be bleeding from the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis), tongue, mouth, eyes, and gastrointestinal tract. The image below shows multiple flat non-pulsating telangiectasias in a patient with Osler-Weber-Rendu disease:

[[figure-4]]
question: Which of the following is the most common form of vascular ectasia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the facial port-wine stain as seen in the image are characteristic of Sturge-Weber syndrome.

This is characterized by a triad of:

  • Facial port wine nevus - usually found in the distribution of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
  • Glaucoma
  • Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis can lead to seizures, mental retardation, or hemiplegia, and is seen as intracranial tram-track calcifications on CT, as given below.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option B: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is an autosomal disease characterised by hemangioblastomas of the central nervous system with pancreas, liver, and kidney involvement.

Option C: Osler Weber Rendu syndrome, also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, is an autosomal dominant disorder with multiple aneurysmal telangiectasia and is associated with serious hemorrhage.

Option D: Ataxia telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ataxia, neurological deficits, and vascular malformations, causing telangiectases.
question: A young girl presents with recurrent seizures, mental retardation and a skin lesion as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Assure the parents about spontaneous regression of the tumor
explanationHtml:
Capillary hemangiomas are present from birth and initially increase in size, but many eventually regress spontaneously. They are generally benign.

Images show the gross and microscopic pictures of capillary hemangioma:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option B: Retroviral infections are associated with vascular tumors such as Kaposi sarcoma.

Option C: Exposure to polyvinyl chloride is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, which is a rapidly growing malignant endothelial tumor. It often involves the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver. It is locally invasive and can readily metastasize

options.text: Explain about the risk of malignant transformation of the tumor
Test the child for retrovirus infection
Enquire about history of exposure to polyvinyl chloride
Assure the parents about spontaneous regression of the tumor

question: A child is brought by her parents to the OPD with complaints of a swelling on the right thigh. Further evaluation led to the diagnosis of capillary hemangioma in this patient. What is the most appropriate next best step?

explanationHtml:
von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas. These vascular lesions are commonly found in the cerebellum, brain stem, retina, pancreas, and liver.

Cavernous hemangiomas are large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma. They are infiltrative and involve deep structures. They do not regress spontaneously.

The given image shows the microscopic appearance of cavernous hemangioma:

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma is diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease. This condition is associated with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The vascular lesions commonly seen in Turner syndrome are cavernous lymphangiomas of the neck.

Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are massively dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells and separated by connective tissue stroma. They are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and rarely in the retroperitoneum. They can be enormous, causing gross deformities around the neck.

The image shows a cavernous lymphangioma of the neck associated with a girl having Turner syndrome:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Pyogenic granuloma are capillary hemangiomas that present as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa. They bleed easily and are often ulcerated.

They commonly occur in the oral mucosa and in the gingiva of pregnant women, likely due to increased estrogen promoting VEGF(vascular endothelial growth factor) in the macrophages; these are called granuloma gravidarum. They spontaneously regress and sometimes may undergo fibrosis, which might require surgical excision

Option B: Capillary lymphangioma are small, slightly elevated or pedunculated lesion spanning up to 1 to 2 cm in diameter that occurs on the skin and oral mucosa.

Option C: Capillary hemangioma generally occurs in the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and mucous membranes of the oral cavities and lips, as well as the liver, spleen, and kidneys. They consist of thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma.
question: Which of the following vascular lesions are commonly seen in patients with Turner syndrome?

correctAnswer: A. It is caused by a bacterial infection
explanationHtml:
The given image shows a pyogenic granuloma. It is not caused by bacterial infection. The term pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer as it neither contains pus nor is it a granulomatous lesion.

These are capillary hemangiomas that appear as red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa. They are most commonly benign. They tend to grow rapidly, bleed easily, and are often ulcerated.

A histologic image of a pyogenic granuloma is given below:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: It is caused by a bacterial infection
It is a type of capillary hemangioma

question: A middle aged male patient presents with a swelling on his left thumb as shown in the image below. Which of the following statements about this swelling is false?

explanationHtml:
The vascular tumor arising from arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation is a glomus tumor.

These tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies, which are specialized arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation. They are benign but extremely painful due to an abundance of nerve fibers. These are commonly found in the distal portion of the digits, especially under the fingernails.

Histopathology shows branching vascular channels separated by stroma containing glomus cells in nests:

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option A: Hemangioendothelioma is a borderline tumour between benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas.

Option B: Capillary hemangiomas are the most common hemangiomas that occur in the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and oral cavity, as well as the liver, spleen, and kidneys

Option C: Hemangiopericytoma is a rare type of fibroblastic tumor derived from the pericytes surrounding the blood vessels.
question: Which of the following vascular tumors arising from arteriovenous structures is involved in thermoregulation?

explanationHtml:
The clinical vignette and the microscopic findings suggest the diagnosis of bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella henselae.

Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family, like Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana.

These lesions can involve the skin, bone, brain, and other organs. They contain stromal neutrophils, nuclear dust, and causal bacteria. Histology shows capillary proliferation with endothelial cells exhibiting nuclear atypia and mitosis.

Modified silver (Warthin-Starry) stain is used for demonstrating clusters of tangled bacilli.

Detection of Bartonella DNA in tissue specimens by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay or of Bartonella antigens by immunohistochemical methods is diagnostic.

Failure to distinguish Kaposi sarcoma from bacillary angiomatosis is problematic because bacillary angiomatosis, unlike Kaposi sarcoma, responds dramatically to antibiotic therapy. Furthermore, bacillary angiomatosis may be life-threatening if untreated.

Treatment: Erythromycin or doxycycline for 3 months.

The given image shows the histopathological appearance of bacillary angiomatosis:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option B: Human Herpes Virus - 6 causes sixth disease or roseola infantum and can cause encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts.

Option C: Bartonella bacilliformis is a pleomorphic gram-negative rod and causes Oroya fever, also known as Carrion's disease. It presents with progressive anemia due to bacterial invasion of the erythrocytes and fever.

Option D: Human Herpes Virus - 8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular neoplasm in immunocompromised patients, and is highly associated with AIDS. Other diseases caused by HHV-8 include multicentric Castleman disease and primary effusion lymphoma.
question: A 46-year-old HIV-positive female patient presents with fever, weight loss, and cutaneous lesions as shown in the image.  Microscopic examination reveals capillary proliferation and neutrophilic infiltration. Which of the following is the causative organism?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are most suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma.

Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpes virus 8 (HHV8) and is highly associated with AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). Classic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in older men of Eastern European and Mediterranean descent. It has the following three clinical stages:

  • Patches: These are red-purple macules on the distal lower extremities
  • Plaques: Patches progress to large violaceous raised plaques. Lesions spread proximally.
  • Nodules: Lesions develop into nodules with more neoplastic features. This stage also progresses to involve nodes and viscera.

Diseases caused by HHV-8 infection primarily in patients with HIV infection include:

  • Kaposi sarcoma
  • Multicentric Castleman disease (MCD)
  • Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL)

The given image shows sheets of proliferating spindle cells in Kaposi sarcoma:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Cavernous hemangiomas are usually benign tumors consisting of large dilated blood vessels filled with blood. They are often infiltrative and are found in the liver.

Option C: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular, proliferative form of Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana infection that occurs primarily in immunocompromised people and is the second-most-common cause of angiomatous skin lesions in persons infected with HIV.

It is characterised by proliferating cystic blood-filled spaces surrounded by a fibromyxoid matrix containing the bacteria.

The gross and histopathological images of bacillary angiomatosis are given below:

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Option D: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm. It is a vascular tumor arising from the endothelial cells. It is associated with vinyl chloride exposure.

Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci are the most common agents responsible for lymphangitis.

Lymphangitis represents acute inflammation elicited by the spread of bacterial infections into lymphatics. It is manifested by red, painful subcutaneous streaks (the inflamed lymphatics) and painful enlargement of the draining lymph nodes (lymphadenitis).

Other options:

Option A: Filaria causes obstructive lymphedema and chronic lymphadenitis.

Option C: Staphylococci can cause infections such as folliculitis, carbuncles, abscesses, cellulitis, and impetigo. In severe cases, the exfoliative toxin can cause staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

explanationHtml:
Hypertension is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure.

Left-sided heart failure can be divided into systolic and diastolic failure. Diastolic failure predominantly occurs in patients older than age 65 years. Here, the left ventricle is abnormally stiff and cannot relax during diastole.

Causes of diastolic heart failure:

  • Hypertension: most common
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Obesity
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis

Systolic failure is due to insufficient ejection fraction, i.e., pump failure. It occurs when the contractile function of the left ventricle is deranged.
question: What is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure?

correctAnswer: C. Increased left ventricular cavity size
explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, an increase in the size of the left ventricle is not normally seen in the heart of an elderly person. The size of the left ventricular cavity is decreased in the aged heart, particularly in the base-to-apex dimension. This change is exacerbated by systemic hypertension.

Changes in the aging heart:

  1. Chambers:
    • Increased left atrial cavity size
    • Decreased left ventricular cavity size
  2. Valves:
    • Fibrous thickening of valve leaflets
    • Aortic and mitral valve calcific deposits
  3. Epicardial coronary arteries:
    • Diminished compliance
    • Calcific deposits
    • Atherosclerotic plaques
  4. Myocardium:
    • Increased subepicardial fat
    • Brown atrophy
    • Lipofuscin deposition
    • Basophilic degeneration
    • Amyloid deposits
  5. Aorta:
    • Dilated with a rightward shift
    • Elastic fragmentation and collagen accumulation
    • Atherosclerotic plaque

explanationHtml:
Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages. They are telltale signs of previous episodes of pulmonary edema.

In cardiac failure, red cells and plasma proteins extravasate into the edema fluid within the alveolar spaces. These are then phagocytosed and digested by macrophages. The iron recovered from haemoglobin is stored in the form of hemosiderin.
