question: What type of cells are heart failure cells?

explanationHtml:
Isolated right-sided heart failure is not caused by left-sided heart failure.

Isolated right-sided heart failure is not common and usually occurs in patients with disorders affecting the lungs. Therefore, it is often referred to as cor pulmonale. It is caused by disorders of the lung parenchyma and pulmonary vasculature. It is also caused by conditions that cause pulmonary vasoconstriction, like obstructive sleep apnea and altitude sickness.

Pulmonary hypertension is the common feature of these disorders, which leads to hypertrophy and dilation of the right side of the heart.

Right-sided heart failure is most commonly caused by left-sided heart failure. This is because an increase in pressure in the pulmonary circulation from left-sided failure burdens the right side of the heart.
question: Which of the following does not cause isolated right-sided heart failure?

correctAnswer: B. Right ventricular dilation without hypertrophy
explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the patient has acute cor pulmonale. This causes right ventricular dilation without hypertrophy. On cross-section, the normal crescent shape of the right ventricle is transformed to a dilated ovoid.

The main pathophysiology behind cor pulmonale is pulmonary hypertension and increased right ventricular (RV) afterload, which is sufficient to cause RV dilation with or without hypertrophy. Sustained pressure overload leads to RV dysfunction and failure.

In chronic cor pulmonale, the right ventricular wall thickens. The hypertrophied right ventricle may compress the left ventricular chamber. It can also cause regurgitation and fibrous thickening of the tricuspid valve.
question: A massive pulmonary embolism occurs in a patient with acute cor-pulmonale. What pathological changes do you expect in the heart of this patient?

explanationHtml:
In the image, the liver specimen shows a nutmeg liver appearance, which occurs in congestive hepatomegaly. This is secondary to passive congestion due to right heart failure.

In right heart failure, congestion occurs in the hepatic and portal vessels, with the most significant congestion around the central veins. This results in an increased liver size and weight. The pericentral zones become congested and red-brown. The periportal regions usually are tan. This leads to a nutmeg liver appearance. With longstanding failure, the central areas can become fibrotic, eventually culminating in cardiac cirrhosis.

Pathological changes are also seen in the spleen and the gastrointestinal tract. Portal venous hypertension also causes the enlargement of the spleen, with platelet sequestration. This is known as congestive splenomegaly. This can also contribute to chronic congestion and oedema of the bowel.

Other options:

Option A: Liver cirrhosis would show a gross appearance of multiple regenerative nodules throughout the liver, separated by bridging fibrosis. The following image shows the gross appearance of the liver in alcoholic liver cirrhosis:

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Haemochromatosis presents with a gross image of dark brown discoloration of the liver, as well as the other involved organs, with hepatomegaly.

Option D: Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis is characterised by fibrosis around the portal vein without the architectural changes of cirrhosis and is due to increased portal pressure. Gross appearance may vary, ranging from normal to shrunken.
question: The liver specimen obtained after the autopsy of a patient is given below. What could be the likely cause of this finding?

correctAnswer: B. Viable myocardium appears brick red and infarct appears pale
explanationHtml:
Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution imparts a brick-red colour to the viable non-infarcted myocardium. The infarct appears unstained and pale.

Myocardial infarcts < 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to identify the area of necrosis. This is done by immersing the tissue slices in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution.

The histochemical stain imparts a brick-red colour to intact, noninfarcted myocardium. Here, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity is preserved. LDH leaks out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, so an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

The image given below shows an ischemic brain after immersion in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution. The pale unstained region is the infarcted zone.

[[figure-1]]

explanationHtml:
Relaxation of myofibrils is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction.

Myofibril relaxation, mitochondrial swelling, and glycogen loss can be detected by electron microscopy within half an hour of myocardial infarction.

Note: Microvascular injury begins >1 hour after the onset of ischemia.
question: What is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction?

explanationHtml:
The earliest light microscopic change that can be observed in the heart of this patient is the waviness of myocardial fibres. This is seen within ½-4 hours at the border of the infarct.

These changes are a result of the forceful contractions of viable fibres. The contractions cause stretching and buckling of immediately adjacent, noncontractile dead fibres.

Myocyte vacuolization or myocytolysis may also be seen in the infarct margins. It is due to the accumulation of salt and water in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Such myocytes are viable but poorly contractile.

The image below shows microscopic features of myocardial infarction, showing wavy myocardial fibres. There are wavy fibres that are elongated and narrow, as compared with normal fibres. The widened spaces between the dead fibres contain edema fluid and scattered neutrophils.

[[figure-1]]

However, it is prominent between 1 to 3 days after myocardial infarction.

explanationHtml:
The given autopsy finding of hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture occurs most frequently 3-7 days after myocardial infarction (MI). During this time, the lysis of the necrotic myocardium is maximum. Thus, most of the infarct has been converted to friable granulation tissue.

The risk factors for free-wall rupture are:

  • Age > 60 years
  • Female gender
  • First MI
  • Large, transmural and anterior MI
  • Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Preexisting hypertension

It is less frequent in patients with prior MI because associated fibrotic scarring inhibits myocardial tearing.

Complications of MI:

  1. Heart failure -
    • This is due to ventricular dysfunction caused by the infarct and ventricular remodelling
    • Usually occurs within a day
  2. Cardiogenic shock -
    • This is usually seen in severe multivessel coronary artery disease due to extensive involvement of the myocardium
    • Usually occurs within a day
  3. Arrhythmias - the most common complication, occurring usually 2 days after infarction
    • Most common arrhythmia within one hour of MI - ventricular fibrillation
    • Most common arrhythmia after one hour of MI - supraventricular tachycardia
  4. Myocardial rupture - occurs when there is transmural necrosis of a ventricle. It includes the following -
    • Left ventricular free wall rupture (most common) - leads to cardiac tamponade
    • Interventricular septal rupture - leads to an acute ventricular septal defect (VSD)
    • Papillary muscle rupture - leads to severe mitral regurgitation
  5. Mitral regurgitation (MR) - this can occur due to -
    • Transient papillary muscle dysfunction - mid-systolic or late-systolic murmur
    • Rupture of papillary muscle - pansystolic murmur
  6. Dressler syndrome (post-MI syndrome) -
    • This is an immune-mediated reaction and presents as pericarditis, pleurisy, and fever
    • It can occur even 48 hrs after MI, but usually occurs 1–6 weeks after MI and often subside after a few days
  7. Ventricular aneurysm
  8. Infarct expansion associated with mural thrombus

It is the gross appearance of the heart with bands of yellow myocardium alternating with normal myocardium. The fatty degeneration creates prominent broken stripes in the subendocardium.
question: What causes tigered myocardium?

explanationHtml:
In reperfusion injury, the maximum damage is caused by free radicals.

Reduced blood flow to the myocardium caused due to an infarct which ultimately leads to ischemic myocardium can be combated by reperfusion. Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. Once the flow is restored, there is bleeding.

On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes. These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres.

Reperfusion injury may be mediated by:

  • Oxidative stress
  • Calcium overload
  • Inflammatory cells recruited after tissue reperfusion

Other options:

Option A & B: Neutrophil aggregation followed by monocyte activation leads to occlusion of the microvasculature and contributes to the no-reflow phenomenon and further exacerbates proteases and elastases that cause cell death.

Option C: Calcium overload results in augmented and uncontrolled contraction of myofibrils, causing cytoskeletal damage and cell death.
question: Which of the following causes the maximum damage in reperfusion injury?

explanationHtml:
Heart muscle contains MM and MB isoenzymes of creatine kinase.

Creatine kinase (CK) has three isoenzymes:

  • CK-1 (BB) - brain, nerve tissue, prostate (small amounts), intestine, lung, bladder, kidney, uterus, thyroid
  • CK-2 (MB) - heart and skeletal muscle
  • CK-3 (MM) - skeletal and heart muscle

Elevation of the CK-MB isoforms is seen in MI. CK-MB is less sensitive and less specific; therefore, troponins are preferred for the diagnosis of MI. CK-MB begins to rise within 3-12 hours of the onset of MI. It peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal within approximately 48-72 hours.
question: What creatine kinase isoenzymes do the heart muscle contain?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of acute myocardial infarction (MI). Enzymes elevated after 4 to 8 hours of MI are CK-MB (creatine kinase MB) and troponins.

When cardiac troponin is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI. If it is the only assay available, it can be used, but it is far less sensitive and less specific.
question: A patient comes to the hospital after 3 hours of the onset of chest pain. ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads. Which of the following enzymes would be elevated in this patient?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, on post-MI day 7, troponin and LDH will be raised. Troponins are highly specific for MI and remain elevated for 7 to 10 days.

Troponins are proteins that regulate calcium-mediated contraction of the cardiac and skeletal muscles. It is the single biomarker preferred for diagnosing MI, late diagnosis of MI, and diagnosis of reinfarction. Troponin I is more important than troponin T.

Cardiac troponin increases rapidly in patients with reinfarction. Sometimes, the cardiac troponin concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. Then the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement.

Myoglobin is the earliest enzyme to increase after MI. It is a protein that is found in the skeletal and cardiac muscles, which binds oxygen. It is a very sensitive indicator of muscle injury. But it is not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle. Myoglobin and SGOT levels come to baseline before day 1.

You suspect that the patient's chest pain was due to myocardial infarction. If so, blood levels of which of the following would be elevated now?

question: The blood levels of various cardiac biomarkers are measured in a patient following myocardial infarction. This is represented in the given graph. Which biomarker does the yellow curve depict?

explanationHtml:
Loss of function mutation in K+ channel genes KCNQ1 and KCNH2 produces the long QT syndrome. The gain-of-function mutation produces the short QT syndrome.

Long QT syndrome manifests as arrhythmias associated with excessive prolongation of cardiac repolarisation. Stress-induced syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD) are common presentations.

Other options:

Option B: Short QT syndrome presents with arrhythmias associated with abbreviated repolarisation intervals. They also present with palpitations, syncope, and SCD.

Option C: Brugada syndrome manifests as ECG abnormalities like ST-segment elevations and right bundle-branch block. This occurs in the absence of structural heart disease. Here, patients classically present with syncope or SCD during rest or sleep or after large meals.

Option D: Familial atrial fibrillation is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in genes coding potassium channels.
question: Loss-of-function mutation in potassium channel gene KCNQ1 results in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The mechanism behind sudden cardiac death (SCD) is most often a lethal arrhythmia, e.g., asystole or ventricular fibrillation.

Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of SCD, responsible for 80% to 90% of cases. But, the mechanism of SCD is most often a lethal arrhythmia. Infarction need not occur. Most of the patients who have SCD but are successfully resuscitated do not show any enzymatic or ECG evidence of myocardial necrosis.

Ischemic injury can directly affect the major components of the conduction system. But, most cases of fatal arrhythmia are triggered by electrical irritability of the myocardium.
question: What is the most common mechanism behind sudden cardiac death?

explanationHtml:
Patients with hyperlipidemia have an increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease (CAD).

Hyperlipidemia is considered the second most common risk factor for CAD worldwide after hypertension. Hypercholesterolemia was implicated in 55% of cases with combined hyperlipidemia in 41% cases.

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin D deficiency is associated with accelerated atherosclerosis and CAD, but it is not the strongest risk factor for coronary artery disease.

Option B: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most commonly inherited bleeding disorder due to abnormal von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is an adhesive protein that promotes the adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen and stabilises factor VIII, and is not associated with CAD.

Option D: Amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy resulting from the extracellular accumulation of protein fibrils that form insoluble β-pleated sheets. It can also be asymptomatic, manifest as dilation or arrhythmias, or mimic ischemic or valvular disease, but it is not the strongest association for CAD.

Note: Estrogen reduces the risk of myocardial infarction in women in the reproductive age group. Accelerated coronary artery disease is associated with the postmenopausal decline in estrogen production. However, postmenopausal hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) is not beneficial.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions has the most strongly associated increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease?

explanationHtml:
Lipoprotein a [Lp(a)] contains the apolipoprotein B-100 portion of LDL linked to apolipoprotein A (apo A). It is an altered form of low-density lipoprotein (LDL).

Increased Lp(a) levels are associated with coronary and cerebrovascular disease risk. It is independent of total cholesterol or LDL levels.

apo A: It is the main protein component of HDL. It facilitates reverse cholesterol transport, moving cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver.

apo B100: It is the main structural component of VLDL, IDL, and LDL, produced in the liver. It is crucial for the assembly and secretion of these particles and serves as the ligand for the LDL receptor, enabling cellular uptake of LDL.

apo B48: It is responsible for chylomicron formation and transport of fats.

apo E: It acts as a ligand for receptors that clear chylomicron remnants and VLDL remnants from the blood.
question: What is lipoprotein a [Lp (a)] composed of?

explanationHtml:
Reperfused myocardium shows eosinophilic contraction bands on light microscopy. They occur in irreversibly injured myocytes with damaged membranes, when the blood supply is restored 12-24 hours after MI.

Ischemia leads to a rise as a result of damage to the sarcolemma, causing dysfunctional calcium regulation. This leads to augmented and uncontrolled contraction of myofibrils after reperfusion.

On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes. These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres.

Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. This leads to bleeding after the flow is restored.
question: Histology of reperfused myocardium:

explanationHtml:
The most common type of cardiomyopathy is dilated cardiomyopathy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the least frequent.

Cardiomyopathies affect the myocardium, causing changes in the ventricles, such as hypertrophy or dilatation. The dysfunction can be mechanical and/or electrical.

Primary cardiomyopathies primarily involve the heart. Secondary cardiomyopathies are associated with a systemic or multiorgan disorder. They occur in the absence of any coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, congenital heart disease, or systemic arterial hypertension.

Types of cardiomyopathy:

  • Dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy
  • Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
  • Left ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy

Note: A mutation in TTN, the gene that encodes titin, accounts for 20% of all cases of dilated cardiomyopathy. Titin is the largest protein expressed in humans. It is the third myofilament in cardiac muscle and consists of a single giant polypeptide that extends from the Z-disk to the M-band region of the sarcomere.

question: What is the most common type of cardiomyopathy?

explanationHtml:
Alcohol abuse is strongly associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Alcohol and its metabolites, especially acetaldehyde, have a direct toxic effect on the myocardium, which leads to the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy:

  • Acquired causes :
    • Infectious and non-infectious myocarditis: the most common cause globally
    • Alcohol is the most common cause in India
    • Pregnancy:
      • Pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy (PACM)
      • Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM)
    • Stress-induced: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
    • Drug-induced:
      • Doxorubicin (anthracycline)
      • Trastuzumab
      • Cyclophosphamide
    • Nutritional deficiency:
      • Beriberi (thiamine),
      • Keshan disease (selenium),
      • Carnitine deficiency
    • Endocrine: Hypo and hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, diabetes mellitus
    • Others:
      • Cobalt toxicity,
      • Heavy metals (lead, mercury, arsenic, lithium)
  • Familial causes (50%):
    • Mutation in the cardiac myocyte titin gene
    • Haemochromatosis
    • Syndromes: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Becker’s muscular dystrophy

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario of sudden cardiac death in a previously healthy man during a stressful situation suggests takotsubo cardiomyopathy. It is a form of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is also called broken heart syndrome, apical ballooning Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or stress-induced cardiomyopathy, occurs during extreme psychological stress when there is a surge of catecholamines. This surge causes microcirculation spasms, leading to transient myocardial stunning. It is most commonly observed in middle-aged women.

It leads to left ventricular contractile dysfunction. The left ventricular apex is most often affected, which leads to apical ballooning. This resembles a “takotsubo,” which is Japanese for “fishing pot for trapping octopus”.

Histologically, acute cases may show microscopic areas of necrosis characterized by myocyte hypercontraction known as contraction band necrosis. Chronic cases may exhibit microscopic foci of granulation tissue.

question: The histological examination of the heart of a patient who died due to heart failure is given below.  What underlying condition did the patient most likely have?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the patient suffered from sustained ventricular tachycardia secondary to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). ARVC is associated with Naxos syndrome, which is a form of cardiocutaneous syndrome.

ARVC is an autosomal dominant cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement in the myocardium of the ventricles. It most commonly affects the right ventricle. It is due to mutations in the gene encoding desmosome-associated protein plakophilin 2. This leads to defective cell-adhesion proteins in the desmosomes that link adjacent cardiac myocytes.

As shown in the image below, Naxos syndrome is characterized by woolly hair and palmoplantar hyperkeratosis.

[[figure-1]]

Morphology shows severe thinning of the right ventricular wall due to loss of myocytes, accompanied by extensive fatty infiltration and fibrosis.

The image given below is a gross photograph of the heart showing dilated right ventricle and near transmural replacement of its free wall with fat and fibrosis.

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option B: Nelson syndrome is a complication that occurs after bilateral adrenalectomy to treat Cushing's disease, which could lead to unchecked growth of an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor, causing hyperpigmentation, headache, and visual disturbances.

Option C: Carvajal syndrome is a cardiocutaneous syndrome and a variant of Naxos disease, but it is associated with dilated cardiomyopathy. It is most commonly due to a mutation in desmoplakin.

Option D: Takotsubo syndrome, also called broken heart syndrome, apical ballooning syndrome, or stress-induced cardiomyopathy, is characterized by a transient myocardial stunning from microcirculation spasms due to a catecholamine surge during stress. It is usually seen in middle-aged women. It is a self-resolving condition.

question: A 14-year-old boy who collapsed while playing basketball was brought to the emergency room and was resuscitated. On evaluation, he was found to have sustained ventricular tachycardia secondary to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Which syndrome is associated with this?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and autopsy findings are suggestive of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). The image provided is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy as seen in HCM.

HCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults. It is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of >15mm on ECHO. The left ventricular myocardium is poorly compliant. This leads to abnormal diastolic filling and intermittent ventricular outflow obstruction, i.e., primarily diastolic dysfunction.

It is an autosomal dominant disease, and the majority is due to missense mutations in the following sarcolemmal protein genes: myosin binding protein C (MYBC) and beta myosin heavy chain (MYH7).

The gross features of HCM are:

  • Massive myocardial hypertrophy, usually without ventricular dilation
  • Asymmetric septal hypertrophy - disproportionate thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the left ventricle free wall
  • Banana-shaped left ventricle - due to bulging of the ventricular septum into the lumen

The image given below shows changes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared to a normal heart. HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and a thickened left ventricle wall.

[[figure-1]]

Histologic features of the HCM are:

  • Massive myocyte hypertrophy- with transverse myocyte diameters frequently greater than 40 μm, normal is approximately 15 μm.
  • Myofiber disarray - haphazard disarray of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractile elements in sarcomeres within cells
  • Interstitial fibrosis and replacement fibrosis

The image given below is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy seen in an abnormal HCM septum.

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option A: Ischemic cardiomyopathy, also known as chronic ischemic heart disease, is progressive congestive heart failure due to accumulated ischemic myocardial damage, which most instances having a prior myocardial infarction.

Option B: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder that manifests with right-sided heart failure and rhythm disturbances that can cause sudden cardiac death. It most commonly involves mutations in cardiac desmosomal proteins.

Option D: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is characterized by a transient myocardial stunning from microcirculation spasms due to a catecholamine surge during stress.

question: An autopsy was done for a young patient who had a sudden cardiac death. It revealed massive myocardial hypertrophy without ventricular dilation. The image obtained on microscopy is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is caused by hemochromatosis, ergotamine, amyloidosis and carcinoid syndrome. Trastuzumab causes dilated cardiomyopathy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is characterized by increased ventricular stiffness causing impaired diastolic filling of the ventricles. The stiffness is secondary to an underlying disease causing accumulation of intra and intercellular substances in the myocardium.

Causes of RCM:

  • Infiltration disorders
    • Amyloidosis (most common)
    • Sarcoidosis
  • Storage disorders
    • Fabry’s disease
    • Glycogen storage disease (type II>> III)
    • Hemochromatosis (DCM>RCM)
  • Fibrotic disorders
    • Scleroderma
    • Endomyocardial fibrosis
      • R-Radiation
      • E-Ergotamine
      • S-Serotonin
      • T-Tropical Endomyocardial fibrosis
      • C-Carcinoid syndrome
  • Miscellaneous: post open heart surgery, diabetes.

Morphology of RCM:

  1. Ventricles are of almost normal size or slightly enlarged
  2. The myocardium is non-compliant
  3. Biatrial dilation is commonly observed
  4. Patchy or diffuse interstitial fibrosis

Which of the following can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy?

  2. Ergotamine

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, the patient has progressive dyspnoea along with hypereosinophilia. This is suggestive of Loeffler's endocarditis. It leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy.

There is peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic infiltrates in multiple organs, including the heart. Major basic protein (MBP) is a toxic product released from eosinophils. This initiates endomyocardial necrosis followed by scarring. It leads to endomyocardial fibrosis, typically with large mural thrombi.

Many patients with Loeffler's endocarditis have a myeloproliferative disorder. This is associated with chromosomal rearrangements involving platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGF)-α or - β genes.

Other options:

Option A: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with mutations in genes that encode sarcomeric proteins, such as myosin-binding protein C, and typically presents with asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

Option B: Dilated cardiomyopathy usually does not present with eosinophilic infiltrates, although Loeffler's endocarditis can develop dilated cardiomyopathy later on secondary to chamber dilation, but it is not the primary pathophysiology.

Option C: Some restrictive conditions, like amyloidosis, can initially cause a restrictive pattern, which may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy as a result of long-term stress weakening the myocardium.

question: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive dyspnoea on exertion for one week along with a diffuse rash. Blood investigations are significant for an absolute eosinophil count of 4600 / mm³. Which of the following is caused by the patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
In this scenario, the decrease in ventricular compliance indicates restrictive cardiomyopathy. Endocardial fibroelastosis is an uncommon restrictive heart condition characterized by fibroelastic thickening that typically involves the left ventricular endocardium.

It is most common in the first 2 years of life. It results from several insults, including viral infections (e.g., intrauterine exposure to mumps) or mutations in the gene for tafazzin. These mutations affect mitochondrial inner membrane integrity.

Other options:

Option A: Endomyocardial fibrosis is a disease of children and young adults in Africa and other tropical areas. It is characterized by fibrosis of the ventricular endocardium and subendocardium that extends from the apex upward. The aetiology is unknown.

Option B: Loeffler endomyocarditis causes endomyocardial fibrosis, usually with large mural thrombi. Its overall morphology resembles that of the tropical disease. Besides the cardiac changes, there is often peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic infiltrates in multiple organs, including the heart.

Option D: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant disorder that causes mutations in genes encoding desmosomal junctional proteins, such as plakoglobin and proteins that interact with desmosomes, as well as desmin. It typically manifests as right heart failure and rhythm disturbances like T wave inversion and epsilon wave.

question: A 2-year-old girl was brought to the outpatient department with complaints of difficulty in breathing and fatigue. The child had a history of intrauterine exposure to mumps. Viral infections are the most common cause of myocarditis. Coxsackie viruses A and B and other enteroviruses account for most of the cases.

Myocarditis is a diverse group of pathologic entities in which infectious microorganisms and/or a primary inflammatory process cause myocardial injury.

explanationHtml:
Transthyretin is the major component of senile cardiac amyloid deposits. It is a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein.

Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or it may be localized. This is particularly seen in the elderly (senile cardiac amyloidosis). It has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis.

Presentation of cardiac amyloidosis:

  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy- most common
  • Asymptomatic
  • Dilation
  • Arrhythmias
  • Ischemic disease
  • Valvular disease.

The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls. Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface, particularly on the left.

Histologically, hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid are found in:

  • Interstitium
  • Conduction tissue
  • Valves, endocardium
  • Pericardium
  • Small intramural coronary arteries.

The image given shows an endomyocardial biopsy of a patient with cardiac amyloidosis stained as follows: A) Congo red only, B) Apple-green birefringence under polarized light:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Haptoglobin is an acute-phase reactant and is involved in binding free hemoglobin and reducing oxidative stress.

Option C: Fibronectin is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that is involved in cell adhesion and wound healing.

Option D: Amylin, also known as islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) is a peptide hormone secreted along with insulin in the pancreas and forms amyloid deposits in the pancreas and is not involved in senile cardiac amyloidosis.

question: Which serum protein is the major component of senile cardiac amyloid deposits?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests post-myocardial infarction fibrinous pericarditis. It is the most common type of pericarditis.

Clinically, a loud pericardial friction rub is present. There is a rubbery fibrin mass loosely gluing the parietal and visceral pericardium together (bread and butter). It may resolve or become organized to produce adhesive pericarditis.

It is usually seen following:

  1. Myocardial infarction
  2. Rheumatic fever
  3. Trauma
  4. Uremia
  5. Radiation
  6. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
  7. Severe pneumonia

Other options:

Option A: Caseous pericarditis can be due to tuberculosis or a malignant neoplasm (from the lung or breast). It can also be seen following cardiac surgery. Caseous pericarditis is almost always tubercular in origin.

Option C: Hemorrhagic pericarditis is composed of blood mixed with a fibrinous or suppurative effusion. It is most commonly caused by the spread of a malignant neoplasm to the pericardial space; cytologic examination of fluid removed through a pericardial tap often reveals neoplastic cells. It usually follows cardiac surgery and is occasionally responsible for significant blood loss or even tamponade, requiring reoperation.

Option D: Purulent/Suppurative pericarditis: It may be caused by bacterial, mycotic, or parasitic invasion. The inflammation may extend into the surrounding mediastinum. It usually results in organization and, therefore, constrictive pericarditis with clinical sequelae. The entry of the pathogen into the pericardium may be by:

  • direct extension
  • seeding from blood
  • lymphatic spread
  • seeding by instrumentation

question: One week following a diagnosis of myocardial infarction,  a patient experiences precordial pain and develops a fever of 101.5°F. Physical examination is remarkable for a loud friction rub. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, fever, pericardial pain, and effusion 4 weeks after MI are suggestive of Dressler's syndrome. The aetiology of Dressler's syndrome is autoimmune.

It is also known as post-myocardial infarction (post-MI) cardiac injury syndrome. It occurs one week to as long as two to three months after MI.

A fibrinous or fibrinohemorrhagic pericarditis usually develops around the second or third day following a transmural infarct. It is a result of the underlying myocardial inflammation.

Dressler's syndrome is believed to have an autoimmune aetiology. There is an inflammatory reaction to myocardial neo-antigens formed as a result of MI.

question: A 52-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction 4 weeks back,  develops fever,  pericardial chest pain and pericardial effusion. What is the aetiology behind the patient's present condition?

explanationHtml:
Concretio cordis occurs in advanced cases of constrictive pericarditis.

In constrictive pericarditis, a thick 0.5 - 1cm fibrous scar tissue is formed. This can obliterate the pericardial space and sometimes calcify. In extreme cases, it can resemble a plaster mold and is known as concretio cordis.

Constrictive pericarditis may be idiopathic or can occur following:

  1. Pericarditis - serous or caseous
  2. Cardiac surgery
  3. Heavy irradiation

Adhesive mediastinopericarditis occurs when adhesion and fibrosis extend from the parietal pericardium into the mediastinum

Note: Soldier’s plaque is a focal, pearly, thickened epicardial plaque. It is indicative of healed pericarditis.

explanationHtml:
Myxomas are the most common primary tumours of the heart in adults.

90% of myxomas are located in the atria. The left-to-right ratio of the myxoma is approximately 4:1. The region of the fossa ovalis in the atrial septum is the favoured site of origin.

Histopathological examination shows stellate or globular myxoma, “lepidic," cells. Peculiar vessel-like or gland-like structures are characteristic. Major clinical manifestations are fever and malaise (due to IL-6). Valvular “ball-valve” obstruction or embolization can occur.

Important points on cardiac tumors:

  • Most common cardiac tumour: metastasis
  • Most common benign cardiac tumour: atrial myxoma
  • Most common primary cardiac tumour in adults: atrial myxoma
  • Most common primary cardiac tumour in children: rhabdomyoma

The image given below shows an abundant amorphous extracellular matrix. It contains scattered multinucleate myxoma cells in various groupings, including abnormal vessel-like formations.

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following is the most common primary tumour of the adult heart?

explanationHtml:
Atrial myxomas most commonly occur in the left atrium.

Myxoma is usually single, but can rarely be multiple. The region of the fossa ovalis in the atrial septum is the favoured site of origin. Mobile tumours exert a “wrecking-ball” effect, causing damage to the valve leaflets.

They can be sporadic or familial.

Sporadic Type Myxoma Familial Type Myxoma
Single Multiple
Postoperative recurrance NIL Present
Younger age
Left atria - Most common site

The image given below shows a gross picture of an atrial cardiac myxoma arising from the region of the fossa ovalis and extending to mitral valve orifice:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Cardiac myxomas are present in 30–40% of Carney complex patients. Null mutations in the PRKAR1A gene are seen in Carney's complex. The PRKAR1A gene encodes a regulatory subunit of a cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase (Carney complex).

Skin lesions are the most common manifestation of the Carney complex. The most common type of endocrine tumour in the Carney complex is the primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD). It is a form of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia that leads to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-independent Cushing syndrome.

NAME syndrome and LAMB syndrome are subsets of the Carney complex. The LAMB acronym refers to Lentigines, Atrial Myxoma, and Blue nevi. NAME refers to Nevi, Atrial myxoma, neurofibromas, and Ephelids.

Components of Carney Complex:

  • Skin pigmented lesions (lentigines, blue nevi, other)
  • Myxomas (cutaneous, mucosal, cardiac, other)
  • PPNAD (Cushing Syndrome)
  • GH-PRL-producing adenomas (acromegaly)
  • Leydig or Sertoli cell tumors
  • Ovarian cystadenoma or carcinoma
  • Thyroid adenoma or cancer
  • Psammomatous melanotic schwannoma
  • Breast ductal adenoma
  • Osteochondromyxoma
  • Cancers (liver, pancreas, adrenal)

Carney triad:

  • Extra-adrenal paraganglioma
  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
  • Pulmonary chondroma

Carney–Stratakis Syndrome: Familial paraganglioma and gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

Mutations in GNAS1 are associated with McCune-Albright syndrome. It is also associated with myxomas.

question: What is the most common site of a cardiac myxoma?

explanationHtml:
The given histological slide shows abundant spider cells. They are seen in rhabdomyoma.

Microscopically, they are composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes. Routine histologic processing often artifactually reduces the abundant cytoplasm to thin strands that stretch from the nucleus to the surface membrane. This appearance is referred to as “spider” cells.

Rhabdomyoma is the most frequent primary tumour of the pediatric heart. 50% of cases are associated with tuberous sclerosis, with mutations in the tumour-suppressor genes TSC1 and TSC2. They are usually multiple and occur in the ventricles preferentially. They often regress spontaneously and may, therefore, be considered as hamartomas.

explanationHtml:
The single most important long-term limitation of cardiac transplantation is allograft arteriopathy.

It is the single most important long-term limitation for cardiac transplantation. It is a late, progressive, diffusely stenosing intimal proliferation in the coronary arteries, leading to ischemic injury. It can lead to silent myocardial infarction since transplant patients have denervated hearts and do not experience angina. Progressive congestive heart failure and sudden cardiac death can also occur.

Other complications following cardiac transplantation:

Allograft rejection: It is the primary concern that requires close surveillance. Both classic cellular rejection and antibody-mediated rejection are recognized. Cellular rejection is characterized by interstitial lymphocytic inflammation, with associated myocyte damage.

Infection and malignancies, particularly Epstein–Barr virus-associated B-cell lymphomas, can happen but are not the main long-term limitation.

The image given below shows allograft arteriopathy. There is severe diffuse concentric intimal thickening producing critical stenosis. The internal elastic lamina and media are intact (Movat pentachrome stain, elastin black).

[[figure-1]]

question: The single most important long-term limitation of cardiac transplantation is ________

explanationHtml:
The image shows a heart with left ventricular hypertrophy. The most common cause of left ventricular hypertrophy is chronic hypertension due to chronically increased afterload.

Other options:

Option A: Malignant hypertension causes acute cardiac injury, rather than the gradual hypertrophic changes.

Option C: Amyloidosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy characterized by abnormal protein deposits stiffening the myocardium. The ventricular thickening is due to infiltration, rather than hypertrophy, of the muscle cells.

Option D: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy involves asymmetric thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the left ventricle free wall. On longitudinal sectioning, the normally round-to-ovoid left ventricular cavity may be compressed into a “banana-like” configuration by bulging of the ventricular septum into the lumen.

question: What is the most common cause of the condition shown in the given image?

correctAnswer: D. A patient who is a marathon runner who came for a pre-run evaluation
explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, a marathon runner will have cardiac hypertrophy with increased capillary density. Aerobic exercise, e.g., long-distance running, is associated with volume-load hypertrophy accompanied by an increase in capillary density. This is not seen in other forms of hypertrophy. This decreases resting heart rate and blood pressure.

In hypertrophy due to pressure or volume overload, there is a sustained increase in mechanical work. This cause myocytes to increase in size thus increasing the size and weight of the heart. The hypertrophied heart has an increased oxygen consumption but decreased supply. This is because hypertrophy is not accompanied by a proportional increase in capillary numbers. This leads to ischemia-related decompensation, which can evolve to cardiac failure and eventually lead to death.

The causes and consequences of hypertrophy are summarized in the below image.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: A patient with systemic hypertension has pressure-overload hypertrophy.

Option B: A patient with an echo finding of an aortic valvular area of 0.6cm² is suggestive of aortic stenosis. There is pressure-overload hypertrophy.

Option C: A patient with a high-pitched holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex is suggestive of mitral regurgitation. There is volume-overload hypertrophy.

Note: Heart weight, rather than wall thickness, is the best measure of hypertrophy in dilated hearts.

explanationHtml:
Most congenital heart diseases arise from faulty embryogenesis during gestational weeks 3 to 8 when major cardiovascular structures form and begin to function.

The most common congenital heart disease is ventricular septal defect (VSD), whereas the 2nd most common is atrial septal defect (ASD).
question: Most congenital heart diseases arise between what weeks of embryogenesis?

explanationHtml:
Char syndrome is associated with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

The clinical presentation of this syndrome includes PDA with facial dysmorphism and abnormal fifth digits.

The following images show the facial dysmorphism associated with Char syndrome, such as flattened cheekbones, depressed nasal bridge, broad and prominent nose with a short philtrum.

[[figure-1]]
question: What congenital heart defect is associated with Char syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Coarctation of the aorta is a feature of Turner's syndrome, not Down's syndrome.

Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common cause of congenital heart disease (CHD). Cardiac defects in Down's syndrome are due to endocardial cushion defects.

Cardiac defects in various chromosomal anomalies are as follows:

Syndrome Cardiac defects
Down's syndrome (Trisomy 21)
  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Atrial septal defect
Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13)
  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Atrial septal defect
Edward's syndrome (Trisomy 18)
  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Atrial septal defect
  • Dextroposition
Turner syndrome (Monosomy X)
  • Bicuspid aortic valve
  • Coarctation of the aorta
  • Dilated ascending aorta
question: Which of the following cardiac defects is not associated with Down's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is the most common type of ASD.

ASDs are abnormal, fixed openings in the atrial septum caused by incomplete tissue formation that allow communication of blood between the left and right atria.

It results in a left-to-right shunt. Excess blood flow through the ASD and/or the pulmonary valve results in a murmur. They are generally well-tolerated and usually do not become symptomatic before the age of 30 years.

ASDs are classified according to their location:

  • Secundum ASD (90%) - usually isolated defects, can be of any size, multiple or fenestrated
  • Primum anomalies (5%) - occur adjacent to the AV valves, often associated with AV valve defects and/or VSD
  • Sinus venosus defects (5%) - located near the SVC entrance and can be associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return to the right atrium

The following image portrays different types of ASD:

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the most common type of atrial septal defect?

explanationHtml:
Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) is a feature of the tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), not left ventricular hypertrophy.

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common congenital cyanotic heart disease. It is a conotruncal anomaly; the four cardinal features of TOF are as follows:

  1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
  2. Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonary stenosis)
  3. An aorta that overrides the VSD
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy

It is the most common type of cyanotic congenital heart disease (CHD). The heart is typically enlarged and is classically boot-shaped due to marked right ventricular hypertrophy.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following is not a feature of tetralogy of Fallot?

explanationHtml:
The given features are suggestive of Williams (Williams–Beuren) syndrome. It is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis.

This condition is due to deletions on chromosome 7, which includes the gene for elastin. These mutations may cause supravalvular stenosis by disrupting elastin–smooth muscle cell interactions during aortic morphogenesis. There is thickening of the ascending aortic wall and consequent luminal constriction.

Other features of the syndrome include:

  • Elfin facies - wide mouth, chubby cheeks, long philtrum, small nose, and delicate chin (as shown in the image)
  • Cognitive abnormalities
  • Intellectual disability (usually mild)
  • Personality changes - over-friendliness to strangers
  • Hypotonia
  • Connective tissue abnormalities
  • Endocrine abnormalities (hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, hypothyroidism, early puberty)

[[figure-1]]
question: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD for evaluation of cognitive impairment. Parents report that the child is overly-friendly with strangers. On examination, elfin facies and hypotonia are noted. Investigations reveal hypercalcemia. Which of the following cardiac defects is associated with this syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease. Mitral stenosis is the most common lesion in rheumatic heart disease.

In rheumatic mitral stenosis, calcification and fibrous bridging across the valvular commissures create fish-mouth or buttonhole stenosis. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is associated with a loud S1.

The most common causes of various valvular diseases are:

  • Aortic stenosis (AS) - calcification due to normal aging or congenitally bicuspid aortic valves
  • Aortic regurgitation (AR) - dilatation of the ascending aorta, often secondary to hypertension and/or aging
  • Mitral regurgitation (MR) - myxomatous degeneration (mitral valve prolapse)
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of mitral stenosis?

correctAnswer: C. It is due to abnormal fusion of valve commissures
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario and echo findings are suggestive of calcific aortic stenosis secondary to bicuspid aortic valve (2 functional cusps). It is due to incomplete separation of valve commissures during development, not abnormal fusion.

In a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve, the 2 functional cusps are usually of unequal size. The larger cusp has a midline raphe that results from incomplete commissural separation during development. The raphe is frequently a major site of calcific deposits.

This condition is associated with mutations in the following areas:

  • Chromosomes 18q, 5q, and 13q
  • Chromosome 9q - loss-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 gene

Late complications include:

  • Aortic stenosis or regurgitation
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Aortic dilation and/or dissection.
  • Predisposed to progressive calcification - Approximately 50% of cases of aortic stenosis in adults.

Note: Acquired bicuspid valves result from abnormal fusion of valve commissures because of an acquired deformity (rheumatic valve disease). It produces a conjoined cusp that is generally twice the size of the nonconjoined cusp.

[[figure-1]]

Midline of larger cusp is major site of calcification

question: A 42-year-old man presented with chest pain and exertional dyspnea for the past 2 months. He has no history of cardiac disease. Examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography was done, which revealed an aortic valve with 2 functional cusps and a valve area of 0.8 sq. cm. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features and echocardiography findings are suggestive of mitral valve prolapse (MVP) or Barlow syndrome. It is not associated with degenerative calcified deposits (seen in calcific valvular degeneration, not MVP).

Barlow syndrome is more common in females. It may be an isolated condition or, less commonly, can be associated with connective tissue disorders, such as Marfan's syndrome.

In this condition, there is mitral annular dilatation, accompanied by floppy mitral valve leaflets. They prolapse or balloon back into the left atrium during systole. The following pathological changes are seen:

  • Interchordal ballooning (hooding) of the mitral leaflets
  • Thick, rubbery, redundant leaflets
  • Thickened mural endocardium

The main histologic change is marked thickening of the spongiosa layer with deposition of mucoid called myxomatous degeneration.

Most individuals diagnosed with MVP are asymptomatic. On auscultation, a mid-systolic click, sometimes followed by a mid to late systolic murmur, is heard. Chest pain mimicking angina and dyspnea occur rarely.

The complications include:

  • Infective endocarditis
  • Mitral insufficiency
  • Stroke or other systemic infarcts
  • Arrhythmias
  • Sudden cardiac death (rarely)

Note: Degenerative calcified deposits are usually seen in aortic stenosis
question: A 45-year-old woman who came for a routine check-up was incidentally found to have a late systolic murmur with a mid-systolic click. Echocardiography revealed thickening and redundancy of mitral leaflets with bulging into the left atrium. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. Mitral stenosis is not a feature of cardiac involvement in this condition.

Carcinoid heart disease refers to the cardiac manifestations caused by the bioactive compounds released by carcinoid tumors. It mainly produces 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, a metabolite of serotonin.

The classic findings in this disease are the primary involvement of the right heart endocardium and valves which show fibrotic plaque-like thickening of the endocardium and tricuspid regurgitation. Pulmonary stenosis may also be seen. Involvement of the myocardium is less common.

The left side of the heart is less commonly affected because the pulmonary vascular bed degrades the mediators. However, left heart carcinoid lesions can occur in the setting of ASD or VSD, or in the case of primary pulmonary carcinoid tumors.
question: A 48-year-old man presented with dull aching abdominal pain and diarrhea for the past 2 months. On examination, his face and chest appeared flushed. In a 24-hour urine sample, 5HIAA levels were elevated. CT scan of the abdomen revealed a mass in the terminal ileum. Cardiac involvement in this syndrome is characterized by all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
The clinical presentation, characterized by skin flushing, wheezing, and watery diarrhea, accompanied by elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels, suggests a diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid heart disease most commonly affects the tricuspid valve. The described systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, which increases during inspiration, is classically seen in tricuspid regurgitation, also known as Carvallo's sign.

The most common features seen in carcinoid heart disease are tricuspid regurgitation followed by pulmonary stenosis. Although pulmonary stenosis can occur in carcinoid syndrome, the described murmur is typically associated with tricuspid regurgitation.

The left-sided valves are usually spared, as the pulmonary vasculature metabolizes the compounds secreted.
question: A 45-year-old patient presents with episodes of skin flushing, wheezing, and watery diarrhea that have persisted for the past five months. explanationHtml:
Acute rheumatic fever is an immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease that typically develops a few weeks after an infection with Group A streptococcus (GAS). It is caused by an autoimmune reaction triggered by molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal antigens that cross-react with host tissues.

The least commonly affected valve in acute rheumatic fever is the pulmonary valve, as it is a low-pressure system and so would have less interaction with immune complexes due to less turbulent flow and mechanical stress. Whereas the left-sided valves are more likely to interact with immune complexes and are commonly affected.

The most commonly affected valve is the mitral valve, followed by the aortic valve.

This condition classically occurs a few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis or, less commonly, skin infections. The antibodies to streptococcal cell-wall antigen cross-react with myocardial antigen, resulting in macrophage activation and inflammation.

Acute rheumatic carditis is a common manifestation of active RF and may progress over time to chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD), mainly manifesting as valvular abnormalities. Damage to heart tissue may be caused by a combination of antibody and T-cell-mediated reactions.

Infective endocarditis is classified into two forms: acute and subacute.

  • Acute - infection of a previously normal heart valve by a highly virulent organism
  • Subacute - infection in previously deformed valves by organisms of lower virulence (S.viridans, S. epidermidis, HACEK). It has a more indolent course.

question: A 50-year-old man with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis underwent prosthetic mitral valve insertion. In the first 2 months following surgery, he is at the highest risk of infection with which of the following organisms?

explanationHtml:
The given features and the image showing painful Osler nodes are suggestive of infective endocarditis. An echo showing a valve-related mass is a major criterion according to Duke’s criteria.

Infective endocarditis (IE) is a microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural endocardium. The aorta, aneurysms, other blood vessels, and prosthetic devices can also become infected. Most infections are bacterial.

Vegetation on heart valves is the classic hallmark of IE. They are friable, bulky, potentially destructive lesions. They contain fibrin, inflammatory cells, bacteria, or other organisms. The mitral valve is most commonly involved.

Complications of infective endocarditis:

  • Cardiac complications - valvular insufficiency or stenosis, myocardial ring abscess, suppurative pericarditis
  • Embolic complications - left-sided (brain, spleen, kidney) or right-sided lesion (lung infarct and abscess)
  • Renal complications - embolic infarcts, focal (more common) or diffuse glomerulonephritis (less common)
question: A 30-year-old man presented with a high-grade fever, chills, and breathlessness for 4 days. He has no other known medical conditions but has a history of IV drug abuse. explanationHtml:

Other options:

Option C: Partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, not complete dehiscence of prosthetic valve, is a part of the major criteria

Option D: Documentation of four minor criteria suggests a possible diagnosis rather than a definitive clinical diagnosis. Definite diagnoses include:

  • Pathological criteria: microorganisms or active endocarditis identified in a vegetation/intracardiac abscess from cardiac tissue, prosthetic material, or arterial embolus.
  • Clinical criteria: if 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor of the criteria are met.

question: A 40-year-old woman presented with chest pain and breathlessness for 1 month. Examination revealed a regurgitant murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed vegetations on both sides of mitral valve leaflets. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in infective endocarditis.

Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Aortic and mitral valves are the most commonly affected; however, in some cases, the right heart valves may be involved.

Vegetations may be single or multiple and may involve one or more valves. Embolization often occurs and may lead to septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms at the site of lodgement due to the presence of virulent organisms in the emboli.

question: Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in which condition?

explanationHtml:
The rightly matched vegetations with the conditions that they are seen are as follows: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B

Rheumatic heart disease often presents with rheumatic fever phase, where small, warty 1- 2 mm vegetations, also called veruccae, extend along the lines of closure of the valve leaflets. The cardinal anatomical changes of the mitral valve in chronic RHD are:

  • Leaflet thickening
  • Commissural fusion and shortening
  • Thickening and fusion of the tendinous chords

Infective endocarditis features large, irregular, friable masses on the valve cusps that can extend onto the chordae. These vegetations can be solitary or multiple and may involve one or more valves. They are potentially destructive lesions containing fibrin, inflammatory cells, bacteria, or other organisms. They can erode into the underlying myocardium and produce a ring abscess. They are prone to embolizations, leading to abscess formation wherever they lodge due to the presence of virulent organisms. Consequently, this may result in sequelae such as septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms.

Subacute infective endocarditis contains less destructive vegetations. They contain granulation tissue at their bases, indicative of healing. Fibrosis, calcification, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate can develop over time.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis is characterized by one or more small, 1-5 mm, sterile vegetations that are usually attached at the line of closure. They are seen associated with hypercoagulable states like chronic DIC or malignancy. They are loosely attached to the underlying valve and are non-destructive. They do not cause any inflammatory reaction, but they can be a source of systemic embolization.

Libman-Sacks endocarditis involves small to medium-sized, 1-4 mm, sterile vegetations associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. These can appear on one or both sides of the leaflets, on the valve surface, chordae, or anywhere on the endocardium. The vegetations form due to immune complex deposition and complement activation. They cause severe valvulitis, leading to fibrinoid necrosis of the valve tissue. Continued damage to the valves can result in scarring and leaflet fusion.
question:

  1. Rheumatic heart disease (RHD)
  2. Infective endocarditis (IE)
  3. Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis

correctAnswer: B. Vegetations > 5 mm size are seen
explanationHtml:
Vegetations in non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) are 1 to 5 mm in size.

NBTE is seen in patients with debilitating conditions such as cancer and sepsis or systemic hypercoagulable states. Hence, it is also called marantic endocarditis.

Small sterile thrombi are deposited loosely on the leaflets of cardiac valves, forming either single or multiple vegetations along the lines of closure of the leaflets or cusps. These thrombi are non-invasive and do not provoke an inflammatory response. They may serve as a source of systemic emboli.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario in this child is strongly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change disease (MCD). It is distinguished by the lack of immune deposits observed in biopsy and histopathological examination.

It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peaks between 2–6 years).

Biopsy findings of MCD are as follows:

  • Light microscopy - glomeruli appear normal (hence called 'minimal change')
  • Immunofluorescence studies - no Ig or complement deposits
  • Electron microscopy - diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells (podocytopathy)

Other options:

Option A: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis, which occurs due to immune complex deposition in the mesangium following a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection and usually presents with hematuria. It generally occurs within a week after infection

Option B: Low C3 levels are typically linked to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which occurs 1 to 3 weeks after infection and is marked by a high ASO titer. Immune complex deposits of IgG, IgM, and C3 with a characteristic lumpy-bumpy appearance are observed.

Option D: Alport syndrome is an inherited defect of type IV collagen that affects the glomerular basement membrane, leading to glomerulonephritis and potentially progressing to end-stage renal disease. It is usually associated with other sensory features such as anterior lenticonus and sensorineural hearing loss.

question: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of generalized swelling of the body and frothy urine. Urinary examination revealed grade 3 proteinuria and the presence of hyaline and fatty casts. There were no red blood cells in the urine. explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. It can be caused by mutations in the following components of the glomerular filtration barrier:

  • Nephrin and podocin are molecular components of the slit diaphragm complex
  • Alpha-actinin 4 is a component of the foot process cytoskeleton

Megalin is not a component of the glomerular filtration barrier. It is present in proximal convoluted tubular cells. Mutations in megalin may lead to some proteinuria but not nephrotic syndrome because glomerular filtration of proteins is not affected.

Note: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is diagnosed when proteinuria persists after a full steroid dose for 4 weeks in children and 4 months in adults. The treatment plan typically includes a renal biopsy to identify the underlying pathology, followed by calcineurin inhibitors like tacrolimus or cyclosporine.
question: A 10-year-old boy is brought for a follow-up visit. He was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome 3 months ago and had been started on a course of oral prednisolone. explanationHtml:

Other options:

Option C: Factor V Leiden mutation leads to resistance to degradation by activated protein C; it is not associated with membranous nephropathy

Option D: Protein C is an anticoagulant, and nephrotic syndrome results in the urinary loss of both protein C and protein S, thereby contributing to a hypercoagulable state.

question: A 67-year-old man presents with sudden onset flank pain and hematuria. Ultrasound reveals enlargement of both kidneys. He is a known case of membranous nephropathy. What is the likely pathophysiology for his current presentation?

It is a podocytopathy characterized by degeneration and focal disruption of visceral epithelial cells, along with effacement of foot processes. explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, immunofluorescence findings, and the image showing proliferating mesangial cells and capillary endothelial cells are suggestive of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type 2 (MPGN type 2) or dense-deposit disease.

This condition belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies and primarily affects children and young adults. It is associated with a dysregulation in the alternative complement pathway. It is clinically and morphologically similar to MPGN type 1 but pathogenetically distinct from it.

In this condition, a circulating autoantibody called C3 nephritic factor is present, which stabilizes the C3 convertase enzyme. The stabilized C3 convertase enhances C3 activation and consumption causing hypocomplementemia. Patients will have consistently decreased serum C3 levels, but normal C1 and C4 levels.

The prognosis is poor, with about half of these patients progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
question: A 29-year-old man presented with complaints of blood in his urine.  Urine analysis was positive for proteins and red cell casts.  A renal biopsy was done as shown below. This results in beta-gamma bridging, characterized by a "bridge" appearance between the beta and gamma regions. This phenomenon is not specific and may occur in other conditions as well.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis. It is usually preceded by an acute streptococcal sore throat or impetigo around 1-4 weeks prior.

It usually presents with features of nephritic syndrome, including:

  • Hematuria
  • Red cell casts in the urine
  • Azotemia, oliguria
  • Hypertension
  • Mild to moderate proteinuria
  • Edema

On microscopy, the following findings are seen:

  • Light microscopy - enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with influx of leucocytes (endocapillary proliferation)
  • Electron microscopy - subepithelial humps
  • Immunofluorescence - granular IgG and C3 deposits on glomerular basement membrane and mesangium

question: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops fever, oliguria, periorbital edema and smoky cola-colored urine 2-weeks after recovery from sore throat. His renal biopsy image is given below. Which of the following statements is false about the given condition?

correctAnswer: A. Proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and WBCs in Bowman space
explanationHtml:
The given image shows a crescent-shaped mass of proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and leukocytes within the Bowman capsule. It is a characteristic feature of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) or crescentic glomerulonephritis.

[[figure-1]]

RPGN is a type of nephritic syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury with necrosis and formation of crescents. It is usually immune-mediated and may be associated with circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs), anti-GBM antibodies, and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

Injury to the glomerular capillary wall leads to the escape of procoagulant factors and cytokines into the Bowman space. This triggers:

  • Proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells - mostly parietal, but also some visceral cells
  • Recruitment of leukocytes and fibroblasts
  • Pathognomonic crescents - due to the circumferential accumulation of these cells and fibrin

The crescents progressively compress the capillary tuft. This results in a rapid decline of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and, consequently, acute kidney injury (AKI). Thus, the degree of crescent formation correlates with the severity and the prognosis of the disease.

Other options:

Option B: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall may indicate membranous nephropathy. It is characterized by irregular spikes from the basement membrane, best visualized with silver stains. The light microscopy image is given below.

[[figure-2]]

Option C: Proliferating mesangial cells and increased matrix deposition in the mesangium can be seen commonly in IgA nephropathy, but also in other proliferative conditions; another more appropriate option is present.

Option D: Proliferation of capillaries with fibrin deposition can be seen in various conditions, such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; a more specific description for the HPE is present.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is seen in HIV, SLE, CLL, and Hepatitis B.

MPGN is caused due to immune-mediated injury. It often presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture.

The causes of MPGN are as follows:

  • Primary MPGN (Idiopathic)
  • Secondary MPGN
    • System lupus erythematosus (SLE)
    • α1-antitrypsin deficiency
    • Infections - hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, schistosomiasis, endocarditis, infected ventriculoatrial shunts, chronic visceral abscesses
    • Malignancies - chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

MPGN is characterized by the proliferation of cells predominantly in the mesangium and the capillary loops. Hence, it is also called mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis. There are 2 types of MPGN:

  • Type I - It is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes along with mesangiocapillary proliferation. Electron microscopy shows subendothelial deposits with the characteristic double contour/tram-track appearance.
  • Type II - It is now known as dense-deposit disease, as electron microscopy shows intramembranous dense deposits. It belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies.

Light microscopy findings of MPGN are as follows:

  • Lobular glomeruli with proliferating mesangial cells, capillary endothelium, and infiltrating leukocytes (endocapillary proliferation)
  • Duplication of the basement membrane gives a double contour or tram-track appearance. It is especially evident in silver or PAS stains.

The gross image suggests that the patient had autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This condition is not associated with hepatic fibrosis. However, patients with autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) have congenital hepatic fibrosis.

ADPKD is associated with mutations in PKD1, encoding polycystin 1, and PKD2, encoding polycystin 2. The multiple expanding cysts of both kidneys ultimately destroy the renal parenchyma and cause renal failure. Cysts arise from the tubules throughout the nephron and, therefore, have variable lining epithelia.

The common extrarenal manifestations of ADPKD include:
  • Hepatic cysts - most common
  • Seminal vesicle cysts can result in infertility
  • Arachnoid membrane cysts are usually asymptomatic, but they can potentially raise the risk of developing a subdural hematoma
  • Pancreatic cysts
  • Splenic cysts
  • Intracranial berry aneurysms
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhages
  • Mitral valve prolapse
There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients, but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proven. ADPKD patients have a three times higher risk of developing bronchiectasis.

question: A 35-year-old man died in a road traffic accident. On autopsy, the following appearance of the kidney was noted. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

The polycystin-2 mutation is less commonly involved and less severe.

Polycystin-1 is encoded by the PKD1 gene located on chromosome 16p13.3. It is expressed in tubular epithelial cells, particularly those of the distal nephron. It contains domains that are usually involved in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. Mutations in PKD1 account for about 85% of cases of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) and it causes a more severe form of the disease.

Polycystin-2 is an integral membrane protein that is expressed in all segments of the renal tubules and in many extrarenal tissues. It functions as a Ca2+ cation channel. Overall, it causes a less severe form of ADPKD disease.

The most common extrarenal site of cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the liver.

Cysts occur much less frequently in the spleen, pancreas, and lungs. There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients, but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proven.

explanationHtml:
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is caused by mutations in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21-p23, which encodes fibrocystin.

The gene is highly expressed in adult and fetal kidneys, and also in the liver and pancreas. Fibrocystin has been localized to the primary cilium of tubular cells.

The serious manifestations of ARPKD are usually present at birth and may cause death by renal failure. The following gross findings are seen:

  • Enlarged kidneys with a smooth external appearance
  • Sponge-like appearance due to numerous small cysts in the cortex and medulla
  • Dilated, elongated channels at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing the medulla and cortex

Microscopic examination reveals cylindrical, or less commonly, saccular dilation of all collecting tubules lined with cuboidal cells. In nearly all cases, the liver contains cysts associated with portal fibrosis and proliferation of the portal bile ducts, known as congenital hepatic fibrosis.

It is a benign epithelial neoplasm. Grossly, these tumors appear tan or mahogany brown and relatively homogeneous. They are usually well encapsulated with a central scar in one-third of cases.

The most important determinant of malignant potential in the papillary type of renal tumor is the size of the tumor.

The papillary type of renal tumors includes:

Small renal papillary growths are fairly common and incidentally found. Ruling out of malignancy is one of the processes carried out during the evaluation of donor transplant kidneys.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the second most common type of renal cell carcinoma and it arises from proximal tubules. It can be multifocal or bilateral. It is typically hemorrhagic and cystic, especially when large.

It is often a circumscribed tumor composed of papillae formed by delicate fibrovascular cores that often contain foamy macrophages and Psammoma bodies.

It has two histological types:

  • Type 1 papillary RCC - single layer of cells on the basement membrane and low-grade nuclear features
  • Type 2 papillary RCC - pseudostratification of cells and usually has high-grade nuclear features

question: Which of the following subtypes of renal cell carcinoma is matched incorrectly with its respective cytogenetic patterns?

explanationHtml:
Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma is the most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for 70% to 80% of renal cell cancers.

It is most likely to arise from the proximal tubular epithelium as solitary lesions. It has a characteristic tendency to invade the renal vein. The histological features are:

  • Rounded or polygonal tumor cells
  • Abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids
  • Arranged in a solid to trabecular (cordlike) or tubular pattern

explanationHtml:
Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient renal cell carcinoma does not show papillary architecture. It is associated with a bubbly appearance of histopathology.

It is a malignant epithelial tumor associated with germline mutations in the SDH gene. It is composed of vacuolated, eosinophilic-clear cells arranged in a solid, nested, or tubular pattern. The presence of the vacuoles imparts the characteristic bubbly appearance, as shown below.

They are arranged in solid sheets with a concentration of the largest cells around blood vessels.

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma can differentiated from oncocytoma and clear cell RCC as follows:

  • Oncocytoma does not show perinuclear halo whereas chromophobe RCC shows perinuclear halo
  • CK7 is diffusely positive in chromophobe RCC but it is negative in clear-cell RCC.

Chromophobe RCC cannot be histologically graded because of its innate nuclear atypia.

explanationHtml:
The renal tumor commonly associated with Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It has an excellent prognosis.

It constitutes 5% of all renal carcinomas. It arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Cytogenetic testing of the tumor shows multiple chromosomal losses and extreme hypodiploidy.

Collecting duct carcinoma or Bellini duct carcinoma shows a characteristic hobnail pattern and prominent desmoplastic stroma on microscopy.

The hobnail pattern refers to the bulbous nuclear projections of epithelial cells that protrude into the lumen as little bumps. It is associated with tubular, tubulopapillary, or tubulocystic pattern.

Collecting duct carcinoma arises from the principal cells of the renal collecting ducts of Bellini. The majority of these tumors are associated with poor outcome, due to their highly aggressive clinical course.

Individuals with the sickle cell trait are at a higher risk of developing medullary renal cell carcinoma.

It is a rare, highly aggressive neoplasm and is morphologically similar to collecting duct carcinoma.

The hypoxic microenvironment in the renal medulla created by hyperosmolarity, low pH, and stasis enhances red blood sickling and ischemic damage. This leads to chronic regenerative proliferation of medullary epithelium and activation of hypoxia-induced signaling pathways, which in turn promote neoplastic change.

The histological section of renal medullary carcinoma showing prominent cytological atypia is shown below:

It is also associated with Psammoma bodies.

This condition is caused by translocations of the TFE3 gene located on Xp11.2, which results in overexpression of the TFE3 transcription factor. It often occurs in young patients and is associated with a poor prognosis.
