question: A pathologist is studying the histopathological slide from a nephrectomy specimen from a patient with renal carcinoma. He observes neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm and papillary architecture. Which of the following subtypes of renal carcinoma is this likely to be?

correctAnswer: D. It occurs commonly in females
explanationHtml:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is more common among males, with a male to female ratio of 2:1.

Renal cell carcinoma may arise from the proximal convoluted tubules (PCT). The classical clinical features of renal cell carcinoma are costovertebral pain, palpable mass, and painless hematuria. It characteristically invades the renal vein and has a high tendency for distant metastasis.

Paraneoplastic manifestations of renal cell carcinoma include:

  • Polycythemia
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypertension
  • Hepatic dysfunction
  • Feminization or masculinization
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Eosinophilia
  • Leukemoid reactions

  • Lungs

Collecting duct renal cell carcinoma has the worst prognosis of all renal cell carcinoma subtypes.

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma has the best prognosis.

explanationHtml:
Renal cell carcinoma is CK7 negative and CK20 negative.

The most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma is clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, which is CK7 negative. Therefore, in determining the origin of cancer of unknown primary, immunohistochemistry (IHC) expression of renal cell carcinoma will generally be CK7 negative and CK20 negative. explanationHtml:
Hunner ulcers are chronic mucosal ulcers that are characteristic of interstitial cystitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome.

It is a rare idiopathic condition that occurs most frequently in women. It presents with intermittent severe suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, urgency, hematuria, and dysuria.

The following cystoscopic findings are seen in the bladder mucosa:

  • Fissures
  • Punctate hemorrhages (glomerulations)

The microscopic findings include:

  • Mucosal ulceration covered by fibrin and necrotic material
  • Increased numbers of mucosal mast cells
  • Submucosal edema

In later stages, transmural fibrosis may occur, leading to a contracted bladder. Biopsy must be done to rule out carcinoma in situ, which may clinically mimic interstitial cystitis.

The following image shows a Hunner's ulcer in a patient with interstitial cystitis.

question: A 36-year-old woman presented with intermittent suprapubic pain, increased urinary frequency, and dysuria for 2 months. A cystoscopy revealed the presence of Hunner ulcers. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario with the presence of Michaelis-Gutmann bodies is suggestive of malakoplakia.

Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory reaction resulting from acquired defects in phagocyte function, commonly affecting the urinary bladder. It can also be seen in other organ systems like the gastrointestinal tract, female genital tract, and central nervous system.

It is seen in chronic bacterial infection, mostly by Escherichia coli or occasionally Proteus species.

Grossly, it presents as soft, yellow-brown, slightly raised mucosal plaques. Microscopically, the following findings are seen:

  • Large, foamy macrophages containing -
    • Abundant granular cytoplasm due to undigested bacterial products
    • Michaelis-Gutmann bodies - PAS-positive basophilic concretions due to iron and calcium deposits in lysosomes
  • Occasional multinucleated giant cells and lymphocytes

[[figure-1]]

Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.
question: A 31-year-old man presented with a history of recurrent UTIs and hematuria. Urine culture showed growth of E. coli. Flexible cystoscopy revealed yellow-brown soft plaques with a central umbilication. Microscopy of the plaque showed Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of polypoid cystitis is indwelling catheters.

Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from mucosal irritation. It may also be associated with radiation therapy and malignant tumors. It usually involves the posterior wall of the bladder.

Grossly, it may show bulbous or papillary appearance and may be confused with papillary urothelial carcinoma. Microscopically, the papillary projections are broad-based, non-branching, and without atypia. Stroma is edematous with minimal inflammation.

Options A and D: Adenovirus infection and the use of anti-cancer drugs like cyclophosphamide cause hemorrhagic cystitis.

Option B: Systemic allergic disorders cause eosinophilic cystitis.
question: What is the most common cause of polypoid cystitis?

explanationHtml:
Malakoplakia is not a metaplastic lesion of the bladder. It is a type of chronic granulomatous cystitis due to defective phagocytic function that may mimic malignancy.

Metaplastic lesions of the bladder include the following:

  • Nests of urothelium (Brunn nests) may grow downward into the lamina propria resulting in the following lesions -
    • Cystitis glandularis - epithelial cells in the center of the nest undergo metaplasia and take on a cuboidal or columnar appearance
    • Cystitis cystica - epithelial cells retract to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium
  • Squamous metaplasia - in response to injury, urothelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium.
  • Nephrogenic adenoma - due to implantation of shed renal tubular cells at sites of injured urothelium, resulting in replacement of urothelium by cuboidal epithelium with a papillary growth pattern
question: A pathologist observed a metaplastic lesion in a biopsy sample taken from the bladder mucosa of a patient. Which of the following is not a differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common tumor of the urinary bladder is transitional cell carcinoma or urothelial carcinoma.

Other epithelial tumors like squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and small cell carcinoma may also occur.

Sarcomas are distinctly uncommon in the bladder. However, the most common sarcoma in infancy or childhood is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and the most common sarcoma in the bladder in adults is leiomyosarcoma.
question: What is the most common tumor of the urinary bladder?

explanationHtml:
The image shows oval-shaped eggs with the terminal spine which is characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium. It is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

The ova are deposited in the bladder wall and incite a brisk chronic inflammatory response. This induces progressive mucosal squamous metaplasia and dysplasia and, in some instances, neoplasia.

Schistosomal infection can less frequently result in adenocarcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma.
question: A 57-year-old man presented with chronic hematuria and dysuria. Microscopic examination of urine showed the following parasitic eggs. What type of bladder carcinoma is commonly associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Isopropyl alcohol is not implicated in the causation of bladder cancer.

Benzidine, arylamines, and phenacetin are well-established risk factors for bladder cancer.
question: Which of the following is not a carcinogen for bladder cancer?

correctAnswer: B. Activating mutations in the NRAS
explanationHtml:
Activating mutation in HRAS (not NRAS) is responsible for bladder carcinoma.

Genetic changes associated with carcinoma bladder:

  • Noninvasive low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma is associated with:
    • Gain-of-function mutations of FGFR3 and HRAS genes
    • Chromosome 9p and 9q deletions
  • High-grade invasive urothelial carcinoma (either papillary or flat) is associated with:
    • Loss-of-function mutations of TP53 and RB genes

Note: Erdafitinib (kinase inhibitor) is the first targeted drug therapy approved by the FDA for the treatment of metastatic urothelial carcinoma especially in patients with mutations of FGFR3 or FGFR2.
question: Which of the following genetic changes is not associated with bladder carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
The most consistent and persistent feature of carcinoma bladder is painless hematuria.

Bladder tumors produce a wide range of clinical features including:

  • Painless hematuria - classical feature and may be the only clinical manifestation
  • Irritative urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, dysuria) - diffuse tumors or tumors at the bladder neck
  • Pyelonephritis or hydronephrosis - when the ureteral orifice is involved
  • Obstructive symptoms, palpable suprapubic mass, or lower extremity edema - late presentation with a large tumor mass
  • Weight loss and/or localized bone pain - metastatic disease
question: The most consistent and persistent feature of bladder carcinoma is:

explanationHtml:
International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) grading system classifies papillary urothelial carcinoma into 2 grades - low grade and high grade. The classification of papillary urothelial carcinoma into grades 1, 2, 3 was was part of the earlier WHO classification.

Grading of urothelial (transitional cell) tumors:

WHO/ISUP grades:

  1. Urothelial papilloma
  2. Urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
  3. Papillary urothelial carcinoma, low grade
  4. Papillary urothelial carcinoma, high grade

WHO grades (old classification):

  1. Urothelial papilloma
  2. Urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
  3. Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 1
  4. Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 2
  5. Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 3

question: Which of the following is not included in the latest International Society of Urological Pathology grading of urothelial tumors?

explanationHtml:
The staging (extent of spread) at the time of initial diagnosis is the most important prognostic factor in infiltrating urothelial carcinoma.

The prognosis of bladder carcinoma depends on the histologic grade and the stage at diagnosis. As most infiltrating urothelial carcinomas are high-grade, staging becomes the major factor to determine the prognosis.

Cystic remnants of mesonephric ducts in the cervix and vagina are termed Gartner duct cysts.

The mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts normally regress in females. Its remnants may persist into adult life as epithelial inclusions adjacent to the ovaries, tubes, and uterus. In the cervix and vagina, these ducts may be cystic and are termed Gartner duct cysts.

question: The following histological image depicts a pathology in which of the following sites?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides).

It is an uncommon vaginal tumor composed of malignant embryonal rhabdomyoblasts. It is most frequently found in infants and in children < 5 years of age. They are locally invasive tumors that cause death by penetration into the peritoneal cavity or by obstruction of the urinary tract.

Grossly, polypoid, rounded, bulky masses that appear like grape clusters can be seen. On microscopy, small tumor cells with oval nuclei, and small protrusions of cytoplasm from one end resembling a tennis racket (tadpole cells) can be seen. Beneath the vaginal epithelium, the tumor cells are crowded in a cambium layer, in the dermis.
question: A 3-year-old girl presents with a mass protruding from the anterior vaginal wall that appears like grape clusters. Histopathological examination reveals tadpole cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. LSIL progress directly to invasive carcinoma
explanationHtml:
Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) does not progress directly to invasive carcinoma. They initially progress to a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), then invasive carcinoma.

The WHO currently recommends a 2-tier system of classification for cervical lesions - low and high-grade intraepithelial lesions (LSIL and HSIL). HPV-16 is the most common HPV type associated with both LSIL and HSIL

LSILs are 10 times more common than HSILs. Most of these lesions regress spontaneously. Progression to invasive carcinoma is unpredictable and can take place over years.

question:

LSIL: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

explanationHtml:
Human papillomavirus (HPV)-16 is the most common type of HPV causing cervical carcinoma. It accounts for almost 60% of cervical cancer cases.

The ability of HPV to act as a carcinogen depends on the viral proteins E6 and E7. These proteins interfere with the activity of tumor-suppressor proteins that regulate cell growth and survival.

  • E6 - binds with p53 gene and promote its degradation
  • E7 - binds with RB gene and promotes its degradation
question: What is the most common type of human papilloma virus causing cervical carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Cervical cancer screening test, commonly known as Pap smear, is stained using the Papanicolaou method.

The time for initiating Pap smear screening is 21 years, regardless of the age of first sexual intercourse.

The sample is collected using Ayre's spatula and endocervical brush. 2 samples are taken:

  • 1st slide - prepared from a sample taken from portio vaginalis of the cervix
  • 2nd slide - prepared from the sample taken from the endocervix (transformation zone)

95% ethanol is used to preserve and fix the pap smear specimen.

It is a highly specific test. Colposcopic examination and biopsy are recommended in case of abnormal Pap smear results.
question: A young woman comes to the gynecology OPD for cervical cancer screening. What is the staining technique used for this?

correctAnswer: C. Smoking is a high risk factor
explanationHtml:
Smoking is strongly associated with mucinous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, but not endometrial carcinoma.

Endometrial carcinoma is the most common invasive cancer of the female genital tract. Type 1 endometrial carcinoma shows endometrioid morphology and is associated with:

  • Unopposed estrogen exposure (endometrial hyperplasia)
  • Obesity
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypertension

PTEN tumor-suppressor gene is mutated in approximately 20% of endometrial hyperplasias.

Genomic sequencing of endometrial carcinoma has revealed 4 major molecular subtypes of endometrioid and serous carcinomas:

  • Ultramutated/ POLE tumors - mutations in DNA polymerase ε (POLE)
  • Hypermutated/ MSI (microsatellite instability) tumors - mutations involving mismatch repair genes
  • Copy number low/ MSS (microsatellite stable) tumors - mutations involving the PI3K/AKT pathway
  • Copy number high/ serous-like tumors - TP53 mutations and numerous genomic copy number variants

question: Which of the following is incorrect about type I endometrial carcinoma?

Nulliparity, family history, and heritable mutations play a role in the development of these tumors. Mutations in the oncogenes KRAS, BRAF, or ERBB2 result in low-grade tumors, and mutation in TP53 is associated with high-grade tumors.

explanationHtml:

It occurs principally in middle adult life and is rare before puberty and after menopause. The surface of the ovary is rarely involved, they are rarely bilateral. It is associated with the mutation of KRAS proto-oncogene.

question: Which of the following is false regarding mucinous tumors of the ovary?

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Dermoid cysts or mature teratomas are benign tumors, usually found in young women during the active reproductive years. It is bilateral in 10% to 15% of cases.

Microscopically, the cyst wall is composed of tissues from all 3 germ layers. This includes stratified squamous epithelium, with underlying sebaceous glands, hair shafts, and other skin adnexal structures. Sometimes cartilage, bone, thyroid, and neural tissue can be seen.

About 1% of the dermoids undergo malignant transformation, most commonly to squamous cell carcinoma. It can also transform into other cancers (e.g., thyroid carcinoma, melanoma).

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

The component tissue of immature malignant teratomas resembles embryonal and immature fetal tissue. It often consists of primitive neuroepithelial cells. The tumor is found chiefly in prepubertal adolescents and young women, the mean age being 18 years.

Monodermal or specialized teratomas:

  • Struma ovarii - composed entirely of mature thyroid tissue, which may be functional and cause hyperthyroidism.
  • Ovarian carcinoid - arises from intestinal tissue, may be functional causing carcinoid syndrome in the absence of hepatic metastasis
question: A 30-year-old woman underwent an evaluation for an abdominal mass. A laparotomy was decided upon for the removal of the mass. The gross appearance of the mass is as follows. Histopathological examination revealed no malignant change. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and histopathology showing Call-Exner bodies are suggestive of granulosa cell tumor.

Call-Exner bodies are small, distinctive, glandlike structures filled with an acidophilic material resembling immature follicles. Additionally, small, cuboidal to polygonal cells are seen which may grow in anastomosing cords, sheets, or strands.

Granulosa cell tumors are composed of cells that resemble granulosa cells of a developing ovarian follicle. It can be of adult and juvenile types. Elevated tissue and serum levels of inhibin, a product of granulosa cells, are associated with this tumor.

Mutations of the FOXL2 gene are seen in most adult granulosa cell tumors.
question: A 45-year-old woman presented to the gynecology OPD with a history of abdominal pain and distension of abdomen. Ultrasound imaging revealed tumor in the right ovary. Serum level of inhibin was raised. The histopathology of the tumor is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

The Schiller-Duval body is a glomerulus-like structure composed of a central blood vessel enveloped by tumor cells within a space that is also lined by tumor cells.

It is the second most common malignant tumor of germ cell origin. It is a unilateral tumor usually affecting children or young women.

question: A 40-year-old woman presented with bilateral adnexal masses. Histopathological examination of the resected specimen showed sheets of mucin-producing signet-ring cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. The genetic material is completely maternally derived
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image showing grapelike vesicles are suggestive of a complete mole. It results from the fertilization of an egg that has lost its female chromosomes, and as a result, the genetic material is completely paternally derived.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

The pathogenesis of complete mole is as follows:

  • Androgenesis (most common) - 46XX karyotype stemming from the duplication of the genetic material of 1 sperm
  • Dispermy - 46XX or 46XY karyotype due to fertilization of an empty egg by 2 sperms

Microscopically, thin-walled, cystic, grapelike structures consisting of hydropic villi are seen. Trophoblastic proliferation involving the entire circumference of the villi is seen.

The embryo dies very early in development and, therefore, is usually not identified. Patients have a 2.5% risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma and a 15% risk of the persistent or invasive mole.

Malignant mixed Müllerian tumors (MMMTs) are carcinosarcomas whose genetic profile closely resembles endometrial carcinomas.

They involve mutations in the same genes - PTEN, TP53, and PIK3CA. The usual genetic alterations found in sarcomas are absent in MMMTs.

MMMTs are endometrial adenocarcinomas with malignant mesenchymal components. The mesenchymal component may resemble uterine mesenchymal elements (stromal sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma) or contain heterologous malignant cell types (striated muscle, cartilage, adipose tissue, and bone).

It occurs in postmenopausal women and presents with bleeding. It is associated with a poor outcome.

explanationHtml:

Dysgerminomas and testicular seminoma are analogous. They may occur in childhood, but most commonly occur in the 2-3rd decades. It may occur in patients with gonadal dysgenesis, including pseudohermaphroditism. The majority of these tumors are unilateral. They express OCT-3, OCT4, and NANOG.

All dysgerminomas are considered malignant, but the level of histological abnormality can differ. Around 33% of these tumors exhibit more severe or invasive characteristics. However, dysgerminomas generally respond well to chemoradiation therapy, and the overall survival rate for affected individuals exceeds 80%.

Bowen's disease starts as a premalignant lesion and transforms into an infiltrating squamous cell carcinoma in approximately 10% of patients, usually over a span of many years.

Bowen's disease occurs in the genital region of both men and women, usually in those older than age 35 years. These lesions have a strong association with infection by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly type 16.

Grossly, it appears as a solitary, thickened, gray-white, and opaque plaque.

  1. Erythroplasia of Queyrat
  2. Condyloma acuminatum

Bowenoid papulosis occurs in young, sexually active adults. It presents as multiple reddish-brown papular lesions, and it is histologically indistinguishable from Bowen's disease, but virtually never develops into invasive carcinoma.

question: All of the following are true regarding Bowen's disease except:

explanationHtml:
The given histopathological features are strongly suggestive of cryptorchidism.

Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:

  1. Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization
  2. Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis
  3. Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells.

Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac. It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.

Phases of testicular descent:

  • Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis. This phase of descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.
  • Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac. This phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.

The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, Müllerian inhibiting substance, gonadotropins, and estradiol from the placenta are thought to play a role. It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma).
question: The biopsy of a resected inguinal mass from a patient shows marked fibrotic changes with prominent Leydig cells and hypoplastic Sertoli cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. a 30-year-old man with torsion testis
explanationHtml:
Torsion testis does not cause testicular atrophy. It may cause intense congestion to widespread hemorrhage to testicular infarction.

Causes of testicular atrophy:

  • Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the blood supply in old age
  • End-stage of an inflammatory orchitis
  • Cryptorchidism - associated with progressive tubular atrophy and sterility
  • Hypopituitarism
  • Generalized malnutrition or cachexia
  • Irradiation
  • Prolonged administration of antiandrogens (treatment for advanced carcinoma of the prostate)
  • Liver cirrhosis - may cause testicular atrophy as a result of increased levels of circulating endogenous estrogens not metabolized by the diseased liver
  • Exhaustion atrophy, which may follow persistent stimulation by high levels of the follicle-stimulating pituitary hormone
  • Occasionally occurs as a primary failure of genetic origins, such as in Klinefelter (XXY) syndrome

The histological image below of testicular atrophy shows small tubules with few or no germ cells, thickening of the basement membrane of the spermatic tubules, and prominent Leydig cells. The near-normal seminiferous tubules are seen side-by-side with atrophic seminiferous tubules.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Testicular atrophy is not seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario depicts that the patient is having Sertoli cell-only syndrome, and patients with this syndrome will have increased levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).

The below image shows normal histology of testis:

[[figure-1]]

In normal males, as spermatogenesis and testosterone production increase, the Sertoli cells produce inhibin, which inhibits the release of FSH. The Sertoli cells are supporting cells that are under the action of FSH. Leydig cells, which are present in the interstitial spaces, are under the action of luteinizing hormone(LH) and produce testosterone. Testosterone has a feedback inhibition on LH.

In Sertoli cell-only syndrome, within the seminiferous tubules, only Sertoli cells are seen and no germ cells. Hence, there are no spermatozoa and there is no feedback inhibition, which results in increased FSH levels. So, testosterone levels, and LH levels remain unaffected since Leydig cells are not affected. Hence, the patient will have male secondary sexual characters.

The most important indication of testicular biopsy is infertility workup.
question: A 30-year-old man undergoes testicular biopsy as part of infertility work-up. Sperm count shows oligospermia. Microscopy shows only Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules. What is the most likely finding seen in the condition?

correctAnswer: D. Intense congestion, hemorrhage, and areas of infarction
explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is testicular torsion. The pathological changes range from intense congestion to widespread hemorrhage to testicular infarction. In advanced stages, the testis is markedly enlarged and consists entirely of soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Adult torsion is typically seen in adolescence and presents with the sudden onset of testicular pain. Neonatal torsion can occur either in utero or shortly after birth and the cause is unknown.

It results from a bilateral anatomic defect that leads to increased mobility of the testes (bellclapper abnormality). Twisting of the spermatic cord typically cuts off the venous drainage of the testis. But, thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement, followed by hemorrhagic infarction. If the testis is manually untwisted within approximately 6 hours of the onset of torsion, there is a good chance that the testis will remain viable.

Dysplastic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, koilocytic atypia
Intense congestion, hemorrhage, and areas of infarction

question: An 18-year-old boy presents with acute onset of testicular pain. On examination, the left testis is enlarged, tender and positioned higher than the right at an unusual angle. Pain is not relieved on elevation of the scrotum. What histopathological changes can be seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Syphilis and mumps affect the testis primarily and later spread to surrounding structures.

Syphilis can affect both the testis and epididymis, but invariably, the testis is involved first as gummas and diffuse interstitial inflammation.

Mumps most commonly affects school-aged children, but testicular involvement is uncommon in this age. Mumps infection in postpubertal males can lead to acute interstitial orchitis in 20 to 30% of cases.

Gonorrhea and tuberculosis affect the epididymis first, which can later spread to the testis.
question: Which of the following infections primarily affects the testis?

explanationHtml:
Germ-cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) is a common precursor lesion of seminoma.

Most testicular germ-cell tumors originate from a precursor lesion called GCNIS. It is believed to arise in utero and stay dormant until puberty, after which it may progress to seminoma or non-seminomatous tumors.

The exceptions to this rule are:

  • Prepubertal yolk-sac tumors
  • Teratomas
  • Adult spermatocyte tumors

The lesion consists of atypical primordial germ cells, which have large nuclei and a clear cytoplasm and fail to develop into spermatogonia. This is because these cells retain the expression of the transcription factors OCT3/4 and NANOG, which maintain the pluripotency of germ cells and prevent their maturation.
question: Which of the following testicular tumors is derived from germ-cell neoplasia in situ?

correctAnswer: B. Pure choriocarcinoma has an excellent prognosis
explanationHtml:
Pure choriocarcinoma is a rare, but aggressive, tumor and has a poor prognosis.

It generally does not cause any testicular enlargement. It spreads rapidly via the bloodstream. This results in the frequent involvement of the lung and liver. However, pure germ-cell tumors (GCTs) are rare and about 60% of testicular GCTs are mixed tumors.

Teratomas in children usually follow a benign course. But, in the postpubertal male, all teratomas are regarded as malignant because they are capable of metastatic behavior.

question: What is the most common testicular tumor in infants?

explanationHtml:
The gross specimen showing a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface that bulges around the surrounding parenchyma is characteristic of a seminomatous germ-cell tumor or seminoma.

The histological image shows sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and central nucleus, with a prominent nucleolus (fried-egg appearance), delicate fibrous septa containing a lymphocytic infiltrate.

[[figure-1]]

Seminoma is the most common type of GCT. The peak incidence is in the 3rd decade and almost never occurs in infants. It is the testicular equivalent of an ovarian dysgerminoma. Immunohistochemistry is positive for KIT (regardless of KIT mutational status), OCT3/4, and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP).

Other options

question: A 30-year-old man presented with a painless testicular mass. Inguinal orchidectomy was done and the gross and histological image is given below.  What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario of the germ-cell tumor is suggestive of embryonal carcinoma.

It is a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCTs) that occurs mostly in the 20 to 30 year age group. These tumors are more aggressive than seminomas. Embryonal carcinomas share some markers with seminomas such as OCT 3/4 and PLAP but differ by being positive for cytokeratin and CD30 and negative for KIT.

Most patients present with a testicular mass, which can be painful due to rapid growth and may be mistaken for torsion.

Grossly, the tumor is often variegated, poorly demarcated at the margins, and punctuated by foci of hemorrhage or necrosis.

Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary convolutions; the neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and exhibit hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli.

explanationHtml:
In post-pubertal males, teratomas are considered malignant, regardless of the presence of immature elements.

Teratomas are non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCTs), which are characteristically composed of more than one germ layer derivative (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

Teratomas have complex histopathology, and 2 variants may be seen:

  • Mature: Adult-type, well-differentiated cells or organoid structures
  • Immature: Embryonal-type, undifferentiated cells or primitive neural elements

In ovarian teratomas, the presence of immature elements indicates malignancy. However, the level of immaturity is clinically insignificant in testicular teratomas. In prepubertal children, testicular teratomas have a benign course. However, in postpubertal males, teratomas are considered malignant.

question: All of the following are true for spermatocytic tumors except:

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Leydig cell tumor of the testis.

It is the most common sex-cord stromal type of testicular neoplasm. It is mostly benign and invariably unilateral. Most cases occur between 20 and 60 years of age. However, they can present at any age.

The most common presenting feature is testicular swelling or gynecomastia (~15% of cases). In children, hormonal effects manifested primarily as sexual precocity, are the dominant features. Tumors of Leydig cells may secrete androgens and estrogens, and even corticosteroids.

Grossly it shows golden brown, homogeneous circumscribed nodules <5 cm in diameter.

Histologically:

  • large, round, or polygonal cells
  • round central nucleus and prominent nucleoli
  • abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm containing lipid droplets, vacuoles, or lipofuscin pigment
  • crystalloids of Reinke, rod-shaped eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies are seen in about 25% of the tumors

Nodular hyperplasia or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the most common benign prostatic disease in men above 50 years. It arises from the inner aspect of the prostate gland, i.e., the transitional zone. It is characterized by benign, hyperplastic proliferation of prostatic stroma and epithelial elements, which is driven by dihydrotestosterone. This growth progressively compresses the urethra resulting in urinary obstructive symptoms.

The normal prostate contains several distinct regions, including a central zone (CZ), peripheral zone (PZ), transitional zone (TZ), and periurethral zone, as shown in the image below.

question: A 61-year-old male patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia is planned for transurethral resection of the prostate. Which of the following is removed during the procedure?

correctAnswer: D. Gleason Score is reported from 1 to 10.
explanationHtml:
The Gleason score is currently reported from 6-10.

The modified Gleason score is a histopathological grading system that corresponds with the clinical behavior of prostate cancer. It is one of the key methods used in the confirmation of the diagnosis, prognostication, and staging of prostate cancer (adenocarcinoma).

The Gleason grading system is primarily based on analyzing the architecture of the tumor cells in the biopsy specimens obtained. The architecture, i.e., the Gleason Patterns are classified as:

    • Pattern 3: Well-formed glands
    • Pattern 4: Poorly formed/Fused/Cribriform glands/Glomeruloid glands
    • Pattern 5: Sheets of the tumor, individual cells, cords, and solid nests of cells, Comedo necrosis
    • Pattern 1 and 2 are no longer defined

Most tumor specimens contain more than one pattern. Therefore, a numeric grade is assigned to both the primary pattern and the next most frequent secondary pattern. The sum of the numeric grades provides the Gleason score.

  • Scores 2–5 are no longer assigned.
  • Scores of 6 - 7 are potentially treatable cancers
  • Scores 8 - 10 are advanced cancers that are less likely to be cured.

Based on the gleason score, they are classified into the following grade groups:

  • Grade group 1: score<=6
  • Grade group 2: 3+4=7
  • Grade group 3: 4+3=7
  • Grade group 4: score 8
  • Grade group 5: scores 9-10

options.text: Grade group 1 represents the most well-differentiated tumors.

    • Pattern 5- Sheets of the tumor, individual cells, cords and solid nests of cells, Comedo necrosis
    • Pattern 1 and 2 are no longer defined

2) Gleason Score:

The current Gleason score ranges from 6–10. Scores 2–5 are no longer assigned.

3) Grade group:

    • Grade group 1: score ≤6
    • Grade group 2: 3+4=7
    • Grade group 3: 4+3=7
    • Grade group 4: score 8

The upper-age-specific reference value of serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in men of age 70–79 is 6.5 ng/mL.

PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium secreted in the semen. Measurement of serum PSA levels is widely used to assist the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of prostate cancer. Older men have a higher serum PSA level than younger men, so the normal range varies with age.

Age Upper age-specific PSA(ng/mL)
40–49 yrs 2.5
50–59 yrs 3.5
60–69 yrs 4.5
70–79 yrs 6.5

The serum PSA levels as a screening test for prostatic cancer has poor sensitivity and specificity. This is because various other factors such as trauma, infections, BPH, instrumentation/digital exam of the prostate, and ejaculation can increase serum PSA levels. A value of ≥4 ng/mL usually warrants serial testing or further evaluation.

In an effort to improve the sensitivity and specificity of serum PSA levels, many novel indices are used:

  • Age-specific PSA reference ranges
  • PSA velocity: Rate of change of PSA values with time. It is considered that PSA velocity of 0.75 ng/mL per year measured at least 3 times over a period of 1.5 to 2 yrs is significant to diagnose Prostate cancer.
  • PSA density: Serum PSA/volume of the prostate gland
  • The ratio of free to bound serum PSA

Pathogenesis behind this condition is generalized mitochondrial dysfunction with structural and functional alterations of mitochondria in the liver, brain, and muscle. Liver is enlarged, but jaundice is absent or minimal. It is characterized by clinical features such as:

  • Signs of progressive CNS damage
  • Signs of hepatic injury

question: Which of the following serological markers can be used to diagnose hepatitis B infection during the window period?

Over a period of months, the IgM anti-HBc antibodies are replaced by the IgG anti-HBc antibodies. Thus, a decline of IgM antibodies in the presence of rising total anti-HBC indicates that the IgM is being converted to IgG and thus the infection is chronic.

HBeAg, HBV-DNA, and DNA polymerase appear in serum soon after HBsAg, and all signify active viral replication.

Occasionally, mutated strains of HBV emerge that do not produce HBeAg but are replication-competent and express HBcAg.

explanationHtml:
Wilson's disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene. It is an autosomal recessive condition.

The ATP7B gene is located on chromosome 13q. The gene encodes a copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B), which has 2 functions:

  • Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin
  • Helps excrete free copper in bile.

The resulting ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper and impaired excretion of free copper. This causes excess deposition of free copper in the tissues, particularly in the liver, brain, and eye.

Note: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive condition characterized by impaired copper absorption and resulting copper deficiency. Here, the mutation is in the ATP7A gene.

question: A 35-year-old man with tremors and chronic hepatitis is found to have the following ophthalmic finding. This patient is also likely to have which of the following?

Low serum ceruloplasmin, raised 24 hr urinary copper, and Kayser-Fleischer rings are diagnostically helpful.

Estimation of hepatic tissue copper is the gold standard for diagnosis. It is measured using neutron activation analysis / atomic absorption spectrometry.

The liver biopsy image shows periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase-resistant round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes. These are characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding that results in impaired secretion of α1 antitrypsin into the serum. α1AT deficiency results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase, causing panacinar emphysema. It also causes liver disease as a consequence of an abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes. Cutaneous necrotizing panniculitis also occurs in a minor subset of patients. Hepatocellular carcinoma develops in 2% to 3% of cases.

question: A 35-year-old male patient with emphysema was found to have elevated liver transaminases. His liver biopsy image is given below.  What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin is located on the long arm of chromosome 14. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a plasma glycoprotein synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes.

For α1-antitrypsin genes, the general notation is “Pi” for “protease inhibitor." An alphabetic letter is given for the position on the isoelectric gel.

This gene has different alleles that produce different amounts of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT).

  • M allele - normal levels of the AAT protein
  • S allele - moderately low levels
  • Z allele - very low levels

The alleles are expressed in a codominant manner.
question: On which chromosome is the gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin present?

explanationHtml:
The most common clinically significant mutation causing α1-antitrypsin deficiency is PiZ. Homozygous individuals with PiZZ have only 10% of normal circulating α1-antitrypsin. So, they are at high risk of developing clinical disease.

Other options:

Option A: PiMM is the most common genotype seen in normal individuals, present in about 90% of individuals.

Option C: Pi-null is a rare variant with no detectable serum alpha-1 antitrypsin.

Option D: PiS variant is clinically asymptomatic.

correctAnswer: D. Bile duct injury and granulomas
explanationHtml:
Bile duct injury and granulomas are uncommon in autoimmune hepatitis except in cases of overlap with primary biliary cirrhosis.

Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is characterised by extensive inflammation, fibrosis, and ultimately cirrhosis. The pathologic features include:

  • Emperipolesis - Lymphocytes and plasma cells within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes.
  • Interface hepatitis or piecemeal necrosis.
  • Rosette formation due to necrosis of groups of hepatocytes and resultant regeneration.

The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic interface hepatitis.

question: An 11-year-old girl with persistently elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) has been diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis. Which of the following pathological features would you not expect in this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows antinuclear antibodies (ANA).
explanationHtml:
Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-liver kidney microsomal autoantibodies (anti-LKM1) and anti–liver cytosol-1 (ACL-1) antibodies, not ANA.

Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-nuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA), and anti–soluble liver antigen/liver pancreas antigen (anti-SLA/LP) antibodies. It less commonly shows anti-mitochondrial (AMA) antibodies.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disorder characterized by continuing hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. It can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure.

Histocompatibility haplotypes such as HLA-B1, HLA-B8, HLA-DR3, and HLA-DR4 are common in patients with autoimmune hepatitis.

Histopathological features include:

  • Plasma cell predominance in inflammatory infiltrates
  • Extensive interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis)
  • Hepatocyte rosettes

The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis, showing characteristic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and interface hepatitis.

[[figure-1]]

It can progress to liver failure.

explanationHtml:
Onion-skin fibrosis is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

The smaller ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis show a striking circumferential “onion skin” fibrosis around an increasingly atrophic duct lumen. This eventually leads to the obliteration by a “tombstone” scar.

The image shows primary sclerosing cholangitis. There is a degenerating bile duct that is entrapped in the dense concentric onion-skin fibrosis.

question: The histopathological findings obtained after a liver biopsy is given below. What would be the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. There is dilation of preserved segments.

On histopathologic examination, large ducts show acute neutrophilic inflammation of the epithelium. The inflamed areas develop strictures. Small ducts show onion-skin fibrosis around the atrophic duct lumen. There is an obliteration of ducts by a tombstone scar.
question: Which of the following is not a feature of primary sclerosing cholangitis?

explanationHtml:
Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with Sjogren's syndrome. Other associated conditions are:

  • Thyroiditis
  • Scleroderma
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Celiac disease

PBC is an autoimmune disease. It is characterized by nonsuppurative, inflammatory destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts. Large intrahepatic ducts and the extrahepatic biliary tree are not involved. It is a disease of middle-aged women, with a female predominance of 9:1. Antimitochondrial antibodies are the most characteristic laboratory finding in PBC.

Histopathologic examination shows diagnostic florid duct lesions. These are lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with or without granulomas centred around the bile duct. They also show Mallory–Denk bodies.

The image given below shows primary biliary cholangitis.

[[figure-2]]
question: Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver.

It appears as a red-blue, soft nodule, usually < 2 cm in diameter. It may be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for a metastatic tumor.

The following histopathological image depicts a cavernous hemangioma of the liver with blood-filled vascular channels separated by dense fibrous stroma.

question: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver?

correctAnswer: D. β-catenin-activated adenoma has no risk of malignant transformation
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatic adenoma. β-catenin-activated adenomas have a high risk of malignant transformation.

Hepatic adenomas are benign tumors of hepatocytes. Spontaneous rupture of the hepatic adenoma may cause intra-abdominal bleeding, which is a surgical emergency.

Hepatic adenomas are classified into 3 subtypes:

  • HNF1-α (Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor-1 alpha)-inactivated adenomas -
    • No risk of malignant transformation
    • Often associated with oral contraceptive pill use (OCP) and MODY-3
  • β-catenin-activated adenoma -
    • High risk of malignant transformation
    • Associated with oral contraceptive pills (OCP) and anabolic steroids usage
  • Inflammatory adenomas -
    • Associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
    • Upregulation of C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid A
    • 10% may have concomitant β-catenin activating mutations
    • Moderate risk of malignant transformation

The gross specimen of hepatic adenoma is shown below.

[[figure-1]]

Hepatoblastoma is the most common malignant liver tumor of early childhood, usually < 3 years. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the most important clinical marker for hepatoblastoma. It remains the key clinical marker of malignant change, response to the treatment, and relapse.

explanationHtml:

Risk factors for hepatoblastoma include:

  • Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome

explanationHtml:
Pure fetal histology hepatoblastoma is associated with a very good prognosis. They may be cured by surgical resection without adjuvant chemotherapy.

question: Which of the following parameters indicates a good prognosis in hepatoblastoma?

explanationHtml:
Gardner syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome is associated with hepatoblastoma.

Activation of WNT signaling plays a major role in hepatoblastomas. This occurs by a variety of mechanisms including mutations in APC gene. Hence, patients with FAP syndromes frequently develop hepatoblastomas.

The following syndromes are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma:

  • Hereditary tyrosinemia
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin defeciency
  • Familial hemochromatosis

question: Which one of the following syndromes is associated with a higher incidence of hepatoblastoma?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma is chronic hepatitis B virus infection. More than 85% of cases of hepatocellular carcinoma occur in countries with high rates of chronic hepatitis B virus infection.

Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma are:

  • Hepatitis B virus
  • Hepatitis C virus
  • Alcohol
  • Aflatoxin
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
  • Tyrosinemia
  • Smoking

Activation of β-catenin and inactivation of p53 are the two most common early mutational events seen in hepatocellular carcinoma.

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Focal nodular hyperplasia and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are not precursors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

The precursors of HCC include:

  • Hepatocellular adenoma - especially those with β-catenin-activating mutations
  • Small cell and large cell change - cellular dysplasias
  • Dysplastic nodules - low-grade and high-grade

Which of the following are the precursor lesions for hepatocellular carcinoma?

  1. Hepatocellular adenoma
  2. Small cell change
  3. Nodular regenerative hyperplasia
  4. Large cell change
  5. Focal nodular hyperplasia

correctAnswer: D. It is associated with liver cirrhosis
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibrolamellar carcinoma. It is usually not associated with liver cirrhosis.

Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a distinctive and rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It usually occurs < 35 years of age. There is no gender predilection and no identifiable predisposing conditions. It has a good prognosis compared to the classical HCC. The majority (50-75%) of these tumors are resectable.

It usually presents as a single large, hard scirrhous tumor with fibrous bands coursing through it. Microscopically, it is composed of oncocytes growing in nests or cords separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagen bundles.

The histological section of fibrolamellar carcinoma is given below. It shows malignant-appearing, oncocytic hepatocytes separated by dense bundles of collagen.

[[figure-1]]

Further investigations reveal elevated neurotensin levels and negative hepatitis B serology. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to arsenic, thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.

Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm. There is equal gender predilection. The tumor may occur at any site, but most often involves the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.

Tumor

question: Which of the following agents is not associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?

explanationHtml:
The most common tumors of the liver are metastatic tumors.

The common primary sources of liver metastasis are:

  • Colon carcinoma
  • Breast carcinoma
  • Lung carcinoma
  • Pancreatic carcinoma

question: Which of the following is the most common tumor of the liver?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a metastatic liver tumor.

Metastases are the most common malignant neoplasms of the liver. The most common primary sources are the colon, breast, lung, and pancreas, although any cancer at any site of the body may spread to the liver.

Patients with metastases typically have multiple nodules replacing the normal liver parenchyma. There may be no clinical or laboratory evidence of hepatic insufficiency. Often, the only telltale sign of secondaries in the liver will be hepatomegaly.

question: A 53-year-old patient with anorexia and weight loss is found to have non-tender hepatomegaly on physical examination. CT scan of the abdomen shows multiple nodules in the liver and investigations reveal elevated ALP and AST levels, with no elevations in AFP. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml:
Typhoid carriers are not at risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma.

Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary malignant tumor of the liver after hepatocellular carcinoma. It is a malignancy of the biliary tree, arising from bile ducts within and outside of the liver.

The risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma include the following:

  • Infestation by liver flukes (particularly Opisthorchis and Clonorchis)
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis and other chronic inflammatory diseases of the large bile ducts
  • Chronic hepatitis B and C infections
  • Cirrhosis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Diabetes mellitus, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
  • Alcohol and tobacco
  • Precursor lesions -
    • Biliary intraepithelial neoplasias
    • Mucinous cystic neoplasms
    • Intraductal papillary biliary neoplasia
lessonTitle: Neoplasms Of Liver And Biliary Tract
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk for cholangiocarcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Klatskin tumors are extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas located in the perihilar region.

These tumors are located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Distal tumors arise in the common bile duct posterior to the duodenum. Regardless of the site, the prognosis is poor.

question: What does Klatskin tumor refer to?

correctAnswer: D. It usually has a good prognosis
explanationHtml:
Gallbladder carcinoma carries a poor prognosis because it is typically detected late due to non-specific symptoms.

Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. Most carcinomas of the gall bladder are adenocarcinomas.

Gallbladder cancer is at least twice as common in women as in men. The most important risk factor for gallbladder cancer (besides gender and ethnicity) is gallstones, which are present in 95% of cases. Her-2/neu is overexpressed in around 2/3 of the cases, and therefore, they can be targeted for therapy.

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding gallbladder carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder is the Phrygian cap. It refers to an inward folding of the fundus of the gallbladder. It is named for its resemblance to a conical hat.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

The other common congenital anomalies of the gallbladder are:

  • Agenesis - absence of all or any portion of the hepatic or common bile ducts
  • Biliary atresia - hypoplastic narrowing of biliary channels
  • Choledochal cysts - congenital dilations of the intra and/or extrahepatic biliary system
question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows pigmented gallstones, which are not associated with hyperlipidemia syndromes.

Pigmented gallstones are made of bilirubin and calcium salts. They can occur in:

  • Chronic hemolytic syndromes
  • Ileal resection
  • Biliary infection
  • Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency

Cholesterol stones are made of crystalline cholesterol monohydrates. Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for the development of cholesterol gallstones.

The following image shows cholesterol gallstones:

[[figure-1]]
question: A 24-year-old man presented with severe right upper quadrant pain for 8 hours associated with nausea and vomiting. A diagnosis of acute cholecystitis was made and he underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The specimen is shown below. This finding is associated with all the following conditions except:

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario of chronic cholecystitis and the image showing lipid-laden xanthoma cells are suggestive of xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis. This condition results from the rupture of Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses.

[[figure-1]]

Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses are bile-filled outpouchings of the gallbladder mucosa through the gallbladder wall. They develop in reaction to chronic inflammation of the gallbladder. Eventually, they may rupture through the wall of the gallbladder. This results in the accumulation of macrophages that have ingested biliary phospholipids, which are called xanthoma cells.

[[figure-2]]

Chronic cholecystitis may have other sequelae:

  • Porcelain gallbladder - dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall
  • Hyalinizing cholecystitis - replacement of the gallbladder wall by dense fibrosis, with or without calcification (leads to a higher incidence of gallbladder carcinoma)
  • Hydrops of the gallbladder - atrophic, obstructed, dilated gallbladder containing clear fluid

Acute cholecystitis includes the following variants:

  • Emphysematous cholecystitis - acute infection of the gallbladder by gas-forming organisms
  • Acalculous cholecystitis - due to gallbladder stasis and ischemia

options.text: Dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall

question: A 52-year-old man was rushed to the ER with right upper quadrant pain for the last 6 hours. He had been diagnosed with gallstones 10 years ago but had not undergone any treatment. Imaging revealed gallbladder wall thickening. He underwent a cholecystectomy which revealed a shrunken and nodular gallbladder with a thick wall. The following was noted on microscopy. This condition is associated with:

explanationHtml:
Pancreas divisum is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas.

The pancreas develops by the fusion of the larger dorsal and smaller ventral pancreatic buds. The dorsal duct is the dominant duct during development, and it drains into the minor papilla. The ventral duct drains into the major papilla. After fusion, the following ducts are formed:

  • Main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) - formed by fusion of the ducts of the dorsal and ventral buds, drains into the major papilla
  • Accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) - formed by the proximal portion of the dorsal duct, drains into the minor papilla

In pancreas divisum, the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse. Hence, the majority of the pancreas continues to drain through the dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor papilla, while the ventral duct, along with the bile duct, drains into the major papilla. These patients are more prone to pancreatitis.

[[figure-1]]

The other congenital anomalies of the pancreas are:

  • Annular pancreas - a band-like ring of normal pancreatic tissue encircling the 2nd part of the duodenum, may cause obstruction
  • Ectopic pancreas - common in the stomach, duodenum, and jejunum (found in about 2% of postmortem exams)
  • Agenesis - rarely seen, associated with mutations of PDX1 (homeobox gene)
question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas?

correctAnswer: D. Hypocalcemia is an important triggering factor this condition
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario in a young patient with a positive family history of similar episodes is suggestive of hereditary pancreatitis. Acute episodes of pancreatitis can be precipitated by hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.

The following genes are implicated in hereditary pancreatitis:

  • Gain-of-function mutation in trypsinogen gene (PRSS1) - most common
  • Loss-of-function mutation in the trypsin inhibitor gene (SPINK1)
  • Loss of CFTR - abnormal secretions that promote protein plugging, duct obstruction, leading to pancreatitis

Hereditary pancreatitis is associated with a 40% lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

question: A 19-year-old boy presented with severe abdominal pain for the last 24 hours with radiation to the upper back. He has had multiple similar episodes since his childhood. Family history revealed similar episodes in the father. Investigations revealed elevated serum levels of amylase and lipase. Which of the following statements is not true about the given condition?

explanationHtml:
The presence of the above clinical symptoms with migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and elevated serum levels of CEA and CA 19-9 in an elderly man points to a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. The most frequently associated mutation with this condition is K-RAS.

It is attributed to the production of platelet-aggregating factors and procoagulants from the tumor or its necrotic products. Both venous and arterial thrombi can occur. Venous thrombi can embolize to the lungs.

Molecular alterations involved in pancreatic carcinogenesis are:

Gene Type Chromosome
KRAS (most common oncogene) Oncogene (activated by point mutation) 12p
CDKN2A (most common tumor-suppressor gene) Tumor suppressor gene 9p
TP53 Tumor suppressor gene 17p
SMAD4 Tumor suppressor gene 18q

The following genes are associated with an inherited predisposition to pancreatic cancer:

  • BRCA2 mutation - pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and ovarian cancer
  • PRSS1 mutation - pancreatic carcinoma secondary to hereditary pancreatitis
question: A 65-year-old man presented with vague abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss for the last 6 months. He also reported spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules at different locations on his body. On examination, thrombophlebitis and epigastric tenderness were noted. Investigations revealed elevated serum CEA and CA 19-9. Which of the following genetic mutations is most frequently associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Mucinous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas have dense stroma, similar to the ovarian stroma.

These tumors have large cystic cavities filled with thick, tenacious mucin. They are lined by columnar, mucin-producing epithelium with dense stroma. This results in similarity to ovarian stroma.

They usually arise in the tail of the pancreas and can be precursors to invasive carcinomas. They are associated with mutations in the KRAS oncogene, and the tumor-suppressor genes TP53 and RNF43.
question: A pathologist was studying a biopsy specimen from a patient with pancreatic cancer. He observed that it resembled ovarian stroma. What is it likely to be?

correctAnswer: B. Carcinoma of body of pancreas often present with jaundice
explanationHtml:
Patients with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas develop jaundice due to obstruction of the biliary tract.

Cigarette smoking doubles the risk of pancreatic cancer and is the leading preventable cause. The clinical features vary depending on the tumor's location.

  • Head - painless, palpable gallbladder with mild jaundice is suggestive of malignancy (according to Courvoisier's law)
  • Body and tail - may remain asymptomatic until later stages, as they do not impinge on the biliary tract and do not cause jaundice

Other common pathological features of this condition are:

  • Desmoplastic reaction - growth of fibrous or connective tissue
  • Perineural invasion, as well as lymphatic and large vessel invasion

options.text: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor
Carcinoma of body of pancreas often present with jaundice

question: Patients with which of the following have the highest risk of pancreatic cancer?

explanationHtml:
The esophagus is the most common site of fistulization in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT).

A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea. The fistula is usually present near the tracheal bifurcation, with or without esophageal atresia. A blind proximal pouch with a distal tracheooesophageal fistula is the most common type of tracheooesophageal fistula (Type C).

10% of the patients have associated VACTERL anomalies (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb).
question: What is the most common site of fistulization in GIT?

explanationHtml:
The most frequent site of the ectopic gastric mucosa is the upper third of the esophagus, where it is referred to as an inlet patch.

It is congenital and mostly asymptomatic. Occasionally, it can release acid, which can result in dysphagia, esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, or, rarely, adenocarcinoma.
question: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and barium swallow image are diagnostic of Zenker’s diverticulum. It occurs due to a defect in the Killian's triangle (Killian's dehiscence).

Killian's triangle is an anatomical triangular area bordered superiorly by the firm oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle and inferiorly by the horizontal fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It is located immediately above the upper esophageal sphincter.

Although the Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is an anterolateral defect, it is rarely symptomatic.
question: A 57-year-old man came with complaints of difficulty in swallowing and a persistent feeling of something stuck in his throat. He also reports bad breath and regurgitation of food particles. Barium swallow revealed the following. This condition occurs due to a defect in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Paterson–Brown–Kelly or Plummer–Vinson syndrome is associated with non-progressive dysphagia, especially with incompletely chewed food.

This syndrome is common in women aged >40 years. The other components of this syndrome are:

  • Post-cricoid webs in the upper esophagus
  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Glossitis
  • Cheilosis

Esophageal webs are idiopathic, semi-circumferential lesions composed of fibrovascular connective tissue and overlying epithelium. They are usually limited to the proximal esophagus and may cause obstruction. They are associated with:

  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
  • Chronic graft-versus-host disease
  • Blistering skin diseases

The images below show endoscopic and barium swallow appearances of esophageal webs.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: All of the following may be seen in patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome except:

explanationHtml:
The given image shows an esophageal ring. Rings located above the gastroesophageal junction are classified as type A esophageal rings.

Esophageal rings are circumferential and thick. They include mucosa, submucosa, and occasionally, hypertrophic muscularis propria. There are 3 types:

Type A rings Type B or Schatzki rings Type C rings

Caused by normal physiologic smooth muscle contractions

Most common type

Note: Steakhouse syndrome refers to intermittent food impaction causing complete obstruction due to the presence of Schatzki rings.
question: A 45-year-old woman presented with complaints of difficulty in swallowing solid foods. An upper GI endoscopy revealed the following finding just above the gastroesophageal junction. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and barium swallow showing the bird-beak appearance are suggestive of achalasia cardia. With respect to this patient's travel history, Chagas' disease due to infection with Trypanosoma cruzi must be suspected.

The infection destroys the myenteric plexus which results in failure of peristalsis and esophageal dilatation. Duodenal, colonic, and ureteric myenteric plexuses can also be affected by Chagas' disease.
question: A 52-year-old woman is being evaluated for dysphagia and chest pain. She traveled to Brazil on a business trip 5 months ago. Barium swallow reveals the following finding. Which of the following could have caused this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal part of esophagus
explanationHtml:
Achalasia cardia is characterized by decreased release of NO(nitric oxide) and VIP(vasoactive intestinal polypeptide) in the distal part of the esophagus.

Normally, NO and VIP are secreted by the inhibitory neurons of the Auerbach's plexus in the distal esophagus. This leads to relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). In achalasia cardia, these inhibitory neurons degenerate, leading to decreased release of NO and VIP. This causes increased LES tone.

The triad of achalasia cardia is as follows:

  1. Incomplete relaxation of LES
  2. Increased tone of the LES
  3. Absent peristalsis (aperistalisis)

Decreased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter

explanationHtml:

Additionally, elimination of allergenic proteins from the diet as it is is associated with atopy and exposure to food allergens like cow’s milk and soy products.

question: Which of the following is incorrect about eosinophilic esophagitis?

explanationHtml:
The symptoms of the patient in the above case scenario and the image showing calcinosis are the characteristic findings of the CREST syndrome or limited scleroderma. Patients with this condition characteristically have antibodies directed against centromeric proteins (anti-centromere antibodies).

CREST syndrome is characterized by the following:

  • Calcinosis
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Esophageal dysmotility
  • Sclerodactyly
  • Telangiectasia

In the esophagus, progressive atrophy and fibrous replacement of the muscularis propria lead to hypomotility and dysphagia. The lower 2/3 of the esophagus develops a rubber-hose–like inflexibility. The associated dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter gives rise to gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett metaplasia, and stricture.
question: A 47-year-old woman comes to you with progressive heartburn and difficulty in swallowing. She also describes episodes of painful blanching and bluish discoloration of her fingers and toes on exposure to cold. The following findings are noted on examination. Antibodies to which of the following are most likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a Mallory–Weiss tear. They require only conservative management, and healing tends to be rapid and complete.

They are longitudinal mucosal tears that may cross the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ). Forceful retching or vomiting, along with failure of reflex relaxation of the gastroesophageal musculature, results in tears involving the mucosa and submucosa. It usually occurs secondary to conditions like acute alcohol intoxication or hyperemesis gravidarum.

Boerhaave syndrome is a much more serious disorder characterized by transmural rupture of the distal esophagus. This results in acute mediastinitis with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Such patients generally require urgent surgical intervention.

options.text: It is due to longitudinal mucosal tears
The gastroesophageal musculature fails to relax
The tears cross the gastroesophageal junction

question: A 50-year-old man presented with blood in his vomitus. He gives a history of binge drinking followed by multiple episodes of vomiting the prior night. He is hemodynamically stable.  Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?

explanationHtml:
The most frequent cause of esophagitis is reflux of gastric acid into the lower esophagus.

The most common cause of gastroesophageal reflux is transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Reflux esophagitis leads to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). This can cause Barrett's esophagus and eventually can cause adenocarcinoma.
question: What is the most frequent cause of esophagitis?

explanationHtml:
Esophagitis in healthy individuals can be caused by the Herpes simplex virus. However, it is relatively uncommon.

In immunosuppressed individuals, infections can be caused by:

  • Herpes simplex virus
  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Candida
question: Which organism can cause esophageal infections in healthy individuals?

explanationHtml:
Infection with Herpes simplex virus (HSV) typically results in punched-out ulcers in the esophagus.

HSV esophagitis commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients. The edge of the ulcer is the preferred site for biopsy. The following microscopic findings are noted:

  • Ballooning degeneration
  • Ground-glass changes in nuclei
  • Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusion bodies

[[figure-1]]

Note: CMV esophagitis causes shallow ulcerations. The biopsy is taken from the base of the ulcer and shows characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions bodies.
question: Punched-out ulcers in the esophagus are caused by:

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing bleeding esophageal varices are suggestive of hepatic schistosomiasis. It is the second most common cause of varices worldwide.

Liver cirrhosis, mostly in association with alcoholic liver disease, is the most common cause of varices.
question: A 28-year-old patient with haematemesis is found to have the following finding on upper GI endoscopy. He has traveled to Zambia several times over the past 3 years. What could be the likely cause of this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma
explanationHtml:
Barrett's esophagus increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.

Barrett's esophagus is a complication of GERD and it is estimated to occur in as many as 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Microscopically, it is seen as the replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).

[[figure-1]]

The following images show endoscopic and microscopic images of Barrett's esophagus:

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma

explanationHtml:
The given image is of Barrett's esophagus showing intestinal metaplasia. The special stain used here is Alcian blue, which stains the acid mucin present in the goblet cells.

The following stains are used for mucin:

question: A 60-year-old man with chronic dyspepsia underwent upper GI endoscopy. The biopsy findings are shown below. What is the special stain that has been used?

correctAnswer: A. The most common site of extranodal lymphoma in GIT is the esophagus
explanationHtml: The most common site of extranodal lymphoma in GIT is the stomach, not the esophagus.

options.text: The most common site of extranodal lymphoma in GIT is the esophagus
The most common benign tumour of esophagus is leimyoma
The most common esophageal cancer overall is squamous cell carcinoma
The most common esophageal cancer in Western countries is adenocarcinoma

question: Which of the following statements is false?

explanationHtml:
Mediastinal fibrosis does not predispose to esophageal carcinoma. Risk factors for esophageal carcinoma include the following:

  • Alcohol and tobacco use
  • Poverty
  • Caustic alkali burns
  • Diverticula
  • Achalasia
  • Tylosis
  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome
  • Frequent consumption of very hot beverages
  • Radiation exposure to the mediastinum
  • Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection - squamous cell carcinomas
question: Which of the following is not a predisposing factor for esophageal cancer?

correctAnswer: B. Decreased risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus
explanationHtml:
Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with decreased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Long-standing H. pylori gastritis (chronic inflammation) causes multifocal gastric mucosal atrophy, which in turn results in decreased parietal cell mass and acid secretion. This leads to a lower incidence of Barrett's esophagus and a reduced risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

H. pylori infection, however, increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

options.text: Increased risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus
Decreased risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus
Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus
Decreased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus

question: A patient with recurrent gastritis has been diagnosed with Helicobacter pylori infection. Which of the following is true in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given images showing an esophageal exophytic growth on endoscopy and apple core appearance in the middle 1/3 of the esophagus on barium swallow are suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma. The characteristic histopathological finding in this condition are nests of stratified malignant cells and keratin pearls, which are noted in image 4.

[[figure-1]]
