question: Endoscopic and barium swallow images of a lesion in the oesophagus of a patient are as shown below. What is the expected histopathological finding?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It is associated with exposure to azithromycin.

Risk factors for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis:

  • Turner syndrome
  • Trisomy 18
  • Erythromycin or azithromycin exposure in the first 2 weeks of life, either orally or via mother's milk.

Hyperplasia of the pyloric muscularis propria obstructs the gastric outflow tract.

It is three to five times more common in males. Generally presents between the 3rd and 6th weeks of life as new-onset regurgitation, often projectile and non-bilious vomiting after feeding. Physical examination reveals a firm, ovoid, 1 to 2 cm abdominal mass. In some cases, abnormal left-to-right hyperperistalsis is seen.

Note: Treatment is the surgical splitting of the muscularis (Ramstedt pyloromyotomy).
question: A 3-weeks-old baby presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after every meal. Abdominal examination reveals prominent peristalsis in the epigastrium and an olive-sized mass is felt on deep palpation of the right upper abdomen. Which of the following drug exposures is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
The endoscopy findings of the watermelon stomach are suggestive of gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE).

In GAVE, endoscopy reveals longitudinal stripes of edematous erythematous mucosa that alternate with less severely injured, paler mucosa, giving the appearance of watermelon. GAVE is responsible for 4% of non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Dieulafoy lesion is a non-stress-related cause of GI bleeding. It is due to a submucosal artery that does not branch properly within the stomach wall. It is shown in the image below.

[[figure-1]]
question: Endoscopy of a patient with chronic upper gastrointestinal bleeding showed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Patients with renal failure develop acute gastritis as a consequence of uremia.

In uremia, gastric injury is due to inhibition of gastric bicarbonate transporters by ammonium ions.

Causes of acute gastritis:

  • Alcohol
  • Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
  • Smoking
  • Ischemia/shock
  • Steroid use
  • Uremia
  • Chemical ingestion
  • Stress

Note: Histologically, the presence of neutrophils above the basement membrane in direct contact with epithelial cells signifies acute gastritis.
question: A 60-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes mellitus is on dialysis for chronic renal failure. Which of the following forms of gastritis is the patient at risk of development?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of chronic gastritis is infection with the bacillus Helicobacter pylori.

Causes of chronic gastritis:

  • Helicobacter pylori - 1st most common
  • Autoimmune gastritis - 2nd most common
  • Radiation injury
  • Chronic bile reflux
  • Mechanical injury (e.g., an indwelling nasogastric tube)
  • Systemic diseases such as Crohn's disease, amyloidosis
  • Graft-versus-host disease

Other options:

Options B and C: Acid hypersecretion and alcohol ingestion are the causes of acute gastritis.

Option D: Autoimmune gastritis is the most common cause of diffuse atrophic gastritis.
question: What is the most common cause of chronic gastritis?

explanationHtml:
The given slide shows the GI mucosa, which has been stained with Warthin-Starry silver stain, demonstrating the Helicobacter pylori bacilli.

On antral biopsy, H. pylori organisms are seen abundantly within the surface mucus layer, but they are difficult to visualize with routine hematoxylin (H&E) stains. Organisms are most easily demonstrated with special stains like Warthin-Starry silver stain or Giemsa stain.

The image given below is a GI biopsy stained with Warthin-Starry silver stain.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

The below image is a Giemsa stain showing Helicobacter pylori in a case of chronic gastritis.

[[figure-3]]
question: A patient with a history of peptic ulcers underwent an upper GI endoscopic biopsy of the stomach. The biopsy was stained with a special stain as shown in the image. Identify the special stain used.

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of H. pylori gastritis. The preferred site for biopsy is the antrum, as H. pylori is most often found in the antrum of the stomach.

H. pylori display tropism for gastric epithelia and are generally not found in the duodenal epithelium. Long-standing H. pylori gastritis may extend to involve the body and fundus, resulting in patchy mucosal atrophy.

The image below is a Warthin-Starry silver stain showing Helicobacter pylori colonized on the surface of the regenerative epithelium of the antrum.

[[figure-1]]

The following image depicts parts of the stomach for better visualisation of the antrum.

[[figure-2]]
question: A 34-year-old man presents with nausea and upper abdominal pain. He experiences vague discomfort mostly in the afternoon and night, which is relieved by food. The urea breath test is positive. Upper GI endoscopy reveals a small ulcer with a clean base in the duodenum. From which of the following sites should the biopsy be taken to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Autoimmune gastritis typically spares the antrum.

Autoimmune gastritis causes diffuse mucosal damage of the acid-producing mucosa within the body and fundus. It accounts for less than 10% of cases of chronic gastritis. CD4+T cells directed against parietal cell components, including the H+/K+ ATPase, are considered to be the principal agents of injury in autoimmune gastritis.

Characteristic features of autoimmune gastritis:

  • Antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor
  • Reduced serum pepsinogen I concentration
  • Hypergastrinemia
  • Endocrine cell hyperplasia leads to carcinoid tumors
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia)
  • Defective gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria)
question: In patients with autoimmune gastritis, what part of the stomach is least likely to get involved?

correctAnswer: A. Anterior wall of the duodenum
explanationHtml:
The most common site of peptic ulcer is the anterior wall of the proximal duodenum, within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve.

Gastric peptic ulcers are predominantly located along the lesser curvature near the interface of the body and antrum.

Locations of peptic ulcers (in decreasing order of frequency):

  1. Duodenum (first part)
  2. Stomach (lesser curvature near the junction of the body and the antrum)
  3. Gastroesophageal junction in gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or Barrett’s esophagus
  4. Margins of jejunostomy
  5. Stomach, duodenum, and/or jejunum in patients with Zollinger–Ellison syndrome
  6. Ileal Meckel’s diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa

The image below shows a peptic ulcer with a round to oval, sharply punched-out defect and a clean mucosal margin.

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the most common site of peptic ulcers?

explanationHtml:
The most common complication of peptic ulcers is bleeding.

An ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenum causes bleeding from the gastroduodenal artery. Gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach causes bleeding from the left gastric artery.

Other complications are perforation, obstruction, and malignant transformation.

Note: The most common cause of death in peptic ulcers is perforation, followed by bleeding. Perforation accounts for two-thirds of ulcer deaths.
question: A 55-year-old man presents with periodic abdominal pain. The pain is associated with meals and is relieved by antacids. Physical examination is unremarkable. Endoscopy shows a mucosal ulcer. What is the most common complication of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Curling's ulcers are associated with severe burns or trauma.

Curling's ulcers occur in the proximal duodenum. Systemic hypotension or reduced blood flow caused by stress-induced splanchnic vasoconstriction results in gastric mucosal injury.

Note: Cushing's ulcers arise in individuals with intracranial disease. They occur in the stomach, duodenum, and esophagus and carry a high incidence of perforation.
question: A 26-year-old man with severe burns is most likely at risk of developing which of the following ulcers?

explanationHtml:
The given endoscopy image showing irregular enlargement of the gastric rugae in the body is suggestive of Ménétrier disease. It is due to excessive secretion of transforming growth factor α (TGF-α).

Menetrier disease is one of the causes of hypertrophic gastropathy. It is associated with diffuse hyperplasia of the foveolar epithelium and hypoproteinemia due to protein-losing enteropathy. There is an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma in adults.

The below histological image shows hyperplasia of foveolar mucous cells. The glands are cystically dilated and elongated with a corkscrew-like appearance.

[[figure-1]]
question: The upper gastrointestinal endoscopy of a patient is shown below. Excessive secretion of which of the following is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Fundic gland polyps are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

Fundic gland polyps may also occur sporadically or with proton pump inhibitor use. They occur in the gastric body and fundus.

They may be asymptomatic or associated with nausea, vomiting, or epigastric pain.

Dysplasia and neoplasia can occur in FAP-associated fundic gland polyps. Another gastric polyp linked to FAP is gastric adenoma.

The histological image below of a fundic gland polyp shows cystically dilated, irregular glands lined by flattened parietal and chief cells. Inflammation is typically absent or minimal.

[[figure-1]]
question: Fundic gland polyps are associated with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The most common site of gastric adenoma is the antrum.

Gastric adenomas are premalignant neoplastic lesions. Patients are usually between 50 and 60 years of age. Males are affected three times more often than females.

The majority of adenomas are composed of intestinal-type columnar epithelium that exhibits varying degrees of dysplasia.
question: What is the most common site of gastric adenoma?

explanationHtml:
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is not a predisposing factor for the development of gastric adenoma. It may predispose to carcinoid tumors.

Risk factors for gastric adenoma:

  • Chronic gastritis with atrophy
  • Intestinal metaplasia
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis

Note: The risk of adenocarcinoma in gastric adenomas is particularly increased in lesions greater than 2 cm in diameter. Overall, carcinoma may be present in up to 30% of gastric adenomas.
question: All are predisposing factors for the development of gastric adenoma except:

explanationHtml:
Familial gastric cancer (diffuse type) is strongly associated with germline loss-of-function mutations in the tumor suppressor gene CDH1. It encodes the cell adhesion protein, E-cadherin.

Half of the sporadic diffuse gastric cancer cases occur due to loss-of-function mutations in CDH1. In the remaining cases, E-cadherin expression is decreased due to hypermethylation and silencing of the CDH1 promoter. Thus, the loss of E-cadherin is a key step in the development of diffuse gastric cancer.

Sporadic intestinal-type gastric cancers are strongly associated with increased signaling via the Wnt pathway (loss-of-function mutation of APC/gain-of-function mutation of β-catenin).

Mutation of TP53 is also found in the majority of sporadic gastric cancers, regardless of their type.
question: Which germline loss-of-function mutation is strongly associated with patients diagnosed with familial gastric cancer?

explanationHtml:
Linitis plastica or leather bottle stomach or Brinton's disease is seen in diffuse gastric cancer.

Diffuse gastric cancer is an infiltrative tumor and often evokes a desmoplastic reaction that stiffens the gastric wall. When there are large areas of infiltration, diffuse rugal flattening, and a rigid, thickened wall may impart a leather bottle appearance as shown below.

[[figure-1]]
question: Linitis plastica is seen in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma does not form bulky tumors. It grows in a diffuse infiltrating pattern that stiffens the gastric wall (linitis plastica). In contrast, the intestinal type tends to form bulky masses.

Loss of E-cadherin is the key step in the development of diffuse gastric cancer, resulting in discohesive cells. These single cells have large, intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery, creating a signet-ring cell morphology. Mutation of TP53 is found in a majority of sporadic gastric cancers of both diffuse and intestinal types.

The below H&E-stained smear shows normal gastric mucosa (red arrow) and the characteristic signet cells (green arrows) in a patient with diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.

[[figure-1]]

Note: Loss of E cadherin is also seen in lobular carcinoma of the breast.
question: All are true about diffuse gastric cancer except:

explanationHtml:
The right axillary lymph nodes are least likely to be involved in gastric cancer metastasis.

Sites most commonly involved in gastric cancer metastasis include the following:

  • Virchow node (Supraclavicular sentinel lymph node)
  • Sister Mary Joseph nodule (Periumbilical nodes)
  • Irish node (Left axillary lymph node)
  • Krukenberg tumor (involvement of the ovary)
  • Blumer shelf (in the pouch of Douglas)
question: A 55-year-old woman with severe unintentional weight loss was found to have gastric cancer. This cancer is least likely to metastasize to which of the following sites?

explanationHtml:
The most common translocation in gastric MALToma is t(11;18)(q21;q21).

Three translocations are associated with gastric MALToma:

  1. t(11;18)(q21;q21) - Most common
  2. t(1;14)(p22;q32)
  3. t(14;18)(q32;q21)

Note: t(11;18) translocation results in a fusion gene leading to the formation of the API2-MALT1 fusion protein, which activates the NF-κB pathways and inhibits apoptosis.
question: What is the most common translocation seen in patients with gastric MALToma?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of gastric MALToma. The tumor cells express the B-cell markers CD19 and CD20. They do not express CD5 or CD10.

They are positive for CD43 in about 25% of cases, a T-cell marker that can be diagnostically helpful.
question: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing chronic gastritis undergoes an endoscopic biopsy. The biopsy showed dense lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions in the gastric glands. The cells of this tumor are likely to express all of the following markers except:

explanationHtml:
Gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors can secrete all of the above-mentioned secretory products except noradrenaline.

Carcinoid products at different sites:

  • Stomach - Histamine, somatostatin, serotonin
  • Duodenum - Gastrin, somatostatin, cholecystokinin
  • Jejunum and ileum - Serotonin, substance P, polypeptide YY
  • Colon - Serotonin, polypeptide YY.
question: Which of the following is least likely to be secreted by gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors?

explanationHtml:
The most aggressive carcinoid tumors of the GIT are seen in the jejunum and ileum.

Carcinoid tumors occur throughout the GI tract. The most common site is the appendix followed by the ileum and rectum.

Ileal carcinoid with metastasis to the liver causes carcinoid syndrome because the vasoactive substances escape the filtering actions of the liver. This is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

The behavior of the carcinoid tumors differs according to their location:

  • Foregut carcinoid tumor
    • Stomach; duodenum, proximal to the ligament of Treitz; and esophagus
    • Gastric carcinoid tumors originate from gastric enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells
    • Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors
    • Variable behavior
    • Rarely metastasize and are generally cured by resection
    • Gastric carcinoid tumors without predisposing factors are often more aggressive
  • Midgut carcinoid tumor
    • Arise in the jejunum, ileum, and appendix
    • Often multiple
    • Tend to be aggressive
  • Hindgut carcinoid
    • Arise in the colorectum
    • Appendiceal tumors are usually < 2 cm in diameter and are almost always benign
    • Metastasis of rectal carcinoid tumors is uncommon

Gastric carcinoid tumors may be associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis, MEN-I, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.
question: At which site are the most aggressive carcinoid tumors of the gastrointestinal system seen?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of carcinoid tumors. The most important prognostic factors include the degree of histological differentiation, mitotic rate, and Ki-67 proliferative index.

The diagnosis of carcinoid tumor is made by increased levels of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) in a 24-hour urine sample. It is positive in larger tumors or if metastases are present.

Note: The most important prognostic factor for esophageal carcinoma and stomach carcinoma is the depth of invasion.
question: A 50-year-old woman presents with complaints of abdominal pain and diarrhea. On examination, her face appears flushed and her pulse is 120/min. Increased levels of 5-HIAA are observed in a 24-hour urinary sample. Which of the following is not a prognostic factor for this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal, or pacemaker cells, of the gastrointestinal muscularis propria.

It is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen. The peak age of incidence is 60 years.

In sporadic GIST, the most common mutations seen are gain-of-function mutations in KIT (75-80%) and PDGFRA mutation (8%). Inherited/germline GIST is seen in Carney–Stratakis syndrome. It is due to a loss-of-function mutation of SDH, which has an increased risk for GIST and paraganglioma.

GIST at a younger age is associated with the following:

  • Carney triad:
    • Gastric GIST
    • Paraganglioma
    • Pulmonary chondroma
  • Neurofibromatosis type 1

Grossly, it usually forms a solitary, well-circumscribed, fleshy mass covered by ulcerated or intact mucosa.

Histologically, the tumor is composed of spindle cells (most common), epithelioid cells, or mixed cell types.

The image below shows microscopy of GIST composed of bundles, or fascicles, of spindle-shaped tumor cells

[[figure-1]]

Complete surgical resection is the primary treatment for localized gastric GIST.

Imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat CML, can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA.
question: A 62-year-old man underwent resection of a localized gastrointestinal tumor arising from the stomach. Histopathological examination showed a gain-of-function mutation in the KIT gene and positivity for CD117 and CD34. What is the most likely origin of the tumor?

explanationHtml:
The most specific marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is DOG-1.

KIT (CD117) is the best diagnostic marker (most sensitive marker) of GIST. However, 5–10% of GIST lack KIT expression. DOG-1 is expressed in all GIST, including CD117-negative cases. Hence, DOG-1 marker is most specific for GIST.
question: What is the most specific marker for a gastrointestinal stromal tumor?

explanationHtml:
Gastric adenocarcinoma is an epithelial tumor of the stomach.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common malignancy (90% cases) of the stomach.

Other options:

Option A: Carcinoid tumor is a neuroendocrine tumor.

Option B: Lymphoma is a lymphoid tumor.

Option C: GIST is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen.
question: Which of the following is an epithelial tumor of the stomach?

explanationHtml:
The eosinophilic appearing cells marked as A are the parietal cells, the absence of which is not associated with Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. The cells marked as B are Chief cells.

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome is caused by gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumors, which leads to parietal cell hyperplasia. Gastrinomas are almost always found in the small intestine or pancreas. The most remarkable feature found in the stomach is an increase in oxyntic mucosal thickness due to massive parietal cell hyperplasia.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A and C: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies that impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF) that is released from the parietal cells, which is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The actions of each of these include:

  • Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intrinsic factor (IF).
  • Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
  • Autoantibody type III acts against the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.

These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.

Option B: Gastric carcinoid tumors originate from gastric enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. They are referred to as well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. The peak incidence of carcinoid tumors is in the 6th decade. These tumors occur throughout the GI tract, commonly in the appendix, ileum, and rectum. Gastric carcinoid tumors may be associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis, MEN-I, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. Ileal carcinoid may cause carcinoid syndrome, which is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.
question: The absence of the structure marked as A will present with all except:

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children < 2 years of age is intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a segment of the intestine, constricted by a wave of peristalsis, telescopes into the immediately distal segment. It is usually idiopathic at younger ages. However, it can be associated with viral infections and rotavirus vaccines, perhaps due to reactive hyperplasia of Peyer patches.

Untreated intussusception may progress to intestinal obstruction, compression of mesenteric vessels, and infarction.

Note: The most common form of congenital intestinal atresia is imperforate anus. It occurs due to the failure of the cloacal diaphragm to involute.

The image below depicts intussusception of the bowel telescoping into the distal segment.

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children younger than 2 years of age?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of celiac disease or gluten-sensitive enteropathy. It is associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 alleles.

It is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by the ingestion of gluten-containing foods such as barley, rye, oats, and wheat (mnemonic: BROW) in genetically predisposed individuals.

In these individuals, digestion of the gluten-containing diet leads to the formation of gliadin peptides. These peptides result in the following immune reactions:

  • They can activate the epithelial cells to express certain cytokines (IL-15), which results in CD8+ T cell proliferation
  • They undergo deamidation and interact with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 on the antigen-presenting cells. This leads to CD4+ T cell stimulation and further cytokine production

These mechanisms result in epithelial tissue damage.

Antibodies associated with celiac disease are:

  • Anti-gliadin antibodies
  • Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (anti-ttG)
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies

Microscopic findings include:

  • Loss of villi
  • Epithelial infiltration by T cells
  • Hyperplasia of crypts
question: A 30-year-old man presented with a history of long-standing diarrhea. Serologic evaluation showed positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Duodenal biopsy showed crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. Which of the following HLA alleles is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and histopathology findings are suggestive of celiac disease. Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is the most common cancer associated with celiac disease.

[[figure-2]]

Small intestinal adenocarcinoma is also associated with celiac disease.

Celiac disease or celiac sprue or gluten-sensitive enteropathy, is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the 2nd part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum.

Antibodies associated with celiac disease are:

  • Anti-gliadin antibodies
  • Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies

MARSH's score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis occurs in about 10% of patients with celiac disease.
question: A 34-year-old male patient presented to the clinic with a history of diarrhea and poor appetite. He has been having 4-5 episodes of non-bloody, loose stools per day for the last 3 months. In cystic fibrosis, malabsorption occurs due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, not intestinal mucosal defects.

Cystic fibrosis is caused by pathogenic mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7 that encodes the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein.

The absence of the CFTR protein interferes with Na+, HCO3-, and water secretion, resulting in defective luminal hydration. This leads to the formation of pancreatic intraductal concretions and results in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

question: A 33-year-old man presented to the ER with severe abdominal pain. He gives a history of fever for the past 2 weeks. On examination, faint salmon-colored macules were noted on the trunk and abdomen. Which of the following diseases would you suspect?

In Whipple's disease, the cause of malabsorption is impaired lymphatic transport.

In Whipple disease, clinical symptoms occur because organism-laden macrophages accumulate within the small intestinal lamina propria and mesenteric lymph nodes, causing lymphatic obstruction. These bacteria-laden macrophages also gather within mesenteric lymph nodes, synovial membranes of affected joints, cardiac valves, and the brain.

The clinical presentation of Whipple disease is usually a triad of diarrhea, weight loss, and arthralgia.

explanationHtml:

Distended foamy macrophages inside the lamina propria of the duodenum can be seen in:

As both organisms are PAS-positive, PAS staining cannot differentiate between the two diseases. On the other hand, acid-fast staining can confirm the diagnosis because only mycobacteria are acid fast, while Tropheryma whipplei is not.

Rotavirus is a common cause of severe childhood diarrhea and diarrheal mortality worldwide. Rotavirus selectively infects and destroys mature enterocytes in the small intestine. This causes repopulation of the villus surface by immature secretory cells.

Giardia lamblia is the most common parasitic pathogen in humans.

It causes giardiasis, which usually develops after a 2 week incubation period. The transmission is by ingestion of resistant mature cysts in contaminated food, water, or by fecal-oral route. Often the infected individuals are asymptomatic, but some present with diarrhea with fat malabsorption, i.e., greasy stools.

Diagnosis is made by identification of the cyst in stool examination, or antigen or antibody detection by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunofluorescence tests.

The following image shows a teardrop (pear)-shaped Giardia with paired nuclei:

Treatment is with metronidazole 250 mg thrice a day for 5-7 days, and a single dose of tinidazole 2 g.

Histology of carcinoid typically reveals islands and nests of uniform cells with scant, pink, granular cytoplasm and salt-and-pepper chromatin. Electron microscopy reveals cytoplasmic dense-core neurosecretory granules.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Carcinoid tumors most commonly occur in the gastrointestinal tract. The most common sites in decreasing order of frequency are the appendix, ileum, and rectum. These tumors may cause carcinoid syndrome, which is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) markers for carcinoid tumors are:

question: A 55-year-old man who presented with diarrhea and flushing was found to have an ileal tumor. The histological image of the resected specimen is given below. Which of the following markers will these cells be positive for?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of autoimmune enteropathy or IPEX syndrome. Definitive diagnosis requires gene sequencing to identify mutations in the FOXP3 gene.

FOXP3 is a transcription factor expressed in CD4+ regulatory T cells.

Autoimmune enteropathy is an X-linked disorder characterized by severe, persistent diarrhea and autoimmune disease in young children. A particularly severe familial form is termed IPEX, an acronym denoting.

  • Immune dysregulation
  • Polyendocrinopathy
  • Enteropathy
  • X-linked inheritance.

The characteristic IPEX triad includes:

  • Autoimmune enteropathy causing diarrhoea

question: A 10 month old infant is brought to the OPD with complaints of intractable diarrhea. His past history is significant for autoimmune thyroiditis. explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of microvillus inclusion disease (MVID), which is associated with mutations in the MYO5B gene.

Microvillus inclusion disease, also known as Davidson disease, is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from mutations in the MYO5B gene. This gene encodes a motor protein that is required for the transport of normal nutrients, ions, water, and plasma membrane components. Hence, it leads to defective vesicular transport that causes deficient brush-border assembly.

Clinical features of MVID are:

  • Profuse watery, secretory diarrhea - before 3 months of age (often in the first few days of life)
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Hypotonic dehydration

Diagnosis of MVID includes:

  • Electron microscopy -
    • Inclusion containing microvilli in the apical cytoplasm of the intestinal cells.
    • Brush border microvilli are poorly developed, with only a few/blunted microvilli
  • Immunostaining of villin (the brush border protein)
  • CD10 immunohistochemistry to detect microvilli inclusions

Treatment is total parenteral nutrition and small bowel transplantation.

The following electron microscopy image shows characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions lined by intact microvilli along the absorptive surfaces of intestinal cells.

[[figure-1]]

Condition Site

A true diverticulum is a blind outpouching of the alimentary tract that communicates with the lumen and includes all three layers of the bowel wall. The most common true diverticulum is Meckel's diverticulum. It most commonly occurs in the ileum. It appears as a result of the failed involution of the vitelline duct, which connects the lumen of the developing gut to the yolk sac.

The following image shows a Meckel's diverticulum.

On the other hand, false or acquired diverticula either lack the muscularis entirely or have an attenuated muscularis propria.

Though Crohn's disease most commonly occurs in the terminal ileum, it may happen in any area of the GI tract.

Polyps are most common in the colorectal region. They can be sessile (without a stalk) or pedunculated (with a stalk). Intestinal polyps can be classified as non-neoplastic or neoplastic in nature. The nonneoplastic polyps can be further classified into three categories as inflammatory, hamartomatous, or hyperplastic. The most common neoplastic polyp is an adenoma.

correctAnswer: A. Failure of migration of neural crest cells
explanationHtml:
Hirschsprung disease occurs due to the failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the bowel wall.

During normal embryogenesis, the neural crest cells migrate from the caecum to the rectum. The enteric neuronal plexuses develop from these migrated neural crest cells.

In Hirschsprung disease, there is an arrest in the migration of these cells, leading to the development of a distal intestinal segment that is devoid of the Meissner (submucosal) and Auerbach (myenteric) plexuses. Hence, this segment is referred to as the aganglionic segment.

As a result, there is a lack of coordination in the peristaltic contractions and functional obstruction, which further leads to dilation of the intestine proximal to the affected segment, resulting in congenital megacolon. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating the absence of ganglion cells in biopsy sections.

[[figure-1]]

Some conditions may cause acquired megacolon. These include:

  • Chagas disease, due to the loss of ganglion cells
  • Visceral myopathy
  • Obstruction by neoplasm or inflammatory stricture
  • Toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis
  • Functional psychosomatic disorders

options.text: Failure of migration of neural crest cells

question: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. It is associated with Down syndrome.

Hirschsprung disease is also known as congenital aganglionic megacolon. 10% of all cases occur in children with Down syndrome.

The premature arrest of normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum produces aganglionosis of the distal intestinal segment. This results in a functional obstruction of the affected bowel and proximal dilation. The absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment in the biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

[[figure-1]]

Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Down's syndrome include:

  • Duodenal atresia
  • Annular pancreas
  • Hirschsprung disease

Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) include:

  • Meckel's diverticulum
  • Malrotation

Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) include:

  • Omphalocele
  • Incomplete rotation of the colon
  • Meckel's diverticulum

Risk factors for Clostridium difficile colitis are:

question: A pathologist is examining the following histopathological specimen from a patient with watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Crohn's disease. It is strongly associated with mutations in the nucleotide oligomerization binding domain 2 (NOD2) gene.

Crohn's disease occurs due to the host response against microbes. NOD2 encodes an intracellular protein that binds to bacterial peptidoglycans and activates the NF-κB pathway. Antibodies against the bacterial protein flagellin may be seen in NOD2-associated disease.

Other Crohn's disease-related genes are autophagy-related 16-like (ATG16L1) and immunity-related GTPase M (IRGM), which are critical for cellular responses to intracellular bacteria.

Crohn's disease most commonly involves the terminal ileum but can affect all parts of the GIT. The following microscopic changes may be seen:

  • Aphthoid ulcerations
  • Focal crypt abscesses
  • Non-caseating granulomas can be found in all layers of the bowel, lymph nodes, mesentery, peritoneum, liver, and pancreas

Note: Ulcerative colitis-associated genes are ECM1 and HNFA.
question: A 30-year-old man presented with loose stools and right lower abdominal pain for the past 6 months. Endoscopy was done which showed skip lesions with a cobblestone appearance. Extraintestinal manifestations of Crohn's disease include the following:

Histologically, sessile serrated polyps appear like hyperplastic polyps, but a serrated architecture throughout the full length of the glands and lateral growth is the differentiating feature. They lack cytological features of dysplasia.

The most common site of juvenile polyps is in the rectum.

Juvenile polyps are focal malformations of the epithelium and lamina propria. They may be sporadic or syndromic. They typically present with rectal bleeding in children < 5 years.

  • Sporadic juvenile polyps - solitary lesions, also called retention polyps
  • Juvenile polyposis - an autosomal dominant syndrome with multiple hamartomatous polyps that have malignant potential
question: Which of the following sites is most commonly involved in patients with juvenile polyps?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features and the histopathological image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts and glands are suggestive of a juvenile polyp.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Juvenile polyps are malformations of epithelium and lamina propria commonly located in the rectum. It is seen in children <5 years of age. The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes there may be a proliferating rectal mass.

The disease may be sporadic or syndromic.

  • Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and are called retention polyps.
  • Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterised by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant.

Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable.

  • Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth, reddish lesions with cystic spaces.
  • Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.

Note: Complex glandular architecture and the presence of smooth muscle cutting through the lamina propria are seen in Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) requires ≥100 polyps.

The current definition of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) requires evidence of any one of the following:

  1. Germline mutation in the APC gene
  2. ≥100 colorectal adenomatous polyps (classical definition)
  3. Any colorectal adenomas < 30 years in a patient with a family history of FAP
  4. Intra-abdominal desmoid fibromatosis, osteoma of the mandible, or multiple epidermoid cysts in a patient with a family history of FAP

Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops in 100% of untreated FAP patients, often before the age of 30 years and nearly always by the age of 50 years.

Attenuated FAP is a less severe form of FAP with the following features:

  • Usually <100 adenomas
  • First appear usually in late childhood
  • Adenomas usually remain ≤1 cm until adulthood
  • Adenomas are fewer and later
  • Adenomas and carcinomas 60–75% right-sided
  • The mean age of carcinoma is 55 years

It occurs due to defective DNA mismatch repair. It is caused by inherited mutations in genes that encode proteins responsible for detecting, excising, and repairing errors that occur during DNA replication. They include MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 or EPCAM genes.

It is the most common syndromic cause of colon cancer. It tends to occur at younger ages than sporadic colon cancers and often involves the right colon. Familial clustering of cancers occurs at several sites, including:

Atelectasis refers either to an incomplete expansion of the lungs (neonatal atelectasis) or to the collapse of the previously inflated lung.

The main types of atelectasis in adults are:

  • Compression atelectasis occurs whenever significant volumes of fluid, tumor, or air accumulate within the pleural cavity. E.g. pneumothorax, pleural effusion.

Microscopically, the hyaline membranes are primarily made up of fibrin admixed with necrotic cell debris. Grossly, the lungs are of normal size, solid, airless, reddish-purple, and they usually sink in water.

question: An infant born to a diabetic mother develops difficulty in breathing within 30 minutes of birth. Within a few hours, cyanosis becomes evident. Fine rales are heard over both lung fields. In this disorder, a lack of production of surfactant leads to severe respiratory failure in neonates. There is a transient improvement with the administration of exogenous surfactant, but it worsens once surfactant therapy is stopped. It is also known as acute lung injury and is clinically characterised by the abrupt onset of significant hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in the absence of cardiac failure. question: A 68-year-old man presented with episodes of shortness of breath and coughing at night that awaken him from sleep. He was diagnosed with COPD 7 years ago. On examination, distended neck veins were observed and S3 was heard on auscultation. Bronchoalveolar lavage of this patient is given below. Identify the marked cells.

explanationHtml:

ARDS is characterised by bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxemia in the absence of heart failure. The causes of ARDS are:

  • Sepsis
  • Diffuse pulmonary infections

question: A pathologist is examining the following histopathological section of an alveolus. All of the following can be associated with this finding except:

explanationHtml:
In the stage of gray hepatization in pneumonia, there is disintegration of RBCs within the alveoli.

Bacterial pneumonias can be classified morphologically as:

  • Lobular pneumonia (bronchopneumonia) - patchy consolidation of the lung
  • Lobar pneumonia - consolidation of an entire lobe

Stages of lobar pneumonia are as follows:

Stages Duration Description
Congestion 1-2 days RBCs and exudate fluid in the alveoli
Red hepatization 2-4 days Accumulation of neutrophils, RBCs and fibrin in the alveoli

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a cytomegalic pneumocyte containing a characteristic intranuclear basophilic inclusion surrounded by a clear halo known as the owl’s eye appearance. In conjunction with the given clinical scenario, this is suggestive of cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia.

CMV is a β-group herpesvirus. It causes the following conditions:

  • Immunocompetent individuals - asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like infection
  • Neonates - devastating systemic infections
  • Immunosuppressed individuals - serious, life-threatening, disseminated CMV infections of the lungs (pneumonitis) and gastrointestinal tract (colitis)

Other options:

Option A: Small-cell carcinoma has small cells with scant cytoplasm, salt-and-pepper chromatin with inconspicuous nucleoli.

Option C: In cryptococcal infection, encapsulated yeasts are seen on direct microscopy.

question: A 65-year-old HIV-positive man presented with fever and breathlessness for 2 weeks. Imaging shows dense infiltration in the lower lobe and the lung biopsy showed the following finding. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and image showing massive neutrophilic infiltration are suggestive of Mendelson’s syndrome or aspiration pneumonitis.

Mendelson's syndrome is a chemical pneumonitis caused by the aspiration of sterile gastric contents during general anesthesia, especially during pregnancy. The most common cause of maternal mortality associated with general anesthesia is either due to a pulmonary aspiration or a failed endotracheal intubation.

The risk factors for Mendelson's syndrome include:

  • Gastric volume > 25 mL (0.4 mL/kg)
  • Gastric pH < 2.5

Incidence of aspiration can be reduced by the administration of:

  • Non-particulate antacids like sodium citrate 30-45 minutes before intubation
  • H2 receptor antagonists like intravenous ranitidine
  • Metoclopramide 1-2 hours before induction

Other options:

Option B: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is a type of ILD associated with Masson bodies and plugs of loose connective tissue on histology.

Option C: CMV pneumonia is associated with the owl's eye appearance on histology.

Option D: Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia is associated with black-walled cysts on silver staining.

explanationHtml:
The given histopathological image clearly shows a granuloma with refractile granules indicative of a foreign body. It is seen in aspiration pneumonia due to vegetative matter (such as food).

In this condition, the chest x-ray usually shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates, especially in the right middle and lower lobes. Patients with altered sensorium are at high risk (stroke, medications).

Chest x-ray showed bilateral diffuse infiltrates with predominant involvement of right middle and lower lobes. The patient could not be revived despite treatment. On autopsy, the lungs appeared grossly normal. The histopathology image of the lung is as shown below. Which among the following is the appropriate cause?

question: A 25-year-old man presented with fever, productive cough, and breathlessness of 2 months duration. CECT chest revealed bilateral upper lobe fibrotic lesions and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Lymph node biopsy revealed the following. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given x-ray of this patient with tuberculosis shows an infraclavicular lesion. It is known as Assmann's focus.

Primary tuberculosis typically occurs following the first exposure and involves the lower part of the upper lobe and the upper part of the lower lobe. The following findings may be seen:

  • Ghon's focus - focus of infection located subpleurally
  • Ghon's complex - Ghon's focus with lymph node involvement
  • Ranke complex - a calcified Ghon's complex

Secondary tuberculosis occurs due to the reactivation of TB. It affects the apex. The following findings may be seen:

  • Puhl's complex - supraclavicular lesion
  • Assmann's complex - infraclavicular lesion

Disseminated or miliary tuberculosis is characterised by 1-2 mm disseminated lesions all over the lung. The following findings may be associated:

  • Simon's focus - early hematogenous seeding in the apex of lungs
  • Rich focus - tuberculous caseous foci in the brain, meninges and spinal cord
question: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to several weeks of occasional hemoptysis, weight loss, and fever. He has lost 7 kg over the past 3 months.  Sputum culture grows acid-fast bacilli and his chest X-ray is shown below. What is this lesion called?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with the gross image showing individual lesions that are small (2-mm) foci of yellow-white consolidation scattered throughout the lung parenchyma, is suggestive of miliary tuberculosis.

Miliary tuberculosis (TB) refers to the widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis via hematogenous spread. It occurs when organisms draining through the lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lungs. Miliary TB may infect any number of organs, including the lungs, liver, and spleen.

The adjective 'miliary' is derived from the resemblance of these foci to millet seeds. The Mantoux test is negative in miliary TB.
question: A 61-year-old man presented with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. The patient subsequently died a few weeks later. Gross specimen of the lung is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Pancytopenia may be seen due to infiltration of the bone marrow
explanationHtml:
The given history, clinical features, and chest X-ray point towards a diagnosis of miliary tuberculosis. Pancytopenia may be seen due to infiltration of the bone marrow in such cases.

The second X-ray shows acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Chest x-ray appearance of ARDS varies depending on the severity and typically appears as bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities with dependent atelectasis in some cases. The opacities may have a patchy ground-glass appearance. The cause of death here is likely ARDS. (option A)

In immunodeficient individuals (eg, a patient having HIV), there may occur widespread dissemination of M. tuberculosis via the hematogenous route (option B) that leads to the seeding of bacteria in various organs (hepatosplenomegaly). This is known as miliary TB.

It is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis, and not extrapulmonary (option D)

The risk factors of miliary TB include-

  • Extremes of age
  • Alcohol use
  • Malignancy
  • HIV
  • Corticosteroids
  • Connective tissue disease
  • Renal failure
  • Diabetes, and pregnancy

question: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough with sputum, and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of α1-antitrypsin deficiency. The α1-antitrypsin is encoded by the proteinase inhibitor (Pi) locus on chromosome 14.

α1-AT is a polymorphic gene located on chromosome 14. The most common clinically significant mutation in α1-antitrypsin deficiency is PiZZ.

α1-antitrypsin is normally present in serum, tissue fluids, and macrophages, is a major inhibitor of proteases (particularly elastase) secreted by neutrophils during inflammation. The absence of α1-antitrypsin activity results in excessive digestion of elastic tissue by elastase.

Patients with α1-antitrypsin deficiency have a markedly increased tendency to develop panacinar emphysema.
question: A 25-year-old man is being evaluated for dyspnea and cough for 2 months. He is not a smoker. Workup revealed emphysematous changes at lung bases. question: A 55-year-old man was brought to the ED with fever, cough with expectoration, and difficulty in breathing for 1 day. He is a chronic smoker and he has had similar progressive symptoms for the last 4 years. Past PFT findings showed reduced FEV1 and increased RV with normal diffusion capacity. Which of the following is the most common organism implicated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the sputum microscopy showing Charcot–Leyden crystals (arrows in image below), lakes of mucus, and numerous eosinophils, are diagnostic of bronchial asthma.

[[figure-1]]

Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction caused by airway hyperresponsiveness to a variety of stimuli. Atopic asthma is caused by a TH2 and IgE-mediated immunologic reaction to environmental allergens (type-1 hypersensitivity reaction). Triggers for non-atopic asthma are less clear but include viral infections and inhaled air pollutants.

Genetic susceptibility for developing asthma:

  • Chromosome 5q - site of the susceptibility locus for asthma
  • IL-13 gene polymorphisms (on 5q chromosome) - most consistent associations with asthma or allergic disease
  • IL-4 receptor gene variants - associated with atopy, elevated total serum IgE, and asthma

The sputum of patients with bronchial asthma shows:

  • Charcot–Leyden crystals - made of an eosinophilic membrane protein called galectin 10
  • Curschmann spirals - spirals of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous gland ducts or bronchioles
  • Creola bodies - desquamated epithelial cells
  • Numerous eosinophils

Note: The hygiene hypothesis was previously used to explain the development of asthma and other hypersensitivity disorders.
question: A middle-aged woman presented with recurrent episodes of breathlessness, wheeze, and chest tightness. Auscultation of the chest revealed bilateral wheeze. Sputum microscopy reveals the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The image above shows markedly distended bronchi involving the middle and lower lobes of the lung, which is seen in bronchiectasis.

Bronchiectasis is a suppurative lung disease with abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi. It is an end-stage condition of various diseases that result in the destruction of the bronchial wall and its surrounding supporting tissues.

The normal clearing mechanisms are impaired, either due to congenital causes or due to bronchial obstruction. This results in pooling of secretions, secondary infection, and inflammation, often with necrosis, fibrosis, and eventually cystic dilation of airways up to four times the normal size.

Note: Kartagener syndrome is a primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.
question: A resected specimen of a lung is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The image above shows alveolar spaces filled with balls of fibroblasts (Masson bodies). This is characteristically seen in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).

Masson bodies are polypoid plugs of loose organizing connective tissue within alveolar ducts, alveoli, and bronchioles, along with foci of fibrosis.

[[figure-1]]

The clinical presentation of COP is the development of nonspecific systemic and respiratory symptoms. It is associated with the filling of the lung alveoli, which is visible on a chest X-ray as patchy, unilateral, or bilateral consolidation.

COP was previously known as bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP).
question: Transbronchial biopsy from a patient showed the following microscopic finding. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Silicosis is the most common form of pneumoconiosis worldwide.

Silicosis is caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica (e.g., quartz). Individuals involved with the concrete work, sandblasting, stone carvers, and jewelers using chalk molds are at high risk.

Pneumoconioses encompass a group of chronic fibrosing diseases of the lung resulting from exposure to organic and inorganic particulates, most commonly mineral dust.
question: What is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world?

explanationHtml:
Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure.

They are well-circumscribed plaques of dense collagen, often containing calcium. They develop most frequently on the parietal pleura and over the domes of the diaphragm. They do not contain asbestos bodies, and only rarely occur in persons without prior asbestos exposure.

Asbestos occurs in two distinct forms - serpentine chrysotile (more common) and amphibole (more pathogenic). Exposure may result in the following conditions:

  • Localized fibrous plaques or, rarely, diffuse pleural fibrosis
  • Pleural effusions
  • Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)
  • Lung carcinoma
  • Mesotheliomas
  • Extrapulmonary neoplasms, including laryngeal, ovarian, and colon carcinomas

The image below shows fibrous pleural plaques seen on the diaphragmatic pleural surface in asbestosis.

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the most common manifestation of asbestosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing typical asbestos bodies are suggestive of asbestosis.

Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis associated with asbestos exposure. The disease-causing capabilities of the different forms of asbestos depend on concentration, size, shape, and solubility. This condition is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis.

Asbestos bodies are a typical finding. They are golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods with a translucent center. They consist of asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material and arise when these fibers are phagocytosed by macrophages.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Other inorganic particulates may become coated with similar iron-protein complexes and are called ferruginous bodies.

Asbestosis is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis and the presence of multiple asbestos bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Centrilobular emphysema may develop in simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis.

Option B: Increased susceptibility to tuberculosis is seen in silicosis, which can cause pneumonia.

Option C: Occupational asthma may be triggered by fumes (epoxy resins, plastics), organic and chemical dust (wood, cotton, platinum), gases (toluene), or other chemicals (formaldehyde, penicillin products).
question: A 60-year-old man presented with dyspnea and cough. Chest X-ray revealed irregular linear densities, particularly in both lower lobes. Histopathological examination of lung biopsy is shown below. This patient has a higher risk of developing:

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image showing the lesion of lupus pernio point towards sarcoidosis. It is a multisystemic disease characterized by polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.

Lupus pernio is seen in cutaneous sarcoidosis and presents as infiltrated erythematoviolaceous plaques involving the nose, cheeks, ears, lips, forehead, and fingers. On the cheeks, telangiectasia is characteristic. It is usually painless. As it does not ulcerate, it is not as mutilating as lupus vulgaris.

Immunological abnormalities include:

  • Polyclonal hyperglobulinemia
  • A CD4/CD8 ratio > 3.5
  • T- cell expansion and macrophage activation
  • Impaired dendritic cell function
  • Anergy to common skin tests.

The hallmarks of sarcoidosis include:

  • B/L hilar lymphadenopathy
  • Non-caseating granulomas
  • Lupus pernio
  • Erythema nodosum (acute sarcoidosis)

Syndromes associated with sarcoidosis are:

  • Mikulicz syndrome - sarcoidosis combined with uveoparotid involvement
  • Lofgren's syndrome - acute presentation of sarcoidosis, consisting of arthritis, erythema nodosum, and bilateral hilar adenopathy

The image below shows the characteristic non-caseating sarcoid granuloma.

[[figure-1]]

The image below shows stellate inclusions known as asteroid bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

The image below shows laminated concretions composed of calcium and proteins known as Schaumann bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.

[[figure-4]]

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of low-grade fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. Examination reveals the following painless skin lesion. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lung biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) is the most common gene mutation in pulmonary hypertension. Inactivating mutations in this gene are found in 75% of the familial cases of pulmonary hypertension and 25% of sporadic cases.

The BMPR2 receptor is a cell surface protein belonging to the TGF-β receptor superfamily. It is involved in the regulation of growth, differentiation, and apoptosis of pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells.

Due to the mutation, there is enhanced proliferation and reduced apoptosis of vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, leading to pulmonary hypertension.
question: What is the most common gene mutation associated with pulmonary hypertension?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and microscopy showing alveoli filled with a dense, amorphous, protein-lipid granular precipitate are suggestive of autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP). It is caused by circulating neutralizing antibodies specific for granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).

PAP is a condition characterized by the accumulation of surfactants in alveoli and terminal airways. It can be due to impaired clearance or abnormal production of surfactants.

PAP can be of three forms:

  • Primary (most common): There is impaired GM-CSF-dependent surfactant clearance by the alveolar macrophages. It can be due to:
    • Autoantibodies against GM-CSF (acquired/idiopathic/autoimmune PAP)
    • Mutation in GM-CSF receptors (hereditary PAP)
  • Secondary: There is a reduction in the number or ability of alveolar macrophages that causes impaired surfactant clearance. It can be due to:
    • Silicosis
    • Immunodeficiency disorders
    • Hematopoietic disorders and malignancies
  • Congenital: It affects neonates and children. There is abnormal surfactant production due to mutation in the genes coding for:
    • Surfactant protein B
    • Surfactant protein C
    • ATP binding cassette protein member 3

It is the most common form of lung cancer. It is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation. The tumor cells produce mucin. It is usually located peripherally (it arises from the terminal bronchiole).

Molecular genetics show frequent mutations in EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, and RET (Receptor tyrosine kinase genes) or KRAS mutations.

Histologically, lepidic growth patterns are seen. It refers to the pattern of spread of the tumor in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septae and resemble butterflies resting on a fence.

Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns, including acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid with mucin formation. Tumor cells are positive for mucin and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1)

Tumors 3 cm or less in diameter, characterized by a lepidic growth pattern without stromal invasion, are now called adenocarcinoma in situ (formerly called bronchoalveolar carcinoma).

TTF-1 is required for normal lung development. It can be used to distinguish primary adenocarcinoma of the lungs (TTF-1 positive) from other histological types of lung cancers, metastatic adenocarcinoma, and mesothelioma (TTF-1 negative).

Chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56 are the markers for small-cell lung carcinoma.

Malignant mesothelioma is a rare malignant tumour of the pleura, associated with heavy asbestos exposure (shipping factory). The lifetime risk of developing mesothelioma in heavily exposed individuals is as high as 7% to 10%.

It has strong male predilection (3:1). There is a long latent period of 25 to 45 years for the development of asbestos-related mesothelioma.

The image below shows a lung autopsy sample with mesothelioma.

[[figure-1]]

Grossly, it appears as a diffuse lesion arising either from the visceral or parietal pleura. The affected lung becomes ensheathed by a thick layer of soft, gelatinous, grayish pink tumor tissue.

Microscopically, they are of three types: epithelioid (60%), sarcomatoid (20%), and mixed (20%).

Electron microscopy in mesothelioma will show numerous long, slender microvilli and abundant monofilaments, but absent microvillous rootlets and lamellar bodies.

question: A 75-year-old man presents with a cough and shortness of breath. He has been working in a shipping factory for 40 years. explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchial carcinoid. Bronchial neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) arise from Kulchitsky cells.

WHO divides neuroendocrine neoplasms into four categories:

  • Typical carcinoid
  • Atypical carcinoid
  • Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
  • Small-cell carcinoma

Carcinoid tumors are low-grade malignant epithelial neoplasms that represent 1% to 5% of all lung tumors. It is not related to smoking. Carcinoids may occur in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

On gross examination, these tumors appear as fingerlike or spherical polypoid masses that extend into the bronchus lumen or as collar button lesions, penetrating the bronchial wall and spreading into the peribronchial tissue.

Histologically, the tumor is composed of organoid, trabecular, palisading, ribbon, or rosette-like arrangements of cells separated by a delicate fibrovascular stroma. On electron microscopy, the cells exhibit dense-core neurosecretory granules.

Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for serotonin, neuron-specific enolase, bombesin, calcitonin, or other peptides.

10% of the cases may produce carcinoid syndrome.

Most carcinoids follow a relatively benign course and have a good prognosis.
question: A  59-year old man presented with persistent wheezing, episodes of hemoptysis, and dry cough. Bronchoscopy revealed a mass occluding the left bronchus. Biopsy of the specimen revealed polygonal cells with fine stippled chromatin and eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests. The tumor was positive for CD 56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. explanationHtml:
Approximately 10% of bronchial carcinoids give rise to the carcinoid syndrome.

Most bronchial carcinoids follow a relatively benign course, do not have secretory activity, and do not metastasize to distant sites.

Classic carcinoid syndrome is characterized by intermittent attacks of diarrhea, flushing, bronchospasm and cyanosis.

Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialised product of tryptophan metabolism by argentaffin cells (cells in the carcinoid tumor). It is then metabolised and excreted in urine.

If urinary levels of 5-HIAA exceed 25 mg/day, a diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome can be made.

It is a benign clonal neoplasm associated with chromosomal aberrations involving either 6p21 or 12q14-q15.

Lung hamartoma is usually discovered as an incidental coin lesion on a routine chest radiograph.

Pituitary adenomas are usually found in adults. The most common genetic alterations in pituitary adenomas are mutations in G proteins (particularly GNAS).

Depending on their size, they are classified as:

  • Microadenomas - diameter < 1 cm
  • Macroadenomas - diameter > 1 cm

They may be functioning or non-functioning. The most common type of functioning pituitary adenomas is prolactinomas.

The clinical features of prolactinoma include:

    • Visual field disturbances (bitemporal hemianopia) - due to compression of the optic chiasm

Serum prolactin concentrations tend to correlate with the size of the adenoma. The normal range of serum prolactin is 5-20 μg/L. The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 μg/L.

Pituitary carcinoma is extremely rare (< 1% of total tumors). They are associated with activating mutations of the HRAS oncogene.

The diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma cannot be made based on histologic appearance alone. Though pituitary adenomas normally show cellular monomorphism and the absence of a reticulin network, they can have some overlapping features with malignant tumors, such as:

The most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia (isolated hypercalcemia without signs or symptoms) is primary hyperparathyroidism. It is also the most common cause of hypercalcemia overall.

Primary hyperparathyroidism results in autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), resulting in elevated levels. It usually results from an adenoma or hyperplasia of parathyroid tissue.

The most common cause of symptomatic hypercalcemia is malignancy. The most common mechanism through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is the secretion of the PTH-related peptide (PTHrP).

Parathyroid tumors may be associated with cyclin D1 gene inversions and MEN1 mutations. Hyperparathyroidism refers to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH). It is classified into:

  • Primary - autonomous overproduction of PTH
  • Secondary - compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia
  • Tertiary - persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after correction of prolonged hypocalcemia. (e.g., after renal transplant)

question: A 40-year-old woman presented with bone pain and abdominal cramps for the past 1 week. She has had multiple prior hospital admissions for management of recurrent renal calculi. The clinical scenario and lab findings point towards a diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism. The bone finding associated with this condition is osteitis fibrosa cystica.

This condition is also called brown tumor or von Recklinghausen disease of bone.

In hyperparathyroidism, high levels of PTH result in increased osteoclast activity. This results in bone loss, which predisposes to microfractures and secondary hemorrhages. This results in the following changes:

  • An influx of macrophages that form giant cells
  • Mass of reparative fibrous tissue
  • Increased vascularity, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin deposition - results in brown color

This clinical scenario is suggestive of hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinemia. As C-peptide is a marker of endogenous insulin secretion, its levels would help in identifying the source of insulin:

question: A pathologist is studying a Congo red-stained slide of pancreatic tissue. He observes it under polarized light and notes the following finding. This finding is commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: C. Increased anticoagulant effect on endothelial cells and macrophages
explanationHtml:
Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) result in increased procoagulant effects on endothelial cells and macrophages, not anticoagulant effects.

AGEs are formed by nonenzymatic reactions between intracellular glucose-derived dicarbonyl precursors with the amino groups of proteins. They bind to a specific receptor (RAGE) that is expressed on inflammatory cells (macrophages and T cells), endothelium, and vascular smooth muscle.

The detrimental effects of the AGE-RAGE signalling axis within the vascular compartment include:

  • Release of cytokines and growth factors, including TGF-β - leads to deposition of excess basement membrane material
  • Generation of reactive oxygen species in endothelial cells.
  • Increased procoagulant activity on endothelial cells and macrophages.
  • Enhanced proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and synthesis of extracellular matrix

These effects are responsible for the microvascular and macrovascular complications in diabetes mellitus.

Graves' disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.

It is an autoimmune disorder due to the production of TSH-receptor stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) which cause hyperthyroidism.

It is characterized by the triad of:

explanationHtml:
Hashimoto thyroiditis is not associated with hyperthyroidism. It is associated with transient thyrotoxicosis, followed by chronic hypothyroidism.

Thyrotoxicosis is a hypermetabolic state caused by elevated levels of free T3 and T4, leading to a range of clinical symptoms. It can be classified into two main types:

  • Thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism – This occurs when the thyroid gland itself is overactive. It is further subdivided into:
    • Primary hyperthyroidism – due to intrinsic thyroid pathology.
    • Secondary hyperthyroidism – due to excessive stimulation of the thyroid by TSH or other factors.
  • Thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism – In this type, thyroid hormone levels are elevated, but the thyroid gland itself is not overactive and the gland functions normally.

[[figure-1]]

In thyroid hormone resistance, tissues are somewhat resistant to thyroid hormones. To compensate, the pituitary often increases TSH secretion, stimulating the thyroid to produce more T3/T4, and occasionally, patients develop symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.
question: Which of the following disorders does not lead to hyperthyroidism?

correctAnswer: D. Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping colloid
explanationHtml:
The given image shows follicular hyperplasia with a scalloping colloid. The clinical scenario along with the image is suggestive of Graves' disease.

In Graves' disease, the thyroid is diffusely hyperplastic. The follicles are lined by tall columnar epithelial cells that project into lumina. The cells actively resorb the colloid in the center of the follicle which results in a scalloped appearance of the edges of the colloid.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

options.text: Dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centre

question: What is the finding seen in the following histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen from a patient with an enlarged thyroid?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture and image showing Hurthle cells are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

In this condition, the following microscopic features are seen:

  • Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well developed germinal centers
  • Atrophied thyroid follicles
  • The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm (oncocytes)
    • This is called oncocytic metaplasia
    • These cells are called Hurthle cells
    • Ultrastructurally, these cells have numerous mitochondria

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease, characterized by the gradual destruction of the thyroid gland leading to thyroid failure. It is commonly seen in women between 45 to 65 years of age. It is caused by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase.

Morphologically, there is a diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland, with an intact capsule. It is well demarcated from the adjacent structures.

Note: Oncocytes can arise in various tissues and are referred to as follows:

  • Hurthle cells/ Ashkenazy cells - thyroid gland
  • Oxyphilic cells - parotid gland
  • Apocrine metaplasia - breast
question: A 50-year-old woman presented with diffuse thyroid swelling for the past 6 months. She says that it has increased in size over the last 1 month. Investigations reveal elevated TSH levels. Histopathological examination is done, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Orphan-Annie eye nuclei are a feature of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, not Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure.
It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient.

The thyroid gland is often diffusely enlarged, painless, with some degree of hypothyroidism. This may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis (Hashitoxicosis). It is associated with an increased risk of:

  • Other autoimmune conditions
  • Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphomas
  • Papillary carcinoma

Histologically, the following findings are seen:

  • Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well developed germinal centers
  • Atrophied thyroid follicles
  • The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm
    • This is called oncocytic metaplasia
    • These cells are called Hurthle cells

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following findings will you not observe in a thyroid gland biopsy taken from a patient suffering from Hashimoto thyroiditis?

explanationHtml:
Autoimmune hypothyroidism is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world.

The thyroid gland is typically enlarged. The circulating autoantibodies found in this disorder are:

  • Antimicrosomal antibodies
  • Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies
  • Antithyroglobulin antibodies

Note: Wolff-Chaikoff effect refers to iodine-induced hypothyroidism.
question: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical condition is suggestive of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

It is the most common cause of a painful thyroid. It is also known as painful subacute thyroiditis, de Quervain thyroiditis, or migratory thyroiditis (this is because the pain can shift to different locations in the thyroid).

Option A: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis (postpartum thyroiditis) is typically painless. It often occurs after pregnancy and is characterized by lymphocytic inflammation in the thyroid.

Option B: Riedel's thyroiditis is a rare disorder characterized by a painless, rapidly growing thyroid mass with extensive fibrosis involving the thyroid and contiguous neck structures.

Option C: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that presents as painless enlargement of the thyroid associated with some degree of hypothyroidism in middle-aged women.
question: A 48-year-old woman presented with fever, malaise, and painful enlargement of the thyroid gland after a few days following viral fever. On investigation, thyroid antibodies were normal and serum T4 was slightly raised. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Nodules in younger patients are less likely to be malignant
explanationHtml:
Nodules in younger patients are more likely to be malignant than those in older patients.

The solitary thyroid nodule is a palpably discrete swelling within an otherwise apparently normal thyroid gland. A higher incidence is seen in areas with endemic iodine deficiency. They are more common in women than in men.

Malignant transformation is more common in:

  • Solitary nodules > Multinodular goiter
  • Solitary nodules in males > females
  • Cold nodules > Hot nodules

However, benign neoplasms are more common than thyroid carcinomas by a ratio of nearly 10:1.
