Solitary nodules are more likely to be malignant than are multiple nodules
Nodules in younger patients are less likely to be malignant

question: Which of the following statements about solitary thyroid nodule is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
The most common thyroid cancer is papillary carcinoma.
Major subtypes of thyroid carcinoma and their relative frequencies are as follows:

  • Papillary carcinoma - most common
  • Follicular carcinoma
  • Medullary carcinoma
  • Anaplastic carcinoma - least common

Thyroid carcinomas are derived from the thyroid follicular epithelium, except medullary carcinoma which is derived from parafollicular C cells.
question: Which of the following is the most common thyroid cancer?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows psammoma bodies, which are seen in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. This type of carcinoma is associated with a history of long-standing unresected thyroglossal cyst.

[[figure-1]]

Psammoma bodies are concentrically calcified structures often present within the cores of papillae in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. These structures are almost never found in follicular and medullary carcinomas. They arise from:

  • Infarction and dystrophic calcification of papillae tips
  • Calcification of intra-lymphatic tumor thrombi.

Psammoma bodies are seen in:

  • Papillary carcinoma (thyroid, kidney, endometrium, lungs)
  • Prolactinoma
  • Meningioma
  • Papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary
question: A patient with a long-standing history of thyroglossal cyst develops a neck swelling. The biopsy of the lesion is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The presence of empty appearing nuclei, also called Orphan Annie eye nuclei as seen in the above image is diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

Microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma include:

  • Branching papillae with fibrovascular stalk
  • Covering epithelium is simple or stratified cuboidal
  • Orphan Annie eye nuclei -
    • Empty-appearing nuclei due to dispersed chromatin
    • They are diagnostic, regardless of papillary architecture
  • Psammoma bodies - concentric calcified structures
  • Foci of lymphatic invasion

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Note: Orphan Annie refers to a comic book character with empty appearing eyes, as shown below.

[[figure-3]]
question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a solitary, non-tender, firm nodule on the left side of her neck. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. A fine-needle biopsy revealed malignant cells. The tumor was excised and examined under light microscopy as shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Hematogenous spread is rare in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Metastases to lymph nodes are more commonly associated with this condition.

It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation. The presence of nuclear features such as Orphan Annie eye nuclei (empty-appearing nuclei) are diagnostic, regardless of papillary architecture.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Diagnosis can be made based on nuclear features, even in the absence of typical architecture
It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation

question: Which of the following statements regarding papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
The FNAC image is suggestive of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Among the given options, the most common site of metastasis is the lungs.

[[figure-1]]

The histological features of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid are:

  • Papillary architecture
  • Nuclear findings (enough to diagnose the condition even in the absence of papillary architecture)
    • Nuclear overlapping, grooving, crowding
    • Ground-glass appearance (Orphan Annie eye nuclei)
    • Dusty and pale chromatin
    • Intranuclear inclusion bodies

The most common mode of spread overall is through the lymphatic route, with lymph node metastases being common at initial presentation.
question: A pathologist is studying the following FNAC from a patient's thyroid nodule. Which is the most common site of metastasis for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is associated with gain-of-function mutations in the following genes:

  • NTRK1 (receptor tyrosine kinase)
  • RET (receptor tyrosine kinase)
  • BRAF (serine/threonine kinase)
question:
In patients with papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, which of the following genes may be involved?

  1. NTRK1
  2. BRAF
  3. RET
  4. TP53
  5. RAS

explanationHtml:
The most common variant of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is the follicular variant.

It has the following features:

  • Characteristic nuclear features of papillary carcinoma
  • Almost entirely follicular architecture
  • Can be either -
    • Encapsulated - favorable prognosis (or)
    • Poorly circumscribed and infiltrative - requires aggressive treatment

The variants of papillary carcinoma include:

Variant

Description

Tall-cell variant

50% of cells with height 2 times the width

Seen in older individuals

Have higher frequencies of vascular invasion

Extrathyroidal extension, and cervical and distant metastases

Diffuse sclerosing variant

In younger individuals, including children

Diffuse fibrosis throughout the gland

Lymph node metastases are present in almost all cases.

Lacks BRAF mutations

Cribriform variant

Associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

Beta-catenin mutation

Columnar-cell variant

Elongated nuclei with pseudostratification of the nuclei

Poor prognosis

Solid variant

More common in children

Associated with Chernobyl nuclear accident

Note: According to the latest WHO classification of thyroid tumors, the non-invasive encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC) has been renamed as non-invasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) to better reflect the indolent course of this tumor. This was done to prevent potential overtreatment and reduce the burden to patients of a cancer diagnosis.
question: Which of the following is the most common variant of papillary thyroid cancer?

correctAnswer: A. A 30-year-old man with papillary carcinoma thyroid
explanationHtml:
Papillary thyroid cancers have the best prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate seen in more than 95% of the patients.

The prognosis of papillary thyroid cancers is dependent on several factors, including age (being less favorable among patients older than 40 years), the presence of extrathyroidal extension, and presence of distant metastases.

The thyroid cancer with the worst prognosis is anaplastic carcinoma.

options.text: A 30-year-old man with papillary carcinoma thyroid
A 45-year-old woman with follicular carcinoma thyroid
A 78-year-old man with anaplastic carcinoma thyroid
A young man with MEN- II syndrome having medullary carcinoma thyroid

question: Which of the following patients is likely to have the best prognosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the given histopathological image showing uniform sheets of cells with capsular invasion by tumor cells is suggestive of follicular carcinoma thyroid.

The following images show follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Option A: In follicular adenoma, there is no capsular invasion.

Option C: Anaplastic carcinoma is associated with rapidly progressive swelling with obstructive features and undifferentiated cells on histopathology.

Option D: In medullary carcinoma, amyloid stroma is seen on histopathology.
question: A 56-year-old woman coming from a hilly area presents with a hard swelling in the neck which moves up with deglutition and does not move with protrusion of the tongue. The biopsy of the frozen section is given below. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
RAS mutations are associated with follicular carcinoma.

It is also associated with acquired mutations in the PIK3CA gene (PI3K/AKT arm of the receptor tyrosine kinase signaling pathway) and the PAX8-PPARG fusion gene.
question: Which of the following mutations may be found in patients with follicular carcinoma?

p53 is is a tumor-suppressor gene and not an oncogene.

question: Which of the following is not a proto-oncogene implicated in carcinoma of thyroid?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and histological appearance showing amyloid stroma are suggestive of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. This condition can occur in the setting of MEN2A (Sipple syndrome) or MEN2B.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Medullary carcinomas of the thyroid are neuroendocrine neoplasms derived from the parafollicular cells or C cells of the thyroid. They may be:

  • Sporadic (70%)
  • Familial or associated with MEN2 syndromes (30%) -
    • More aggressive and metastasize more frequently than sporadic
    • Usually bilateral and multicentric

Both forms can be associated with RET mutations.

These tumors may present with:

  • Mass in the neck
  • Dysphagia
  • Hoarseness
  • Diarrhea due to the secretion of VIP
  • Cushing's syndrome due to ACTH secretion

Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles. Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. These lesions secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen.
question: A middle-aged woman presents with thyroid swelling. The histology of the swelling is as shown below. Investigations reveal elevated calcitonin levels. Which of the following is associated with this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Corticotroph cells with homogenous and pale cytoplasm
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. In this condition, the normal basophilic cytoplasm of the corticotrophs of anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and pale. This is termed the Crooke hyaline change and is due to the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm.

This change occurs due to high levels of circulating glucocorticoids in Cushing's syndrome.

[[figure-1]]

Based on the cause of Cushing's syndrome, the following pathological changes are seen in the adrenals:

  • Iatrogenic - atrophy of zona fasciculata and zona reticularis (as zona glomerulosa functions independently of ACTH)
  • ACTH-dependent - diffuse hyperplasia (due to high ACTH levels)
  • ACTH-independent - nodular hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma

Note: Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells are called spironolactone bodies. They are seen in Conn's syndrome.

options.text: Corticotroph cells with homogenous and pale cytoplasm
Accumulation of keratin filaments in adrenal cells
Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells
Basophilic nuclear inclusion bodies in corticotroph cells

question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the OPD with rapid weight gain and easy bruisability over the past 1 month. She was started on oral prednisolone for dermatomyositis 2 months ago. On examination, moon facies and abdominal striae are noted. Her BP is 160/110 mm Hg. Which of the following pathological changes is seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Obesity is the most common clinical feature of Cushing's syndrome.

Clinical features of Cushing’s syndrome are attributed to the glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid actions of cortisol. They include:

System Clinical features
Body fat
  • Central or truncal obesity (most common)
  • Buffalo hump (fat deposition behind the neck)
  • Moon facies
Skin
  • Purple striae (over abdomen & flanks)
  • Acne and Hirsutism
  • Easy bruising
  • Facial plethora
  • Hyperpigmentation
Musculoskeletal
  • Proximal myopathy
  • Osteoporosis
Metabolic
  • Poorly controlled hyperglycemia
  • Dyslipidemia
Reproductive
  • Oligomenorrhea
  • Amenorrhea
Renal
  • Hypokalemic alkalosis
CVS
  • Atherosclerosis
  • Diastolic Hypertension
  • Edema
Hematologic
  • Hypercoagulable state
  • Lymphopenia
  • Neutrophilia
  • Eosinopenia
CNS
  • Depression
  • Psychosis
  • Anxiety
question: What is the most common clinical feature of Cushing syndrome?

correctAnswer: B. High ACTH and high renin levels
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario and the image showing hyperpigmentation of palmar creases and oral mucosa are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency. It presents with low aldosterone, high renin, and high ACTH levels.

In primary adrenal insufficiency, lack of aldosterone production results in compensatory rise in ACTH and renin levels. The high ACTH results in hyperpigmentation. The most common causes are autoimmune in developed countries and tuberculosis in developing countries.

In secondary adrenal insufficiency, there is pituitary dysfunction leading to low ACTH levels. Renin and aldosterone levels are normal, as they function independently of ACTH.

options.text: High ACTH and low renin levels
High ACTH and high renin levels
Low ACTH and normal renin levels
Low ACTH and low renin levels

question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, and dizziness for the past 3 days. On examination, the following findings are noted. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and blood glucose is 48 mg/dl. Which of the following would you expect in this patient?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing bilateral adrenal hemorrhage are suggestive of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not a cause of this condition.

It is caused by highly virulent organisms such as:

  • Neisseria meningitidis or meningococci (classically)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae or pneumococci
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Haemophilus influenzae
  • Staphylococcus species

This condition is more common in children. Overwhelming bacterial infection leads to bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, thereby causing acute adrenal insufficiency. This is likely a result of direct bacterial seeding of small vessels and endothelial dysfunction caused by microbial products and inflammatory mediators.

It usually presents with rapidly progressive hypotension and shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with widespread purpura. Without prompt recognition and treatment, death occurs within hours to a few days.
question: A 6-year-old boy was referred with fever, altered sensorium, and non-blanching rash for the past 2 days. He developed rapidly progressive shock and DIC. Despite resuscitation measures, he died. The following appearance of his adrenals was noted on autopsy. All of the following can cause this condition except:

explanationHtml:
Bilateral nodular hyperplasia of the adrenal glands is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism.

Adrenal adenoma is the second most common cause. It is usually solitary, but multiple adenomas may occur occasionally. Other rare causes include:

  • Ectopic aldosterone-producing tumors
  • Familial idiopathic hyperaldosteronism - due to germline mutations of KCNJ5 (encodes a potassium channel)
question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism?

explanationHtml:
The underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome is adrenal adenoma.

Hyperaldosteronism may be primary or secondary.

Primary hyperaldosteronism is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone with resultant suppression of RAAS. It can occur due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma. It presents with the following features:

  • Hypertension (most common)
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Polyuria (due to ANP)
  • Polydipsia (due to polyuria)
  • Muscle weakness

It is confirmed by elevated ratios of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (PAC / PRA).

When primary hyperaldosteronism is due to an aldosterone-secreting adenoma, it is called Conn syndrome. Patients are usually treated with spironolactone followed by surgical removal of adenoma. In patients treated with spironolactone, the adenomas contain eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions called spironolactone bodies.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

In secondary hyperaldosteronism, aldosterone release occurs in response to the activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAAS).
question: What is the underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
MEN2B syndrome is associated with pheochromocytoma and medullary carcinoma of thyroid, not adrenocortical carcinoma.

Adrenocortical carcinoma is associated with the following hereditary cancer syndromes:

  • Li–Fraumeni syndrome - due to germline TP53 mutations
  • Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome - a disorder of epigenetic imprinting
  • MEN1 syndrome - due to mutations of MEN1 gene
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk of developing adrenocortical carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of autoimmune polyendocrinopathy (APS) type 1. It is also called APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy).

The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene is mutated in this condition. This gene usually increases tolerance of central T-cells to peripheral tissue antigens. When this function is lost, the T-cells become more prone to mount immune reactions against tissue antigens, promoting autoimmunity. These patients form autoantibodies against IL-17 and IL-22, which are crucial for protection against fungal infections.

It manifests in childhood with the following features:

  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
  • Ectodermal dystrophy (abnormalities of the skin, dental enamel, and nails)
  • Organ-specific autoimmune disorders such as -
    • Autoimmune adrenalitis
    • Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism
    • Idiopathic hypogonadism
    • Pernicious anemia

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS) type 2 usually presents in early adulthood as a combination of the following:

  • Adrenal insufficiency
  • Autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes
question: A 7-year-old boy is brought for the evaluation of recurrent seizures over the last 3 months. Past history is significant for chronic oral candidiasis for 2 years. On examination, nail dystrophy is noted. Further investigation reveals serum calcium of 6.9 mg/dl and prolonged QT interval. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma. This patient does not need to be examined for a shagreen patch. It is a feature of tuberous sclerosis syndrome, which is not associated with pheochromocytoma.

Familial syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma are:

Syndrome Clinical manifestations
Neurofibromatosis

Café-au-lait spots

Axillary and inguinal freckling

Optic nerve glioma

Lisch nodules
von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome

Hemangioblastomas

Renal cell carcinoma

Pancreatic endocrine neoplasms
MEN2A syndrome

Medullary thyroid carcinoma

Parathyroid hyperplasia
MEN 2B syndrome

Medullary thyroid carcinoma

Marfanoid habitus

Mucocutaneous ganglioneuromatosis

Even patients with no family history must be evaluated for findings of these genetic syndromes, as they may occur sporadically in some cases.
question: A 24-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations, headaches, and sweating. Her BP was 155/95 mm Hg and HR was 135/min. Investigations revealed elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines and a right adrenal mass on CT abdomen. She should be examined for the presence of all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common manifestation of Wermer’s syndrome or MEN-1 syndrome.

MEN1 syndrome is due to germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor-suppressor gene, which encodes a protein called menin. The most commonly secreted products are pancreatic polypeptides.
question: Which of the following is most commonly involved in Wermer syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The definitive diagnosis of malignancy in pheochromocytomas is based exclusively on the presence of metastases to regional lymph nodes as well as distant sites like the liver, lung, and bone.

Capsular and vascular invasion may be encountered even in benign lesions. Malignant and benign pheochromocytomas resemble each other in almost every aspect. Hence, typical histological criteria like cellular atypia, mitotic spindles, and vascular invasion are insufficient to confirm malignancy in pheochromocytomas.
question: Which of the following is an indicator of malignant transformation in a patient with pheochromocytoma?

explanationHtml:
The given histopathology slide shows nests of cells arranged in an organoid pattern, with fibrovascular septae, and finely granular cytoplasm. This is called the zellballen pattern. It is typically seen in paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas.

Paragangliomas are benign neuroendocrine tumors arising from paraganglia in the neck or abdomen. They are composed of chief and sustentacular cells arranged in an organoid pattern.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: A pathologist is studying the following slide from the biopsy of a patient with an abdominal mass. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a paraganglioma (ectopic pheochromocytoma) located in the abdomen. They commonly arise from the organ of Zuckerkandl, located at the bifurcation of the aorta. It is part of the vertebral paraganglia (clusters of chromaffin cells along the autonomic nerve chains).

Other sites of origin of paragangliomas include:

  • Urinary bladder - rarely
  • Carotid and aortic bodies
  • Ganglion nodosum of the vagus nerve
  • Jugulotympanic ganglia
question: A 38-year-old woman was being evaluated for persistent hypertension. Workup revealed a tumor located near the bifurcation of the aorta. Surgical excision was done and HPE examination revealed a zellballen pattern of cells. Where did this tumor likely originate from?

explanationHtml:
Familial paraganglioma is most likely associated with mutations in the SDH (succinate dehydrogenase) gene.

The SDH complex is involved in mitochondrial electron transport and oxygen sensing. It is believed that SDH mutations also lead to the upregulation of HIF-1α, which is a key oncogenic driver in this type of tumor.
question: What mutation is likely to be seen in patients with familial paraganglioma syndrome?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing mucosal neuromas are suggestive of MEN2B syndrome. This condition is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.

The MEN syndromes are a group of inherited diseases of multiple endocrine organs. Tumors occur at a younger age than sporadic tumors, either synchronously (at the same time) or metachronously (at different times).

MEN2 syndrome occurs due to abnormal activation of the RET gene. Medullary carcinoma is seen in both MEN 2A and 2B syndromes. However, it tends to be more aggressive and metastasizes more frequently in MEN2B syndrome.

Note: RET gene is deactivated in Hirschsprung disease.
question: A 21-year-old young man presents with a neck mass. Past history is significant for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma 6 months ago. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the following finding. Which of the following should the patient be screened for?

explanationHtml:
Polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome occurs due to germline mutations in the EPAS1 gene. This syndrome presents with neuroendocrine tumors and early-onset polycythemia.

RET gene mutation is seen in MEN2A and MEN2B syndromes.

SDHD and SDHB mutations are seen in hereditary paraganglioma 1 and hereditary paraganglioma 4 syndromes respectively.
question: What gene is mutated in polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Periductal mastitis arises from the large lactiferous ducts.

It is also known as squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, recurrent subareolar abscess, or Zuska disease.

The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is the basic functional and histopathological unit of the breast. Successive branching of large ducts eventually leads to the TDLU. Sclerosing adenosis, blue dome cyst, and carcinoma breast arise from the TDLU.
question: Which of the following lesions does not arise from the terminal duct lobular unit of the breast?

explanationHtml:
Duct ectasia and Paget's disease arise from the large ducts of the breast.

Normal anatomy of the breast includes ducts, lobules, and stroma. Successive branching of the large ducts eventually leads to the terminal duct lobular unit.

Atypical hyperplasia arises from the terminal ducts and lobules, whereas, fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumors arise from the intralobular stroma.
question:
Which of the following lesions arise from the large ducts of the breast?

  1. Duct ectasia
  2. Fibroadenoma
  3. Paget's disease
  4. Atypical hyperplasia
  5. Phyllodes tumor

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute mastitis. The most common cause of acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess). It is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses.

Option A: Breast abscess caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is uncommon, only a few cases have been documented in immunocompromised patients.

Options B and C: Streptococcal infections tend to spread throughout the breast in the form of cellulitis.
question: A 28-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast. On examination, you notice her nipple is erythematous and tender with a purulent exudate. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Periductal mastitis is strongly associated with a history of smoking. More than 90% of the affected individuals are smokers.

Periductal mastitis is also called recurrent subareolar abscess or squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts or Zuska disease. In this condition, a relative deficiency of vitamin A associated with smoking or toxic substances in tobacco smoke alters the differentiation of the ductal epithelium.

Histologically, there is keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the nipple ducts. Keratin shed from these cells is trapped and plugs (keratin plug) the ductal system, causing dilation and eventually rupture of the duct. This results in keratin spillage into the surrounding periductal tissue forming a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response.

It presents with a painful erythematous subareolar mass that clinically mimics bacterial abscess. It has a high recurrence rate.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with a history of smoking?

explanationHtml:
The typical history of a breast lump following trauma and mammography findings of a radiolucent cystic lesion with rimmed calcification suggests a diagnosis of fat necrosis.

About half the affected women with fat necrosis of the breast have a history of breast trauma or previous surgery. It can present as a painless palpable mass, skin thickening or retraction, or mammographic densities or calcifications.

Histologically, necrotic adipose tissue with foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and chronic inflammatory cells are seen often with hemosiderin deposits, fibrosis, and calcification.

The following image shows an area of fat necrosis within breast tissue.

[[figure-1]]

Note: Calcifications are seen on mammography in the following conditions -

  • Apocrine cysts
  • Hyalinized fibroadenomas
  • Sclerosing adenosis
  • Duct ectasia
  • Breast carcinoma- shows irregular densities and small, numerous, clustered calcification (microcalcifications).
question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a painless palpable lump in her left breast. She had sustained a traumatic blow to her left breast 1 month back. Mammography showed a radiolucent cystic lesion with rimmed calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Papillomas are classified under proliferative breast diseases without atypia.

Proliferative breast lesions without atypia are not clonal and usually have no genetic changes. Thus they are predictors of risk but are not true precursors of carcinoma.

Benign epithelial lesions are classified into three groups, according to the subsequent risk of developing breast cancer. These are:

  • Non-proliferative breast changes
  • Proliferative breast disease without atypia
  • Atypical hyperplasia

Note: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) has recently been classified as a benign lesion with associated risk for developing carcinoma in the future but not as a malignancy capable of metastases.
question: Which of the following is a proliferative breast lesion?

explanationHtml:
Duct ectasia is a non-proliferative breast change.

Radial scar, sclerosing adenosis, and florid hyperplasia belong to proliferative breast lesions without atypia.

Proliferative breast lesions without atypia are not clonal and are not commonly found to have genetic changes. Thus they are predictors of risk but unlikely to be true precursors of carcinoma.
question: All of the following lesions are proliferative breast lesions without atypia except:

explanationHtml:
The most common clinical presentation seen in patients with duct papilloma is nipple discharge. More than 80% of large duct papillomas produce a nipple discharge.

Papillomas grow within a dilated duct and are composed of multiple branching fibrovascular cores. It can be serous or bloody.

  • Serous discharge - due to intermittent blockage and release of normal breast secretions or irritation of the duct by the papilloma
  • Bloody discharge - due to torsion of the stalk, causing infarction
question: What is the most common clinical presentation seen in patients with duct papilloma?

explanationHtml:
The image given depicts gynecomastia. Seminoma is not a cause of this condition.

Gynecomastia occurs due to increased estrogenic action. The most common causes of gynecomastia include:

  • Cirrhosis of the liver
  • Alcohol
  • Marijuana, heroin
  • Antiretroviral therapy
  • Anabolic steroids
  • Klinefelter syndrome (XXY karyotype)
  • Functioning testicular neoplasms such as Leydig cell or Sertoli cell tumors

Microscopically, there is an increase in the dense collagenous connective tissue. It is associated with epithelial hyperplasia of the duct lining with characteristic tapering micro-papillae. Lobule formation is almost never observed.
question: A young man presents to your clinic with the following finding. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Apocrine change does not increase the risk of cancer as it is a non-proliferative change.

Moderate or florid hyperplasia, fibroadenoma with complex features, and sclerosing adenosis are classified under proliferative disease without atypia with a 1.5- to 2-fold increased risk of carcinoma.

Both breasts are at increased risk, although the risk to the ipsilateral breast may be slightly higher.
question: A biopsy was performed on a female patient who presented with a lump in her right breast. Presence of which of the following findings is not associated with an increased risk of cancer?

explanationHtml:
The given image is suggestive of the comedo type of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Myoepithelial cell markers like p63 can differentiate DCIS from invasive carcinoma.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

DCIS is a malignant clonal proliferation of epithelial cells limited to ducts and lobules by the intact basement membrane. It is rarely palpable and is almost always detected by mammography.

Myoepithelial cells (basal cell layer) are preserved in involved ducts or lobules in DCIS. Hence the myoepithelial cell markers like p63, basal cytokeratin (CK 5/6), calponin will be positive in DCIS whereas it will be absent in infiltrating ductal carcinoma. However, myoepithelial markers may be diminished in high-grade DCIS compared to surrounding normal ducts or lobules.

Once the tumor cells penetrate through the basement membrane and grow within the stroma, they are considered to be invasive carcinoma.

[[figure-3]]

Note: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) has recently been classified as a benign lesion with associated risk for developing carcinoma in the future but not as a malignancy capable of metastases.
question: While undergoing a routine mammogram, a 45-year-old woman was found to have clusters of microcalcification in her right breast. A needle biopsy was done and revealed the following. Which of the following markers can be used to rule out invasive disease?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario showing a red eczematous rash over the areola of the breast is suggestive of Paget's disease of the nipple. The next best step in management is biopsy of the nipple.

Paget's disease can be mistaken for eczema, and hence, biopsy of the nipple should be the initial management of choice. Paget cells are readily detected by nipple biopsy.
question: A 55-year-old woman presents with persistent soreness and itching in her right nipple. On examination, the following finding is noted. What would be the next best step in her management?

correctAnswer: A. The cells are ER positive
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image showing Paget's cells (malignant cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei) are suggestive of Paget's disease of the nipple. These cells are ER-negative.

Paget's disease of the nipple is a rare form of ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS). The characteristic Paget's cells are scattered individually throughout the squamous epithelium. They do not breach the basement membrane but extend via the lactiferous sinuses into the nipple skin.

The following images show Paget's cells that do not breach the basement membrane.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

It presents as a unilateral erythematous eruption with a scale crust. A palpable mass is seen in about half the patients with this disease.

The underlying carcinomas are usually poorly differentiated, ER-negative, and overexpress HER2. The prognosis of Paget's disease depends on the features of the underlying carcinoma.

Paget's disease may mimic the following conditions:

  • Eczema (clinical appearance) - can be differentiated by the presence of malignant cells on biopsy
  • Superficial spreading melanoma (histological appearance) - Paget's cells are PAS-positive and diastase resistant unlike melanoma cells

Note: Paget's disease of the bone is a distinct condition that results in abnormal bone metabolism due to osteoclastic overactivity.

options.text: Prognosis depends on the underlying carcinoma
The cells show overexpression of HER2

question: Histopathological examination of a middle-aged woman who presented with redness and itching over the nipple of her left breast is given below. Which of the following statements is incorrect about her condition?

explanationHtml:
Early full-term pregnancy (younger than 20 years) is protective against breast cancer. It halves the risk of developing breast cancer compared to that of nulliparous women.

Women with very dense breasts on mammography have a four- to six-fold higher risk of both ER-positive and ER-negative breast cancer compared to women with low density.

Obese women under the age of 40 years have a decreased risk as a result of anovulatory cycles and lower progesterone levels. In contrast, postmenopausal obese women are at an increased risk, which is attributed to the synthesis of estrogens in fat depots.

Early menarche, late menopause, and nulliparity are risk factors of breast cancer due to hyperestrogenemia. Exercise and breastfeeding are protective against breast cancer.
question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for breast cancer?

explanationHtml:
The upper outer quadrant is the most common site of carcinoma in the breast.

Approximately 50% of carcinomas are located in the upper outer quadrant, 10% in each of the remaining quadrants, and about 20% in the central or subareolar region.

A palpable mass is the most common clinical sign of invasive breast carcinoma.

Triple assessment is recommended for the diagnosis of any palpable breast lump. It includes:

  • Clinical examination
  • Radiological assessment (mammography/USG)
  • Pathological assessment (FNAC/biopsy)

Techniques of palpation for breast examination are:

  1. Vertical strip/lines pattern
  2. Circular pattern
  3. Wedges or radial spokes pattern

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the most common site of carcinoma in the breast?

explanationHtml:
BRCA2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 13 (13q12.3).

Mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are responsible for 80 to 90% of single gene familial breast cancers and about 3% of all breast cancers.

ER-positive, HER2-negative cancers (luminal type) is the most common subtype of breast cancer in individuals who inherit germline mutations in BRCA2. This gene is associated more frequently with male breast cancer.

Single gene mutations associated with familial breast cancer can be categorized into:

  • High penetrance germline mutations (>4 fold increased risk) - BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PTEN, STK11, CDH I, PALPB2
  • Moderate penetrance germline mutations (2-4 fold increased risk) - ATM, CHEK2
question: On which of the following chromosomes is the BRCA2 gene located?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of triple-negative breast cancer (ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative). TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).

Common gene mutations in the 3 major molecular types of invasive breast carcinoma are:

Molecular Subtype Common gene mutations
Luminal (ER+/HER2-)

Luminal A: PIK3CA (more common), TP53

Luminal B: PIK3CA (more common), TP53
HER2 Positive (HER 2+) TP53 (more common), PIK3CA
TNBC (ER-/ HER2-) TP53 (more common), PIK3CA
question: Immunohistochemical testing was performed on a biopsy sample taken from a patient with breast cancer. It revealed lack of expression of ER, PR, and HER2. Which of the following genes is most commonly mutated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining shows positive ER, PR (brown nucleus), and negative Her-2 (no membrane-bound brown stain) expression, which is suggestive of luminal A molecular subtype. It shows a poor response to paclitaxel.

Hormone receptors (ER, PR) are present in the nucleus. Therefore ER, PR–positive breast cancer cells will stain dark in the nucleus on IHC. Her-2 receptors are membrane-bound receptors, and hence, cells having these receptors are darkly stained on the membranes.

Luminal A type is more commonly associated with BRCA2 mutations.

Hormone receptor-positive tumors are responsive to hormonal chemotherapeutic agents like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors. In Her-2 negative cases, trastuzumab is not effective as it is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody directed against HER-2.

The following image shows ER/ PR/ Her-2 positivity:

[[figure-1]]

Note: At least 10% of luminal type A breast cancers express tp53 mutations. tP53 mutations are associated with triple-negative tumors as well.

options.text: It is not associated with tP53 mutations

question: A 44-year-old woman has been diagnosed with breast carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry staining of a tissue biopsy specimen of this patient is given below. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?

explanationHtml:
Carcinomas with immunohistochemistry ER and HER2/ν negative are all of the above except mucinous carcinomas. Mucinous carcinomas are usually ER-positive and HER2/neu negative (luminal A type)

ER-negative, HER2-negative (triple-negative) molecular subtype commonly includes the following histological subtypes:

  • Medullary
  • Adenoid cystic
  • Secretory
  • Metaplastic
  • Spindle cell
  • Squamous
  • Matrix-producing
question: Immunohistochemistry test of a breast cancer patient was reported negative for ER and HER2. This molecular subtype includes all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
ER-positive, HER2-negative status on immunohistochemistry is suggestive of the luminal type of breast carcinoma, which does not include secretory carcinoma.

The ER-positive, HER2-negative molecular subtype (luminal type) commonly includes the following histological subtypes:

  • Well and poorly differentiated lobular carcinoma
  • Tubular carcinoma
  • Mucinous carcinoma
  • Papillary carcinoma

Secretory carcinomas are usually ER-negative and Her2/neu negative (basal type).
question: Patients with all of the following conditions have ER-positive and HER2-negative tumors except:

explanationHtml:
Lobular carcinoma is the most common type of breast carcinoma to present as an occult primary carcinoma.

Lobular carcinoma of the breast is seen bilaterally and with multicentricity. Loss of E-cadherin is the hallmark of lobular carcinoma. They also have characteristic patterns of metastatic spread, often involving the peritoneum and retroperitoneum, leptomeninges (carcinomatous meningitis), gastrointestinal tract, ovaries, and uterus.

The histological hallmark of lobular carcinoma is the presence of discohesive infiltrating tumor cells, often arranged in a single Indian file pattern or in loose clusters or sheets.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following breast cancers most commonly presents as an occult primary carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
There is no or very slight desmoplastic response seen in lobular carcinomas.

Desmoplasia refers to collagenous stromal proliferation induced by tumor cells which is essential for tumor growth and spread. It results in hard and stony tumors. However, this is not seen in lobular carcinoma. This is likely due to the loss of expression of CDH1, the gene that encodes e-cadherin (normally maintains intercellular adhesiveness). This also results in disaggregation of cells.

Lobular carcinomas are often bilateral and multicentric. It shows characteristic metastatic spread, often involving:

  • Peritoneum and retro peritoneum
  • Leptomeninges (carcinomatous meningitis)
  • Gastrointestinal tract
  • Ovaries
  • Uterus

Histopathological image of invasive lobular carcinoma of breast showing discohesive cells with few signet ring cells.

[[figure-1]]

Note: Individuals with heterozygous germline mutations in CDH1 (loss of E-cadherin) also have a greatly increased risk of gastric signet-ring cell carcinoma.
question: Which of the following is not a feature of lobular breast carcinoma?

correctAnswer: C. There is obstruction of dermal lymphatics by neoplastic cells
explanationHtml:
T4d in the TNM staging of carcinoma breast points toward a diagnosis of inflammatory breast carcinoma. It shows extensive invasion and proliferation of tumor cells within the dermal lymphatics leading to obstruction.

Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. The hallmark of this condition is the overexpression of e-cadherin. This results in increased tumor cohesion and the formation of tumoral clumps which can result in emboli. It has a particularly poor prognosis.

These tumors are usually of high grade but do not belong to any particular molecular subtype. More than half (60%) are ER-negative and 40% to 50% overexpress HER2. There is no association with trauma.

Due to lymphatic obstruction, it results in brawny induration, erythema with a raised edge, and edema called peau d’orange appearance. This may mimic non-neoplastic inflammatory lesions like mastitis. A breast lump may or may not be present.

The following image shows a peau d’orange appearance of the right breast.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: There is loss of e-cadherin expression
It has a relatively favorable prognosis
There is obstruction of dermal lymphatics by neoplastic cells
History of trauma to the breast is usually present

question: A 53-year-old woman with breast cancer is found to have TNM staging of T4dN0M0. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?

explanationHtml:
The immunohistochemistry (IHC) pattern of patient C reveals moderately strong circumferential staining (faint brown color) in >10 % of cells, which is classified as 2+ or equivocal staining. Hence, she should be subjected to fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm HER2-positive gene amplification status.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

The following are classified as HER2-positive tumors:

  • Tumors that show 3+ staining on IHC (here FISH is not needed).
  • Tumors with 2+ staining on IHC, followed by HER2-gene amplification confirmed by FISH

Once HER2-positive status is confirmed, targeted therapy against HER2 can be initiated with trastuzumab or lapatinib.
question: Immunohistochemistry for HER2 protein expression is performed in 3 patients with breast carcinoma, with the following results. Which of the following patients should be subjected to fluorescence in-situ hybridization?

explanationHtml:
HER2 overexpression in a patient with carcinoma breast is associated with poor survival.

Prediction of response to agents like trastuzumab that target the HER2 receptor, is the main significance of the HER2 status of a breast malignancy.

Prognostic and predictive factors in breast carcinoma:

question: A middle-aged woman is diagnosed with low-grade mucinous carcinoma of the breast. IHC showed HER2 overexpression and a low Ki67 index. Which of the following would be considered as a poor prognostic factor?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing duct proliferation are suggestive of fibroadenomas. The use of cyclosporin-A after transplantation is associated with fibroadenomas that regress after cessation of the treatment.

[[figure-1]]

Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumor of the female breast. Nearly 2/3 cases are associated with mutations in the MED12 gene.

They are frequently multiple and bilateral and usually occur in women <30 years of age. They are solid, well-defined, highly mobile masses (also known as breast mice).

Fibroadenomas can be classified into 2 types:

  • Without complex features - classified as a non-proliferative condition
  • With complex features -
    • Associated with cysts > 0.3 cm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine change
    • Classified as proliferative changes without atypia
question: A 30-year-old woman on cyclosporin-A following renal transplantation developed multiple bilateral breast lumps that regressed after cessation of treatment. Her biopsy finding is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Both epithelial and stromal components can metastasize
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image are suggestive of phyllodes tumor. Here, only the stromal component is involved in metastasis.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Phyllodes tumor is a fibroepithelial tumor arising from the intralobular stroma. It presents as a smooth, rapidly growing, multinodular, painless breast lump that is usually palpable. It most commonly presents in the 6th decade of life and is associated with:

  • Gain in chromosome 1q
  • HOXB13 overexpression

Phyllodes tumors show stromal cellularity next to the epithelium (subepithelial or periepithelial regions). This feature helps to differentiate it from intracanalicular fibroadenoma.

The prognosis of phyllodes tumors depends on their histological grade. Most phyllodes tumors are low grade, with limited stromal cellularity. They recur only occasionally and do not metastasize.

The features of malignant (intermediate and high grade) phyllodes tumors are:

  • Markedly increased stromal cellularity
  • Stromal overgrowth - absence of epithelial elements
  • Nuclear atypia
  • Increased mitosis (>10/ 10 hpf)
  • Highly recurrent

Regardless of the grade, lymphatic spread is rare in phyllodes tumors. Hence, axillary lymph node dissection is contraindicated.

options.text: Stromal cellularity is increased next to the epithelium
Absence of epithelial elements suggests malignancy
Both epithelial and stromal components can metastasize

question: A 58-year-old woman presented with a large, rapidly growing painless breast lump. On examination, a smooth, multinodular breast lump was noticed. Microscopic examination of the core biopsy sample is shown below. Which of the following is an incorrect statement regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Angiosarcoma is the most common stromal malignancy in the breast.

It arises in the interlobular stroma and accounts for < 0.05% of breast malignancies. It is a high-grade tumor with a poor prognosis. It can either be sporadic or occur in association with radiation therapy. The mean age of affected individuals is 35 years.
question: What is the most common stromal malignancy in the breast?

explanationHtml:
BRCA-2 mutation does not predispose to the development of renal cell carcinoma.

BRCA-2 mutation predisposes to the development of prostate and pancreatic cancer. It is also associated with an increased risk of male breast cancer.
question: BRCA-2 mutation does not predispose to the development of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of colloid or mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloid carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intracellular and extracellular mucin deposition.

On histopathological examination, extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei, arranged in clusters, floating in lakes or pools of mucin. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the periphery to form a signet ring appearance.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Option B: Microscopic image of papillary carcinoma of the breast showing true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue lined by the tumor cells is shown below.

[[figure-3]]

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. Histopathological examination of the mass showed cells in mucin pools and faint nuclei. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Osteoclasts are specialized multinucleated macrophages derived from circulating monocytes that are responsible for bone resorption.

Osteocytes are formed when osteoblasts are embedded in the matrix within lacunae and canaliculi. They control calcium and phosphate levels in the microenvironment.

Osteoblasts are mesenchymal cells that rim the bony spicule, responsible for bone synthesis and mineralization.

Chondrocytes are specialized cells that produce and maintain the extracellular matrix of cartilage.

question: What are the specialized multinucleated macrophages in bone called?

explanationHtml:
Osteocalcin is not a bone resorption marker.

It is a protein secreted only by osteoblasts. Thus, it is a bone formation marker (osteoblastic marker).

question: Which of the following is not a marker of bone resorption?

explanationHtml:
Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor.

It is a benign cartilage-capped tumor. 85% of osteochondromas are solitary. The remainder is seen as part of the multiple hereditary exostosis syndromes, an autosomal-dominant hereditary disease.

Lesions arise from the metaphysis near the growth plate of long tubular bones, especially near the knee. They are either sessile or pedunculated and range in size from 1 to 20 cm. Histologically, the cap is composed of benign hyaline cartilage varying in thickness and is covered peripherally by perichondrium.

Osteochondromas can progress to chondrosarcoma.

The image below shows the histopathological specimen of osteochondroma, displaying a cartilage cap lined by perichondrium contiguous with mature bone.

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: Which of the following is the most common benign bone tumor?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteogenesis imperfecta type II.

The type II variant of osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is uniformly fatal in utero or during the perinatal period. Type II OI is characterized by extraordinary bone fragility with multiple intrauterine fractures.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is caused by deficiencies in the synthesis of type I collagen. It can be separated into four major clinical subtypes that vary widely in severity. The severity of the disease is based on the location of the mutation within the protein.

Individuals with type I OI have a normal life span, but experience childhood fractures that decrease in frequency following puberty.

question: A woman delivered a child who died a few minutes after birth. The infant was found to have blue sclera and fractures of the right humerus, ulna, and femur at birth. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This given clinical scenario is suggestive of achondroplasia.

Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia and a major cause of dwarfism. It has autosomal dominant inheritance.

It occurs due to the gain of mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR3). This leads to abnormal cartilage proliferation at growth plates and affects endochondral bone growth. Infants present with:

  • Short stature
  • Rhizomelic shortening of limbs
  • Frontal bossing
  • Midface deficiency

The condition is not associated with changes in longevity, intelligence, or reproductive status.

The image below shows a baby affected with achondroplasia. Note the prominent forehead, triangular face, and body asymmetry in the image (a); a low nasal bridge in the image (b); trident hands in the image (c); and scoliosis in the image (d).

[[figure-1]]

question: A 29-year-old woman gives birth to an infant with less than 5th percentile length. The head and torso are of normal size but extremities are short. The head circumference is at the 95th percentile, and frontal bossing is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Albers-Schönberg disease or osteopetrosis is also known as marble bone disease.

The term osteopetrosis reflects the stone-like quality of the bones. The bones are abnormally brittle and fracture easily, like a piece of chalk. It occurs due to reduced bone resorption and diffuse symmetric skeletal sclerosis because of impaired formation or function of osteoclasts.

Note: Osteogenesis imperfecta is also called brittle bone disease. Paget's disease is also called osteitis deformans; it presents with mosaic pattern of lamellar bone.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: Which of the following is also called marble bone disease?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteopetrosis. It occurs due to autosomal recessive defects in the gene for the enzyme carbonic anhydrase II.

Carbonic anhydrase II is required by osteoclasts and renal tubular cells to generate protons from carbon dioxide and water (acidification). The absence of carbonic anhydrase II prevents osteoclasts from acidifying the resorption pit and dissolution of calcium hydroxyapatite within the bone matrix. It also blocks the acidification of urine by the renal tubular cells. This leads to reduced bone resorption and diffuse symmetric skeletal sclerosis.

Due to deficient osteoclast activity, bones involved by osteopetrosis lack a medullary canal giving it a bone-in-bone appearance. The ends of long bones are bulbous (Erlenmeyer flask deformity) and misshapen. The neural foramina are small and compress the exiting nerves, leading to cranial nerve palsies.

Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis leads to leukopenia and prominent hepatosplenomegaly. Due to mutations in the gene encoding CA II, a depletion in the otherwise extensively available carbonic anhydrase II can be seen which results in a condition called marble brain disease or Guibaud-Vainsel syndrome.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: An infant is being evaluated for multiple fractures over the last 3 months. On examination, hydrocephaly, cranial nerve defects, and hepatosplenomegaly are noted. Imaging reveals generalized sclerosis and a bone-in-bone appearance. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme to be deficient in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteoporosis. Cytokines stimulate osteoclast recruitment and activity in osteoporosis by increasing the levels of RANKL.

RANKL helps in diminishing the expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG), increasing osteoclast proliferation, and preventing osteoclast apoptosis.

Decreased estrogen levels after menopause actually increase both bone resorption and formation. However, the latter does not keep up with the former, leading to a high turnover. Decreased estrogen appears to increase the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with sudden severe back pain. There is no history of trauma. X-ray findings are given below. MRI shows thinning of trabecular plates of the vertebrae and vertebral collapse. Levels of which of the following will be increased in her condition?

explanationHtml:
Histologically normal bone with decreased density is the hallmark feature of osteoporosis.

In advanced osteoporosis, both the trabecular bone of the medulla and the cortical bone are markedly thinned leading to progressive microfractures.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Inadequate mineralization in osteomalacia leads to a thickened osteoid matrix.

Option C: Paget's disease presents with a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone.

Option D: Dissecting osteitis cystica is seen in severe hyperparathyroidism.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: In patients with which of the following conditions will you see a histologically normal bone?

correctAnswer: C. It is polyostotic in about 15% of cases
explanationHtml:
Paget disease is monostotic in about 15% of cases and polyostotic in the rest of them.

Paget disease (osteitis deformans) is a disorder of increased, but disordered and structurally unsound, bone mass. The onset is in late adulthood (average age at diagnosis, 70 years).

It occurs due to mutations in the SQSTM1 gene. This increases the activity of NF-κB, which then increases osteoclast activity.

Three sequential phases exist:

  • Initial osteolytic stage
  • Mixed osteoclastic-osteoblastic stage
  • Final burned-out quiescent osteosclerotic stage

The axial skeleton or proximal femur is involved in up to 80% of the cases. The typical x-ray findings are as follows:

  • Enlargement of the craniofacial skeleton: leontiasis ossea or lion face
  • Invagination of the skull base (platybasia)
  • Chalk stick-type fractures in the long bones of the lower extremities

The pathological hallmark is a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone, seen in the sclerotic phase as shown below. It shows a jigsaw-like pattern produced by unusually prominent cement lines, which join haphazardly oriented units of lamellar bone.

[[figure-1]]

Laboratory findings show elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and urinary hydroxyproline (normal serum calcium and phosphorus).

Following tumors can develop in the affected bones in Paget's disease:

  • Benign tumors -
    • Giant cell tumors
    • Giant cell reparative granuloma
    • Extra-osseous masses of hematopoietic tissue
  • Sarcoma (osteosarcoma or fibrosarcoma) - most dreaded complication. Occurs in < 1 % of all individuals with Paget disease, and in 5% to 10% of those with the severe polyostotic disease.

options.text: It occurs due to mutations in the SQSTM1 gene
It is polyostotic in about 15% of cases
Sarcoma occurs in less than 1% of all individuals

question: A patient presents with back pain, recurrent headaches, and increasing head size. On evaluation, raised alkaline phosphatase and a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone is seen. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Osteopetrosis does not belong to the clinical spectrum of hyperparathyroidism.

The features of hyperparathyroidism are as follows:
  • Osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • Osteopenia/osteoporosis
  • Hyperuricemia and gout
  • Pseudogout
  • Increased production of calcitriol
  • Dissecting osteitis and brown tumors
  • Nephrolithiasis
  • Hypophosphatemia
  • Anemia
Hyperparathyroidism leads to significant skeletal changes related to unabated osteoclast activity. Increased osteoclast activity is most prominent in cortical bone, but the medullary bone is not spared. Osteoclasts may tunnel into and dissect centrally along the length of the trabeculae, creating the appearance of railroad tracks, diagnostic of dissecting osteitis. Generalised osteoporosis may be seen in the phalanges, vertebrae, and proximal femur.
Brown tumor presents with bone loss leading to microfractures and secondary hemorrhages which causes influx of macrophages and ingrowth of reparative fibrous tissue. Generalized osteitis presents with increased bone cell activity, peri-trabecular fibrosis, and cystic brown tumors.

question: In patients with hyperparathyroidism, which of the following is least expected?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of acute pyogenic osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of culture-positive pyogenic osteomyelitis.

Osteomyelitis denotes inflammation of bone and marrow, almost always secondary to infection. Organisms may reach the bone by

  1. Hematogenous spread
  2. Extension from a contiguous site
  3. Direct implantation
The common causative organisms include:
  • Staphylococcus aureus - the most common cause overall
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa - most common cause in IV drug abusers
  • Salmonella - common in patients of sickle cell anemia
  • Haemophilus influenzae - was a common causative organism in children, less common now due to vaccination
  • Streptococcus pyogenes - most common in neonates
  • Escherichia coli, Klebsiella- most common cause in patients with genitourinary tract infections

question: A 7-year-old child presented with fever,  pain, and swelling around the knee joint for 3 days. Lab investigations showed a WBC count of 23,500/mm3. An MRI was done, which demonstrated an intramedullary abscess of the proximal tibia. Which of the following is the most common causative organism of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Salmonella enteritidis is commonly implicated in osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia.

The common causative organisms include:
  • Staphylococcus aureus - the most common cause overall
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa - most common cause in IV drug abusers
  • Salmonella - most common in patients of sickle cell anemia
  • Haemophilus influenzae - was a common causative organism in children, less common now due to vaccination
  • Streptococcus pyogenes - neonates
  • Escherichia coli, Klebsiella- most common cause in patients with genitourinary tract infections

question: Patients with sickle cell disease are particularly susceptible to osteomyelitis caused by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The patient is most likely suffering from TB osteomyelitis. Brodie's abscess is not a complication of this condition.

In tuberculous osteomyelitis, weight-bearing joints - spine (Pott's disease), hips, and knees, are most commonly affected.

Complications of tuberculous osteomyelitis include:

  • Scoliosis or kyphosis (gibbus)
  • Neurologic deficits secondary to spinal cord and nerve compression leading to paraplegia -
  • Tuberculous arthritis
  • Sinus tract formation
  • Psoas abscess - may be due to paravertebral “cold” abscess
  • AA amyloidosis

question: A patient who is a known case of TB presents to the orthopedic OPD with a 4-month history of progressively worsening back pain. He also complains of fatigue and irregular fever for 2 weeks. X-ray reveals lytic destruction of the anterior portion of the vertebral body and increased anterior wedging. All of the following are the complications of his condition except

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteoblastoma.

Histopathology shows well-circumscribed lesions composed of randomly interconnecting trabeculae of woven bone that are prominently rimmed by a single layer of osteoblasts. Stroma surrounding the neoplastic bone consists of loose connective tissue that contains many dilated and congested capillaries.

The image below shows the histopathological findings in osteoblastoma.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma are benign bone-producing tumors that have identical histologic features. The differentiating features between them are given below:

Osteoid osteoma Osteoblastoma
Less than 2 cm in diameter Larger than 2 cm in diameter

Predilection for the appendicular skeleton

 involves the posterior spine (laminae and pedicles)

Thick rind of reactive cortical bone is seen on radiography

Usually, no marked bony reaction is seen on radiography

Pain that is relieved by aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents

 Pain which is unresponsive to aspirin

question: A 25-year-old man presents with back pain that is unresponsive to aspirin. Radiographs show a well-demarcated lesion in the posterior spine. A biopsy is done and the histopathological finding is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given history and classic sunburst appearance on the X-ray are highly suggestive of osteosarcoma. Mutation of p53 (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) is associated with a greater risk of sarcomas, particularly osteosarcoma.

The image given below shows sunburst pattern seen in osteosarcoma.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Translocation (X;18) is characteristic of synovial sarcoma.

Option B: Translocation (12;16) is characteristic of myxoid liposarcoma.

Option D: 1p rearrangements are characteristic of conventional chondrosarcoma.

question: A 17-year-old man presents with progressive swelling of the upper end of the humerus. He also complains of arm pain and weight loss for 3 months. X-ray findings are given below. Which of the following is associated with a higher risk of developing this condition?

correctAnswer: A. It usually arises in the diaphyseal region of long bones
explanationHtml:
Osteosarcomas usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the long bones of the extremities. It commonly occurs in the knee (i.e., distal femur or proximal tibia).

The most common subtype is primary, intramedullary, osteoblastic, and high grade. It is a malignant tumor in which the cancerous cells produce an osteoid matrix or mineralized bone. It occurs in all age groups but has a bimodal age distribution.

The formation of fine lace-like neoplastic bone by the tumor cells is diagnostic histopathologically of osteosarcoma as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Radiography shows a large destructive, mixed lytic and blastic mass with infiltrative margins, which breaks through the cortex and lifts the periosteum, resulting in reactive periosteal bone formation. The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised ends of the periosteum, known radiographically as the Codman triangle, is characteristic of osteosarcoma. This is shown in the radiograph below.

[[figure-3]]

options.text: It usually arises in the diaphyseal region of long bones
It has a bimodal age distribution
Codman triangle is characteristic of the tumor
Most common subtype is osteoblastic and high grade

question: Which of the following statements is false about osteosarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are nonhereditary disorders characterized by multiple enchondromas. Maffucci syndrome is, in addition, distinguished by the presence of spindle-cell hemangiomas.

Enchondromas are benign tumors of hyaline cartilage that usually occur in bones of enchondral origin. They are usually diagnosed in individuals 20 to 50 years of age. They present as solitary metaphyseal lesions of tubular bones of the hands and feet.

The radiographic features consist of circumscribed lucencies with central irregular calcifications, a sclerotic rim, and an intact cortex. They are usually smaller than 3 cm. They are gray-blue and translucent, composed of well-circumscribed nodules of hyaline cartilage containing cytomorphologically benign chondrocytes.

The enchondromas in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are sometimes more cellular than sporadic enchondromas and exhibit cytologic atypia, making them more difficult to distinguish from chondrosarcomas.

The image below displays the histopathological picture of an enchondroma showing lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by bone and covered by perichondrium (fibrous tissue).

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question: Which of the following bone tumors is characteristically seen in patients with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome?

correctAnswer: B. Clear cell and the mesenchymal variants occur in older patients.
explanationHtml:
The clear cell and the mesenchymal variants of chondrosarcoma occur in younger patients (teens or 20s).

Chondrosarcomas are malignant tumors that produce cartilage. They commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs.

They are subclassified histologically as following variants:

  • Conventional (hyaline cartilage producing) - 90% cases
  • Clear cell
  • Dedifferentiated
  • Mesenchymal

In multiple hereditary exostosis, osteochondromas can progress to chondrosarcoma. Increased thickness of the cartilage cap has been reported as an indicator of potential malignancy. The average age of secondary chondrosarcoma is younger than patients with primary tumors.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone

options.text: Conventional central tumors constitute about 90% of chondrosarcomas.
Clear cell and the mesenchymal variants occur in older patients.
Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton.
In multiple hereditary exostosis, osteochondromas progress to chondrosarcoma.

question: Which of the following statements is not true about chondrosarcoma?

explanationHtml:
Osteochondromas, multiple enchondromas, and synovial chondromatosis can progress to become chondrosarcoma.

The average age of patients with secondary chondrosarcoma is 35 years (less than that of those with primary tumors). These tumors most commonly affect the pelvic bones. The increased thickness of the cartilage cap (normally 1–3 mm) is considered an indicator of potential malignancy.

Multiple enchondromas in the setting of Ollier’s disease or Maffucci's syndrome carry a significantly higher risk of transformation to secondary chondrosarcoma than solitary enchondromas. Histological findings of abundant myxoid change, cyst formation, and permeation of existing trabeculae suggest malignancy.

Secondary malignancy in synovial chondromatosis has been reported, but it is rare.
lessonTitle: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone
question:
Which of the following can progress to become chondrosarcoma?

  1. Osteochondroma
  2. Multiple enchondromas
  3. Synovial chondromatosis
  4. Chondromyxoid fibroma
  5. Solitary chondroma

correctAnswer: B. It arises in the epiphysis of long tubular bones
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Ewing sarcoma. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis.

Ewing sarcoma follows osteosarcoma as the second most common group of bone sarcomas in children. It generally affects patients < 20 years. Boys are affected slightly more frequently than girls. Usually, the tumor arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis.

Fever, elevated sedimentation rate, anemia, and leukocytosis may be seen. Plain radiographs show a destructive lytic tumor with permeative margins that extend into the surrounding soft tissues. Periosteal reaction leads to the deposition of reactive bone that resembles onion-skin. It arises in the medullary cavity and usually invades the cortex, periosteum, and soft tissue.

On microscopy, sheets of uniform, small, round cells with scant cytoplasm are seen, which may appear clear because they are rich in glycogen. The presence of Homer–Wright rosettes indicates a greater degree of neuroectodermal differentiation.

The image given below shows the histopathological findings in Ewing sarcoma.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Most Ewing sarcoma family tumors contain an (11;22) (q24;q12) translocation. Variant translocations fuse the EWS to other members of the ETS transcription factor family. CD99(MIC2), FLI1, and NSE would be positive in ES/PNET.
